## Chapter 1: The Bird With the Broken Wing

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko solves an easy case, deals with somewhat irritating presences in his life, and encounters an unexpected guest.

### Text

It was a dark and stormy night.

Zuko leaned backwards in his chair, exhausted from the long hours spent chasing the scum of the world. The good news was that he was in the perfect place to relax: a dimly lit bar at one in the morning, with a dusty counter, worn-out leather stools, and no one around but the two owners and him. Here, he could half-close his eyes and detach himself from the world.

The cold metal counter would have bothered his hands, but he was used to exchanging money in the dark, over a cold metal counter, usually with shady types who knew better than to trust the authorities, but who had a good heart in the end. That was how Zuko liked it. He was a private eye, but he had no patience for anyone trying to trick or trap anyone else. Zuko worked for people who pursued justice, people who wanted to do what was right, but didn’t mind sidestepping the rules.

The door behind the counter opened, and Chan walked through, quickly followed by his business partner, Ron-Juan. Chan and Ron-Juan weren’t the type of people Zuko usually worked with. They had no morality, and were pretty much nothing more than spoiled idiots who ran a bar and drank a lot of their own wine. Still, Zuko didn’t always have to love his clients, as long as the endgame was what he wanted. Someone had contaminated a vat of Chan and Ron-Juan’s best beer (which wasn’t worth trying *before* the contamination, if you asked Zuko.) Even if Chan and Ron-Juan were assholes, messing with their drinks was still dishonest. So Zuko had taken the case.

It had been an easy job, over and done within a few days, useful for the cash so that Zuko could keep his apartment near the center of Ba Sing Se. The saboteur hadn’t been very careful, and had left fingerprints all over the beer vat. He had been drunk when Zuko found him, and had probably been drunk when he had contaminated the beer, too.

Still, thought Zuko as he stared across the counter at the very beer that had been contaminated just days ago, he hadn’t been easy to catch. Once he had found out that Zuko was after him, Lee (Zuko had only found out his name later, and it hadn’t been of any use, considering how many Lees there were), had managed to disappear, using back alleyways and restaurant basements and a million other sneaky tricks Zuko wouldn’t have imagined him to have. Still, after a few hours of speedy car rides and crashing through doorways, Zuko had caught up to him. Now, all there was to do was to sit in Chan and Ron-Juan’s bar and wait for the money.

Sure enough, the money soon arrived, the bills spilling out of Chan’s leather wallet and into Zuko’s hand. Unlike most private eyes, Zuko didn’t crave the money. The money was something he needed, a side perk of the real prize: justice.

Squinting at the bills through his better eye, Zuko fanned the money through his left palm, about a half second slower than he had to, for the effect. “This is only nine-tenths the amount you promised me.”

Chan’s face flushed bright red, and Ron-Juan looked as though he was about to faint on the floor. *Amateurs* , thought Zuko. “What?’ cried Chan. “No! You must have counted wrong!”

Zuko sighed, leaning forward and looking Chan directly in the eye. “I’m a detective, Chan. You own a bar, and you’re drunk. Believe me, I *never* count wrong.”

Chan’s eyes frantically darted towards Ron-Juan, whose teeth were practically chattering in fear. “Of course you don’t!” Chan’s voice radiated false confidence. “We were just playing a trick! Ron-Juan, go get that other money we keep in the back!”

“Right away!” said Ron-Juan, in a voice about two octaves higher than his normal one. Zuko was having a hard time keeping himself from laughing. He almost never used his status as a private eye with a penchant for handling danger to scare people, but Chan and Ron-Juan were rich, cheating assholes, just like the guy he’d caught for them. They deserved it.

Ron-Juan returned with a box full of cash. It was clear from the layer of dust on top of it that this was some sort of emergency stash. Knowing Chan and Ron-Juan, they had landed themselves in trouble with someone important, and needed the means to run away if that person ever found them again. Quick as lightning, Chan reached out and yanked the box out of Ron-Juan’s hands. Throwing open the lid, he pulled out a few bills and slammed them forcefully into Zuko’s hand. “There’s your money! Happy now?!”

Zuko smirked at them as he slid out of his stool and began to walk out of the bar. “Couldn’t be happier.”

Chan and Ron-Juan’s bar, despite being dingy and far from a social hotspot, was located in the middle of Ba Sing Se, only a couple of blocks away from Zuko’s apartment. Ba Sing Se was a city of division. There were no walls between the neighborhoods, but there might as well have been. Each part of the city had its own purpose, and those who lived there fulfilled it. Almost no one dared leave their district.

Zuko’s neighborhood, the Middle Ring, was mostly home to businesses: stores, restaurants, and other little things, usually with their owners living in apartments of varying sizes just above them. For Zuko, his apartment also included his office, because why bother having them in different places when you didn’t like taking a taxi and didn’t have a car?

After about ten minutes of walking in the pouring rain through nearly empty streets (it *was* one thirty in the morning, after all), he arrived at his apartment. For a city apartment, it was pretty big, especially considering how little money Zuko actually had. Two bedrooms, a kitchen, a living room, an office, and a bathroom was a lot for Ba Sing Se, but Zuko had had the good luck of solving a case for a real estate agent about a year and a half ago now. The apartment had been a gift.

He turned the key in the door, eyes already drooping shut with exhaustion. He may have been used to late nights, but that didn’t mean he liked them. He was almost ready to collapse on the sofa, not even bothering to walk to his bedroom.

He was lucky he didn’t, because when he entered his apartment, there were already two people sitting on his sofa.

Stopping just short of falling on top of them, he sighed, placing a hand on the coffee table instead. “I *knew* I made a mistake giving you the key to this place.”

Katara stood and put her hands on her hips. “What do you expect?! You said you’d call in two hours, and it took eight! We had the right to be worried!”

“I was on a job. You didn’t need to worry.”

“Oh, sure!” said Sokka, rising to his feet to stand next to his sister. “*Why* would we worry about our friend the detective who’s out chasing down *dangerous* *criminals*?! Wow, I have no idea!”

Zuko rolled his eyes. “I’ve told you both a thousand times. You aren’t my friends.”

Sokka grinned, that goofy, ridiculous grin that made Zuko’s pulse race in irritation. “Uh-huh. But you let us in here. And you let us talk to you.”

“You begged me to give you the keys to my apartment and then you kept using them to come in without my permission.”

Sokka shrugged, unbothered. “That’s just what friends do.”

Katara punched her brother in the arm. “ *No* , Sokka, breaking and entering is *not* what friends do!” Sokka laughed nervously. Katara turned to face Zuko. “I think what Sokka’s trying to say is that you need people to check in on you, even if you think you don’t need it. That’s what friends are for.”

“Besides,” chimed in Sokka, “if we weren’t here, how would you have any fun?!” His arm swung around, giving him an awkward clap on the shoulder. Zuko nearly fell onto his face from the surprising strength of the blow, and felt his face go red in embarrassment. “You take life too seriously!”

Zuko rolled his eyes. “I solve crimes. I need to take that seriously.”

Sokka rolled his eyes right back. “I’m a student studying to solve crimes. That doesn’t mean I can’t tell a joke!”

“Right,” said Katara. “He can’t tell a joke even *without* being a forensics student.”

Zuko felt his fist tightening on the edge of the sofa. Sokka and Katara were good people, of course, but the ease with which they interacted, the lightness in the air when they spoke, how *casual* everything was...it wasn’t for Zuko. After seventeen years with his father and two with criminals, Zuko wasn’t exactly a master of friendly conversation.

He only ever made things harder. It was better to be alone. Alone, he couldn’t hurt anyone, and no one could hurt him.

“Will you two please *leave* ?” His voice came out harsher than he meant it too, and his words hung in the air like smoke.

Katara blinked. “Zuko, we were just trying to help!”

“We wanted to make sure you weren’t *dead* !”

“Well, I’m not dead, '' mumbled Zuko, turning his back to them. “Now, can you please leave?”

They didn’t respond, but Zuko heard the door shut behind him, and he knew they were gone. His legs finally gave in to exhaustion, and he fell backwards onto his sofa. It was now two in the morning, and even with a bright light directly over his head, his eyes were already drooping shut.

Of course, just as he was beginning to drift off to sleep, his phone rang, the irritating, high-pitched noise entering his head like a drill, causing his eyes to shoot open.

Grumbling in irritation, he made his way over to his phone, which was sitting on the wooden table on the other side of the living room. Glancing at the name, he nearly threw the phone across the room just to shut it up. His tired eyesight was so blurry that he could barely click on the “Reply” button.

“Uncle, what’s going on? It’s two-fifteen in the morning.”

His uncle’s voice came through the phone, as unbearably calm as usual. “I just wanted to see how you were doing, Detective Zuko.” For some reason, his uncle always used his “official” name, as though it mattered at all what he called him. “I heard your last case was a bit of a challenge.”

“It wasn’t,” Zuko said bitterly. “I had to chase someone across the city. It took a little longer than I expected. Then I caught them. That’s it.”

“Ah,” said Iroh. His voice sounded exhausted; he must have stayed awake for this. “Well, I’m glad to hear that it went well.”

“Why do you care?” muttered Zuko. “It’s not like you’ll ever let me know any of your White Lotus secrets. Those could be the key to some of my cases.”

Zuko heard Iroh’s sigh from the other end of the phone. “Zuko, I am part of a society that is the backbone of this city. It is naturally my priority. But that does not mean that I do not care about you.”

“Just leave me alone. We both know that’s a lie.” Zuko let his voice become harsh, like earlier. He let his words stay in the air.

The phone went silent long before he put it down.

Why did all of these people pretend to care so much? Zuko knew better than to trust them. He had thought his father cared about him, and look where that had landed him.

But if they did care...well, they were even more stupid than Zuko had thought. He did dangerous work, and he did it with a lot of messing up and guessing wrong, because that was how Zuko was. If these people were truly good enough to care, then they certainly didn’t deserve to be stuck with him.

Sighing as the heavy thoughts settled in his brain, Zuko turned off the light and fell onto his bed, at last in his own bedroom, ready to fall into a heavy sleep. Thunder was crashing outside, and Zuko found the noises strangely calming.

There was another ringing sound, this time the sound of the downstairs doorbell.

Who the hell would be ringing Zuko’s doorbell at three in the morning? Zuko had no idea. Carefully, he crept down the stairs to the front hall of the building, where the doorbell was ringing again.

Cautiously, he opened the door, to make sure there was no instant attack of any sort waiting for him. When there wasn’t, he took a deep breath and flung open the door. Lightning flashed, illuminating the face in front of him.

He didn’t know what he’d expected to see, but this was not it. Standing before him was a face he hadn’t seen in two whole years, not since he’d run away. It was a face he’d thought he’d never see again.

Yet here it was.

What was *she* doing here?

“Azula?”

## Chapter 2: The Lady on the Stairs

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko tries to deal with someone he hasn't seen in a long time. Azula learns some things about the people of Ba Sing Se.

#### Chapter Notes

No TWs for this chapter. Enjoy!  
(In this chapter, an extra space between paragraphs indicates a time jump/change in setting.)

### Text

Azula rolled her eyes with the same exasperated look that Zuko remembered from his childhood, and flipped a strand of hair over her shoulder. “Of course it’s me. Shouldn’t you be able to tell? I thought you were a detective.”

Well, she was as quick to criticize as ever. But what the hell was she *doing* here? “I haven’t seen you in two years, Azula. I’m allowed to be surprised when you show up at my apartment at three in the morning.”

She looked different. Older than he remembered, for one. She’d been fifteen when he left, barely old enough to start high school. Now she was seventeen, almost an adult, and though she hadn’t grown taller, she seemed more ragged, or maybe just a little smarter, as though some part of the world had gotten into her head since he’d last seen her. She looked less prim and proper than he remembered; he always remembered her wearing silk blouses and tightening her hair in buns as a child, but now she was wearing a red leather jacket over a pair of black jeans. Most surprisingly, her hair hung in a ponytail, a style Zuko didn’t think he’d ever seen on her.

Sighing, Azula shoved her way past him and into the lobby. As she did, Zuko couldn’t help noticing the giant backpack on her back.

“Hang on. What are you doing?”

Azula turned and placed her hand on her hip. “I’m on vacation. I need a place to stay. You’re my brother and you live here. Which one is your door?”

At last his groggy, middle of the night brain caught up to him. Zuko raced in front of the stairs, blocking Azula’s path. “Hang on. I haven’t seen you in two years. You can’t just barge into my apartment and act like you own the place!”

“I don’t own it. I’m perfectly aware of that fact.” Under the lights of the lobby, Zuko could see the bags under his sister’s eyes. It was clear that she hadn’t slept enough that night either. “Do you not want me here?” Her voice was hard to read, a mix of irritation, coldness, and possibly even disappointment, or hurt.

“I bought this place to get away from our family, Azula. It’s my way of proving that I’m different. I get to choose who comes here, no one else.” It was hard not to raise his voice as he spoke. He hadn’t had to explain his reasons for running away to anyone in two years; doing it made him feel like he was right back with his father, growing up under that roof all over again.

He expected her to knock him over the railing and barge up the stairs, but instead she just stared at him, another expression that he couldn’t read. It looked almost regretful, but also irritated and cold again. “I didn’t say I wanted to stay here. I said I was on vacation.”

“For how long?”  
Azula shrugged, something that was unlike her in itself. “I’m not sure yet. Father thought that it would be beneficial for me to have some worldly experience. University applications and all that.”

Zuko paused. “So he knows you’re here?”

Azula nodded. “Relax, Zuko, he won’t come looking for you. He gave up on you a long time ago.” Her voice was a mix of pity and disdain, two emotions Zuko hated.

“Don’t talk to me that way.”

“How?”

“Like you’re *better* than me. You’re not better than me just because our father said so. You don’t get to come in here and take over my apartment and act like you run the whole city. I ran away from Father’s life for a reason. You don’t have the right to bring it back.”

There was a small silence, then Azula clapped her hands in slow motion. “Well, I can see my presence has irritated you, but seeing as it’s three fifteen in the morning and I have no other plans, what if I stayed here for one night, and we worked something out in the morning when we aren’t audaciously sleep deprived anymore?”

Zuko sighed. He hated to admit it, but she was right. He was too tired to argue with her anymore. “Fine. One night.”

Azula smirked at him. “I’m glad to see that we’re on the same page. It makes for a promising start.”

Zuko was surprised when he woke up the next morning to find every part of his apartment seemingly intact. His sister wasn’t angry or volatile, unless something deeply triggered her emotions, but she had always had an affinity for tricks as a kid. It was something Zuko still associated with her; the ability to mess things up in small, effortless but irritating ways.

She was already awake when he found her, which wasn’t surprising. Azula had always been an early riser growing up. She was dressed in an outfit similar to the one she’d had on the day before; a tight-fitting shirt with pattern mimicking blue flames, and black straight-legged pants. Her hair was coiled into a topknot with two strands falling on either side of her face, the same style she’d always worn as a child.

The floorboards creaked under Zuko’s footsteps, and Azula turned to face him. She looked a lot more awake and alive than she had the night before, though that was probably due to the fact that she was drinking coffee.

“Where did you get coffee?”

Azula took a sip of her drink, waves of aloofness radiating off of her. This was how he’d always remembered her. But he couldn’t forget the looks she’d given him the night before, full of a kaleidoscope of indiscernible emotions. He’d never seen her look like that before.

“Use your intuition skills, *Detective* . I borrowed your coffee maker.”

Of course, that didn’t mean she *wasn’t* condescending and absolutely bitchy.

“There’s extra if you want it.”

Zuko shook his head. He’d given up on coffee when he’d become a detective. No amount of it could possibly fix the lack of sleep that came with his job, and besides, it gave him a monster headache. “No thanks. Tea is more my thing.”

Azula laughed. “Of *course* it would be.”

With nothing else to say, the air went silent. After a childhood of unintentional separation and two years of literally not seeing each other, the siblings were at a loss for words. Neither of them knew the other, not really. It was almost like they were strangers, meeting for the first time in the middle of the city.

But the mention of tea gave Zuko an idea.

He grabbed his sister by the shoulder, something he hadn’t done since they were kids.

“What are you doing?”

Zuko gave her a sarcastic smirk. “Didn’t you want a tour of the city?”  
“Not in the slightest.”

Zuko sighed. “Just come to the tea shop.”

Azula seemed completely uninterested in anything the tea shop had to offer. She accepted the cup of tea that Iroh offered her, sipping it delicately and staring out the window without engaging in conversation with either of them. She had greeted Iroh coldly, and had said nothing since.

Zuko sighed, carrying a tray back into the kitchen, where his uncle was happily preparing another pot of tea, probably the first of the day. However, the second Iroh saw the look on Zuko’s face, he set the tea tray down and turned to him, face full of concern. “What’s troubling you, Zuko?”

Zuko sighed, slumping into a chair. “I just don’t understand, Uncle. What is Azula *doing* here? Why would she come to see me after two whole years? What does she want?”

“What did she tell you?”

Zuko groaned and rolled his eyes. “That she’s on vacation.”

“But you don’t believe her?”

Zuko gave his uncle a skeptical glance. “Azula always lies. If you’d been there more while we were growing up, you’d know that.” He paused, realizing what he’d said. “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean-”

“It’s all right.”

The room fell silent for a minute, except for the sound of the nearly boiling tea kettle.

“I was hoping that maybe she could stay with you. I can’t afford to have her with me while I’m working on my cases.”

Iroh shook his head. “As much as I would like to better acquaint myself with my niece, I doubt she’d be too thrilled with the idea.” He paused. “Besides, you aren’t working on a case right now, are you?”

“No.” Zuko threw his uncle a suspicious look. “What are you getting at?”

“I am simply saying that the best solution may be the one you have already found.”

“You mean letting her stay with me.”

Iroh nodded. “Zuko, I am well aware that Azula represents a part of your childhood for you that you would rather forget. But it seems to me that she is making you an offer. She would not have sought you out if she did not want to make some sort of amends with you.”

“Are we talking about the same Azula?”

“Is it so hard for you to believe your sister would want to see you again?”

“You didn’t know her growing up.” Zuko sank deeper into the chair. “She never wanted anything to do with me then. It was all about pleasing our father, being perfect, and lording that perfection over me. She never had time for getting to *know* me.” There was a hint of old, un-dealt with bitterness in his voice. Maybe he was being petty, but if he was, he didn’t care.

“It’s been two years, Zuko. A person can change a lot in two years.”

There was a rustling from the front of the shop, and Zuko heard the little bell that his uncle had hung over the door twinkle. He could hear Azula’s voice through the curtain, but not her words. In the absence of any obvious disaster, he turned back to his uncle. “Even if she has changed, that doesn’t solve the problem of my cases.”

“What about them?”

Zuko sighed. “You know by now that I work better alone. It’s easier when you don’t have to worry about other people messing up, or ruining the job for you when people’s lives are on the line!”

Iroh sighed. “Zuko, there’s nothing wrong with accepting help from time to time.”

“I don’t need help. Especially not from *her* .”

Iroh put his tea pot down. “Zuko, you are a detective. It seems to me that you are allowing your memories of your childhood to cloud your judgement.” Zuko opened his mouth, but was cut off. “I am not saying that whatever happened while you were growing up isn’t true, but who you both were as children does not have to be who you both are now. That decision rests on you.”

Zuko turned away, not wanting to look him in the eye. Maybe he was right. Maybe Azula *had* changed.

But maybe she hadn’t. If Zuko had learned anything from his life, first with his father and then fighting scheming criminals, it was that no one could really be trusted except yourself. Even if their intentions were good, they would mess up the job through sheer inexperience. Most of the time, it wasn’t so nice and clean-cut.

Zuko was abruptly pulled out of his thoughts when there was a crash and a shriek from the front of the shop, a shriek in a voice that Zuko recognized right away as Azula’s. This alone was unusual, and enough to make Zuko sprint into the front of the tea shop to see what was happening. He could hear his uncle’s footsteps following close behind.

He found Azula looking completely infuriated, pinned against the counter by a man who wore a familiar dark green scarf around his neck.

Azula caught sight of Zuko and let out a sigh of exasperation. “Finally. Do you really permit this sort of behavior here?”

Zuko eyed the man suspiciously. On the one hand, it was usually a bad thing to have someone pinned against a countertop. On the other hand, it was Azula. “What happened?”

The man turned to him, an angry look on his face. Zuko didn’t recognize him. “This young woman disrespected me in an enormous way! She completely disregarded my authority and my rights as a Dai Li officer! I was simply reminding her who she was talking to.” He turned back to Azula. “I hope you’ve learned your lesson.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “Actually, I haven’t learned anything, because I don’t live here, and I have no idea who you are.”

The man sighed, lowering his hand. “All right. Only because of that, I’ll let it slide this time. But I would tread carefully if I were you.” With that, he turned and walked out of the tea shop, the bell twinkling again as he left.

Azula turned to Zuko, still irritated, her eyes flashing. “Who was that? Why was he acting as though he had some sort of authority over me?”

“It’s because he does,” Zuko sighed, leaning against the counter. “Did you see that green scarf that he was wearing? That means that he’s a member of the Dai Li.”

There was another pause.  
Azula flung her hands up into the air. “Why does every person in this town expect me to know who that is? Do they not understand the words ‘I just got here?’”

“You shouldn’t forget about the Dai Li,” said Zuko, turning to meet her gaze. “That man may not have seemed scary, but there are a lot of Dai Li in this city.”  
“What are they?”

Zuko couldn’t help feeling like he was in some sort of spy movie. “The Dai Li are a society that’s existed in Ba Sing Se for decades. They were formed to maintain order in the city after some riots about sixty years ago. They’ve got a huge network of members, mostly in the police force, some of them in the government.”

“Why was that man threatening me? All I did was tell him that we were closed.”

Zuko sighed. “Some of the Dai Li love to hold their authority over everyone else. With all of their allies in politics, they can sort of do whatever they want.

Azula nodded. “They can’t be punished for breaking the law when they *are* the law.”

“Exactly.”

There was a small pause. Then, Iroh turned and began setting up more tables. “Well, I won’t have any of those threats and bullying happening in my tea shop.”

Azuls raised an eyebrow, sipping a cup of tea that she’d just grabbed off the table. “You seem to really hate these men, Uncle. I wouldn’t have thought you were capable of hating anyone.”

As if on cue, the bell over the doorway twinkled again, and in walked an old man, even older than Zuko’s uncle. Upon seeing the customer, Iroh walked across the room and embraced him, grinning. “Pakku! It has truly been too long.”

“It has indeed,” responded Pakku, looking around the shop with a judgemental eye. “I must say, I was not expecting to see your nephew here.”

“Zuko decided to pay me a surprise visit. It was a pleasure.”

“I see,” murmured Pakku. “And I see that you have also hired a female assistant. That will be good for business.”

Azula raised an eyebrow. “What are you implying?” Her tone was sharp and biting.

Pakku squared his shoulders. “I am simply stating the obvious. It’s something that most women have trouble grasping, don’t work yourself into a fit. “

Azula crossed her arms over her chest. “And if I say you’re deeply wrong and that your beliefs about women are misguided and fucked-up? Who works themself into a fit then?”

Pakku’s face instantly reddened with anger. “You will not disrespect me like that! Do you have the faintest idea of who I am?!”

Azula threw her arms out. “No! How many times do I need to remind people that I do not live in this city?”

Iroh walked over and tried to put his hand on Azula’s shoulder, but she shoved it away. “Pakku is a member of the White Lotus, Azula.”

“And what might that be?”

Pakku narrowed his eyes. “Your ignorance is bordering on complete insubordination, young lady!”

“Well, I won’t be ‘ignorant’ anymore if someone in this room would do me the grand courtesy of telling me what in the name of the fucking sun the White Lotus is.” Azula’s voice was oozing sarcasm.

Pakku groaned, taking on an official-sounding tone. “The White Lotus is one of the oldest societies in the world. We have existed in Ba Sing Se for centuries, to preserve the values of tradition, culture, and freedom. We use our positive influence over entrepreneurs to strengthen small businesses and allow citizens to share their knowledge with the rest of the world.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “Well *that* sounds far too perfect to be that effective in reality.”

Pakku turned to Iroh, ignoring Azula. “I came to inform you that I have been supervising a new exhibition at the Ba Sing Se Museum of Arts and Culture. All members of the White Lotus…” he glanced sideways at Azula, grimacing... “and their families are invited to celebrate the opening at a gala.” He eyed Azula and Zuko with an unimpressed look. “Please attempt to look presentable.” And with that, he left, the bell over the door chiming louder than before. as it met a gust of wind. Azula turned back to them, a smirk on her face. “My first day in town, and there’s already a party? *This* should be exciting.”

Zuko rolled his eyes at her dramatic words. “Don’t get so excited. I’ve been to too many White Lotus events to count, and they’re boring as fuck. Absolutely nothing interesting ever happens.”
