## Chapter 3: The Tragedy at Marsdon Manor

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula and Zuko go to the White Lotus's museum gala. Azula encounters several new faces, is presented with a rivalry, and witnesses a surprise.

#### Chapter Notes

TWs in the end notes for this chapter. (Spoilers!)  
We're getting Azula POV this chapter. She's my favorite character to write, so this one was a lot of fun, if a little shaky as i got used to writing her. Anyway, enjoy:)

### Text

Azula dug through her backpack, trying to find one suitable party outfit among the clothes she’d packed. Of course, it wasn’t easy; she *had* packed in a hurry, after all. Still, she managed to dig a short red party dress out from the bottom of the bag. It was slightly wrinkled, but she supposed it would do. She held it up in front of her body and made a face. Azula *hated* dresses. There was no other item of clothing that could make her feel so exposed, so easy to overpower. Pants were much more practical. But tonight, it seemed, she had no choice.

For some reason, she’d also managed to pack her only pair of high heels, despite hating them almost as much as she hated dresses, so she pulled them onto her feet. Glancing in the mirror, she saw a girl in a short red dress covered in white flowers, gold heels, and her hair in a tight bun on top of her head. In short, she saw a well-dressed girl who looked nothing like her. Still, it would have to do. She would have to make time for a shopping trip soon.

Zuko emerged from his room, looking...interesting. Unlike Azula, he wore no trace of red, the unofficial color of their family. That wasn’t surprising. What *was* somewhat surprising was his long, black coat that he had put on over grey pants and a white shirt.

“Is that the new fashion trend in the city now?”

Zuko looked like he might smother her with the enormous coat. “No. I got this coat on a job.”

“Well, you look like a character out of a children’s cartoon.”

“You know, usually when people demand to stay in someone else’s apartment with no warning, they don’t spend the whole time there criticizing their clothes.

“Well, I’m a special girl.”

Zuko sighed, rolling his eyes. “I guess it’s pretty hard to argue with *that* .”

They walked across town towards the museum, which, according to Zuko, was a dusty old building that you couldn’t miss because it looked like it came from a different century. Azula winced as she walked, her shoes pinching her toes. She should have just worn sneakers; these heels were two years old and a size too small.

“Zuko?”

“Mmmhm?”

“How many of these sorts of parties have you been to before?”

Zuko stopped for a second and turned to look at her. “Too many to count, especially when I first got to Ba Sing Se. The White Lotus loves them. But I’ve been trying to avoid them for a while now.”

“Then why come to this one?”

Zuko sighed. “Uncle asked me to. He said it would be good for you to get to know the town.”

“Do you disagree?”

“I just don’t think the White Lotus is your best introduction to this place. That is, if you’re staying.” He paused and looked at her, clearly expecting some sort of answer.

“I’m not sure.” That, at least, was somewhat true. “When I left on vacation, I didn’t really have a plan.”

“That doesn’t sound like you.”

“I was *attempting* to mix things up.” Her tone sharpened slightly in her defensiveness. “But I do think I’ll be here for a while, yes. There seems to be quite a lot of interesting things in this city.”

Zuko sighed, as though giving in to something. “Well, the spare room in my apartment is open if you want it. But if you mess with any of my cases, it won’t be open anymore.”

Azula blinked at him. Well, *that* was unexpected. “Why would you do that? Aren’t I the very representation of the family you’re trying to escape?”

“Yes,” said Zuko. Well, at least he was being honest. It was more than she could say for herself. “But you’re also my sister.”

“And?”

“And it wouldn’t be right to leave my sister in the city without anywhere to stay!”

“You know I could pay for a hotel, right?”

“It’s not about that,” muttered Zuko. “This is about respect, and honor.”

There was a pause, and then Azula shrugged. “Well, I can’t say I relate to that sentiment, but it works out well for me, so as far as I’m concerned, continue feeling that way, I suppose.”

Zuko was giving her more than she deserved. If he knew everything, he’d take it all away in a second. But Azula didn’t want to think about that now.

They walked in silence the rest of the way to the museum, which was, as Zuko had said, practically prehistoric, and looked completely out of place in the enormous, modern city. Even the door was old looking, wooden and thick, with an enormous door knocker. In the doorway hung an enormous banner that read: *Grand Opening of the History of Love in Artwork, Members Only.*

“Catchy slogan,” muttered Azula sarcastically, as the siblings passed through the open doorway and into the lobby, which was essentially a large room furnished in the same old style as the building. Along the walls were several paintings, as well as several objects in glass boxes, clearly on display. The room was packed with people, most of them looking to be around the same age as Pakku. A few teenagers around Azula’s own age seemed to be scattered about the room, and she wondered what business they could possibly have at what seemed to be the stuffiest event in the world.

Before she could ask her brother about the other teenagers, two figures broke out of the crowd and ran towards them, clearly recognizing Zuko. Both had dark skin, dark hair, and striking blue eyes, and looked alike enough that Azula would guess that they were probably brother and sister. The brother tried to high-five Zuko, but ended up slapping him on the shoulder instead when Zuko didn’t high-five him back. His face flushed. His sister giggled, rolling her eyes in a loving way.

Azula raised an eyebrow. Well, *this* was interesting. “Zuzu, you never told me that you’d made new friends!”

Zuko looked at the floor and turned his back to the two new arrivals. “I haven’t.”

The brother clapped Zuko’s back with his hand (intentionally this time) and grinned. “Sure he has. We’re his best friends. He just won’t admit it.” Despite the confidence of his words, there was a perpetual undercurrent of insecurity in his voice. Interesting.

The sister smiled at Azula. “What’s your name? How do you know Zuko?”

Azula blinked, caught off guard, silly as it was. Back home, she’d lived with her father and their servants. She’d gone to the same elite private school since Kindergarten. She’d had private tutors come to the house for every activity. Suffice to say, she hadn’t had to introduce herself to anyone in years.

Still, she managed. “I’m Azula. Zuko, the idiot who won’t appreciate his friends, is somehow related to me. And you are?”

The sister laughed. “I’m Katara. This is my brother, Sokka.”

Sokka gave her a friendly wave. “Zuko, how come you never told us you had a sister?”

Zuko continued to stare at the floor and look unnecessarily moody. “It never came up.”

Azula wasn’t exactly surprised that he hadn’t told them. After all, this was Zuko’s new life, the one he’d created purposely to get away from his family. From *her* .

“Well, Azula,” said Katara, “welcome to Ba Sing Se. We’d be happy to lend you a hand if you need anything.”

“You don’t need to do that,” said Zuko, still determined not to look either of them in the eye. Katara seemed un-bothered by it, but Sokka kept trying to make eye contact with him. Zuko was certainly persistent in his quest to be a brooding detective, Azula could give him that. “I can handle her.”

Azula raised an eyebrow. “No one is *handling* me. I can handle myself.”

“So that’s why you’re living in my apartment, then.”

Awkward silence descended over the group. Sokka looked around for a way to break it, then grinned. “Look, a food table! Who wants to go get some?” Without waiting for an answer, he grabbed Zuko’s hand and dragged him across the room.

Azula watched them go. Over by the food table, she noticed an odd-looking man dressed in green, eyeing the food almost as excitedly as Sokka had. She turned to Katara. “Who’s that man in green?”

“That’s Mayor Kuei.”

“Is he allied with the White Lotus?”

Katara shook her head. “No, the Dai Li, actually, but he really likes parties. If there’s a party, he’ll be there.”

“Sounds rather superficial.”

Katara shrugged. “Can’t say I blame him. Everyone loves a good party.”

“I suppose that’s true for some people. Not me, and certainly not my brother.”

Katara paused. “So, what’s your story with your brother? It seems...not too easy.”

Azula folded her arms over her chest. “I don’t want to talk about it.”

“That’s okay,” Katara smiled. “But I was serious. If you ever need something from someone you aren’t related to, you know where to find me.”

“Why would you do that?”

Katara blinked. “It’s just the right thing to do.” She sighed. “You and Zuko have that in common.”

“What?”

“You always seem so surprised when someone does something nice for you.”

Azula had no response to that.

She glanced over at the food table, where Sokka was excitedly pointing something out to Zuko, who actually looked the least disinterested he’d looked all night. “Your brother seems to lose his ability to hold a conversation around mine.”

Katara laughed. “Yeah, he’s been that way for a while.”

“Of *course* my idiot brother wouldn’t do anything about that.”

“I’m not so sure he’s the same way.”

Azula smirked, thinking about how easily Zuko had allowed Sokka to pull him across the room. “Oh, believe me, he absolutely is.”

Katara glanced around the room, which, as far as Azula could see, continued to only contain people above the age of a hundred. “So, how come you got invited here?”

“Oh, our Uncle’s a member. He seems somewhat antiquated and overly sentimental to me, so from what I’ve heard about this organization, that checks out.”

Surprisingly, Katara laughed. Azula blinked in surprise. “Wow. I thought everyone in this city worshipped the ground these people walked on.”

Katara shook her head, suddenly serious. “You’d be surprised. A lot of people don’t like the White Lotus, but they have an influence on so many people, and they’ve got a hand in so many businesses, so most people are too scared to do anything.”

“You don’t seem to like them very much. What brings you here?”

Katara shrugged. “I’m a journalism student. I helped get some of the exhibit items from the archives.”

“Well, that’s exciting.”

Katara shook her head. “It was pretty boring, actually.”

Their conversation was interrupted by the return of Sokka and Zuko, both carrying plates of food. Sokka kept telling Zuko how good various appetizers were, and that he *had* to try them.

Azula glanced around the party. “What are we supposed to do now?”

Sokka shrugged. “Why don’t we go around and introduce ourselves to people? See who’s here.”

*Interesting* . Azula had only been to her father’s parties growing up, and at those, her goal had always been to keep up her perfect posture, and say the exact right thing at the exact right moment. This seemed much more...free. At least it appeared to be. Azula couldn’t shake the feeling that whatever you said in the presence of the White Lotus would become important later on.

Zuko seemed completely horrified by the idea of talking to other people. If the thought didn’t make Azula’s stomach tie itself in knots, she would have laughed. But she understood all too well. Learning the ins and outs of the social world after living in their house for seventeen years was difficult, and people were quick to judge if you made a mistake. It was easier to push people away, to not even try.

But Azula wasn’t a quitter. She never had been. She had succeeded at everything her father had asked of her, and now that this was her life, she would succeed at this, too. She *had* to.

“All right, then. Let’s go meet some people.”

Azula couldn’t figure the ancient society out, and it irritated her. They weren’t all sentimental types like her uncle, nor were they old-fashioned assholes like Pakku. Glancing around the party, she could also see several people who looked eccentric, and some who looked completely calm and collected. There was no pattern, and the more she talked to people, the harder the pattern was to find.

“So,” she said politely to the man with white curly hair coming out of his ears, hanging upside-down on the banister with no shirt on, “you’re a...what, exactly?” Next to her, she could hear Katara giggling. “If you know them all, you could just *tell* me,” she hissed in the other girl’s ear, but Katara only kept laughing.

“A wrestler!” cried the man, in a voice that sounded as eccentric as he looked. “Some people might call me an ex-wrestler, but I say I’m still at my prime and they just don’t know it!”

Azula sighed. What good was getting to know people if they were all like *this* ?

Sensing her discomfort, Katara grabbed her hand and pulled her away from the man, who gave them a wave. “Wow. You really *are* new in town, huh?”

Azula groaned. “I didn’t mean to be so obvious. But why are they all so *weird* ?”

Zuko sighed. “This is why I don’t go to parties. I have better things to do than talk to people who want nothing to do with me.”

Sokka gave him a goofy grin. “Oh, come on! Everyone loves you!”

Zuko scowled. This was evidently an untrue statement.

Katara gave the two of them a reproachful look. “Come on, guys! They’re not all bad! Even Bumi!” Azula gave her a quizzical look. “The wrestler. I know he’s weird, but I’m friends with his adopted son, and he can be kind of sweet!”

Azula rolled her eyes. “I’ll believe it when I see it.”

Sokka cocked his head at her. “You’re prickly, aren’t you?”

Zuko smirked. “This is why I’m the social one in our family.”

Azula felt her face flush, a memory of a party when she was fourteen flashing through her head. It was sort of terrifying how right he was. But of course, she could never let him know that. “Oh, please, Zuzu, if you’re the social one, I’m a four hundred foot tall purple platypus with pink horns and silver wings.”

They were interrupted by a very nervous looking old man stumbling right into them. He had a thin grey mustache, and absolutely no hair on top of his head. “Forgive me! I didn’t mean to offend you!”

Azula felt a smile spreading across her face. What better experiment for meeting new people than someone incredibly nervous who couldn’t harm her in any way if he tried?

“Greetings, friend. There is no need to apologize, because we are forgiving people.”

The man ran away, potentially even faster than he’d run in. Azula heard Zuko and snickering. She turned and saw Katara giving her a pitiful stare. “What?!”

Zuko stared blankly at her. “That isn’t how you talk to people.”

Azula felt her face flush slightly. She was deeply mortified, but couldn’t let herself show it. “I live with our father. How am I supposed to learn other than by trial and error?”

Before Zuko could say something else, Sokka grinned and ran towards a table covered in shrimp. With a small smile, Zuko followed him. As Katara went after the rest of them, Azula took the opportunity to slip into the corner. All of this learning was exhausting. It felt like she was in school again, only absolutely none of this came naturally to her. Why did it have to be so *hard* ?

“I see you’re also not an action-oriented guest.”

She turned and saw another old man (Was this society truly made up of solely old men? If so, it made her like it even less.) This one had a thin mustache, a long beard, and a thick head of white hair. She hadn’t seen him before, probably because he’d stayed in the shadows the entire time. Azula could respect that choice; in retrospect, it was probably what *she* should have done.

“I’m trying,” she replied. “But I’m new in town. Trying to navigate these things is a risk.”

“Wise choice,” said the man. “Most people just come to these parties for the spectacle, and the drama.”

Azula crossed her arms over her chest. “Well, I’m so busy learning everyone’s name, which for some reason the entire town already knows, that I can’t be bothered with that. You’re in luck.”

The man let out a low laugh. “You’re not the only one who can’t be bothered.” He held out his hand. “Call me Jeong Jeong.”

Azula hesitated before taking it. “How could you not be here for the spectacle? Aren’t you a part of this?”

Jeong Jeong sighed. “The purpose of the White Lotus is to uphold traditions. Some people’s tradition is spectacle. Mine happens to be something else.”

Satisfied, Azula accepted his hand. “Have you upheld your tradition?”

The man sighed. “I wish.”

Before Azula could ask him to elaborate, another man walked over. This one was slightly younger than Jeong Jeong, though his hair, which he wore in a bun, was still slightly grey. The odd thing about him was that he wore a sabre at his waist. Was *everyone* at this party weird?

The younger man put his hand on Jeong Jeong’s shoulder. “Jeong Jeong, I know you don’t love this. I don’t either, but it’s time to get ready for the unveiling.”

Jeong Jeong nodded. “I can handle it for one night.”

The man with the sabre looked at Azula and offered her a small smile. “I’m Piandao. I don’t believe we’ve met before.”

Azula shook her head to confirm his statement and held out her hand. “Pleased to make your acquaintance.”

Unlike her previous attempt at a friendly greeting, this seemed to go over well, and the man took her hand before disappearing into the crowd. Azula let her gaze follow the two men until they disappeared from view, but when she lost sight of them, she began to feel anxious, an unusual feeling for her. She only really knew three people at this party, if you counted Katara and Sokka as people she knew, and she had lost sight of every single one.

“Are you looking for someone?”

Azula turned and found yet another serious-looking man behind her. This one had dark brown hair and a short, neatly-trimmed beard of the same color. “No,” she lied, grabbing a drink from a passing waiter and taking a sip. “I’m simply taking a moment of quiet.”

The man nodded, still not smiling. He certainly seemed very serious. “Well, my name is Arnook. I’m a member of the White Lotus. Are you new in town?”

Azula was pretty sure she couldn’t convince him otherwise, so she nodded. “I’m on vacation.”

Arnook nodded again. “Well, if you need anything, you can tell me.”

Before Azula got the chance to respond, a younger man with an excited-looking face (the opposite of Arnook’s expression) ran up. He was dressed in only white clothes. “Arnook! The stage is in position for the unveiling, and all the lighting has been verified! The crew is doing their final soundchecks, and soon they’ll be ready!”

Arnook nodded. “Excellent work, Professor Zei. But I will once again remind you that you have already been accepted into the White Lotus. You do not need to prove yourself to any of us.”

Professor Zei nodded, clearly not following what Arnook had said. “Of course! I’m just very excited!” And with that, he disappeared into the crowd again, a checklist in his hand. Arnook raised his hand at Azula, and then he, too, hurried off.

Azula was on the verge of just leaving when she caught a glimpse of Zuko, Katara, and Sokka, all standing together near the stage. Hiding her relief, she walked over and joined them, casually sipping her drink as though she’d never left.

Zuko gave her a suspicious glance. “Where were you?”

Azula rolled her eyes. Her brother had every right to be annoyed with her, she’d give him that, but suspicion? She didn’t know anyone here! What could she possibly do? “I was meeting a secret agent planted in the crowd to construct a massive network of tunnels underneath the city and use them to overthrow the government and eventually wage war on the rest of the world.” She blinked innocently. “Where were you?”

Zuko didn’t find her joke at all amusing, but Katara and Sokka both laughed.

Onstage, the White Lotus members began to file in. As they did, Azula was pleasantly surprised to realize that she recognized every single one, except for one of them. Maybe this was what people meant when they said that mingling could be useful.

The only man she didn’t know stood at the end of the line, and looked to be the most ancient of all. He barely looked like a man, only a dried-out husk of a person. “Who’s that?”

“That’s Yon Rha,” said Sokka. “He joined the White Lotus ages ago after he was in the military. Nobody remembers why he joined. He doesn’t really do anything.”

The crowd fell silent as Professor Zei began to recite the rules of courtesy for the event, but as he talked, Azula could hear strange noises spreading from the back of the room. Katara and Sokka were still watching the stage, but she could see that Zuko had heard them, too. They looked at each other, then slowly directed their gazes towards the crowd behind them. It looked inconspicuous, but Azula caught sight of several green splotches. Upon closer inspection, she realized that they were actually men in what appeared to be a much darker version of an army uniform.

“Who are they?” she hissed at Zuko.

His face looked grim. “Dai Li.”

Azula looked around, watching the green figures slowly move through the crowd. She could feel the wheels of her brain begin to turn. It all made sense. Her uncle had spoken about the Dai Li with venom in his voice, venom she’d never heard from him before. She remembered hearing that the White Lotus was focused on freedom, but the Dai Li on order. Both were enormous societies, no doubt vying for power.

She turned to Zuko. “They hate each other, don’t they?”

Sokka, who had now caught on to the Dai Li’s presence as well, nodded. “It’s actually really terrifying.”

“Why are they here?” murmured Katara. “This is a peaceful event! It does *nothing* to them!”

Azula rolled her eyes. “I met one Dai Li officer. He didn’t seem like a very peaceful person.”

“To be fair,” said Zuko, “you weren’t exactly the most polite with him.”

“I don’t need to be polite with those who don’t deserve it.”

“Guys!” called Sokka. “Look!” He pointed at the stage.

The entire room’s attention was no longer directed at Professor Zei, who hadn’t noticed the Dai Li’s presence, and was continuing to read his infinitely long list of rules. The crowd rustled and murmured, slowly getting louder and louder until there was a crash from the back of the room. Professor Zei’s voice stuttered into shocked silence, and the entire room went quiet as the crowd whirled around to look at the back table. A man in dark green stood on top of it, surrounded by an army of others in identical uniforms. In his hand, he held the bottom of a wine glass. Azula couldn’t see the glass shards covering the table from the other side of the room, but in the near silence, she could hear them crunching under his boots.

On the stage, Professor Zei was shaking in fear. “What do you want?” he cried, his voice coming out as a squeak.

The man at the back of the room smiled cruelly. “I have simply come to share my opinion with the rest of you.”

“You liar!” cried the nervous looking old man who had run away from Azula earlier. His voice sounded like that of a stereotypical grandfather from a children’s cartoon. He was quite possibly the least intimidating person that Azula had ever seen. “You’re just trying to bring us down.”

The man clenched the broken glass tighter, causing more shards to fall at his feet. “Nonsense, Fung. You do value freedom, correct?”

“Not at the expense of others,” said Iroh from the stage, his voice steady but full of anger.

“Well then, you will understand what I have to say,” said the man. “These sorts of events, these grandiose displays of your wealth, they only disrupt the order of this city. They elevate your social status in an extremely unfair way compared to everyone else, and they do nothing to truly preserve culture. A true culture lover would be working to preserve our city instead of these meaningless artifacts.”

Bumi, the wrestler, walked to the front of the stage. “Don’t try lying, Ukano!” he cried. “You Dai Li just want to take all the power for yourselves, and everyone knows it!”

The man (Ukano) laughed. “You fool. You have no idea how destructive you all are. When this city falls, it will be on your shoulders.”

Without another word, he leapt off the table and raced out the door, disappearing into the inky blackness outside. The other men followed suit.

“Well,” hissed Azula, “that was intriguing.”

Zuko nodded. “Something like this happens every time someone tries to change the town. The other group can’t stand the idea.”

“It’s awful,” murmured Katara. “How can two groups of people hate each other so much?”

“Different goals,” said Sokka, at the same time that Zuko said “Bad luck,” and Azula said “Human nature.”

The four of them fell silent, as did the rest of the room. The Dai Li’s impromptu visit had left a feeling of uneasiness in the air. Even though they were gone by now, Azula couldn’t shake the feeling that something was about to go horribly wrong.

The room stayed silent for what felt like hours, but eventually, Professor Zei cleared his throat, and continued reading his long list of rules as though absolutely nothing had happened. Azula, despite the fact that she was impeccable when it came to focusing, couldn’t concentrate on his words, instead glancing around the room for anything suspicious. She found only a crowd of innocent partygoers, seemingly as on edge as she was.

At last, Professor Zei finished his endless list, and retreated to the back of the stage with the rest of the members of the White Lotus. In his place, Pakku stepped up to the microphone. As he opened his mouth and began to speak, Azula found herself drifting into bored oblivion. It wasn’t that the topics Pakku spoke about were uninteresting, but his voice had a quality to it that made her want to not listen to it.

Or maybe it was just the fact that she already knew that he was a misogynistic asshole. That also made her want to not listen to him.

Still, she forced herself to listen to the end of his speech as he folded up the paper he was reading off of. “I hope that you will all take the time to bask in the culture displayed in this incredible new exhibi-”

His voice was cut off, and the crowd gasped. Despite herself, Azula gasped along with them.

A knife had flown through the air, so quickly that no one could see where it had come from, and lodged itself in Pakku’s throat. He clutched at the knife for a second, attempting to save himself, his fingers stained red by his own blood.

A second later, he collapsed to the stage, dead.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

TWs for this chapter: Blood, knives, death (only in the final paragraph.)

Believe me, the worst is yet to come for our detectives.  
I hope you all enjoyed that! If you've got anything to say, please leave a comment or come find me on Tumblr at @theatergirl06.

## Chapter 4: Wasps' Nest

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

In the aftermath of Pakku's murder, the group tries to get their bearings as the party dissolves into chaos. Zuko is offered a special opportunity, Azula reflects on the past, and Katara makes an unusual connection.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Mentions of death, knives and murder, physical abuse, burning. (If you want to skip the last two, skip the part written in italics.)

This one's a little long, and not my favorite chapter if I'm being honest, but I hope you all enjoy it anyway:)

### Text

The room instantly dissolved into chaos. People began to run and scream, pushing and shoving one another this way and that. Some tried to run out the door as fast as they could, others tried to get to the stage. The four teenagers were separated from each other in the mob, each doing their best to follow the path of the crowd and not get trampled.

Katara had been trying to get to the side of the room where she thought the knife had come from when a stampede of middle-aged women in yellow dresses raced by, shrieking all the way to the door and knocking her flat onto her back. For a second, she couldn’t breathe at all as the crowd raced every which way around her. As she struggled to her feet, a hand reached out and pulled her under a table.

Still gasping for breath, Katara turned to see who was there. Sitting next to her was a girl who appeared to be about the same age as her. The most unique thing about her was her hair, which was pure white, and tied into a complicated style that hung loose in places and was braided tightly in others. Her eyes were blue, like Katara’s, but of a much lighter shade, like snow in the moonlight. She wore a pale blue dress that was just a shade darker than her eyes.

“Are you crazy?” hissed Katara, deciding to save her thanks for later. “Why aren’t you trying to leave? You’ll get hurt!”

The girl cocked her head at her, seemingly unoffended. “It didn’t seem like *you* were leaving.”

Katara pulled the notebook she always carried out from under the folds of her dress. “I’m a journalist,” she said, neglecting to mention the “student” part of her title. That could come later. “It’s my job to figure out things like this.”

The girl nodded, somewhat grimly. “Well, that man onstage with a knife in his neck practically raised me. I’m not leaving him behind.”

Katara let out a gasp. “Oh my gosh! I’m so sorry!” She took a closer look at her. “Are you okay?”

The girl shook her head, tears starting to spill from her eyes. It seemed that the reality of the murder was only hitting her now. Katara couldn’t think of anything to do except put one arm around her and let her cry.

On the other side of the room, Sokka had leapt onto a table to stop himself from being run over by the room full of crazy people. So far, standing on the table had worked surprisingly well. The room was starting to empty, and as he looked around, he could see police cars pulling up outside. Considering that the police belonged almost entirely to the Dai Li, this could only end *very* badly.

The last of the party guests had pretty much streamed out the door by the time the Dai Li arrived, leaving only White Lotus members behind. Looking around the room, Sokka couldn’t see Zuko, Azula, or Katara. Knowing Zuko and Katara, he figured they were somewhere nearby. Neither one of them was the type to run away from a murder. He’d known Azula for about half an hour, but she didn’t exactly seem like a wilting flower, either.

Most of the White Lotus members were clustered together around Pakku’s body, talking in hushed whispers that Sokka couldn’t hear from his side of the room. Only Professor Zei, the newcomer, was running around, trying to fix all of the furniture that the crowd had destroyed in its stampede.

Sokka recognized one of the only non-adults at the event leaning against the wall nearby. He was a teenager, a few years younger than Sokka, and probably the most weirdly innocent-looking person that Sokka had ever met. The strangest thing about him was that he had no hair at all, something that Sokka had never seen on a young person before. The boy was shaking, his eyes wide, his hands clasped together. Sokka didn’t blame him. This was scary shit. Sokka was pretty used to blood and things like that, since he was studying forensics, but if this kid knew Pakku? Yeah, that would shake him up for sure.

Not really knowing what else to do, Sokka got up and made his way over. “Hey, you okay?”

Despite the scary circumstances, the kid gave him a smile. Even Sokka, who was (according to Katara) terrible at reading emotions, could tell that the smile was forced. “Yeah, I’m alright. You?” His voice was higher than Sokka had been expecting.

Sokka nodded. “Yeah. I’m sort of used to this stuff.” The boy’s eyes grew wide. “No, not like in a...murderer sort of way! Like, I study it! I’m a forensics student!”

“Oh!” the boy let out a nervous laugh. “That’s cool!”

Sokka nodded, still feeling the awkwardness in the air. “What’s your name?” he asked, mentally scolding himself. Everyone in town knew the White Lotus, but Sokka had never cared enough to learn many of their names, especially the kids, who never really did anything. Now, though, he wished he had.

The boy didn’t seem to mind, though. “I’m Aang.” He extended his hand.

Aang. That was the name of Katara’s best friend from elementary school. Sokka had never met him.

Sokka took his hand. “I’m Sokka,” he replied. “So...did you...know Pakku?” Not the most tactful way to ask, but it was the only way Sokka could come up with.

Aang nodded. “Everyone in the White Lotus does.”

“Oh.” Sokka didn’t know what else to say. “I’m...sorry.”

His attention was brought away from Aang by a crash at the back of the room. The police had all gathered by the doorway. There had to be at least twenty officers, all of them armed. At least half of them wore scarves around their necks, in a color that Sokka (and everyone else) recognized as Dai Li green.

The man in the front (the Chief of Police, Sokka realized), raised a hand, and the room fell silent. “No one is to leave this room!” His voice carried a lot of weight, like someone who had been giving orders for ages, and knew what he was doing. “You are all suspects for murder!”

As the police were beginning to gather up everyone left in the room, grouping them together and keeping an eye on them, calling on them one by one to be interrogated, Zuko felt a hand grab him by the arm and yank him backwards. A second later, he was inside a closet with the door shut. The small room was dark, lit only by one flickering lightbulb. Every surface was covered in dust, making Zuko cough. As he was about to shout, he was spun around by the same pair of hands that had pulled him in, and came face to face with his uncle.

Iroh put a finger to his lips before Zuko could speak. He moved to the front of the closet and put his ear to the keyhole. After a moment or so of listening, he seemed satisfied. He turned to Zuko and nodded.

“What’s going on?” Zuko hissed. “Why did you pull me into a closet during a police interrogation?”

“Because,” whispered Iroh, “my nephew is an accomplished detective, and a very dear friend of mine has just been murdered. This is a society built on loyalty and tradition, and Pakku deserves justice.”

“What’s wrong with the police?”

Iroh sighed. “As much as I would like to put my trust in the police, I know I cannot. They have become too entangled in the ways of the Dai Li. They have a strong vendetta against the White Lotus. I cannot put my dear friend’s murder in their hands.” He looked up. “But I can put it in yours.”

Zuko’s eyes widened. “Uncle...are you asking me to take this case?” It was easily the most important case he’d ever been given. “How do you know I’ll succeed?”

“Perhaps you will not,” whispered Iroh. “But I know that you will fight for justice and honor, and that you will not give up. That is all I ask of you.”

Zuko nodded grimly. A case like this could be dangerous, but Zuko was no stranger to danger. Despite the fact that he didn’t need it, Iroh had always been quick to offer Zuko aid. If Iroh needed Zuko’s help, he would give it. It was only fair.

Azula sighed, rolling her eyes at the police officer sitting across the table from her. They were in a small chamber off to the side of the giant room where the party had taken place. After the murder, she had managed to squeeze herself into a corner and slip into the shadows in order to avoid the insanity of the crowd. Once the police had arrived, though, she had shown herself. She knew that there was no point in hiding in the shadows during a police interrogation. It would only make them suspect her.

Still, these policemen had an exasperating sense of superiority that was evidently unearned. Although she certainly didn’t want to end up as a suspect, she had no qualms about irritating her interrogators.

“Can you repeat the question?”

“I asked how you were acquainted with the victim.” The officer (he hadn’t bothered to tell her his name)’s voice was tight. She was clearly getting on his nerves.

Azula sighed and put on a bored expression. “We met today. We spoke for approximately three minutes and thirty-three seconds.” She gave him a wide grimace. “Is that specific enough for you?”

“According to the testimonies of other party guests, you seemed quite irritated during his speech. Do you deny this?”

Azula thought quickly. The truth could get her in hot water, but a lie would seem too convenient. If she hesitated too long, she would look suspicious. As a newcomer, she already had a target on her back. She wasn’t about to make it bigger. “If I’m being honest, I found him rather irritating. I thought he seemed stuffy, and that he was promoting outdated ideologies.”

The police officer leaned across the table. “Irritating enough to murder him?” His tone was sharp, but Azula didn’t let it scare her.

“Absolutely not. Mild irritation is not motive enough for murder.”

“My sources say that you come from a family that deals in business. Might that have given you a higher tolerance for violence? A willingness to do whatever it takes?”

Another place where lying was too convenient. “It did. But that doesn’t mean I would ever put effort into planning the murder of someone I met that same day for three minutes. Plus, I was in the middle of the crowd. There were at least three people who were standing with me.”

“You could have hired someone else.”

“Who? I know one person in this city, he’s my brother, he was standing right next to me at the party, and he’s a complete disaster, so even if I *were* planning a murder, I would never ask *him* to do it.”

The police officer sighed, tired at last with her antics, and waved his hand to dismiss her from the small chamber. As she re-entered the party room, she noticed that most of the police, as well as Pakku’s body, were gone.

She caught sight of Sokka standing a few feet away from her, and made her way over to him. “Have they finished interrogating everyone already?”

Sokka nodded. “They’re gonna blame someone in the White Lotus no matter what. It’s only really a question of who.”

Azula nodded, twirling a strand of hair around her finger. “Got any guesses?”

Sokka looked thoughtful for a moment. “Maybe Piandao. He’s powerful, plus he’s a fencing master.”

“Seems almost too convenient.”

Sokka nodded. “What do you think?”

“I’ve only just met the vast majority of the potential suspects.”

“Come on, your brother’s a detective. Didn’t you get any of that piecing-clues-together gene?”

Azula laughed, to her own surprise. “If you ask me, they’re going to accuse that nervous old man that keeps running around.”

“Fung?”

“Yes, him. It’s always easier to prey on the weak ones.”

“But what would his motive be?”

“Who cares? It’s not as though anyone’s going to ask. Besides, the quiet ones could always be hiding *something* . That’s why it’s imperative that we keep an eye on them.”

Sokka began to respond, but Azula caught sight of a motion in a nearby dark corner. Looking closer, she could make out Zuko standing in the shadows. He was beckoning to them both.

Azula tapped Sokka on the shoulder, and they walked over, being sure not to attract the attention of the crowd.

Zuko had on his determined face. “Where’s Katara?”

Azula glanced around the party. “I haven’t seen her. I presume she’s safe, though. The police have overturned the entire room. If there was another body, they would have found it by now.”

It took her a moment to realize that both boys were staring at her. “What? I’m simply stating what all three of us were thinking.”

Zuko sighed. “Listen. Uncle asked me to take the case of Pakku’s murder.”

Sokka gasped. “Zuko, that’s great! That’s the biggest job you’ve ever done.”

Azula could have sworn she saw Zuko’s face flush slightly. “I need your help organizing the crowd, Sokka. I need to do interrogations like the police did, but I need real information. I need you to take every person in this room into the side chamber, one by one, and I need you to do it without attracting too much attention. We don’t know who could still be watching this party.”

Sokka nodded and set off.

Azula sighed. “I assume you want none of my help, but my services are available, should you desire them.”

“What do you want?”

“Let me watch your interrogations.”

Zuko looked away from her. “I don’t need your help, Azula. This is a job that needs to be done alone.”

“You just asked Sokka for help.”

“I need one person to do crowd control. That’s not the same thing as helping.”

“So what, you want me to stay out here? You don’t own me. If I want to watch you ask people questions, I’m perfectly free to do so.”

Zuko sighed. “I don’t see how anything good can come from this.”

Azula smirked. “I can become better acquainted with the members of the White Lotus.”

Zuko groaned as they walked towards the side chamber. “I really think you don’t need an interrogation to do that.”

The chamber that they entered was simple. It was small, with only a table and three chairs; one on either side of the table and one in the corner, which Azula took, despite the fact that she would rather sit at the table as well. It was similar to the chamber where Azula had been interrogated by the police, but while that chamber had been furnished with a metal table and fluorescent lights, this one contained only wooden furniture and older lights. It felt warmer and more welcoming, which Azula thought was good for the interrogations. A welcoming ambiance would make their suspects more willing to open up, because they would feel more secure. Azula didn’t know who had set up the room, but whoever it was, she had to give them credit. They had done an exceptional job.

Zuko took a seat on the other side of the table, and pulled a notebook and pen out of the folds of his coat. His face was the picture of gravity; stony and severe, intimidating and full of animosity. If you asked Azula, he looked like something out of a comic book, but she supposed that such a disposition could prove useful in an interrogation. After all, angry people were known to make others nervous, and everyone tended to reveal more when they were nervous.

Azula wasn’t a detective herself, of course. All she knew about interrogations came from her advanced psychology classes, her father’s lessons on human nature and how to take advantage of that, and, if she was being honest, a rather large obsession with crime novels when she was younger. She would never embrace the “brooding private eye chasing justice” mantle the way Zuko seemed to have done, but she’d be lying if she said she didn’t relish in the mystery, in the intricacy of it all, the way each clue fit together to form a picture that was sometimes horrifying, but always made perfect sense at the same time.

Before Azula could think any more about the wonders of mysteries, there was a knock at the door. Zuko looked up, already wearing an expression so intense that Azula almost burst out laughing right then and there. Sokka poked his head in, then nodded. A moment later, and the eccentric wrestler from the party rolled (yes, literally rolled) through the door. What was his name? Bouey? Boonchuy? Booma?

Zuko clicked his pen and stared the wrestler right in the eyes. The interrogations were beginning.

“Name?” Zuko asked only for the sake of his notebook and, he supposed, his sister, because he already knew the answer.

Bumi smiled his usual wide, weird smile in response. “Name’s Bumi!”

“How old are you?”

“One hundred and twenty-two years old!”

Azula let out a laugh of disbelief from the corner where she sat.

Zuko leaned forward. “Bumi, how did you join the White Lotus?”

The wrestler’s eyes grew misty. “Well now, that was a long time ago. I don’t remember everything, if I’m bein’ honest.”

“Can you try?”

Bumi’s eyes grew misty, and he looked pensive for a moment. “It was right around the time when I was retiring, I think. Yes, that’s what it was. I never wanted to retire, and I didn’t have to. I bet I could take you on today, eh?” There was an awkward pause before Bumi cleared his throat and continued. “Anyway, I had a coach, like everybody does, and he pulled me aside one day and told me that I needed to retire to make room for younger talent. I didn’t want to...wrestling was the most fun thing in the world to me, ya see, but it was only fair. So I retired, and I gave a speech. Talked about how fun wrestling was for me, and how I hoped that kind of fun could last forever. That night, I went to the hotel I was staying in and found a note. That’s how I got into the White Lotus.”

“Can you remember which members let you in?”

Bumi let out a laugh. “Oh, they’re all dead now. I’m the oldest member there is.”

“Does that make you the leader?”

Bumi laughed again. “Oh no! The White Lotus is supposed to be about preserving tradition, so Pakku was always really the leader. He always organized the events, and he was the one who really put up a fight against the Dai Li.”

*Interesting* , thought Zuko. A leader meant a lot more potential enemies. “One more question, Bumi. Since Pakku was the leader, did anyone ever think he was...unfair? That he was stopping you from doing something you really wanted?”

“Well, of course,” replied Bumi. “He was strict, like most leaders are. I’d bet most of us were angry at him at one point or another. But mad enough to kill him? I can’t say.”

“What were you mad at him about?” Azula’s voice came from the corner of the room. Zuko shot her a glare, but she ignored it, looking right at Bumi.

“Well, truth be told, I wanted to go back to wrestling sometimes, but Pakku never let me. He said that the White Lotus needed to be my top priority.”

“Couldn’t you have left?”

“I could have, but that would have meant leaving all my friends.”

“That’s enough,” said Zuko. “Bumi, thank you. You can go.”

The wrestler gave him a grin and (literally) skipped out of the room.

Zuko turned to his sister, who was looking innocently up at the ceiling. “I told you to stay quiet!”

“Technically, you never told me anything.”

“You said you wanted to come in and watch! You lied to me!”

“You knew perfectly well that I was going to do this.”

“So I told you not to come in!”

“You have no right!”

“Yes I do!” The room fell silent. “Azula, you are living in my apartment. You are currently living off the money I make from this job. This job is probably the only reason you aren’t sleeping on the streets, so be quiet and let me do it.”

Was that too far?

Azula looked away, and seconds later, there was another knock at the door. Fung, the nervous-looking old man, entered the room. Zuko gave him a smile.

“Could you please tell me your name?”

“Fung, sir.”

“There’s no need to call me sir.”

“Can you tell me how you joined the White Lotus?”

“Well…” the man looked even more nervous than before, “let’s see...I’m not quite sure I remember. That was a very long time ago, you see, and I’m quite old…”

“How old are you exactly?”

Fung rubbed his chin. “Well, let’s see...I’m not quite sure…”

In the corner, Azula narrowed her eyes.

Zuko sighed. “That’s fine, Fung. Did you ever have any reason to be angry with Pakku? Any grudges you were holding?”

“Why, no!” said Fung, almost too adhemently. “None of us did.”

“That is a lie.” Azula’s voice came from the corner, cold and intimidating, almost exactly like their father’s. Zuko felt a chill run down his spine. With Azula’s strange arrival, he’d almost forgotten the reason he hadn’t wanted her there in the first place. This...the way she acted like their father, followed in his footsteps... *this* was why.

If it had been that simple, it would be easy to tell her to just go away. But there were times when Azula seemed like she couldn’t be more different from their father. Like showing up on his doorstep unannounced and asking for a place to stay.

Fung seemed to tremble in his seat. Azula slowly rose and walked over to them. Standing next to Zuko, she leaned forward and cupped the old man’s face in her hand. She ran the other hand over the table, purposely letting her long nails scrape the wood. When she spoke, her tone was low and menacing, her gaze piercing.

“Now listen to me very carefully, Fung. I am a very determined person. As a child, I was often called perfectionistic. That may have been true, but one trait has stuck with me throughout the years.” Azula dug her nails deeper into the table. “I will stop at *nothing* to get what I want.” Sweat poured down Fung’s face. “I haven’t the slightest idea what you’re talking about!”

Azula leaned closer, now placing her other hand on her hip. “Are you sure about that, Fung? Because, as a child, I was also described as being quite observant.” She gripped his face even tighter. “ *Unusually* observant. And I am quite certain that I observed that glint in your eyes that signifies the omission of certain information.” She brought her other hand to his face. He was still trembling. “It would be a shame if such important information were kept out of a case, and all of the blame fell on your frail shoulders, now, wouldn’t it?”

The room was silent. At last, Fung took a gulp of air. “All right, I’ll confess! I didn’t want to sound suspicious because, well...I was scared. But the truth is, I was furious at Pakku. I don’t do a lot around here; mostly I stamp forms and sign papers, but Pakku seemed to hate me! He was always looming over me, giving me more work to do, acting like he had no respect for me, even like he was disgusted by me! It was the worst part of my day! But I never thought about killing him, I swear! I could never kill anyone!”

Seemingly satisfied, Azula released his face and propped herself up against the table. “ *There’s* the statement I was looking for.”

“That’s enough!” Zuko stood, knocking some papers off the table. “Fung, thank you. You can leave.”

The old man all but sprinted out of the room. Zuko whirled to face his sister. “What the fuck was that, Azula?!”

Azula leapt up and sat on the edge of the table with one leg crossed over the other. “ *That* was getting results. If you want full information on everyone’s relationship with Pakku, you can’t expect them to all be honest with you instantly. He was clearly lying.”

“It doesn’t matter if he was lying!” Zuko was nearly shaking in anger. “I fight for justice, Azula. I won’t use interrogation techniques like that on old men, and I won’t associate myself with people like that!”

A flash appeared in Azula’s eyes that Zuko couldn’t quite understand, but it vanished almost as quickly as it had come. “You don’t know he’s innocent,” was all she said, before turning on her heel and walking out the door. Zuko would have slammed the door, but Azula closed it so slowly, carefully, and neatly, that Zuko barely heard it click shut.

*People like that.* Azula hadn’t needed to ask him what he meant. He meant people like her father. The very same people he had run away from two years ago. Cruel, heartless, even monstrous. The worst part was that Azula couldn’t even completely deny it.

*It was five years ago, and Azula remembered it like it was yesterday. She remembered Zuko sitting* *in on one of Father’s business negotiations for the first time. He was so excited; he had run into* *his room to call his uncle, but he hadn’t answered. Azula hadn’t shared his excitement; she’d been* *to a million of Father’s business meetings, and each was the same. Azula had already learned how* *to copy Father’s cold, unflappable façade. She had no need to learn again.*

*She had listened at the door as Father had gone through his usual routine with his guests. They* *were young and nervous this time; coming from a new startup company that their Father was* *trying to acquire.*

*She heard Father’s voice perfectly clearly, even from outside the door. “Now then, we all know* *what we are really here to discuss today.”*

*“Sir, with all due respect, we wish to remain independent! We have the utmost respect for your* *work, but we do not want to be acquired by your company!” Azula couldn’t see whoever was* *responding, but their voice was trembling.*

*“Is that so?” murmured Father, still somehow loud enough for Azula to hear. “What a pity that* *you’ll never get that far. It was the Caldera Bank that loaned you your startup money, correct?”*

*“...yes.” The response was weak, as though the speaker already knew what was coming to them.*

*“You know, I used to work at Caldera Bank, years ago. I was quite well-liked, too. Were you aware* *of that?”*

*“...No, sir.”*

*“I could tell. But wouldn’t it be a shame if all that startup money were to simply...disappear? Why,* *you wouldn’t only lose your company...I believe you’d lose everything.”*

*There it was. The final move. The reveal. The open threat. Azula knew it all too well. Silence fell in* *the room. Azula could hear nothing more.*

*“I see.” The voice of the newcomer was soft, defeated. “Well then, sir, we will be happy to partner* *with Sozin Enterprises.”*

*“No!” Zuko’s voice was loud, full of emotion, everything that did not belong in the meeting room.* *It came so suddenly that Azula nearly jumped into the air, but her shock was quickly replaced by* *fear. What was he doing?*

*Zuko had never been deserving of Sozin Enterprises. He was a weak idiot who was too soft for his* *own good. Not only that, but he was able to love (and be loved) so easily that it made Azula* *furious. He could not have what was hers. And so, she had always done everything in her power to* *stop him from succeeding.*

*But this...this was going to end badly. Perhaps even worse than she’d wanted. Azula could feel her* *heart racing as she put her ear to the door.*

*“You can’t intimidate and blackmail these innocent people! They’re only trying to achieve their* *dreams! What you're doing is despicable! How can you betray these honest people?”*

*The room was silent again. Azula could feel herself holding her breath. Then, all of a sudden, there* *was a crash and a shriek. Azula had just enough time to leap out of the way before the door flew* *open and Father stormed out, pulling Zuko behind him. Zuko struggled, but Father had an iron* *grip on his wrist. Azula followed them silently down the hall.*

*She wasn’t quite fast enough, but she arrived in the kitchen just in time to see Father pull a clay* *dish out of the oven, grab Zuko, and hold the dish to his face, keeping it there and pressing it* *harder and harder into his skin.*

*Azula was sure the whole neighborhood could hear Zuko’s screams. All she could do was stand in* *the doorway, frozen in shock and fear.*

*As Zuko continued to scream, and the smell of burning flesh finally reached Azula’s nose, making* *her nearly gag, Father’s eyes rose up and met her own. They were full of anger, hatred, but most of* *all, they contained power.*

*Under her father’s gaze, Azula stared back at him and smiled a sick, twisted smile. It was all she* *could do.*

*Zuko caught sight of her expression with his unburned eye. Azula could see betrayal flash across* *his face before their father walked over and slammed the door shut, leaving her to listen to her* *brother’s screams echoing in the dark.*

*Zuko had been thirteen, and Azula eleven. Sometimes when she closed her eyes, she could still hear* *him screaming.*

Lost in her memories, Azula had lost track of what was around her. She was brought out of her thoughts by a shriek, and before she knew it, she was on the floor. More surprisingly, there was someone on top of her.

“Oh my gosh!” said the someone. “I’m so sorry! I normally don’t fall when I cartwheel, but you walked right into my path and I didn’t see you and this is just kinda really scary, so I wasn’t paying too much attention and…”

“It’s all right,” said Azula, getting to her feet. She would normally be furious, but this girl’s voice had an innocent quality to it that made it very difficult to be mad at her.

Once standing up, she could see the girl who knocked into her. She was strange, to put it mildly, and somewhat out of place at this party full of old nobles in suits and ball gowns. This girl wore a dress, but it was shorter, more like a summer dress, and instead of white, blue, or gold like nearly everyone else around her, this dress was bright pink. Almost the same color as a pink highlighter. Instead of a fancy updo, she wore her hair in a long braid, which was draped over her left shoulder. Her eyes were wide and full of light, and she wore bright pink lipstick that was the same color as her dress.

Despite her overall strangeness, the girl was undoubtedly pretty, and there was something alluring about her presence. Azula could feel the wheels in her brain turning, and she was suddenly filled with the desire to know more.

The girl was still looking at her, and Azula tried to think of something to say. It was harder than she’d thought it would be; conversation wasn’t at all like Father’s intimidation. She’d learned that years ago, but that didn’t make it any easier. “Uh...really, I don’t usually forgive things like this, but since it’s today, I…” she stopped. That pretty much couldn’t have gone any worse.

Instead of looking hurt, the girl smiled. “Oh, I’m so glad! I hate it when people are angry! It produces so much negative energy!”

Instead of being annoyed by the nonsense about energies, Azula found herself relieved that the girl was still talking to her at all. She didn’t know why.

“Have you got a name?” Could have been better, but at least it wasn’t a complete disaster.

“I’m Ty Lee,” said the girl, still smiling. “What’s your name?”

“Azula.” Her own name felt strange on her tongue.

“Nice to meet you, Azula!” Ty Lee held out her hand, and Azula took it, wondering if she was gripping too tightly, or too loosely. Whatever she was doing, Ty Lee didn’t seem to mind. “What are you doing at this party?”

Somehow, Azula managed to regain part of her analytical functions. This strange girl was a potential source of information. Zuko may not think that Azula was a good person, but she could be a good information gatherer. She did owe him that, at the very least.

“My brother is a detective. He’s attempting to solve this case.”

Ty Lee’s eyes widened in recognition. “Oh, Detective Zuko! Yeah, his uncle’s a White Lotus member! He talks about him all the time, but I never knew he had a sister!”

That wasn’t surprising. Uncle-oh-high-and-mighty would never stoop so low as to mention her, the little girl who had never been *nice* enough for him. He had never bothered with her as a child. Only Zuko.

“What about you?” asked Azula. “Are you involved with the White Lotus? You don’t exactly seem…”

“Like a High Society girl?” interrupted Ty Lee. “It’s all right. I know I’m not. But I am technically a White Lotus member. My family’s been allied with them for years, and when they helped out the circus I was working at a few years ago, my family sent me to live with them.”

“Where do you live?”

Ty Lee laughed. “Wow, you really are new to town! Most of the White Lotus lives in Pakku’s mansion. Well...I guess it’s not his anymore. Everyone at least has a room there, even if they don’t use it.”

Azula leaned forward. Ty Lee was brimming with energy and kindness, and Azula felt strange interrogating her. “Did you like living at Pakku’s mansion?”

Ty Lee leaned back casually. “I did! It was away from my sisters, and they’re sweet, but there are seven of us and we all look alike, so that’s not always very fun. It was kind of lonely from time to time, but I had Aang and Yue as friends, I guess, and most of the adults were nice, too! Especially your uncle, he was hilarious!”

“Were there any parts you didn’t like?”

“Well, I guess that Pakku could be kind of strict sometimes. He was always yelling at me about not cartwheeling and wearing longer skirts.” Ty Lee locked eyes with Azula. “But I would *never* kill him. I would never kill anyone.”

There was a crash from across the room, and Ty Lee leaped up. “I need to see if my friends are okay!” She turned back to Azula. “But it was nice to meet you, Azula! I have a feeling we’ll see each other again!”

Azula watched her run across the room, almost transfixed by the way she moved, bouncing and swinging. The girl was interesting, to be sure. She may have had a bubbly exterior, but despite Azula’s efforts, she had known that Azula was trying to get information the entire time.

Zuko was surprised to see Katara enter the chamber alongside his next suspect. As the girl sat in the chair, Zuko pulled Katara aside. “What are you doing? You know I need to ask these people some questions!”

“You’re perfectly capable of asking questions!” whispered Katara, her tone of voice making it clear that nothing would make her leave the small room. “This girl was practically Pakku’s daughter! She needs support right now! I’m not going to let you grill her like she means nothing while she’s still in this state!”

Zuko sighed. When Katara decided she wanted to help someone, there was absolutely no changing her mind. After all, *he* hadn’t been able to get rid of her for two years.

Zuko took a seat across from the girl, while Katara stood at the back of the room, gazing intensely at him. The message was clear: *if you fuck this up, you are 100% dead.*

The girl did seem shaken. Her eyes were red, her hands still trembling, and her white hair and wide blue eyes made her look so delicate that she was almost like a doll. Almost *too* delicate.

“Can you please tell me your name?”

“Yue.” The girl’s voice was soft, to match her exterior.

“How old are you, Yue?”

“I’m eighteen,” said Yue. “Almost nineteen.”

“Thank you.” Being gentle was challenging, but it was better than an angry Katara. “Yue...could you please tell me about your relationship with Pakku?”

Tears began to fall from Yue’s eyes, and she wiped them away with her hands. “Pakku...he was like a father to me. I have a real father...he’s a member of the White Lotus, too, but he works a lot, so it was always Pakku that I spent time with. He taught me how to do math, how to write essays...he taught me how to do everything. He’s the reason I’ve ended up the way I am today, he…” Yue’s voice broke and she couldn’t speak anymore.

Katara raced forward and put her hand on Yue’s shoulder. “Yue, that was beautiful. Don’t worry. You don’t have to answer any more questions today, I promise.”

“Actually…” Zuko started, but he was cut off by Katara’s glare.

As Katara and Yue walked out the door, Azula walked in. The two siblings stared at each other for a moment, then came to a silent agreement not to talk about their fight earlier. Azula plopped back into the same chair she’d been sitting in earlier, as though she’d never left.

“What have you found?”

Zuko sighed as he flipped through his notebook. “Nothing. That’s the problem. Every single member of the White Lotus has a potential motive.”

“Care to elaborate?”

Zuko groaned. “Bumi wanted to go back to wrestling but Pakku wouldn’t let him, Fung was terrified of Pakku, Jeong Jeong wanted to forbid weapons but Pakku always gave them out behind his back, Piandao didn’t like Pakku because he kept raising the rent on his fencing studio, Arnook didn’t like him because Pakku kept trying to take his place as leader of the cultural society, Professor Zei’s place in the White Lotus depended on keeping Pakku happy, and Yon Rha was even older than Pakku, and didn’t like that he was taking charge.”

“And the children?”

“Even they have motivations! Aang, the bald one, wanted to go out more, but Pakku was always grounding him, and Hahn, the rich boy in the blue velvet, was thirsting after Pakku’s power.”

Azula nodded. “There’s also Yue. Pakku clearly had a huge impact on her, but she seems so shy. It’s possible he weakened her.”

“There’s a fourth one, too, isn’t there?”

Azula’s face flushed for a split second, but the blush disappeared so fast that Zuko wasn’t sure whether or not it had been there at all. “Pakku always scolded her for being herself.”

“That’s definitely a motive.”

“They all have a potential motive. It doesn’t make them guilty.”

Zuko raised an eyebrow. “I never thought you’d be the one to defend people’s innocence.”

Azula shrugged. “I’m only saying that it’s dangerous to jump to conclusions.”

Back in the ballroom, Katara caught sight of Sokka and waved him over. He wrapped his arms quickly around her, then caught sight of Yue. “Who might this be?” His voice was playful, too playful for the scenario.

“I’m Yue,” said Yue. “Are you Katara’s brother? You two look alike.”

Katara scanned Sokka up and down. She didn’t see what Yue meant. “Yes, Sokka’s my brother. Sokka, Yue lives with the White Lotus.”

“Oh,” said Sokka, looking a little unsure of himself. “Does that mean you knew…”

“Yes.”

“Oh,” said Sokka again. “I’m sorry.”

“That’s okay.”

Sighing, Katara spotted Aang, her friend from elementary school, across the room. “Sokka, have you ever met Aang?”

“No, but you did talk about him when you were six. I met him today.”

“Great, why don’t you go talk to him?”

“I…” started Sokka, but Katara was already walking away with Yue.

Yue laughed. “Did you really want him gone that badly?”

Katara groaned. “No. I just…” she dropped her voice and placed her hands on Yue’s shoulders. “I wanted to let you know how brave you were in there. It must be really hard to talk about it.”

Yue smiled at her. “Thank you, Katara. You’ve been so kind to me tonight. I wish there was something I could do to repay you.”

“No.” Katara’s voice came out firmer than she had intended. “Yue, you’re a good person who’s grieving. Helping you is the right thing to do. I don’t need to be repaid. I won’t accept it.”

Yue stared at her. “You seem like a truly amazing person, Katara. I don’t know what I would have done tonight without you.”

Katara blushed. “Thank you. I...don’t always feel that way. Amazing, that is.”

There was a sudden crash before either girl could continue. Turning around, they found the room suddenly filled with police officers once again. This time, however, there were far more. There were so many that Katara couldn’t see anyone besides herself and Yue. They had all vanished behind a wall of green uniforms.

Suddenly, three officers leaped out of the crowd and grabbed Yue by the arms. Yue shrieked and nearly fell backwards, but a fourth officer grabbed her and pinned her down on one of the tables. The other three held her still, pulling her arms behind her back.

“Stop!” At last Katara managed to find her voice. “What are you doing to her?!”

There were more crashes from around the room. In the officers’ arms, Yue struggled, her eyes full of fear.

“Don’t move any more, young lady,” bellowed the officer, holding her still. “You’re under arrest for murder, in cold blood!”
