## Chapter 5: The House of Dreams

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko and Sokka retrace their steps and make a discovery, Katara does what she does best, and Azula finds herself in slightly uncharted territory, in the middle of an an enormous mansion.

#### Chapter Notes

Here again with my daily(ish) update! I hope everyone likes this one! There's lots of semi-flirting (or, my attempt at writing semi-flirting), so hopefully that's fun!  
(TWs at the end for this chapter.)  
Enjoy!

### Text

Sokka sighed as his sister slumped against his shoulder. After Yue had been accused, most of the party guests had retreated, including Azula and Zuko, who had gone home to “review their evidence” (Sokka was pretty sure that all they were going to do was sleep.) Most of the White Lotus had gone to sleep as well, leaving Sokka and a distressed Katara who refused to go home. Instead, they had gone to the police station and waited all night in the lobby. Sokka had drifted in and out of sleep the entire time, but Katara had stayed awake, eyes wide and staring at the front desk, for the past eight hours. Now, at last overcome by her exhaustion, she was sound asleep on Sokka’s shoulder. He was glad for it; the second she woke up again, she’d be back to staring at the desk.

Katara had always been like this. Whenever she saw someone who she thought needed her help, she would give absolutely everything she had in order to help them. It was one of the reasons that she was beloved by many, and it was the reason she was studying journalism. She’d wanted to tell the stories of people who couldn’t tell their own.

Of course, the downside was that everyone who cared about her was swept up in her escapades, for better or for worse. Loving Katara meant staying up all night in uncomfortable lobbies, it meant long days filled with reading articles, and it meant being bossed around constantly. But it was always worth it. If you loved Katara, she would love you back with every cell in her body, and whenever you needed her, she would be there in a heartbeat.

Sokka had never been like that. Sure, he liked helping people. He certainly didn’t want to hurt them. But Katara’s *purpose* had always been helping others. Sokka didn’t know what his purpose was. He liked solving mysteries with Zuko, he supposed. He liked figuring things out and making plans and piecing things together. He liked how easy it was to bounce ideas off of Zuko. Despite Zuko’s constant affirmations that he didn’t need anyone’s help, Sokka could tell that he genuinely appreciated his input. And that made him feel...well, appreciated.

The police finally opened the door. Instantly, Katara shot up and went over to the desk. From across the room, Sokka could hear her asking endless questions. Sokka could hear the receptionist struggling to keep up with his sister.

After a few minutes of conversation, a police officer came out and said something to Katara. She nodded, then followed the young woman through the door.

Sokka leaned back in his chair and let his eyes droop shut.

There was nothing Azula loved more than a bulletin board. Zuko had woken up before her and pinned photos of all the suspects to the bulletin board of his office. He had taken notecards and written down their names, ages, occupations, and potential motives. Beneath the photos was a map of Ba Sing Se with its three rings. She wasn’t an expert on geography, but she could identify the Middle Ring, where they lived. Azula snapped a picture of the board with her phone, then went into the kitchen. Zuko was there next to the coffee pot, and he gestured for her to take a mug, which she gladly did. After last night, she would need the extra caffeine.

They plopped down at the table with coffee, tea and toast. Zuko bent over his notebook, looking at it intensely.

“What’s your plan for today?”

Zuko sighed, clearly annoyed that she’d spoken. He didn’t seem to be in the mood for conversation. “I’m going to investigate the scene of the crime.”

“Alone? You should never investigate a crime scene alone. The killer could be looking for new victims.”

Zuko glared at her, rolling his eyes. “If you’re trying to weasel your way into my case, that won’t work. If it’s so important to you that I go with someone, I’ll call Sokka.”

And with that, he walked into the other room. Azula could hear his voice on the phone, but couldn’t make out his words. She sighed, slumping over the table. This mystery *meant* something to Azula; it made her heart race, and fire run in her blood. The idea of clues and pieces of information sliding together, of following a trail, made Azula feel like herself. It made her feel clever, but clever in a way that was all her own. It was the first time Azula could remember feeling that way.

Zuko wanted nothing to do with her. But that didn’t mean she couldn’t help. After all, she’d always had a talent for puzzles as a child.

Zuko came out of his office. “I’m going to investigate the scene of the crime. Sokka is coming to meet me there as soon as he can, so you don’t have to worry about anything. Just...stay here. This stuff is dangerous.”

Azula rolled her eyes, but said nothing as he closed the door behind him.

She slumped over the table again. What was she supposed to do if she couldn’t leave the apartment at all?

As if summoned by her thoughts, the phone rang. Azula practically leapt out of her chair to answer it.

“Hello?”

“Azula? I was hoping to talk to you!”

Azula blinked in surprise. “Ty Lee? How did you get this number?”

“Your uncle gave it to me!”

“Why are you calling?” Azula genuinely didn’t know. No one had ever called Azula before, not really. Plus, she barely knew this girl.

There was a sigh from the other end of the phone. “I want to help you.”

“What? Why?”

“Because the White Lotus is my family. I may not be super close to them, but they’re the reason I was able to be myself and join the circus. If they’re in trouble, I want to try.”

“That’s awfully noble of you.” Azula couldn’t stop the suspicion from creeping into her brain. It was almost *too* perfect.

“Well, what’s in it for you?” Ty Lee’s voice was full of genuine curiosity, not suspicion. Azula couldn’t help but smile. Ty Lee was brimming with...well, positive energy, and seemed to have her head in the clouds, but it was quickly becoming apparent to Azula that she was anything but stupid. She was smarter than she looked, and would make a useful ally.

It didn’t hurt that Azula also couldn’t help feeling happier when she was around her, even after so little time. It was this weird nervous, fluttery, blissful feeling. She couldn’t quite figure out what the feeling was, or why it was there.

Azula realized that Ty Lee was still waiting for her answer, and didn’t know what to say. Explaining the excitement that mysteries and puzzles brought her was too complicated to explain to Ty Lee, especially over the phone. So she simply said, “I’m looking for an adventure,” and left it at that.

“Great!” said Ty Lee. “I think I can help with that!”

“In what way?”

“Well, I do live at the White Lotus mansion. I don’t think any of us would ever kill Pakku, but it wouldn’t hurt to look around, right? Maybe you’ll find something useful.”

Azula felt a smile spreading across her face. This was exactly the sort of opportunity she’d been looking for. “I think I’ll find that very useful.”

“Awesome! I’ll see you soon!”

“Wait!” Azula almost had to shout to make sure Ty Lee didn’t hang up the phone. “...where *is* the White Lotus mansion?”

Katara took a seat in the interrogation room across from Yue, whose hands were trapped inside metal cuffs that were bolted to the table. She still had on her blue gown from last night, though it had been squished and wrinkled. Her braided hair had fallen into a tangled mess, and the dark circles under her eyes indicated that she hadn’t slept at all.

Still, Katara thought she looked beautiful all the same.

The second Yue caught sight of her, a look of relief crossed her face, and tears began to spill down her cheeks. She could have been crying from sadness, fear, exhaustion, relief, anything, really. Katara didn’t know.

She reached across the table and took Yue’s hands in her own. She didn’t know exactly what had happened to the girl during the night, but she figured that the touch of someone who wasn’t trying to arrest her would provide some sort of comfort. Hopefully.

Yue gave her a weak smile, and Katara smiled back. Seeing a bruise on Yue’s shoulder, however, her expression turned grim. “What did they do to you?”

Yue sighed. “I’m okay. They were just being a bit...rough is all.” Katara could tell she was lying. Her shaking hands, at least, showed that she was terrified.

“If they did anything to really hurt you, I will do ten times worse to each and every one of them.”

Yue blinked, clearly surprised by the ferocity in Katara’s voice. “Katara, what are you doing here? You barely know me.”

Katara squeezed Yue’s trembling hands even more tightly. “Yue, I can tell that you’re innocent. I can tell that you’re a good person, even though I just met you, and I am not going to let a good person go through this alone. You don’t deserve that. Whatever happens, you can count on me. I promise.”

Yue said nothing in response, only gave Katara a smile that said everything that she needed to know. In her hands, Katara could feel Yue stop trembling. Katara smiled back at her.

“Thank you,” was all Yue said, and it was enough for Katara. “Now please, you look exhausted. Go home and get some sleep.”

“But…”

“Katara,” Yue leaned forward. “Do it for me.”

Katara sighed, and let go of Yue’s hands. “Okay,” she said, giving in at last and getting up to leave. “But I know you’re innocent, Yue. And I’ll do everything in my power to help you prove it.”

The entire museum was surrounded by police tape, and the front steps were crawling with officers. Zuko stood behind a parked car halfway down the street, wondering how he was going to find a way in. Sneaking around had never been his best skill, but if he could get close enough to pick the lock, he’d manage.

Zuko had known how to pick locks since before he could read. Azula had, too. In their father’s house, knowing how to pick locks was a necessary skill, like knowing how to walk, or how to eat.

There was a tap on his shoulder, and Zuko nearly jumped. A hand flew over his mouth to keep him from yelping, and he whirled around, ready to fight, but it was only Sokka.

“You almost scared the life out of me!”

Sokka shrugged. “You’re a detective! I guess I thought you’d be more...observant!”

Zuko rolled his eyes. “Wow, thanks.”

Sokka grinned. “Anytime, Great Detective.”

“I thought I told you not to call me that!”

“Sure thing, Great Detective.”

Zuko sighed. “Let’s just focus. Be quiet so I can think of a way to get in there.”

He turned and started scaring again. Hearing a creak behind him, he turned and saw Sokka looking through a telescope.

“Why do you have a telescope?!”

“You’re a detective. Why *don’t* you have a telescope?”

Zuko groaned. Sometimes this happened with him and Sokka. Neither of them could think of the right things to say, so they just fell into a pattern of needling one another. It was a pain, especially since they could get along so easily sometimes.

“Give me your telescope.”

Sokka handed it over, and Zuko stared through the lens. He could now get a closer look at the lock on the door (which looked easy to pick), but the police officers were watching it like hawks. Unless they got a ladder to climb onto the surrounding rooftops and could somehow leap up and across ten feet to the upper window, all without being seen, Zuko was out of ideas.

Unless…

Zuko turned and glanced at Sokka, who was absentmindedly tossing the boomerang he (for some odd reason that Zuko found strangely endearing) always carried around from one hand to the other. Sokka was smart, but also a little bit crazy. He’d never done anything like this before, but it could work…

But asking Sokka for help meant two things. It meant admitting that Zuko needed help, which meant admitting how easily he could be taken out. It meant showing weakness, and it meant getting Sokka involved with the case and potentially putting him in danger, which was the absolute last thing Zuko wanted.

He glanced at Sokka, who was grinning a little too widely at him. Sokka was one of his first real friends, even though Zuko rarely admitted it. He always stood by Zuko’s side, even when he probably didn’t deserve it, and always *tried* to cheer him up, even though it usually didn’t work.

He could trust him, just this once.

Zuko handed the telescope back to Sokka, and placed his hand on his shoulder. “Here’s what I need you to do. If I can get close enough to that door, I can pick the lock, no problem. But you’re...crazy.”

“Wow, thanks.”

“That’s not what I meant! Look, I need you to create some sort of distraction so we can get to that door and I can pick the lock. Can you do that?”

Sokka grinned and pulled out his boomerang. “You bet your potatoes I can!”

“That’s not a real expression.”

Sokka’s face flushed. “I tried!”

Azula tried to ignore her anxiety as she rang the doorbell at the White Lotus mansion. Ringing the doorbell of a house she was trying to investigate in secret seemed strange, but Ty Lee was the one who knew the house, and she had said to ring the doorbell. It was strange, depending on someone else to lead her. Azula had never been allowed to do that growing up. It had been acceptable to depend on exactly two people: herself and occasionally, when it served him, her father.

The door flew open and Ty Lee was standing there. Again, she was wearing pink, this time a pair of overalls painted with butterflies. On anyone else, they would have looked stupid, but the style suited Ty Lee perfectly.

“Azula!” Ty Lee instantly wrapped her in a hug, causing Azula to leap backwards in shock. “Oh my stars, I’m sorry! Are you not a touching kind of person? I really like hugging people, but if that makes you uncomfortable, I can stop!”

The idea of someone being willing to stop doing something because it made her uncomfortable was almost more shocking to Azula than Ty Lee’s hug itself. “It’s all right.” What was it about this girl that made her willing to forgive anything and everything?

Ty Lee smiled. “Oh, good!” With that, she arched backwards and used her hands to spring into the house. “Come on in! Pretty much everyone’s out today!”

“Who else is here?” asked Azula, as she made her way through the door, looking around to see if anyone was observing them.

“Hmm,” started Ty Lee, now standing on her hands, “I think Fung’s here. Yon Rha, too. Your uncle’s out, so is Piandao. Aang and Hahn are here, and so are Piandao and Professor Zei. I think that’s it!”

That didn’t sound like pretty much everyone to Azula, but she said nothing. Instead, she took the opportunity to observe the room around her. The mansion overall was the same size as the house she grew up in, but instead of a dark maze of endless small chambers, this mansion was laid out more like a hotel. There was an enormous central chamber, where they were currently standing, which was surrounded by balconies, each leading to several doors, which Azula assumed led to various bedrooms, lounges, offices, and things like that.

Ty Lee flipped over her head and landed in front of her on the floor. She was a talented acrobat, to be sure. “It’s neat, isn’t it?”

Azula nodded. Even she, who had grown up in a house just as big, could appreciate this place. Ty Lee grinned and leaped to her feet. “So, where do you want to go first? Pretty much everyone who’s here is working, so we can go anywhere we want if we don’t interrupt them.”

Azula realized that she had no idea. She may have liked puzzles, but she’d never actually investigated anything in her life. It was her only real flaw, she reasoned, and one that she could fix with practice and time. She could manage inexperience, because inexperience could be fixed.

Even so, she couldn’t show her flaw, even to Ty Lee, who she trusted. She had no idea who could be watching, waiting to pray on whatever weakness she dared show. “Take me to the room the White Lotus members use the most!”

Ty Lee smiled. “Great idea! Follow me!”

Azula walked up one of the four spiralling staircases, looking for anything that could be a clue as she went up. The staircase was wide for a spiral, and its walls were large enough to hold a myriad of artworks. They must have cost a fortune, seeing as they seemed to be the originals.

The two girls came to a stop at the fourth balcony, and Ty Lee led her down the hallway, to an enormous oak door, accented with intricate carvings of (what else?) lotus flowers.

Ty Lee tapped softly on the door, then leaped back when someone popped their head out. A teenage boy, not much older than Azula and Ty Lee emerged. He had narrow blue eyes, a tall, skinny body, and an incredibly grumpy expression on his face. “Why are you bothering me, Ty Lee?”

Ty Lee sighed. “I didn’t mean to bother you, Hahn, I was just checking to see if anybody was in there!”

Hahn laughed. “Right. Hey, why don’t you just leave this room, and me, alone?”

Ty Lee blinked, looking genuinely hurt. “Hahn, I didn’t mean to offend…”

“No she didn’t.” Azula’s voice surprised even herself, coming out smoothly and calmly, devoid of any emotion other than dangerous anger. “She has just as much right to this room as you do. If I’m not mistaken, you’ve been here all day, so it’s really time to cede it to someone who would actually do something purposeful with it, don’t you think?” She ran her hand over the railing, allowing her long nails to leave marks in the wood. “Now then, I’d be running along if I were you. I’d prefer not to see you again.”

Hahn gave her one last look and walked down the hall, glaring at both of them as she went. Azula smiled coldly.

Ty Lee grinned and pumped her fist in the air. “That was awesome! I had no idea you could do that!”

Azula smiled at Ty Lee, a real smile this time. “I do have my talents.” She turned the knob, and the door opened. The girls entered a room that was clearly meant to be some sort of lounge, although it was more the size of a movie theater. It was full of chairs made of fur and leather that Azula recognized from her childhood. The coffee tables were made of dark wood, and one was even made of petrified wood. It must have cost a fortune. At the other end of the room was an enormous fireplace. Azula hadn’t even seen a fireplace in years. Her father was more the “modern technology and electric fires” type, since his company *did* deal in technology.

Ty Lee plopped into the nearest chair, one made of white fur. “So! This is our sitting room, or that’s what Pakku called it. I don’t come here too much, since the older White Lotus members are usually here, but this is where everyone spends the most time.”

Azula glanced around the room, looking for anything suspicious. It seemed like an ordinary, if incredibly fancy, sitting room, but if Azula had learned anything from her detective stories, it was that very few things were what they seemed.

She heard Ty Lee giggle, and glanced up. “What?”

“You’re just staring at that table really intensely.”

Azula caught her reflection in a mirror on the wall, and saw that her face had turned bright red. She tried not to show it, though, and quickly put on a cocky expression. “What, are you jealous of the table?”

Crap, that had been *way* too far. Curse social interaction and all its difficulties!

Ty Lee stared at her for a moment, shocked, then burst out laughing. “You’re something, Azula! That’s for sure.”

Was *nothing* she did enough to offend this girl? Azula was terrible at this and she knew it, but Ty Lee didn’t seem to care at all. How could that be?

Ty Lee leaped over her head and ducked under the table. “Hmmm, seems like there’s nothing to really be jealous of...oh!”

“What?” Azula crouched down to look under the table, where the entire underside of the petrified wood had opened at the brush of Ty Lee’s fingers, nearly hitting her on the head. Out fell a small golden key. Azula reached out and studied it closely. Ty Lee wiggled out from under the table and stared at the key alongside her.

“You don’t happen to know what this is for, do you?”

Ty Lee stared back at her, a blank expression on her face. “I have no idea.”

Zuko couldn’t have asked for a better outcome. The police had been attentive, of course, but they clearly hadn’t been expecting anyone to show up in broad daylight. In other words, they had underestimated Zuko and Sokka’s craziness. In this case, that worked in their favor.

Sokka threw his boomerang into an alleyway, causing the trash cans in the alleyway to clatter to the ground, making an enormous clatter that sounded almost like gunshots. Zuko smirked. Sokka may have been inexperienced, but he could also be absolutely brilliant. Sometimes Zuko could forget that, but it was one of the things he liked most about his friend.

Startled, all but one of the officers ran into the alleyway. Sokka, whose boomerang had returned to his hand (that thing was good, wasn’t it?), threw the weapon once again into an alleyway on the opposite side of the street, causing an identical clatter. The remaining officer by the door looked conflicted for a moment, then gave in and ran into the alleyway, leaving the door unguarded. Zuko grabbed Sokka’s hand, ignored the fact that his face grew hot the second he did so, and ran towards the door. Once there, it was only a matter of using his pocket knife on the lock. Child’s play.

Inside, the party room looked...well, like a murder scene. The tablecloths were askew, covered in footprints from the crowd trying to race out the door. Broken glass littered the floor, and worst of all, Zuko could still make out blood stains on the stage where Pakku had been standing. Creepy, to be sure.

He made his way to the stage, looking around for anything out of place in the disarray. It was hard to find clues in a chaotic room like this.

“What should I do?” asked Sokka, who was still standing in the doorway. Zuko glanced at him. He could be helpful, but Zuko didn’t want to become the kind of detective who relied on other people. It would only make him weaker.

Zuko checked his watch. “We probably have about five minutes before they come back. I need you to keep track of time and make sure they’re not coming. Got it?”

Sokka sighed. This was a superficial job, and he knew it. “Got it.”

Zuko knelt down on the stage and glanced at the stains. Why nobody had cleaned them up, he didn’t know. There were no marks in the wood, however. Whoever had thrown the knife had had perfect aim. They had only needed to throw it once.

Zuko glanced up. He thought he remembered the knife coming from the left side of the room, but he couldn’t be sure. The killer was long gone by now, so there was really no way to tell.

There was a rustle as Sokka got up on the stage next to him. Zuko groaned. “I thought I asked you to keep track of time!”

Sokka shrugged. “Look, I know you asked me to do that, but I think I can help!”

“I don’t want your help!” Zuko’s voice came out harsher than he’d anticipated, and he wanted to kick himself as soon as he said it. “Sorry, that’s not how I meant to say…”

“It’s okay!” interrupted Sokka, too quickly to be genuine, which made Zuko feel even worse. This was why he worked alone. So that *this* didn’t happen. That and other reasons.

Sokka was angling his boomerang now, right above the red stains. Eyeing it closely, he threw it in a straight line. Unlike usual, it didn’t curve much. It instead landed on a small ledge in the upper left corner of the room, right above the doorway.

Zuko grabbed his pocket knife and raced over, using his momentum to swing himself up onto the ledge. Sokka stared at him from the ground. “That was sick!” he cried, then instantly stared at the ground. Probably wondering if he’d been too nice. That was definitely Zuko’s fault.

Zuko smiled, trying his best to make things less awkward. “You’re not the worst yourself. That boomerang...it was clever.”

Sokka shrugged. “I have my ways.”

Zuko tried to hide his reddening face (again! why?!) as he turned to stare at the corner where the boomerang had landed. It was evident that no one had cleaned this ledge in years, as the entire thing was covered in a thick coating of dust, so thick that it almost made Zuko cough. But looking more closely at the dust in the corner…

Footprints.

As he moved to pick up the boomerang, Zuko noticed something else. In the walls, just above the footprints, were two deep gashes, fresh in the wood and unnatural. The kind of gashes that could only be formed by knives.

There had definitely been a killer here.

Azula and Ty Lee had been trying the golden key on every door in the mansion for the last half hour. The house was so huge that Azula expected another half an hour at least, but the sound of a car engine outside signalled more people arriving home.

Ty Lee glanced out the window. “That looks like Arnook, Bumi, and Jeong Jeong. We might want to put that back if we don’t want to get caught.”

Azula sighed. She would have loved to check all the rooms. But getting caught on the first day wasn’t going to do her any favors. “All right.”

The girls made their way back up the stairs and to the sitting room. They had closed the table again when they left, and luckily, there was no one waiting for them. If anyone had noticed that the key was missing, they didn’t want a direct confrontation right now.

Ty Lee had just finished putting the key back when there was a loud banging coming from the balcony above them, followed by a scream and a crash. They glanced at each other, then raced to the edge of the balcony. All around the mansion, doors flew open as people rushed to the railing to see what had happened.

Lying in the very center of the lobby, his neck bent at an odd angle and lying in a pool of his own blood, was Fung. The nervous man’s constantly darting eyes had gone still, and he was staring up at the ceiling with a blank expression.

Azula felt a chill run down her spine. This killer, whoever they were, wasn’t playing around. They were out for blood, and they weren’t going to stop.

The three new arrivals raced through the doorway at the sight of their fallen camarade. Arnook, who was nearest to the body, knelt down and grabbed something, holding it up to the light.

Azula squinted. “What is he holding?”

Ty Lee leaned over the railing and hung from it by her feet. Instinctively, Azula reached over and grabbed her ankles, but Ty Lee needed no help swinging back up to stand next to her. “Looks like a scrap of fabric.” She pulled out her phone. “Here. You can use this to get a closer look.”

Azula held up the phone and zoomed all the way in. Arnook was indeed holding a scrap of fabric. Not only that, but even as a newcomer to Ba Sing Se, Azula could recognize the color.

“Dai Li green.”

### End Notes

## Chapter 6: The Lernean Hydra

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

The group finally investigates the obvious suspects, but their personal differences come to light as they muddle their way through their interrogations.

#### Chapter Notes

Sorry this chapter was a day late! I don't think there are any TWs (if I missed any, let me know!)  
We’ll be meeting some familiar faces this chapter! I hope you all enjoy:)

### Text

Zuko stared at the scrap of fabric that Azula had managed to steal from the Dai Li mansion. Other than the blood staining the edges, it was undoubtedly Dai Li green.

He turned to face Azula and Sokka, both of whom were sitting on his small sofa. Sokka was wiggling his fingers anxiously, clearly on edge from the second murder. Honestly, who could blame him? Azula, meanwhile, seemed incredibly calm. Almost too calm, given the circumstances. Had she been anyone else, Zuko would have felt terrible knowing that he’d shown them two murders in their first two days in Ba Sing Se.

Zuko did feel somewhat responsible for her. After all, she was his little sister, and she was living in his apartment. But she was Azula. This was the girl who had watched hours of crime shows as a teenager, not even flinching at the blood. This was the girl who had smiled as their father held a hot pan to his left eye. Nothing seemed to faze her. Sometimes it made her seem creepy, but in this case, it actually made her less suspicious. Azula’s calm regarding the murders wasn’t surprising because she’d *always* been this way.

Zuko wouldn’t put it past his sister to double-cross him in some way, but he didn’t think she was behind these murders. She didn’t even know any of the victims. The only possible reason was if Father had sent her, but Zuko didn’t think he would have been so obvious.

For these murders, he thought he could trust her. For now, anyway.

“What’s our next move?” asked Sokka from the sofa. He was starting to calm down a little, Zuko could tell.  
Zuko stared at the scrap of fabric. “If we assume the two murders are connected, this is definitely enough evidence to investigate the Dai Li. But there’s two catches.”

“Which are?”

Zuko sighed. “They’re not going to just let us in. The Dai Li *is* the police force, they’re not going to let anybody other than them investigate the case, especially since we’ve been hired by a member of the White Lotus.”

Sokka rested his chin on his hand, thinking. “What if we disguised ourselves? That might work.”

Zuko thought for a moment. “It might. But that only solves half the problem.”

“The problem is more simple than that,” said Azula from the other side of the sofa. “If we simply act like we deserve to be investigating, they’ll believe it.”

Sokka raised an eyebrow. “That’s gonna take a *lot* of fake confidence. Think they’ll buy it?”

A chill went down Zuko’s spine as Azula’s lips curled into an all-too-familiar smirk. “Why do you think *I’m* here?” She turned to Zuko, her expression all business yet again. “What’s the othe catch?” Her eyes were as piercing as ever, the way they always were when she was solving a puzzle. Zuko sighed. It was going to be even harder to get her off his back now.

Zuko stared at the scrap of fabric again. “This fabric...it seems so obvious. Like they’re *trying* to get us to suspect the Dai Li.”

Sokka sighed. “Even if they are, they’re already enemies with the White Lotus. It’s worth investigating them just for that.”

Azula twirled a strand of her hair. “A limited number of suspects is better, but if we eliminate this entire group of people, we risk eliminating some important information.”

Zuko sighed. “This whole thing feels strange to me.”

“Me too,” said Azula. “But we either act on our new information, or we don’t.”

Sokka stared at the door knocker of one of the largest mansions in town, his stomach still in knots. Zuko and Azula had seemed all too eager to jump into the interrogations and investigate part of this case. That was to be expected, since Zuko was a detective, and Azula...well, Sokka didn’t know her, but she seemed not to be fazed by much. Sokka, on the other hand, was still wrapping his head around the whole *two people are dead* thing.

It wasn’t that he didn’t like the idea of solving a case. He was a literal forensics student and he loved the idea of himself as some sort of investigator. It had intrigued him, ever since he was a kid.

Still, standing here, dressed as government agents and relying on Azula’s acting skills to get them interrogations with one of the most powerful groups of people in the city...everything felt a lot more *real* . It wasn’t a game anymore, and that idea made Sokka nervous.

He wished Katara were here. He had a feeling that she would understand what he was feeling. Not that Azula and Zuko wouldn’t, but he didn’t want either of them (especially Zuko, if he was being really honest), thinking that he was scared, or not up to the task. It had taken such a long time for Zuko to accept any of Sokka’s help at all. He refused to ruin it now.

Azula knocked loudly on the door. Already, Sokka could see that she knew what was doing. Somehow, even the way she knocked radiated confidence and authority. Azula was rather small in stature, so hopefully her confidence would make up for that.

The door opened to reveal Poppy, a rich Dai Li member that Sokka had only crossed paths with a few times. She had seemed sweet, but he didn’t really know her at all.

Azula stared the woman right in the eyes, looking calm. “Good morning, Miss. My colleagues and I are agents of the National Defense Service. We have some questions about recent events in this town.”

Poppy looked around nervously, clearly not knowing what to do. “Um...of course! What do you need?”

Zuko stepped forward. “We need to gather everyone involved with this organization and ask a few questions.”

“Why is that?”

Azula placed her hand on her hip and glared at Poppy. “Are you really so bold as to question our motivations? Do you question the National Defense Service? I don’t remember the last person who did that, do you?”

Sokka and Zuko shook their heads. Personally, Sokka was wondering how on Earth Azula expected this to work. They were pretending to be members of a government organization that didn’t exist, and relying on their acting skills alone. He thought it was a long shot.

Still, Poppy seemed to be falling for it. “Of course not! Come in! I can get the three of you a room right away!”

Azula smiled politely and followed her into the mansion.

The first thing that Azula noticed was that this mansion, though as big as the White Lotus mansion, couldn’t be more different. While the White Lotus mansion was one big open space, with lots of large windows and natural sunlight, the Dai Li headquarters (which Zuko had said belonged to a man named Long Feng) bore a closer resemblance to the house Azula had grown up in. The mansion was all dark, winding corridors, like an endless maze of shadows, hidden corners and locked doors. Azula could have sworn she was right back home, except for the color scheme. Back home, when they had decorated, they had mostly decorated in red. Here, everything was colored in the Dai Li’s signature green. Various police medals and official-looking certificates garnished the walls, which were lit with old-looking lanterns. Azula hoped that this wasn’t a trap, because she wasn’t sure she could find the way back out if she had to. They had taken so many turns that even she (and she had a near-perfect memory) had lost track.

Poppy took them into a room that looked a lot like a police interrogation room. It had probably been modeled after one, Azula reasoned. It was made almost entirely of cement, with fluorescent lights and a metal table. It was odd that the Dai Li possessed a room like this. They did, after all, control the police. If they needed interrogations, why not use the official rooms at the police station?

For the moment, however, that wasn’t Azula’s concern, so she filed the question away in her head for later.

The three of them sat down facing the door, and Poppy gave them a warm smile. “It won’t take me long to gather up everyone who’s here. You should be able to have a short discussion with each of them.”

Azula smiled at her. “That sounds absolutely perfect.”

Once the door closed behind him, Sokka turned to her. “Are you sure this is gonna work? It seems like a long shot. Like a *really* long shot.”

Azula sighed. “One can never be sure, of course. But if you have confidence that your plans will work, so long as you don’t get cocky, they do.”

“You’re doing this all wrong!” snapped Zuko suddenly. “You’re being incredibly reckless. You barely have a plan at all! I can’t believe you’d be this stupid!”

Originally, Azula had had five different plans, and this was the one she’d decided on, but that probably wasn’t what Zuko wanted to hear. Plus, she had different strategies depending on the events that occurred, strategies she hadn’t yet shared. She hadn’t wanted them to panic. “Zuko, if you didn’t want to do this, you could have said something sooner. You’re the detective, after all. It’s your case.”

“You would never have listened to me!”

“Maybe this time, I would have! You wouldn’t know because you always assume I don’t care about anything!”

“Guys!” interjected Sokka. “Not that I don’t love this sibling drama you have going on, but there’s a guy standing at the door watching us!”

The two siblings turned towards the door, where a man with a thin moustache was watching them. Zuko nodded, and he entered the room. Azula didn’t recognize him, but Zuko clearly did.

“Long Feng,” said Zuko, trying to imitate Azula’s confident tone from earlier. “Leader of the Dai Li. Thank you for coming to answer our questions.”

“It’s my pleasure,” said Long Feng, in a slippery sort of voice that made the hairs on Zuko’s arm stand up. “Now...what did you say your job was again?”

“We work for the National Defense Service,” replied Azula, her eyes rising to meet Long Feng’s. He stared at her with a ferocity that Zuko had rarely seen on anyone before, and Azula stared right back, matching the ferocity perfectly. Just like she always had growing up.

“I see,” said Long Feng, leaning forward. “The National Defense Service doesn’t exist, and you’re not from any government. I knew who you were the second I saw that scar you’re trying to hide, *Detective Zuko.* ”

Sokka looked like he was about to jump out of his seat. Zuko tried to keep calm, and looked confused. Next to him, Azula started sobbing. Long Feng blinked in surprise.

“I’m so sorry!” she cried. “This is all my fault! We...we only wanted to find the truth, you see! That’s all Zuko’s ever wanted since we were kids! Our father lied to him so much, and he’s been on this quest to find the truth ever since! I wanted to help him so badly, and I thought this would work! I swear I didn’t want to deceive you! I just never thought you’d trust us if you knew who we were!”

The room was silent for a moment. Everyone was staring at Azula in shock. She continued to sob.

Then Long Feng laughed. “I knew there was a spark in you!” His laugh was cold and sinister, just like the rest of him. “The Dai Li is an organization of order and justice. We will happily welcome young truth-seekers. I think we are going to do great things together.”

And with that he left the room, still laughing as he went.

Zuko glanced at Azula, who still had her head down on the table. “Did you mean what you said?”

Slowly, she raised her head. The tears were completely gone. “We’ve got him exactly where we want him.”

Sokka’s face grew into a smile. “You mean you planned that?”

“Not exactly,” said Azula. “But I did have an idea.”

“You should have told us!” cried Zuko, still angry at her constant secret-keeping. This was his job, and here she was, acting like she was suddenly in charge. It made his skin crawl.

Azula rolled her eyes. “It doesn’t matter. He trusts us now.”

Zuko laughed. “You forget you’re still new to this, Azula. Long Feng doesn’t like us. He wants to use us to infiltrate the White Lotus.”

Sokka shrugged. “Who’s to say we can’t use that to our advantage? We can still get the information we need.”

Azula smirked. “My thoughts exactly.”

Zuko slumped back in his chair. The two of them getting along made him even more furious with Azula than he had been beforehand.

There was another knock at the door, and a couple entered. Zuko recognized them as Ukano and Michi. Zuko had heard of them; Ukano was a city council member who had joined the Dai Li to better implement his policies, and Michi was his wife and political advisor.

Zuko smiled at them. “Welcome, Ukano and Michi. Thank you for being here.”

Ukano remained stony, but Michi gave him a polite smile. “Thank you, Detective.”

Zuko opened his notebook. “Can you tell me about your relationship with the White Lotus, please?”

Ukano huffed. “We don’t speak of those people here. Their ideology is going to corrupt this city! We need more order in Ba Sing Se, not more freedom.”

Michi nodded. “I can respect them, of course, but their ideology is simply shocking.”

To his right, Zuko saw Azula roll her eyes. The woman was clearly just parroting her husband. Still, he smiled. “Thank you. One last question. Where were you this morning, when Fung of the White Lotus was murdered in his own home?”

Ukano huffed, but his wife gave him a gentle nudge. Zuko needed to keep an eye on her. Michi seemed like a standard obedient spouse (like something from an old sexist detective story) at first glance, but Zuko couldn’t forget that she was also her husband’s political advisor. She was smarter than she looked.

“We were in our room here!” said Michi. “We were having a lovely morning of games with our children. You can ask our daughter Mai. I’m sure she’ll remind you all how utterly boring it was.” Her voice grew tight at the end, showing her irritation with her daughter. Zuko smirked.

“Thank you both,” he said, writing their statements down in his notebook. “You can both go. Have a lovely afternoon with your son.”

The two of them left, and Sokka turned to Zuko with a corny smile. “Well, aren’t *you* a gentleman?” His voice came out in a strange tone that left Zuko completely confused. His face grew even darker, then he muttered something about his shoe lace and knelt down. Azula giggled next to him, then turned to face Zuko. “Keep an eye on the wife. She’s the real brains there.”

Zuko rolled his eyes. She could be such a know-it-all. “I already figured that out.”

“Well then, good for you.” She still seemed indignant with him. Fine. Maybe she would leave.

Sokka made a show of chattering his teeth. “Is it just me, or is it really cold in here?” Zuko stared at him, confused. “Cold, like you guys, you guys are being cold...oh, forget it.”

There was another knock, and another couple entered the room. One of the members was Poppy, who had let them in, the other was her husband, Lao. Both were rich nobles who had surprised the whole town when they had joined the Dai Li instead of the White Lotus. Other than that, Zuko didn’t know much about them.

“Thank you both for coming,” Zuko said as they sat down. “I’m going to get right to the questions, if that’s alright with you.” They both nodded, and he continued. “Can you tell us about your relationship to the White Lotus?”

Lao nodded. “When we arrived here, everyone expected us to join them. We do, as you probably know, come from the type of family that would normally join them. But we did not.”

“And can you tell me why that is?”

Poppy chimed in. “We supported the ideology of the Dai Li more so than that of the White Lotus. A safe, orderly city; that’s the kind of world we want our daughter to grow up in.”

“Do you have anything *against* the White Lotus?”

Lao nodded. “We think their ideas are dangerous and preposterous. They all seem like absolute lunatics to me.”

Zuko nodded. “I see. Could you tell me what you were doing this morning, when Fung of the White Lotus was murdered?”

Poppy nodded. “We were supervising our daughter’s lessons.”

“Your daughter is…”

“Our daughter is a fifteen-year-old blind girl. She doesn’t go out much, but we wanted her to be able to defend herself, so she has martial arts lessons once a week. Today, we were supervising.”

Zuko thanked them, and they left. Azula sighed. “Does it always take this long to find important information? I’m the epitome of patience, obviously, but…”

Zuko rolled his eyes at her. “Yes, Azula, sometimes it takes a long time to get information. Not everything just falls into your lap like it did while we were growing up.”

Azula’s mouth dropped open. “Is that what you really think?”

Before they could go any further, there was another knock, and a man entered. Zuko recognized him, too. Chief Song, the Ba Sing Se chief of police. Overall a pretty standard police chief, other than the fact that he would do whatever the Dai Li told him to. It made for quite a few unfair arrests in the streets of the city.

He took a seat, and Zuko plastered on a smile for the third time. “Thank you for coming, Chief Song.”

“My pleasure.” The man seemed anxious, checking his watch while beads of sweat slid down his forehead. Zuko frowned. “Chief Song, is there a problem?”

The chief nodded. “My sincerest apologies, it’s just that...well, with these new cases, there’s a lot of paperwork to be done at the police station. The whole place is sort of in chaos, and I really do need to be there to control the crowds and whatnot.”

“I completely understand,” said Zuko. It wasn’t even a lie; he did understand. “We’ll keep it to one question, then. What were you doing this morning when Fung of the White Lotus was murdered?”

Chief Song sighed. “I was interrogating Yue all morning. We’re quite convinced that she is guilty of Pakku’s murder. I assume you know that already.”

Zuko nodded. “We do. All right, thank you, Chief Song. I won’t keep you any longer.”

The chief practically ran out of the room. “How many more interrogations do we have?” asked Sokka.

Zuko shrugged. “Not too many, I don’t think.”

Almost instantly, there was another knock, and a girl with short auburn hair and blue eyes entered the room. She was gorgeous, and also looked like she could beat Zuko up right then and there. She sat down across the table and gave them a smile. She was the only person he’d met that day who he hadn’t already heard of at some point.

“Can you please tell me your name?”

“I’m Suki,” said the girl. “Can you tell me yours?”

Azula laughed. Zuko smiled. “I’m Zuko, and this is Sokka and Azula.”

“Nice to meet you. Obviously the circumstances could be better.”

Sokka nodded in agreement, clearly slightly in awe of the girl. Zuko narrowed his eyes, annoyed. Why did he have to act like an idiot? They were in the middle of an interrogation!

“Suki, are you a member of the Dai Li?”

Suki shook her head. “Technically not. I’m not old enough to be a member. But my ancestor, Kyoshi, founded the Dai Li, and my parents both died when I was young, so the Dai Li practically raised me.”

“So you’re more like a protegé?”

“Exactly.”

“Are you happy about that?”

Suki grinned. “Absolutely! Kyoshi was one of the bravest, strongest women in history. I’m proud to be following in her footsteps, and I always will be.”

“What’s your relationship to the White Lotus?”

Suki narrowed her eyes. “The Dai Li’s trying to do real good in this city. Anyone who doesn’t support that, or tries to stop them, is automatically a problem in my book.”

“So you see them as the enemy?”

“That’s what they are!”

“Would you ever be open to forgiving them?”  
“If they show that they’re worthy of forgiveness, yes.”

Zuko nodded. “And where were you this morning when Fung of the White Lotus was murdered?”

Suki sighed. “I know it’s not a great alibi for you, because I was alone, but I was training in one of the gyms here in the mansion, like I do most days. Sorry I can’t give you better information.”

Zuko sighed, also disappointed, but didn’t show it. “That’s all right, Suki. Thank you for your time.”

Suki gave him a polite nod and left. Azula cocked her head at the empty doorway. “They’ve certainly done a good job of creating their perfect child protegé.”

Zuko thought that was especially ironic coming from her.

Poppy poked her head through the door to interrupt their conversation. “That’s everyone who’s around.”

Relieved (and slightly exhausted), Zuko stood up to leave. Poppy smiled at them. “Just follow the red lanterns, and they’ll take you right to the exit.”

The group was winding down a maze of hallways, all tired after the day’s events, when two pairs of hands reached out and yanked them around the corner. Sokka started to scream, but a hand clapped over his mouth. The hands released them almost as soon as they had grabbed their arms.

“Shut your mouth, Clue Guy, we’re trying to help you!”

Zuko took in the two people standing before them. Both of them were teenage girls. The older one looked to be between his and Azula’s age, and had her hair in pigtail buns with long strands hanging down in the front. She wore an expression of boredom. The younger girl looked only slightly younger, and significantly shorter, but wore her hair back in a simple headband. Her eyes shone bright white in the reflection of the lanterns: she was blind.

The memories clicked in Zuko’s mind, and he realized that these must be Ukano and Michi and Lao and Poppy’s daughters.

Zuko narrowed his eyes. “What do you want?”

The older girl (Mai, Michi had called her) rolled her eyes. “Toph just said, we’re trying to help you.”

Azula placed her hands on her hips. “How can *you* help *us* ?”

Toph stuck out her tongue. “Because we live with the Dai Li, duh!”

Sokka cocked his head. “Do you know something?”

Mai nodded. “We know a few things that might help you.”

“Just a minute,” piped up Azula. “Why should we trust you?”

Mai smiled dryly. “Because we hate the Dai Li.”

“Yeah!” chimed in Toph. “Do you know how many *rules* they make?! My parents use them to watch me twenty-four hours a day! It’s because of them that I can never *do* anything!”

Mai nodded. “They somehow make this city even more boring than it was before. I almost don’t believe it.”

“All right,” said Zuko, glancing around to make sure no one was watching them. “What can you tell us?”

Toph smirked. “The Dai Li have a secret factory outside of town. They don’t want anyone to know about it. We’ve never been, and we don’t know what it makes, but we can tell you where it is!”

Mai smirked and handed Zuko a piece of paper with coordinates on it. “You’re welcome, losers.”

The two girls disappeared into the darkness, still laughing. Zuko stared at the coordinates in his hand, then looked up at Sokka and Azula.

“Zuko, are you really…” Sokka looked nervous. Zuko nodded. If there was a clue to find, he was going to find it.

“I am.” He ignored his exhaustion and slight fear. He could deal with that later. “I’m going to that factory tonight.”

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

## Chapter 7: The Mystery of the Blue Jar

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko embarks on a dangerous nighttime expedition, Azula does everything in her power to prove her worth, and Katara makes good on her promise to Yue.

#### Chapter Notes

Today is a double chapter day (because I was late with the last one.) This one is one of my absolute favorites that I've written so far (definitely my favorite out of the first ten chapters), so I hope you all like it!

TWs: Falling, toxic substances, allusions to child abuse.

### Text

Zuko sat at his desk, tapping his fingers in anticipation, just like he used to do when he was a kid. He couldn’t remember the last time he’d stayed up late to go out on a case. Most of his recent cases had involved easy work that occasionally stretched into the night. This was different. Staying up until the city had gone dark for the sole purpose of sneaking around felt more dangerous, as though the stakes had been raised. They probably had.

He checked the clock. It was eleven at night. He wasn’t sure, but the factory guards would probably begin to disperse around midnight. He planned to leave in half an hour, and see where it went from there. It would have been better to have a blueprint, or a map of the factory, or something like that, but Mai and Toph had only given him coordinates. It made him wonder if this was a prank, or worse.

His phone dinged, informing him that he needed to leave in ten minutes. He left it on the table and shut it off, to be sure that no one could track him. According to his calculations (even though he’d never been the absolute best at math), the coordinates converged just outside of Ba Sing Se. Ba Sing Se was one of the few cities with an efficient train system, so he could get very close with only that. After that, it was only a fifteen-minute walk.

A gust of cold air blew through the window, making Zuko shiver. He threw on his coat and left the office. Azula would laugh at him for the long coat, but it was the best thing he had for working on cold nights. It was only October, but the temperatures in Ba Sing Se tended to drop at night.

As he walked into the living room, he caught sight of Azula on the sofa, typing something on her phone. She took one look at him in his coat and burst out laughing. Zuko sighed.

“What are you still doing up?”

Azula rolled her eyes at him. “It’s eleven twenty-five, Zuko. I’m seventeen. I don’t go to bed until one in the morning.”  
“That’s a lie. You wake up with the sun.”

“Why can’t I do both?”

Zuko groaned. “Is this your way of telling me that you don’t get nearly enough sleep?”

“How much sleep do *you* get?”

Zuko had no answer to that. Azula leaped up from the sofa, placing her phone down on the coffee table. “Anyway, where are we going?”

Zuko wanted to punch something, but in fairness, he probably should have seen this coming. “ *We* are not going anywhere. *I* am going to investigate the factory. *You* are staying here.”

Azula sighed and stood up straight. “Zuko, what’s the point of having allies if you don’t use them? Besides, you shouldn’t go to a mysterious factory at night alone.”

“You’re *not* my ally, Azula.” Zuko tried to make his voice as firm as he could. “You’re our father’s daughter and my responsibility. If you get hurt while you’re staying here, Father will kill me. And I mean that in the literal sense. I’m not risking that just so you can have a little fun.”

Azula moved her arms and blocked the doorway. “Zuko, I can help. I’m good at observation and puzzles and things like that. You know that.”

She was right, of course, but it didn’t matter. Zuko grabbed her by the arm and pushed her back as he finally managed to walk through the doorway, slamming the door behind them, and locking it shut. “I don’t need your help.”

Sokka and Katara had been working all night, and for the second night in a row, they were about to fall asleep sitting in the waiting room at the police station. Katara had been compiling evidence all day, talking to various White Lotus members, getting testimonies to Yue’s character (over the phone), and she thought she had enough evidence. At least three White Lotus members had seen Yue during the party, meaning that she couldn’t have been up on the ledge that Sokka and Zuko had discovered.

Still, Sokka had been helping her to compile the evidence into a comprehensible, organized list. The neater and more official it looked, the more convinced the police would be. Yue was barely older than Katara, and Katara refused to let her go to prison for a murder she clearly hadn’t committed.

Just as Sokka was starting to doze off next to her, a police officer opened the door to the same metal room she’d been in that morning. Yue was there again, and even though it was less than twenty-four hours later, she looked different. Instead of shocked and tearful, she looked numb, as though she’d already resigned herself to her fate. The sight of it made Katara’s heart break.

Well, even if Yue had given up, Katara refused to. She sat down across the table from Yue and pulled out the binder that she and Sokka had been working on. Not even bothering to say hello, she started talking. “I think Sokka and I have found enough evidence to maybe get you out of here, at least for now.”

Yue blinked. “That was so fast. How did you do that?”

Katara smiled. “I promised you that I’d help you, Yue. I don’t make promises like that lightly.” A glimmer passed through Yue’s eyes, and it was enough to make Katara keep going. “I managed to call up every White Lotus member on the phone, and I’ve gotten six solid testimonies to your character. Plus, Aang, Piandao, Professor Zei, and maybe Ty Lee all say that they saw you during the murder. Sokka and Zuko figured out where the murderer was standing, so if you have people who saw you, you couldn’t have been standing there and in the middle of the party at the same time.” She glanced at Yue, who looked taken aback. “Are you okay?”

Yue nodded. “Given the circumstances, yes, but...this is just so overwhelming. There’s so much information. Do you think it’ll work?”

Katara sighed. “I don’t know. I’m a journalism student, not a police officer. But I’m going to do everything I can.”

Yue smiled and reached out, taking Katara’s hands just as Katara had that morning. “Thank you, Katara. I’ve been all alone here, and you’ve just made this so much more bearable.The world is lucky to have someone like you in it. And so am I.”

Katara felt a blush spread across her face. “You too, Yue. You’re a really good person. I wouldn’t have helped you if I didn’t know that.”

Yue’s face flushed and she smiled, but her smile quickly turned into a concerned frown. “Katara, when’s the last time you slept?”

Katara tried to look awake, but the yawn that she let out betrayed her. She sighed. “I slept for a few hours this morning.” She hadn’t looked in the mirror all day, but she could imagine the dark circles that had undoubtedly appeared under her eyes.

Yue’s eyes widened in worry. “Katara, I appreciate your help more than you’ll ever know. But I couldn’t forgive myself if you were hurting yourself to help me. You may be incredible, but you’re still human, Katara. Please, go sleep.”

“But I still…”

“Katara.” Yue’s gaze was full of care and softness, an expression that made it incredibly hard to say no. “Do it for me.”

After a ride on the empty train through the Lower Ring, and then just outside the city’s wall, Zuko found himself staring at what was undoubtedly the Dai Li’s factory. It was located in a neighborhood of warehouses and empty truck lots. In short, it looked completely unassuming among the other enormous, square buildings that surrounded it. But it was located at the very edge of the neighborhood, right before the dense forest that surrounded the northern edge of Ba Sing Se. The factory was clearly well-guarded, surrounded by a metal wall so high that Zuko couldn’t even see over it. He could, however, see the barbed wire that covered it, and the gate in the center that seemed to need a fingerprint to open. From where he was standing, he could see no visible way in.

“Completely impenetrable,” said a voice from beside him, nearly making him jump. “A very well-designed factory, I’d say. Father would be proud.”

It took a second, but Zuko recognized the voice. He turned to his sister. “What are you doing here? How did you get out of the apartment?”

“As if I’d tell you that,” said Azula. “Then I couldn’t get out the next time you locked me in.”

“You shouldn’t be here, Azula. This is dangerous.”

“Oh, please, I know that. But you shouldn’t be here alone. It’s never wise to do something like this alone.”

“I can’t imagine you care enough about me to actually be worried about whether or not I’m safe.”

Something flashed across Azula’s face. Was it guilt? Anger? Zuko had no idea. “Anyway, you’re lucky we’re still outside. Turn around now, and go home.”

“No.” Azula planted her feet firmly on the ground. “I know I can help you with this. Whatever reason you have for not letting me doesn’t change the fact that two people are dead, and whatever’s behind that wall could hold the key to keeping the entire rest of the city safe. Including our Uncle. So please, Zuko. Put whatever grudge you have against me aside, and let me come.”

Zuko wanted to respond, but had no words, so he nodded reluctantly. “Fine. But you have to do everything I tell you.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “I suppose that sounds like a fair deal.”

Maybe this could get her to leave him alone. “That doesn’t solve the problem of actually getting us in.” The two siblings turned and stared at the wall.

Azula eyed the forest on the other side of the factory. “Would it be possible to climb a tree and jump the fence?”

Zuko followed her gaze. “Probably, but it’s not very likely to work. There has to be another way.” He caught sight of a man walking down the road, pushing a cart full of crates. Around his neck hung a scarf. It was Dai Li green.

For the first time that night, Zuko felt a smile spread across his face. He glanced at Azula, who was also staring at the cart. She clearly understood the idea. He turned to her. “Listen closely. That guard isn’t expecting anything to happen. If we move quickly, we can stay in the dark and leap onto the front of that cart.”

“I see several problems with this plan.”

Zuko rolled his eyes. Of course she had to criticize him. “We’ll work those out later. Stick close behind me and only move *exactly* when I move. Understood?”

Azula rolled her eyes right back. “Yes. I speak English.”

Zuko decided to ignore that last comment and turned his attention back to the cart, which was almost right in front of them. A few feet ahead of them was a patch of shadow, dark enough to move through without being seen if they were quick enough. Trying to stick to the shadows, he ran to the side of it. He couldn’t hear Azula’s footsteps, but she was close enough to him that he could feel her breathing.

The whistling guard rolled the cart into the shadow. The second the front of it breached the darkness, Zuko dropped to his knees and began to run as quickly as he could while staying low to the ground. It felt like an eternity, but he soon leaped onto the front of the cart and curled himself into a ball, hiding in the shadow of the crates. A quick glance assured that Azula was next to him. The two strands of her hair that hadn’t been coiled into her perfect topknot were flapping in the wind. She was staring at the gate with a determined expression on her face. Zuko recognized it from their childhood. When Azula decided she was going to achieve something, there was absolutely no stopping her.

The cart screeched to a halt, and Zuko felt Azula grab his arm to keep herself from falling off. The guard stepped forward, and Zuko held his breath, praying that he wouldn’t look sideways. If he did, there was a chance that it was too dark for him to notice the two siblings. Zuko really, really hoped that was true.

The guard pressed his finger to the gate, and as it opened, he walked back behind it, causing both siblings to sigh in relief. The guard paused for a second, and Zuko hoped they hadn’t been too loud, but after a moment of consideration, he walked back behind the cart and pushed it into the factory.

Inside the yard, Zuko had a clearer view of the factory itself. It was a massive building with a rectangular base and a triangular roof. It was long and flat instead of tall, but its size was apparent. Around the building were several brick walls jutting out of the main outer wall, forming a sort of maze in the cement factory yard. There was one giant door at the front of the building, and above the door was a window. There was a spotlight shining from the window, sweeping the yard.

Zuko realized a second too late that the spotlight was about to fall onto their cart. Frantically, he leaped up, instinctively grabbing Azula’s hand, and began to race to the left, only hoping that the guard didn’t catch sight of them. They ran until they were safely hidden from the spotlight behind one of the brick walls. Zuko stopped, panting. Azula, too, leaned against the brick wall, exhausted from the sudden sprint.

“Make sure no one’s behind us,” hissed Zuko as he leaned out carefully, trying to see where the spotlight was shining. The courtyard was empty now, and the spotlight was on the right side of the factory, leaving the side where they were standing sheathed in darkness. Zuko beckoned to Azula, and the two of them sprinted again, this time towards the open front door.

Before they could enter, Azula grabbed him by the wrist to stop him. Angry, his heart racing with adrenaline from the danger, Zuko whirled around to face her. “What?!”

She looked around, almost as though she were second-guessing herself. But she was Azula, and he had never in his life seen her second-guess herself. “We shouldn’t go in the front door.”

Zuko wanted to slap her. How could she do this? They were losing time already! “Why not?”

She sighed. “It just...it seems too easy. Like a trap.”

Zuko rolled his eyes. “Azula, this isn’t one of your mystery novels. You might think that my life is just a puzzle for you to play so you can win yet another prize, but this is a real case. You can’t think about it like it’s a story. So stop acting like you’re playing another game with me and do what I say, like you agreed to do.”

Azula said nothing more. She just nodded, and the two of them slipped through the side of the front door.

The room they entered was nothing more than a long hallway, clearly just used to get from room to room. Dim, fluorescent lights lined the ceiling but for some reason, none of them were lit. The siblings crept down the hallway in almost complete darkness, passing cement door after cement door. At last they stumbled upon one that was ajar. Zuko gave Azula a silent nod, and they slipped through the open door.

The room they found was so long that they couldn’t see either end from the doorway. The floor was made of cement, the walls were made of brick, and the ceiling looked like it was made of metal. It was dark, with almost no lights that they could see. The only lights were attached to the enormous vats that lined the entire room. The vats were metal, with open tops and ladders going up the sides. Small glass slits allowed people to look through and see what was bubbling inside.

Zuko approached the nearest vat. It was filled with a bubbling substance that was a bright blue he’d never seen before. It was probably toxic, and looked like something that the Dai Li was definitely not allowed to be making.

From a closer viewpoint, Zuko could see a small metal door in the side of the vat. Feeling emboldened by the fact that they weren’t dead yet, he pulled it open. He heard machines clanking somewhere in the vat, and a small test tube fell out of the slot and into his hand.

Before he could stop her, Azula reached over and grabbed the tube out of his hand. From her pocket she pulled various paper strips (Zuko recognized one of them as a pH strip), and began sticking them into the liquid.

“Incredible!” her eyes grew wide. “This chemical doesn’t match any mixture recorded in human history! The Dai Li is creating entirely new substances!”

Seeing Zuko’s confused expression, she shrugged. “I excelled in chemistry class, Zuko. You...uh...weren’t there.”

That didn’t help. Zuko felt his expression sink into an even deeper frown. Azula sighed. “What?”

“How can you say that this is incredible? The Dai Li is probably using this to *hurt* people!”

“I only meant scientifically!”

“Please. You’re probably happy about what they’re doing.”

A look of hurt crossed Azula’s face. “You have no evidence to back up that claim.”

“Yes I do.” Zuko’s voice came out as more of a growl. He could feel his hands shaking with pent-up anger. “You’ve always been this way! You don’t care about other people: you see life as one giant game that you have to win! And now you’re putting yourself in danger because of it, and when you get hurt, I’m going to take the fall for you! Just let me finish this on my own. It’ll be better for everyone.”

Azula was silent again. Zuko couldn’t remember her ever being this quiet when they were kids. Maybe the fact that he finally had *some* power over her had something to do with it. Azula had always had enormous respect for anyone with power.

He began climbing the ladder to get a closer look at the blue liquid from above.

“Wait!” Azula’s whisper cut through the darkness like a knife. Zuko sighed, turning around halfway up the ladder.

“What the fuck do you have to say to me now? Do you not understand how much you’re messing up my life already?”

Azula threw her arms up in the air. “New substances can be incredibly unstable! That blue thing could bubble up at any moment, and you could get seriously hurt!”

A memory of Azula stopping Zuko from leaving home when he was sixteen because “he could get hurt” surfaced. She’d been tricking him then, and she was probably tricking him now. “I’m done listening to you, Azula.”

“I’m serious!”

Zuko rolled his eyes. “I grew up with our Father, Azula. I knew what *getting hurt* was long before you did. Believe me, I can handle myself.”

He finished climbing the ladder, not knowing or caring if she was still standing there. Tomorrow, she could leave, and the last vestige of the childhood Zuko wanted to forget would be gone. Maybe then, he could finally have peace.

At the top of the ladder, he leaned over the blue liquid. From the top, it somehow managed to look even more sinister, like something an evil sorceress would brew to poison children. Maybe that’s what it was. The smell of it made Zuko feel dizzy. If he’d been leaning out any further, he would have worried about falling in.

All of a sudden, the liquid began to bubble faster. In his daze, Zuko didn’t realize it until a second too late. In a flash, the liquid was rising up in a geyser, shooting right at him.

A second before the blue potion enveloped him, arms wrapped around his waist and yanked him backwards. Thrown off balance by the weight of another person, Zuko fell backwards onto the factory floor, landing with an enormous crash.

Sitting up, Zuko found Azula lying on the cement floor next to him. She looked more worn out than he felt, which made sense, considering that he’d fallen on top of her. He stared at her, speechless for the first time that night. Had she really pulled him off the ladder? Azula had surprised him many times, but never like this.

She groaned, using her arms to push herself up.

“I grew up with our father, too, Zuko. I can protect myself.”

Before either of them could say anything else, alarm bells were ringing, and lights were turning on. Still shaken from the fall, the siblings got to their feet and began to run. Zuko barely noticed where he was going, or how he got there. He just kept running, ignoring the shouts, the clanging, everything. Ignoring the threats.

He didn’t need to look at Azula to see if she was there. For the first time since she had arrived, he felt the same sort of silent understanding that had been sprinkled throughout their childhood. Getting along with Azula, talking to her, had never been easy. In fact, it had been downright awful most of the time. But only they had known what it was like to live in their strange world. There had been a lot of running and hiding, and a lot of needing to communicate without moving, without saying a word.

Zuko was partially amazed that they hadn’t forgotten how.

After running for what felt like an eternity, the siblings were finally at the train. Both bruised and exhausted, they took their seats, staring off into space. Neither had the energy to say anything more to the other. They simply spent the ride in silence. For once, the air between them felt calm.

When they finally got back to Zuko’s apartment, Zuko locked the door behind them, feeling Azula’s eyes on him. It made him remember the nights they had spent together as children, always locking their door so that they could pretend they were safe.

Turning around, he saw that Azula had fallen asleep on his sofa. She was breathing evenly. For the first time in a while, her face wasn’t an unreadable mask, and she didn’t look menacing. She looked...human. Smiling, he turned off the light and went into his office. He would sleep soon, but not yet. For the moment, he had too many questions.

What did Azula want with him? Was she really just an extension of their Father, as he’d believed for so long, or was she something else?

More importantly, what was the Dai Li really trying to do with their hidden factory and their never-seen-before chemicals?

Why were they trying to hide it?
