## Chapter 8: The Dressmaker's Doll

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula and Zuko attempt to find an obvious solution, and find themselves at odds with their own emotions, and with each other.

#### Chapter Notes

So sorry for the delay in posting this one (again!) I keep forgetting to post, but I'm trying to work on that!  
TWs for this chapter: Manipulation, mentions of murder.

That's all! I hope you enjoy this one!

### Text

Azula woke up the next morning to find sun streaming through the windows of Zuko’s apartment. She sat up, groaning. Had she fallen asleep on the sofa? Zuko was lucky enough to have a second bedroom that she’d been using, and since she wasn’t there, that was the only explanation. How humiliating.

Still tired from the events of the night before, Azula forced herself to get up off the sofa and make her way to her room, where she threw on the first set of clothes she found, something she never did. Luckily for her, everything she owned was impeccably designed and tailored, so it wasn’t as though there were any wrong choices. She glanced at herself in the mirror. Despite the sunshine, there was already a chill that had drifted into the apartment, so her red sweater with the big collar seemed to suit the conditions just fine. She twisted her hair into her topknot (it was really a habit at this point), and made her way to the kitchen. Seeing that Zuko wasn’t there, she turned the coffee pot on herself. She was soon sipping from a steaming mug, and she felt herself slowly growing less sleepy.

After half an hour or so (and more cups of coffee than she could count), Azula started wondering where Zuko was. The door was still locked, so he couldn’t have gone anywhere, and there was no sign of a struggle, so it was unlikely that anyone had taken him by force.

Smirking, she walked into his office, a room she hadn’t been allowed to enter until now, because it was “Zuko’s private work and she could go read a mystery novel if she wanted to solve a puzzle.” Sure enough, Zuko had fallen asleep at his desk, slumped over a stack of papers. His hat, which he’d been wearing the night before (how in the world had it not fallen off then?) was now on the floor. He was sleeping so deeply that he didn’t even stir when she entered the office.

Ordinarily, she would have used this opportunity to play a prank on him, or woken him up and teased him for sleeping so late. She’d done so many times growing up, but for some reason, something stopped her. She wasn’t sure what it was.

She left him to sleep, and went to read a novel on the sofa. Ironically, it wasn’t a murder mystery, but a romance novel that Ty Lee had shoved into her hand when she left the White Lotus mansion. Ty Lee had sworn that it would “make all of her troubles go away.”

Azula had never picked up a romance novel in her entire life. Her father had always called them “distracting fluff that rotted your brain when you could have been intellectually improving yourself.” She still thought he was right, but it was the only book Azula had at the moment, and it wasn’t as though he was around to punish her.

There was something about the ability to read whatever she pleased without fear that made Azula feel powerful, as though she could fly to the moon and back. It wasn’t the sort of power given to by her father’s praise. That felt like the sort of dangerous power that you had to be careful with if you wanted to survive. This kind of power felt more like...freedom.

Azula didn’t know how long she read for, but it felt as though no time had passed at all. She fell quickly into the world of the story: the two women, starting as strangers, but forming an instant, inexplicable connection, then traversing continents to find one another. The story invoked a sort of emotion in her that she’d never experienced before.

She was just getting to the part where one of the character’s ex-boyfriend made an appearance (a predictable plot device that still managed somehow not to annoy Azula), when Zuko came rushing out of his office, still looking like a complete disaster.

“Why didn’t you wake me?!” His question was angry, but his words lacked the venom they had carried the night before.

Azula sighed. “Forgive me for attempting to let you sleep. I believe you said I didn’t care about other people, so you can blame it on that.” Was it perhaps a bit petty? Yes, but if she was being honest, she was a little angry at Zuko for the night before. He absolutely had good reasons not to trust her, but she had simply been trying to help. He hadn’t had to be so brutal with her.

On the other hand, she supposed she didn’t really have the right to criticize.

“We have a meeting with the Mayor!” cried Zuko, frantically rubbing his hands on his head, and Azula realized that he was looking for his hat.

“What?!” replied Azula, as she ran to get Zuko’s hat from the office floor. “Why do we need to see the Mayor?”

“So we can present our evidence!”

Azula sighed. Her brother could be so naïve sometimes. “Zuko, if you had ever read a mystery novel in your life, you would know that ninety-nine times out of a hundred, the government cannot help you. They’re either useless or being manipulated by someone else.”

“But Mayor Kuei is a good person! I’m the one who lives in this city, and I know it.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “Fine. Suit yourself. Be as naïve as you want.” She turned and went back to her novel. The ex-boyfriend was about to hire an assassin to go after the love interest. Interesting twist.

It took her two minutes before she looked up and realized that Zuko was still standing at the door, looking at her expectantly. She sighed, closing the book. “If I’ve done something wrong, please just tell me. You know that I’m impeccable at fixing errors.”

Zuko seemed to give into something, and sighed, leaning against the door. “Are you coming?” “I’m sorry?”

“Oh come on, I know you heard me.”

Azula let out a bitter laugh. “After last night, you’re asking me if I’m coming? Won’t it be ‘better for everyone’ if I leave you alone?”

Zuko sighed. For once, Azula couldn’t read his expression. He looked regretful, but also as though he was fighting with himself. “Look...I may only keep you here because it’s the right thing to do. But maybe you’re right about not going everywhere alone. So, if you promise to stay quiet this time, are you coming?”

Azula smirked, practically leaping off the sofa. “Why, I thought you’d never ask!”

The Mayor’s office was located in an impressive-looking City Hall, in the center of the Upper Ring. It was made of dark wood, and took up almost an entire city block. On the left side of the building was a tall tower, something Azula had never seen on a City Hall before.

“A bell tower?”

Zuko shrugged. “The Mayor’s...quirky. Sometimes he likes to ring the bells for fun.”

“How did he get elected again?”

“As far as I can tell, the Dai Li basically picked him.”

“What did I tell you about useless politicians?”

“Not everything is a murder mystery trope!”

“Let’s just go inside.”

There was a giant brass knocker on the front door in the shape of a dog. Slowly, Zuko raised his hand and knocked twice. Almost instantly, the door opened, and they were greeted by a man in a suit. They followed the man up two flights of winding stairs, and found themselves in what was clearly a waiting room. It was unlike any waiting room Azula had ever seen, and she had seen many. The floor was covered by a brown carpet patterned with paw prints, and the chairs were made of brown leather that looked as though a dog had scratched at it. Azula took a seat on one of the leather chairs, and noticed how thin and worn-out the leather felt.

They only had to wait a few seconds before the door flew open, and Mayor Kuei popped his head out with an enthusiastic wave. Azula remembered his face from the party. Up close, however, he looked even more strange. He wore tiny glasses that appeared to be purely for show, since they were tinted green. He wore an enormous, neon green hat, and a bow tie decorated with (what else?) paw prints.

“Come in!” cried the Mayor with another enthusiastic wave. In doing so, he accidentally smashed one of the lights on the wall of the waiting room. “Oops! Sorry about that!”

The two siblings followed him into his office. Azula noticed instantly that there were two chairs behind the desk instead of one. Odd.

The Mayor leaped onto the desk, then fell backwards into his chair, which spun around. His flying arms nearly smacked Azula in the face. “Sorry again!” He grabbed onto the desk and pulled himself to a stop. “What can I do for you?”

Azula pulled out the samples she’d taken of the blue substance the night before. Before she could begin describing them, Zujo interjected. “Mr. Mayor, these samples are from an entirely new chemical substance that is being manufactured at a factory just outside of the city. The factory is manufacturing these chemicals illegally and in secret. It’s likely that they’re incredibly dangerous.”

The Mayor nodded. “It *sounds* dangerous!” He leaned forward, placing his elbows on the desk and his chin on his hands. “But tell me, who controls this factory?”

Zuko swallowed. This was the biggest accusation he was going to make. “The Dai Li, Mr. Mayor. The guards there are dressed in Dai Li uniforms.“

An expression of pure fear and confusion passed over the Mayor’s face. Sweat instantly began pouring down his forehead. “I...I think I’m going to call my advisor. If you’ll excuse me for a moment.”

As Mayor Kuei went into the corner with his phone, the siblings exchanged a confused glance. A couple of minutes later, he sank back into the chair, still looking uneasy. “Great news! My advisor is actually still in the building, because we were having a meeting right before you two showed up! He should be here right about now!”

As if on cue, there was a knock on the door, and in walked none other than Long Feng. He slid smoothly into the seat next to the mayor. Azula’s eyes narrowed. Long Feng had the mannerisms of a manipulator, and Azula knew that because she had the exact same ones. She absolutely didn’t trust him, and she had the sense that he had a hand in many dark schemes.

The Mayor swallowed. “Long Feng, these detectives claim that they have discovered a Dai Li operated factory that manufactures illegal, experimental chemicals!” The panic in his voice was apparent.

Long Feng looked right at Azula. His gaze showed no emotion, but his lips were curled into a subtle smirk. “There is no Dai Li factory that makes illegal chemicals, Mr. Mayor. The Dai Li is an honorable organization, isn’t that right?”

“Certainly!” squeaked the Mayor, looking even more nervous under Long Feng’s cold gaze. He turned to Zuko and Azula. “There must be some sort of mistake. The Dai Li are an honorable organization. I’d bet my life on it! They would never manufacture illegal chemicals, and certainly not illegally and in secret!” His eyes darted nervously over to Long Feng, who gave him a small nod of approval. Azula felt her blood boiling. That small nod of approval was something she’d spent her life fighting long and hard for. Seeing it from here made her think that it was even crueller than she’d originally believed.

Zuko pushed himself up from the desk, infuriated. “But we saw the factory with our own eyes! How can you take their evidence over ours? On what grounds?”  
The Mayor looked confused for a moment, but Long Feng quickly placed his hand on his shoulder. “Mr. Mayor, if I may, these...teenagers are detectives, doing the honorable work of trying to uncover the truth in this city. It is my belief that they have simply been led down a false trail. All the while, the Mayor was nodding like a bobblehead doll.

Zuko sighed, slumping back into his chair. They were fighting a losing battle, Azula could tell. But perhaps they could leave a final impression on the Mayor. “Mr. Mayor, I can tell that you’re never going to believe us. I understand. I wouldn’t believe us either. But rest assured, lying is human nature, and the Dai Li are very much capable of it.” She grabbed one of Zuko’s business cards out of his coat pocket and shoved it across the table. “If you ever find yourself doubting them, and desire more information, you know who to call.” She stood up and began to walk towards the door. Zuko already had his hand on the knob. “I believe there is nothing more we can do here.”

Zuko opened the door to reveal a young woman, maybe in her twenties, standing directly on the other side. She rushed into the office, panting. She was wearing a pale green dress that was splattered with mud, her hair had clearly been tossed about by the wind, and her makeup was running down her face. She wore a necklace with a pendant that was Dai Li green.

Long Feng got up from the desk, a surprised look on his face. “Joo Dee, what’s happened?”

Azula looked at Zuko for guidance. “That’s Joo Dee,” he whispered. “The secretary at the police station.”

“Does she always look like that?”

Zuko shook his head. “Joo Dee might be the least messy person in the entire city.”

Joo Dee began to cry as she turned to Long Feng. “It’s Chief Song, sir!”

Azula remembered the hurried police chief she’d met briefly during the interrogations. He hadn’t seemed like much of...well, anything. But she had a feeling she knew what was about to come.

“What about him?” asked Long Feng, though Azula could sense that he already knew, too.

Joo Dee sobbed even more. “He’s...he’s dead! Murdered!”

A third murder. And this time of a member of the Dai Li. Meaning that the White Lotus wasn’t the only target. An interesting development, to be sure.

Shock spread across Long’s Feng’s face for a second, before condensing into one, rage-filled expression. Slowly, he turned to point at Azula and Zuko. “You two. You were in such a hurry to get out of here, weren’t you?”

Azula opened her mouth to reply, but Zuko beat her to it. “Are you accusing us of murder?!”

Long Feng regained his composure but kept his angry stare, smoothing his moustache as he did so. “I’m simply saying that you seemed determined to bring us down two seconds ago. First you say you’ve discovered a secret factory, and now the chief is murdered right as you’re trying to leave? It’s a little...suspicious, to say the least.”

“You can’t accuse us of murder,” said Azula, making sure to match Long Feng’s composed demeanor. “You have no proof.”

“That is fair,” replied Long Feng. “But I can deduce that you were never on my side. You two have been working with the White Lotus to conspire against us this entire time!”

The Mayor gasped. Zuko, in fury, ran at Long Feng, but Long Feng held out his hand to stop him. “How dare you accuse us of something like that?!”

Long Feng laughed bitterly. “I’m a fool for not seeing it sooner! You two are manipulative conspirators, and you have been all along!”

“Conspirators!” yelled the Mayor, who seemed more betrayed by Long Feng’s accusations than Long Feng himself. “Now, get out of my office!”

Azula didn’t argue, and surprisingly, neither did Zuko. The two of them left the building, and walked back to Zuko’s apartment without a word.

Only when they re-entered the building did Azula collapse onto the sofa, exhausted despite the fact that it was only five-thirty in the afternoon. The lack of sleep may have had something to do with it. “Well, that was a complete failure. Not only was the Mayor completely useless, but now we have no access to the Dai Li.”

Zuko smirked at her. “It doesn’t always have to be total success or total failure.”  
“What are you talking about?”

Zuko grinned and pulled a silver key out of his coat. Azula gasped, a smile spreading across her own face. “You never told me you learned how to pick pockets!”

Zuko shrugged. “I learned it from Father. Well, he didn’t teach me. I learned it so that I could steal my phone out of his pocket whenever he took it. He usually didn’t notice.”

The mood in the room suddenly went from lighthearted to very dark. Azula sighed, sitting up and placing her chin in her hands. “Zuko?”

“Yeah?”

“Why am I still here? You’ve made it very apparent that you hate me.”

Zuko sighed, slumping back into his chair. “I...don’t know.”

“You don’t know why you’ve decided not to despise me?”

“I haven’t!” Zuko’s voice came out as a yell. “I still hate you! You’re annoying, and you act cold and manipulative like our father. You spent our entire childhood tormenting me for not being perfect! Now I finally found a way to live on my own, away from him, and you’re here, taking it away from me! You can’t even let me have this one thing! You have to be the absolute best at this, too! It’s not fucking fair, and I hate you for it!” He was breathing hard when he finished. Azula should have been hurt, but his words washed over her like a river. They didn’t hurt. Maybe because she knew they were true.

“Then why am I here?”

Zuko let out a breath. “Because I still feel like I need to take care of you! Because when your little sister shows up on your doorstep, you help her because it’s the right thing to do! Because I know that you lived with our Father, too, even if you had it easy! Because sometimes I see something in you that I think I can reach out to, and I feel like I have to try, because that’s what honorable people do.”

The room was silent for a moment. Azula pondered his words. He had been overprotective of her since she arrived, but she had never considered that it might stem from a sense of responsibility. “You know you don’t have to keep me here. Nobody’s making you. Father won’t be mad if I go home.”

“I know.”

The room was silent again. Then.”I’m gonna ask you the same question.”

“What question?”

“Why are you here?” Azula blinked in surprise at Zuko’s question. “You could have gone somewhere else by now, but instead you stayed with me. And you hate me.”

Azula paused for a second before answering. If only she could tell the whole truth. But she didn’t have that option. She settled for a half-lie. “I...I want what you have.”

“Are you fucking kidding me?” There was venom in Zuko’s voice. “I almost thought you were better than that.”

“It’s not like that.” Azula sighed. “This vacation was Father’s idea, but...I wanted it, too. It was strange, living alone in his world. I wanted a chance to see what was out there. And then I found you. You have this network of people around you who love you unconditionally. You have endless mental stimulation, and you can practice your skills with no one but yourself to make you do it. You’re free here, Zuko.” She paused, remembering who she was talking to. She’d said too much already. She rolled her eyes, and switched to a flippant tone. “I only wanted to observe for a while, that’s all.”

It was half of the truth, anyway. For someone like her, that was pretty good.

“And last night?”

“What?”

“You want to use my life to experience new things. You didn’t have to climb a ladder and risk your perfect self to save me from a vat of blue poison. Why would you do that?”

Azula laughed. “Well, without you, I can’t do any of this, can I?”

The response was cold and cruel, and it hurt Azula even to say it. But she couldn’t afford to put either of them in danger. Not while they had more important, and risky things to do.

Neither of them could think of anything more to say, so they sat in silence, stewing in their own hatred and mistrust. Azula could feel that they wanted to reach one another, but Zuko could never see past his anger, and Azula could never say what she truly wanted to say.

They were fighting a losing battle, and they always had been. What sort of messed-up siblings included a brother who hated his sister and only tolerated her because of a twisted sense of responsibility? For that matter, what sort of siblings included a sister who could never share her feelings and had to be flippant and cruel about death in order to feel free?

This was all her fault. It may have been the biggest mistake she had ever made. But she could still fix it, for Azula had always been impeccable at correcting errors.

She was going to help him solve this case, and she was going to be *perfect* at it.

Perfection was all she knew how to do.

## Chapter 9: The Blue Geranium

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula and Sokka gain access to a new location, but death is hanging over their heads. Katara wears her heart on her sleeve, and Zuko questions whom he can trust.

#### Chapter Notes

Double-chapter day (because I forgot yesterday. Again.)

TW: Descriptions of mutilation, corpses.

Happy reading!

### Text

The siblings had been sitting in silence for hours when, at nine at night, there was a knock at Zuko’s door. Azula was still buried in the same book she’d been reading earlier, so Zuko, having nothing better to do, went and opened it.

Sokka stood on the other side, out of breath and holding a stack of papers in his hand. He tried to race into the apartment, but he tripped, and the papers went tumbling to the floor. Hurriedly, Zuko knelt down and gathered up the papers before they fell down the stairs. He turned back to Sokka, who looked completely mortified.

“Here.” Zuko handed him the papers, not even bothering to look at what was on them. Meanwhile, Azula came up behind Sokka and yanked the papers out of his hands. Zuko groaned. Apparently she was going to pretend like their conversation never happened. That was fine with him. They would solve the case faster that way.

“Blueprints?” mused Azula. “That seems intriguing.”

Sokka nodded, still catching his breath. Had he run all the way across town? That was sort of...sweet, actually. “They’re blueprints of the morgue. It’s next to the police station. I managed to find them on the library computer…”

Zuko raised an eyebrow. “You hacked into the computer, didn’t you?”

Sokka’s face darkened. “All right, fine, but that’s not the point! I found them, and I think I found a way in. I heard about the police chief’s murder today. If you want to look at the body, this could be your chance.”

Zuko stared at Sokka, almost with different eyes. He had known before that Sokka was a good friend. After all, he had followed him onto a murder scene. But this was...different. Sokka had gone and used his time to get something for Zuko. He had taken a risk, and he had done it without even being asked.

For some reason, Sokka seemed to care deeply about Zuko. There was a part of Zuko that completely hated it. Couldn’t he see that Zuko was damaged goods? A ruined teenager who was better off on his own, because knew that almost everyone he interacted with would try to hurt him. Sokka deserved better than someone so closed-off, and Zuko shouldn’t have to bother with such a good friend when he didn’t need or want it.

Still...maybe it wouldn’t hurt to be a little less cold from now on.

He looked Sokka right in the eyes, and Sokka’s face darkened. It did that a lot, noted Zuko. Odd. “Thank you.”

Sokka’s eyes darted to the floor. “What are friends for, right?”

The room filled with an incredibly awkward silence, except for Azula, who looked like she was trying not to laugh. Zuko glared at her.

There was a clattering in the lobby, and Katara suddenly burst through the door, nearly knocking Sokka and his blueprints to the ground. She was dressed nicer than usual, Zuko noticed. Not that Katara wasn’t always nicely dressed, of course, but she was wearing a blue velvet dress and a silver necklace that looked a little bit more formal than what she usually wore. Like Sokka when he had arrived, she had to stop and catch her breath.

“What’s wrong?” asked Sokka. “Did you not sleep again?”

Katara shook her head. “It’s not that,” she panted. “The police just called me. They said I have an opportunity to present my evidence for Yue, but it’s in half an hour, and with these last two murders, it’s the only chance I’ll get for ages.”

Sokka checked his watch. “Katara, the police station isn’t far from here, but if you don’t hurry, you’re gonna be late.”

Katara nodded, still panting. “I know. I just...I was hoping you could come with me. For support or whatever. I just...I could use a friend is all.”

That was something Zuko admired about Katara. She thrived off connections with other people, and when she needed someone, she was never afraid to ask. In other words, she was the opposite of Zuko.

Sokka looked uncomfortably at his blueprints. “Katara, helping you is always important to me. But...I’m the only one who knows how to use these blueprints, and unless we want to do it another time…”

“What are those for?”

Sokka sighed. “We’re breaking into the morgue.”

Instead of getting mad, Katara just rolled her eyes lovingly. “Of course you are. It’s fine, Sokka. You worked hard getting those. I can go to the police station on my own.”

Zuko sighed. He wanted to go to the morgue, too, but after everything Sokka had done for him, he trusted him to investigate it himself, at least as much as Zuko could trust anyone. Besides, he owed him.

“I’ll go with you, Katara.”

Sokka and Katara turned to stare at him, both looking shocked. Zuko stared at the floor. “Look, Sokka. You got me these blueprints. You want to get into the morgue *and* help your sister. The least I can do is help you with that. It’s about…”

“Here it comes,” he heard Azula whisper to Katara.

“...honor,” he finished.

Azula snapped her fingers. “There it is!”

“Will you stop that?”

“Never.”

Sokka offered Zuko a nervous smile. For once, it wasn’t a sarcastic one. “Wow, thanks Zuko.”

Zuko smiled back. “Will you be okay at the morgue alone?”

“He won’t be alone,” said Azula, sliding off the sofa and placing her book on the coffee table. “I can go with him. Unless, of course, you’d rather I go with Katara.” She smirked at Zuko. The teasing undertone of her comment was clear.

Zuko almost laughed. The idea of Azula offering moral support to anyone was even more laughable than the idea of him doing it. “Somehow I don’t think you’re exactly the pep talk queen.”

Azula rolled her eyes, but Sokka laughed. Katara nodded. “So it’s settled, then. We’ll go off and do this, and then we can meet back here later.”

“If we survive the night,” said Sokka in a spooky voice. Katara rolled her eyes.

“Don’t be so dramatic.”

Azula and Sokka stared at Sokka’s blueprints as they hid in an alleyway across the street from the morgue. At this time of night, the building was locked, and only the dim, blue light from the freezers shone through the windows. Despite herself, Azula felt chills going down her spine. The building, especially with the enormous bronze padlock on the door, looked outright creepy.

Azula used her phone as a flashlight, and Sokka looked more closely at his blueprint of the entrance. “Right,” he whispered. “There should be an air vent in the alleyway to the right of the morgue. We can crawl through it and access the center hallway.”

He glanced at Azula. “You’re short. You can fit through the vent better than I can. There’s no one here right now except one guard, and he’s in that office…” he indicated the blueprint “in the front of the building. If you can get to the back door without getting caught, you can let me in, and we can go to the office where they’re keeping the chief’s body.”

Azula nodded. “Not the most intricate plan I’ve ever heard, but I think that it will prove satisfactory.” She noticed Sokka laughing and turned to him, annoyed. “What?”

“Nothing, just...nobody I’ve ever met talks like that.”

The words felt like knives to Azula, though she knew that hadn’t been Sokka’s intention. They shouldn’t have felt that way at all. But the implication that she wasn’t normal because she was using words she’d learned from her father...it touched a deeper part of herself that was usually easier to ignore.

Silently, the pair crossed the street, Sokka looking around as they went to make sure that no shadowy figures were following them. When they arrived in the alleyway that Sokka had circled in red on his blueprints, Azula instantly noticed the vent in the wall. Sokka pulled out his boomerang and began toying with the screws. Azula had to give him credit...for being a literal children’s toy, the boomerang certainly seemed to be a useful tool.

“Where did you get that boomerang?”

Sokka smiled as he fiddled with one of the screws. “My father gave it to me when I was a kid.”

“Is your father…” Azula knew no better way to ask.

Sokka laughed slightly. “No, he’s alive. He just doesn't live in Ba Sing Se, so I don’t see him a lot anymore. My mother...she wasn’t so lucky.”

“I’m sorry,” replied Azula. Then, after a moment,“Neither was mine.”

Sokka paused and stared at her, hurt flashing across his face. “Zuko never mentioned that to me.” Azula almost rolled her eyes. The amount that Sokka somehow cared about Zuko’s opinion was simply astounding.

The grate fell away, leaving the vent open. Azula squeezed herself in. It was a bit of a tight squeeze in places, but she would be able to move through the vents without a problem. She reached back, and Sokka handed her the blueprints. He had marked the path through the vents in bright blue highlighter, so she could see it perfectly. Before crawling into the vents, she turned back. “Don’t take it personally, Sokka. Zuko never tells anyone anything. No one in our family ever does. It’s part of how we grew up.”

“ *You* just told me,” called Sokka as she began to crawl down the vents.

Azula frowned. Fortunately, no one could see her face. “That’s because I’m desperate,” she mumbled to herself, as she crawled her way down the passage.

Katara’s hands were trembling as she stood in front of the panel of police officers. Nobody but her and the police were allowed to be in the room as she presented the evidence she had gathered. It made the process even more nerve-wracking, but it did bring her a small amount of comfort to know that Zuko was standing outside the door. She had spent a lot of time investing herself in Zuko, because she had seen how much he needed true friendship in his life, and because, once you got past his rough exterior, he was actually pretty fun to be around. It was nice to know that she could count on him, too. It made it feel like a real friendship, and not just someone she was trying to help.

She thought about Yue reminding her to sleep, despite where she was, and how hard it was for her to be alone. She hadn’t known Yue for too long, but she was certain that the white-haired girl was a true friend. She smiled.

A policeman across the room cleared his throat, and she was snapped back to reality. She stared at the notecards in her shaking hands, and took a deep breath.

“Honorable officers, I’m here today to prove that Yue of the White Lotus is innocent. She was not responsable for the murder of Pakku, and I have sufficient evidence to prove it.”

They stared at her, unsmiling. Katara took a deep breath and kept going. “To begin with, here are two photos of footprints and knife slashes on a ledge on the left side of the ballroom where the murder took place. Considering that both marks were fresh when they were discovered the day after the murder, we can conclude that the murderer was standing in this spot when they killed Pakku. Four witnesses: Aang, the adopted son of Bumi, Piandao, the fencing master, Professor Zei, the newest member of the White Lotus, and Ty Lee, an acrobat, all confirmed that they saw Yue standing on the dance floor during the murder. If she was on the dance floor, she could not have been standing on the ledge.” She took another deep breath. The police continued to stare at her, unsmiling. “In addition, I have here testimonies from every member of the White Lotus. They all state that Yue is a good person, and would never dream of committing a murder.” She passed them across the table to allow the police to read. “If I remember correctly, some key phrases were ‘Yue is one of the kindest people I have ever known,’ ‘Yue is the most loyal teenager I have ever met, and would never betray her people,’ and ‘when Yue loves someone, she will do anything and everything within her power to protect them.’” She paused. “These words do not paint a murder, honorable officers. They paint a teenage girl.”

The officer sitting in the center of the panel grumbled. “This is all well and good,” he began. “But these people are Yue’s allies. It’s only natural that they would say kind things about her, especially if they were actually accomplices to her murder.”

Katara sighed. She felt tears pricking at the corners of her eyes, and let them roll down her face. “Then use me. I met Yue two days ago at the White Lotus party where Pakku was killed. The first thing she did was pull me under a table to save me from getting trampled by the crowd. She did this even though she was in the middle of sobbing, and grieving the death of the man who was practically her father.” She took another deep breath. “As I’ve visited Yue over the past two days, I’ve gotten to know her. There’s a kindness in her eyes, a deep-running loyalty, and she cares about other people. Even when she had to spend her nights here, she was always reminding me to take care of myself and get more sleep. She...she radiates generosity. She’s one of the best people I’ve ever met. And even though I haven’t known her too long, I can promise you all that this is true.” She smiled, thinking of the sparkle in Yue’s eyes. “Yue is a friend. Not a killer.”

The police continued to show no emotion, instead staring at her for what seemed like an eternity. Katara absolutely wanted to punch them.

At last, one of them cleared his throat. “Thank you, Miss. We’ll let you know if there are any new outcomes in the near future.”

Katara exhaled as she went out into the lobby, where Zuko was standing. All she could do now was wait.

Sokka only had to wait at the back door for around five minutes before Azula appeared, phone and blueprints in her hands, with a cocky smile on her face. Sokka had only known Azula for two days, but he couldn’t think of many instances where he had seen her without that cocky smile. It reminded him of Zuko’s frown: it was like a mask.

Azula handed him the blueprints, and Sokka found the path he’d marked in violet. Beckoning, he began to creep down the halls, turning this way and that. The morgue didn’t look very big from the outside, but from the inside it was more like a maze, with endless winding hallways lit by dim, fluorescent lighting.

“So…” came Azula’s voice from behind him, “your blueprints seemed to do a fine job of impressing my brother.”

Sokka nearly stopped short in the middle of the hallway. He could feel his face heating up. “I don’t know what you mean.”

“Oh, please. Your face might as well permanently be a shade darker whenever Zuko’s around.”

Sokka sighed. “That obvious, am I?”

Azula laughed. “Don’t worry, I don’t think he noticed. Zuko can be absurdly self-absorbed. Frankly, I don’t understand what interests you about him.”

Sokka’s mind flashed to Zuko’s bravery, his determination, his loyalty hidden underneath his bitter exterior. Plus, he wasn’t exactly an ugly duckling.

It took a nudge from Azula to realize he’d stopped walking. “You won’t...tell him, will you?”

Azula laughed again. “No. Believe it or not, I’m rooting for you.”

“Really? I thought siblings were supposed to be all overprotective or something.”

“I certainly have no right to threaten you unless I believe you pose a lethal threat to my brother. Other than overheating from all of the blushing you two do, I don’t think that’s the case. Besides, I actually like you.”

Sokka blinked. “That makes one of you two.”

Azula sighed, grabbing Sokka’s wrist. “Look, Sokka. You have a good head on your shoulders. You’re smart and you’re witty, but you also know how to be loyal and protective. My brother needs that.”

Sokka sighed. “That’s nice of you to say, but it's not like he’ll ever feel the same way. Or even notice.”

Azula laughed. “Well, Zuzu is an idiot. But he’ll figure it out eventually. For what it’s worth, I think he feels the same way about you. He just hasn’t realized it yet.”

Sokka smiled. “Thanks, Azula. That was really nice of you.”

“If you tell anyone that I was this friendly to you, I will dig up your darkest secret and reveal it to every living being on this planet.”  
“Noted.” Sokka paused, glancing at his blueprint. “We’re here.”

The two of them slowly opened the door, and entered an office that had clearly been used that very day. The desk was still covered with unfinished forms, there was a stamp without a lid on it, and a half-full cup of coffee in the trash can. The room was completely spotless, and lit with the same eerie blue glow from the freezer that Sokka had been able to see from outside.

Azula eyed the form sitting on the desk. At the top of the paper, Sokka could see a picture of Chief Song. “Does it say anything important?”

Azula shook her head. “It says he was slashed to death with some sort of blade, in his own office.”

“Is there any security footage?”

Azula shifted through the papers, being careful not to move anything in a noticeable way. “Just one second of a dark figure before the cameras were disabled.”

Sokka gulped, staring at the freezer. He had studied photos and things before in class. He had even done investigations on a real corpse. But this was different. This was someone he had known, if only vaguely. This was a real citizen who had been *murdered*

He turned to Azula. “This won’t...gross you out or anything, would it?”

She shook her head. “We’re inside a morgue, Sokka. I knew what I signed up for.”

“Fair enough,” he sighed. “Ready?” She nodded, and the two of them slowly pulled the freezer open. Sokka almost gasped at the sight. Next to him, Azula’s face grew white, and her eyes widened.

Chief Song hadn’t just been slashed to death: he had been mutilated. Sokka couldn’t even recognize his face anymore: it was too covered with deep wounds and dried blood. His eyes were shut and scabbed over, half of his hair was missing, and several of his teeth were gone, feeding the trail of dried blood that seemed to pour from his mouth.

“This was an incredibly violent murder,” mused Azula, as though it wasn’t already obvious. “Look at how shallow these strokes are. This wasn’t a planned attack. This was fueled by some sort of emotion.”

“But what sort of emotion could cause someone to go this far?” asked Sokka. Azula looked puzzled, but even as he asked, Sokka knew the answer. “Of course.”

“What?”

“The only feelings strong enough to provoke something like this, something that was obviously unplanned, something so violent, are anger and grief.”

“Which means we now know the motivation for Chief Song’s murder.” The two of them glanced at one another. “Revenge.”

Zuko was trying to stop Katara from pacing back and forth in the waiting room when his phone rang. Seeing Sokka’s name on the screen, he ran right into the corner and picked it up. Katara glanced at him, but he mouthed Sokka’s name, and she nodded and went back to pacing, this time with her head in her hands.

“Did you find anything?”

“Yes!” cried Sokka from the other end of the phone. “Listen, we found Chief Song’s body. It *wasn’t* pretty. We were probably traumatized. I’m a forensics student and that body made me never want to see a drop of blood again in my life, let me tell you…”

“Sokka!”

“Right, sorry! Anyway, only emotions could cause a murder this violent, not to mention that we could tell it wasn’t planned.”

“Of course!” mused Zuko. “Revenge?”

“Exactly!” said Sokka excitedly, though Zuko wasn’t sure why he sounded excited. Maybe he was in some sort of shock.

Zuko exhaled. A revenge kill was awful, but it gave him a clear place to look. Only one person, or rather, one group of people, would want revenge on the Chief of Police. The Chief of Police who had arrested their own unofficial daughter, and done virtually nothing to stop the murders of two of their people.

“Thank you, Sokka. Really.”

Sokka’s voice softened. “Of course.”

“And...are you okay?”

“Of course I’m okay. I’ve got you for a friend, don’t I? *Wow* , that was really sappy. Sorry.”

Zuko laughed. “It’s late. Go get some sleep.”

He hung up the phone, but before he could tell Katara his discovery, he was interrupted by a shriek from the other side of the room. Whirling around, he found Katara with her arms wrapped around the white-haired Yue, who was hugging her back as tightly as she could. Zuko could hear their excited voices all the way across the room.

“They let you go?! They think you’re innocent?!”

Yue nodded, tears of joy streaming down her face. “They said I could go home! And it’s all because of you.” She took Katara’s hands and squeezed them. “ *Thank you* , Katara.”

In response, Katara simply leaned in and hugged her back.

Zuko leaned against the wall, thinking. He was happy to see Yue home, but with Sokka and Azula’s discovery, the White Lotus had just become the prime suspects in Chief Song’s murder.

Yue could go home, that should have been a good thing. But...for Yue, home was a secret society full of potential killers.

Was she safe?

#### Chapter End Notes

## Chapter 10: Motive v. Opportunity

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula and Zuko come to a startling conclusion, but the adventure is far from over.

#### Chapter Notes

TWs for this chapter: Mentions of murder (that goes for the whole fic, actually.)

Happy reading!

### Text

Katara smiled as she and Yue walked down the street together, both feeling lighter than they had in a long time. It made Katara’s heart swell with relief and gratefulness just to see Yue’s face light up each time they came to a new intersection, a new building. Over and over again, Katara watched Yue come to terms with the fact that she was free: that each of these buildings was open to her, and would be forever. It was a feeling that Katara couldn’t imagine, but watching it on Yue’s face was absolutely priceless.

Plus, if she was being honest, Yue just looked absolutely gorgeous when she smiled.

“Thanks for taking me home,” said Yue at the end of their walk. “You didn’t have to do that.”

“It was no trouble at all,” replied Katara. “I...I wanted to spend time with you. Actual time, outside of a police station, or an interrogation room. I wanted to get to know *you* . The real you.”

Was it her imagination, or did two spots of color appear on Yue’s cheeks? “I’d like that too, Katara. I’d like it a lot.”

Katara grinned, ignoring the blush that she could feel spreading across her own face. “Well then, I guess we’ll be seeing each other again.”

Yue’s eyes sparkled in the moonlight. “I guess we will.”

The two girls stood in silence for a moment. Slowly, Katara felt Yue’s fingers interlock with hers. They froze for a second, surprised, but their hands stayed where they were.

Yue looked away for a moment. Was that guilt on her face?

“What’s wrong?”

Yue turned back to Katara. She was smiling again, but this smile somehow felt forced. “I’m just wondering how I can make this up to you. You did so much to help me when you barely even *knew* me. I...I just want to give that back to you, somehow.”

“Yue, you don’t have to do that. Just seeing you happy is enough for me, I promise.”

Yue sighed. “Still, there must be something.” Her eyes grew wide, as an idea seemed to strike her. “I know! You’re a journalism student, right?” Katara nodded. “Why don’t you interview me about the White Lotus? They’re a super old organization. You must have tons of questions!”

As much as Katara hated asking for something in return for her help like this (it made her feel like she’d been manipulating Yue all along, even though she hadn’t meant to), Yue was right. She did have tons of questions, and if she could gain new knowledge about the White Lotus, it could help her discover some of the strange truths about the city.

Plus, if she was interviewing Yue for a journalism piece, she could spend even more time with her…

“That sounds like a great idea.”

Early the next morning, Zuko and Azula found themselves at the White Lotus mansion. Sometimes, being in such a big house bothered Zuko because of its resemblance to his childhood, but the White Lotus mansion was so different from the house that he’d grown up in that he was usually fine. Both siblings had brought caffeinated drinks with them, and were blinking sleepily as the mansion slowly woke up around them. It would have been nice to have Katara and Sokka here too, but Katara had fallen into such a deep sleep after Yue’s release that no one could wake her, and Sokka (while apologizing profusely over the phone) had said that he had a project due by the end of the day, but that he would call them later to see how things had gone.

After Azula and Sokka had figured out that Chief Song’s murder stemmed from a desire for revenge, Zuko had decided to do another interrogation of the White Lotus, this time only about Chief Song’s murder. The first round of interrogations had been rough, but this time was easier. Their (hypothetical) motives were all the same, so all Zuko needed from each of them was an alibi.

Azula turned to him. “Are you sure they’re okay with us being here? If I was an ancient organization, I would be too prideful to let myself be interrogated twice for murder.”

Zuko nodded. “Uncle promised me that they would help us, and even if he hadn’t, they wouldn’t stop me. They’re all prime suspects for this murder, and the city deserves to be safe from whoever did this as soon as possible.”

“You know that if we catch Chief Song’s killer, that doesn’t mean that this is all over, right?”

Zuko sighed. “I know.”

The siblings were soon interrupted by a clatter on the stairs and a blur of pink flying towards them. The figure soon came to a halt, and threw her arms around Azula. “Azula! It’s so good to see you again!”

Zuko watched his sister’s face turn a deep scarlet, and tried not to laugh. “Ty Lee! You...uh... didn’t have to wake up so early.”

Ty Lee laughed. “That’s what friends do, silly!”

Azula’s eyes widened. “Is...that what we are? Friends?” Her voice sounded more unsure than Zuko had ever heard, and she looked completely mortified at every word that was coming out of her mouth.

Ty Lee smiled at her. “Of course we’re friends! Friends help each other out, just like we’ve been helping each other.” She cocked her head. “Did you have a toxic friend situation back home or something?”

Azula’s blush deepened, and Zuko sighed, feeling slightly bad for his sister. Sure, she was awful, but to his knowledge, Azula hadn’t had *any* friends growing up. That couldn’t have been very easy for her. After a few seconds, she nodded, a little too strongly. “Yeah. Something like that.”

Despite Azula’s awkwardness, Ty Lee didn’t seem to care. “Well, I’m sorry. That’s never fun. But you just have to find new friends who’ll treat you the way you deserve! There’s always someone out there.” She gave Azula a comical wink. In response, Azula laughed so loudly that even the people on the balconies turned and stared. Her face darkened even more, but Ty Lee just laughed. “Anyway, I’m sure you have investigating to do, but I just came to wish you luck. I’ll see you soon! You can ask me anything!” And with that, she bounced away as quickly as she had appeared.

Zuko smirked at Azula, pleased to finally have something to lord over his sister that didn’t feel like too serious of a threat. “She’s pretty.”

Azula glared at him. “She is forgiving and optimistic, and therefore the perfect candidate for learning how to correctly navigate the topic of friendship. That is all.”

“And that’s why you turned bright red.”

Azula, as he had expected, turned bright red. “I must have gotten a sunburn recently and not noticed.” She turned to stare at him. “But even if there were another reason, it’s not as though it would matter, because that girl is...unattainable. So please, leave it alone.”

The clock on the wall chimed six-thirty. Since it was time to start the interrogations anyway, Zuko did as he was asked, and left it alone. The two of them had set up a table in a small room on the second floor, and Zuko took out his notebook.

It was weird to think that three people were really dead. It was usually all just business to Zuko, notes and interrogations and payment, but sometimes the reality of the situation hit him. It hurt every single time.

There was a knock at the door, and Aang, the bald teenager, came in. Zuko remembered him from the last interrogation. Even though he had had a motive for Pakku’s murder, Zuko found him one of the least likely suspects. Aang was a kid, really. Either that, or he was *really* good at acting.

He offered him a smile. “Hi, Aang.”

“Hey, Zuko.” Aang’s smile showed no indication of nerves or guilt. “How are you today?” Usually, Zuko would see that as a tactic to throw him off, but he knew Aang, at least a little bit through Katara, and knew that Aang was just like that. “I’m doing well, how are you?”

Aang grinned. “Great!” he cried. Then his face turned serious, as he seemed to remember why they were really there. “I mean...as good as I can be, I guess.”

“That’s good to hear.” Zuko turned to his notes. “Aang, can you tell us where you were at 10:58 AM on Thursday, October 13th, when Chief Song of the Ba Sing Se police was murdered in his office?”

Aang tapped his chin, pondering. “Huh, I’m not really sure. It was a Thursday, so I was probably walking Appa, my dog. Or maybe I was playing with Momo, my cat. I could have been playing Pai Sho with Bumi, but I could have also been on my scooter in the backyard with my friend Kuzon.” Zuko sighed. This was completely unhelpful. “Can you do anything to remember more clearly? Maybe narrow it down to one or two possibilities?”

Aang flipped upside-down in his chair. “Uh...yeah! I remember that I had fur all over my clothes that afternoon. I kept breathing it in and sneezing by accident. Momo’s shedding right now, so I was probably playing with him!” As Aang spoke, Zuko spotted a strand of cat fur on his shoulder. Even though no one could confirm Aang’s alibi, that was still relatively solid evidence, especially considering that Zuko often ended up with *no* evidence when he looked for alibis.

The siblings didn’t need to interrogate Yue, who had been locked up all day yesterday, so their next suspect was Hahn, a White Lotus teenager that Zuko didn’t know very well. Upon reading his name in Zuko’s notebook, however, Azula groaned and rolled her eyes.

“What?”

Azula sighed. “He’s an obnoxious asshole is all. I saw how he acted towards Ty Lee. Trust me when I say that you do *not* want to be stuck in a broken elevator with him.”

For once, Zuko took his sister’s word. As Hahn entered the room, he made sure to have his questions ready right away.

“Good morning, Hahn.”

“It is a good morning, isn’t it? After all, you two get to talk to me.”

Hahn sounded like some sort of children’s book character, but his words were backed up by too much genuine confidence for him to be fictional. Somehow, that made Zuko feel even more irritated.

“Hahn, can you please tell us where you were at 10:58 AM on Thursday, October 13th, when Chief Song of the Ba Sing Se police was murdered in his office?

Hahn laughed. “That’s easy! I was at a party with my friends Chan and Ron-Juan! You know them, right? They run a bar! Anyway, there was a game on that morning, so a bunch of guys from school and I went over to the bar to watch. Chan and Ron-Juan grew up down the street from me, so they’re kinda like my older cousins,” (at this point, Hahn flexed his muscles, as though that was somehow impressive) “and they let us use the bar for the morning.”

“How thoroughly exciting,” said Azula, her voice oozing sarcasm. “Do you have any proof of your alibi?”

Hahn rolled his eyes, mumbling “Of course a *girl* would need *proof* ,” and pulled out his phone. He began to play a video showing twenty or so teenagers in sports jerseys watching a game on television. Zuko recognized Chan and Ron-Juan’s bar, and recognized Hahn in the center of the crowd. The video went on for three whole minutes (without any changes in its events) before Zuko cleared his throat. “How much time is on this video?”

Hahn laughed, pausing his phone. “Right! I guess you guys couldn’t handle the awesomeness! Anyway, that video’s about an hour long. My friends and I were gonna put it online, since we look so good in it. You know, for the good of the people and all that.” He flexed his arms again.  
Next to him, Azula was glaring at Hahn with piercing eyes. Hahn didn’t see her gaze, but otherwise, he probably would have been obliterated on the spot. Zuko had had enough, though, so he quickly interjected. “Thank you, Hahn. That’s all for today.”

Hahn flashed them another incredibly annoying smile before leaving the room.

Azula crossed her arms over her chest. “Well, that was literal torture.”

Zuko shrugged. “At least he has an alibi, right?”

Azula groaned. “I’d rather have him be guilty. Then he’d have to go to prison, and I could avoid ever having to encounter him again.”

There was yet another knock on the door, and Ty Lee poked her head in. “Hey guys!” she practically bounced over to the chair.”

Azula was suddenly studying her fingernails very intensely. Zuko smirked at her, then gave Ty Lee a smile. “Hi, Ty Lee. Thanks for helping us out so much.”

“Oh of *course* ! I’d do anything for my friends!”

Ty Lee confused Zuko sometimes. She seemed too happy to be real, but every time he was around her, her joy felt too genuine to be false. It was always hard to know what was true, but he did think that she (for some reason) cared about his sister.

“Okay Ty Lee, neither of us actually think you did this, but for the sake of the paperwork, can you please tell us where you were at 10:58 AM on Thursday, October 13th, when Chief Song of the Ba Sing Se police was murdered in his office?”

Ty Lee grinned. The girl seemed to never stop smiling. “Sure! It was a Thursday, and on Thursdays at noon, the circus I work at always does a show. Everyone has the second two weeks of October off, so it was actually our last show, and I was really excited but also really sad and…”

“Yes, but what were you doing at 10:58?”

“Right! I got to our tent at 10:30 to start prepping, and I was there until the show started at noon. You can check with the man who runs the circus if you like.”

Zuko shook his head. He’d check it out if he had to, but Ty Lee didn’t seem to care very much about the White Lotus in the first place, at least according to Azula. She loved them, but wasn’t close enough to them to murder an innocent man for them. Plus, she was Ty Lee. Unless Zuko had a good reason to suspect her, he was operating on the assumption that she was innocent. “Thanks Ty Lee. That’s all we need for now.”

“Cool.” Rather than getting out of her chair normally, Ty Lee placed her hands on the seat, did a handstand on the chair, arched her legs over the back of it, and launched herself onto the floor. “Azula, maybe I can call you later?”

Azula nodded, looking a little like a deer in headlights. “That would be...nice.”

Ty Lee gave the siblings one last wave before she left the room. Zuko side-eyed Azula. “She’s just a friend, right?”

Azula turned even redder. “Please, she’s my pathway to learning friendship. The only reason I act like...this is because I despise not being perfect at anything.”

“So that’s the only reason you look at her like that?”

Azula slammed her fist on the table. “Zuko, I barely know how friendship works, let alone...what you’re implying. Nothing is going on between me and Ty Lee. I barely know her. So please, just let it go.”

Zuko was debating whether or not to actually let it go this time when there was another knock at the door. Good. The adults would be more straightforward to interrogate than the teenagers.

Yon Rha, the ancient member that almost no one knew anything about, was first. Zuko knew that he had been in the military a very long time ago, but that was all. The old man moved like a willow, each bone creaking like a tree limb in the wind, slowly and jerkily.

Zuko got right down to business. “Yon Rha, can you please tell us where you were at 10:58 AM on Thursday, October 13th, when Chief Song of the Ba Sing Se police was murdered in his office?”

Yon Rha nodded, slowly like the rest of his movements. “Yes...let’s see now...that was Thursday, so I was at the weekly vegetable market in the corner by what used to be the zoo. I go every week, because my mother forbade me when I was a child, but now…”

“Thank you,” interjected Zuko, who was trying to get these over with. “Can you verify this with anything?”

Surprisingly, Yon Rha managed to produce several vegetable stand receipts, solidifying his alibi.

Next was Professor Zei, the new member, the Anthropology professor. He sat in the chair nervously, looking as though he wanted to leap up and run away.

Still, Zuko kept going. “Good morning Professor Zei. For everyone’s sake, I’ll keep this quick. Can you please tell us where you were at 10:58 AM on Thursday, October 13th, when Chief Song of the Ba Sing Se police was murdered in his office?”

Professor Zei nodded. “Why, yes, I can. I’ve recently started teaching classes at Ba Sing Se University, so I was teaching a class that morning. If you like, you can contact my students, and they’ll confirm that I was there.”

Zuko nodded, scribbling the answer in his notebook. Pretty much everyone’s alibi was easy to confirm (or deny) so far, which made his job a lot easier. An open and shut case was better for everyone involved.

The next guest was Arnook, Yue’s father, the leader of the Ba Sing Se Cultural Society, an organization dedicated to preserving ancient artifacts and historical records. According to Yue, he worked a lot, but that was all Zuko knew.

“Good morning, Arnook. Can you please tell us where you were at 10:58 AM on Thursday, October 13th, when Chief Song of the Ba Sing Se police was murdered in his office?”

Arnook nodded, still wearing the same serious expression that Zuko had never seen him without. “Yes. I was visiting my daughter, Yue. I’m sure you’re both aware of her situation the past couple of days. I wanted to be sure that I could support her as much as possible.”

Zuko nodded, noting it down. The alibis were all starting to blur together in his head, as often happened when he had lots of different information to juggle. But he still had three alibis left to gather, so he kept going, and welcomed Piandao, the fencing master and one of Pakku’s best friends, into the chamber. Piandao wore a polite expression, though he still seemed slightly tired, and was sipping a mug of coffee that might have been too big even for Azula.

“Thank you for coming, Piandao. Can you please tell us where you were at 10:58 AM on Thursday, October 13th, when Chief Song of the Ba Sing Se police was murdered in his office?”

Piandao nodded. “I was teaching lessons at my fencing studio, just like I do every day. Feel free to check with my students if you need more clarification.”

Zuko almost hit something. Each alibi could have been cut from a book on how to craft an inconspicuous alibi. Even though a simple alibi made his job easier, *only* simple alibis made it harder. There wasn’t much winning to be done.

The second-to-last interrogation was Jeong Jeong, the quiet head of the university. Apparently he was a pacifist, so Zuko had no idea what would ever push him to murder. Still, everyone was a suspect. That was basically rule number one of detective work. That and *don’t get yourself killed.*

“Good morning, Mr. Jeong Jeong.” Zuko didn’t usually use “Mr.” but Jeong Jeong seemed like he would appreciated it, and the last thing Zuko wanted was to have his suspects thinking that he was rude because he didn’t say “Mr.” “ Can you please tell us where you were at 10:58 AM on Thursday, October 13th, when Chief Song of the Ba Sing Se police was murdered in his office?”

Jeong Jeong nodded. “I know that this isn’t too easy for you, since I can’t confirm it, but I was here on Thursday morning. I was all alone, except for Aang and Bumi, who were in the backyard playing with Aang’s cat. I was in the lounge...I believe your friend showed it to you,” he gestured to Azula as he spoke, “and I was reading my book.”

Zuko wrote the alibi in his notebook and sent Jeong Jeong out of the room. Azula turned to him. “Either he’s innocent, or he’s an absolutely exceptional liar.”

Zuko nodded. “The imperfect alibis usually mean that someone’s innocent. They always sound the least rehearsed.”

Bumi, the wrestler, was their last interrogation of the day. As Jeong Jeong had said, Bumi said he’d been playing with Aang and his cat. Nothing noteworthy there. Zuko did note that Aang seemed to have forgotten that Bumi had been there at all, but he could chalk that up to Aang’s usual flightiness.

After the interrogations were over, Zuko, exhausted, poured over his notes. Each alibi was perfectly crafted, *too* perfect. Maybe they were all true. Maybe they were all lies. It was impossible to tell. Occasionally, Azula peered over his shoulder to offer a thought, but for the most part, she, too, was silent.

It took an hour and a half of staring at Zuko’s notes before Zuko felt something click in his head. His head roaring with sudden adrenaline, he leaped up from his chair, startling Azula, who nearly banged her head on the wall as she jumped back. “What?”

Zuko gave her a quick, intense gaze. “I think one of the alibis might be a lie. Do you have your phone?”

Azula handed it over (without complaint, which was nice), and Zuko dialed one of the few numbers he actually knew.

“Katara?”

“Hi Zuko! How are y-”  
“Listen, I don’t have much time. Do you know if Yue had any visitors while she was at the police station? Besides you, I mean?”

There was a moment of silence as Katara thought. “No. I definitely remember her saying that she was all alone. Why?”

“I don’t have time to explain right now, but thank you!”

Zuko hung up the phone. Azula was still giving him a confused glare. “Arnook is lying. He never visited Yue. *No one* visited Yue except Karara.”

Azula’s face lit up. “Of course! How simple.” Her face fell. “I should have realized he was bluffing.”

Zuko laughed. “I don’t know any detectives who do a perfect interrogation on their first try.”

Azula seemed surprised at his encouragement, but managed a small smile anyway. A second later, her face grew stern. “We need to find Arnook!”

The siblings ran into the lobby, causing every single person in the center and up on the balconies to turn and stare at them. For once, Zuko didn’t care. He spotted Arnook up on the third floor and pointed at him. Even from far away, Zuko saw him freeze. “Everyone! That man lied about his alibi yesterday morning! Whatever you do, don’t let him move! He could be a murderer!”

White Lotus members (Zuko spotted Aang and Ty Lee among them) began streaming down the balcony and swarming around Arnook. Zuko could only hear their yells, but somehow, they managed to bring Arnook in front of them. “I called the police!” shouted Aang from the back of the group, jumping up and down to be seen. “They’re on their way.”

Azula stepped closer to Arnook, a pitiful look on her face as she stared him in the eyes. “Arnook of the White Lotus...you love your daughter, do you not?”

Arnook already looked anxious. “Of course I do. More than anything in the world.”

Azula nodded, as though she understood. “How sad for her, that she has to deal with the news that her father lied during a murder investigation, and potentially murdered an innocent man. She would be so disappointed in you. Why, she may never want to speak to you again.”

Arnook was already so worked up that tears began to spill from his eyes. “Yue means the world to me. I would never bring her into any of that. I don’t even know what you’re talking about!”

Azula leaned in closer. “But don’t you think that Yue would be slightly less furious with you, just a little more willing to forgive, if you did one good thing in the end. Come clean, Arnook. Be honest. It’s what Yue would want, and we all know it.”

There was a moment of silence.

“Fine!” Arnook’s voice came out like a snap. “You want the truth? Fine! The Dai Li murdered Pakku, the best friend I’ve ever known, the man who practically raised my daughter. They killed Fung, who was quiet, but beloved by everyone here! They arrested my daughter for a murder she didn’t commit! That Chief of Police was a corrupted bastard who shouldn’t have had that much power, and who should have stayed away from my daughter.”

“So you killed him?” asked Azula, still examining her nails as though she didn’t care. “Out of a desire for revenge?”

Arnook paused for a second, then nodded grimly. “Yes.”

Azula leaned in closer. “And what do you know about the other murders? Pakku and Fung? Did you commit those, too? Wouldn’t you want to clear Yue’s name, in case she falls under suspicion again?”

Arnook shook his head frantically. “I know nothing about those murders, and I never had! I killed Chief Song out of revenge, and I’ll admit it, but that’s all. I swear on my life, and my daughter’s life! Please, you have to believe me!”

Azula rolled her eyes at his pleading, but before she had the chance to ask any more questions, the police arrived. Arnook was whisked out of the house before they could even take a last glance at him.

The air in the White Lotus mension seemed ten times heavier. Some members milled around and tried to make idle conversation, but most of them just stood there, staring off into space, shocked.

There had been a killer in their midst, and there could be others.  
Azula turned to Zuko, wearing an expression that was a mix of horrified and excited. “This isn’t over.”

Zuko thought of all the information he was missing, the killer (or even two killers) that he still hadn’t caught. “No,” he said, partially to himself. “It isn’t over.”

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

Thank you for reading! I had lots of fun with this chapter, especially the interactions between Katara and Yue and Azula and Ty Lee, because I'm a romantic.

PLEASE tell me your thoughts in the comments if you've got any, or come talk to me on Tumblr at @theatergirl06.
