## Chapter 11: Have You Got Everything You Want?

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula and Zuko are left alone with the evidence they've gathered, but before long, buried emotions bubble to the surface.

#### Chapter Notes

No TWs for this chapter, I think! It's a little on the shorter side, but I really loved writing it, so I hope y'all enjoy it too!

### Text

Azula had risen before the sun the next day, like she always did. Zuko found her at six in the morning, already fully dressed and staring intensely at his bulletin board. Despite the early hour, she didn’t look tired at all. Zuko remembered how late she used to stay up studying when they were kids, and thought she was probably used to functioning without a lot of sleep.

“Have you been awake for long?”

Azula shook her head, her two free strands of hair flying back and forth. “Only about half an hour.”

“That’s...really early. You know *I* don’t always get up that early, right?”

Azula nodded. “Perhaps if you learned true dedication, you would.” Her snarky tone reminded him of a younger version of herself. Since she’d arrived, she’d been...prickly, to be sure, but also different. She seemed less interested in hurting him, and more interested in the mystery they were working on. Obviously she hadn’t stopped teasing him, but there was less malice to it. It was weird.

Zuko sighed. “Do you really think I don’t have dedication?” He didn’t really care what she thought, but he wanted to know.

Azula paused for a moment, then shook her head. “No. I think you didn’t have enough dedication to please Father.”

Zuko hadn’t really had enough of anything to please their father, but the past two years had taught him that that wasn’t always a bad thing. Azula, it seemed, hadn’t learned the same thing.

The conversation was getting too personal for such an early hour of the morning, so Zuko turned to the bulletin board, where he had pinned photos of their suspects. On the board was a photo of every single member of both the White Lotus and the Dai Li. Seeing Arnook’s photo near the top, Zuko grabbed a red marker nearby and put an X over his face.

He sighed as he glanced at Azula. He still didn’t want her working on this case, but if he was being honest, he was sort of starting to get used to her. Besides, he could use someone to bounce ideas off of, and since Sokka had called him last night to tell him that he and Katara would be at their dad’s house for the day, Azula was the only person Zuko had. At least Zuko knew that she would be honest with him.

Azula, too, turned her head to face the clue board. “Who’s your current top suspect right now?”

Zuko thought for a moment. “Long Feng seems...untrustworthy. He seems like someone who would use underhanded tactics to get the jump on other people. He tried to manipulate us, he was puppeting the Mayor, I just...I don’t trust him.” He only realized after he’d finished speaking that there were veins of anger running through his voice.

Azula raised an eyebrow at him. “You seem to hate this man. I agree that he is not to be trusted, but…”

“He’s a horrible person!” cried Zuko, surprised by the volume of his own voice. “He probably threatened people! He probably uses his power to blackmail them! He’s exactly the kind of person who would use his leverage to recruit innocent people! He’s exactly the kind of person who would hurt anyone who spoke out against him!” He was panting by the time he finished.

Azula’s eyes widened. “Zuko,” she began, with uncharacteristic gentleness in her voice, “I know you hate people like that. You...you have every right to hate them. But you don’t have enough concrete evidence against him to prove anything. I agree that he’s worth investigating, but we can’t jump to conclusions.”

Zuko sighed. It was silly, letting his anger get the better of him like that, but he could rarely stop himself. “I’m sorry. I shouldn’t hate these people because of the way they are.”

Azula crossed her arms over her chest. “I never said that. These people are bad, and you can hate them if you want to. You should. I was only arguing against accusation without proper evidence.” There was a twinge of sadness in her voice, and it took Zuko a moment to understand why.

“Azula, when I was talking about manipulative people, I didn’t mean…”

“Yes you did. You said so yourself.” Azula stared at her shoes. “I’m not angry at you, Zuko. After what our father did to you, you hate people like him. There’s nothing I can do about that. Just keep reviewing your suspects.” The familiar coldness had returned to her voice, but there was an undertone of hurt that Zuko couldn’t usually hear.

“What do you think?”

Azula eyed the board, scanning the photos, staring at them intensely like she always did when she was trying to figure something out. “I don’t trust Piandao.”

“Really? Why?”

“He seems *too* nice, I suppose. Plus, a swordsman? It seems a little too convenient.”

Zuko rolled his eyes. “Being nice isn’t a crime, Azula.”

Azula glared at him. “Sure, you say that now. But Piandao probably used his ‘niceness’ to take things from other people. Even if he didn’t earn them. Even if other people worked harder, and did everything in their power, he probably always ended up with everything just because he was so *nice* !”

“How does that connect him to the murders?”

“I’m theorizing. It’s possible that Pakku, whom we both know is *not* nice, got jealous of his achievement, and they had a falling-out. And because Piandao was so ‘nice’ he couldn’t take criticism, and he snapped!” Like Zuko before her, Azula was panting by the time she finished speaking.

“That’s sort of a far-fetched theory…” began Zuko, but Azula cut him off.

“Maybe it is. But it can cut deep to work yourself to the bone for something, to do the only things you know how to do over and over again, and to just be rejected constantly, only to have someone else gain the acceptance you could never have, all because they managed to act *nice* .” She was glaring at him now, even though he had done nothing.

Strangely, he found it almost comforting. Azula’s high intensity was something he was used to. It felt less weird than everything else that was going on. But the things she was saying...well, Zuko didn’t know how to talk about them with her. But if she thought that she had been the unlucky one, she was dead wrong. She didn’t know what he’d been through.

Once again, he felt anger boiling in his chest. “You think being nice is so easy, do you? You think that being nice gets you whatever you want? Look at Professor Zei! He’s new to the Dai Li, he’s *nice,* he’s trying his hardest, but the other members are just walking all over him! They don’t have the right to do that!”

“But they’ve been working longer and harder! They deserve to be above him, at least for now! Are you implying that all the work they’ve put in doesn’t matter?”

“They didn’t work! They just used their status to get whatever they wanted! They’re using their status to screw over all of the ‘nice ones’ who you claim have squirmed their way into everything.”

“Zuko, those people aren’t trying to screw over the nice ones. They’re only working harder. Maybe they can be stuck-up sometimes, but that doesn’t mean you need to label them all as monsters!” She looked away, and dropped her voice. “Being a monster takes more than that. Believe me, I know.”

But Zuko was done with Azula’s soft words and pretending to care. He just wanted an honest answer out of her. “So you think you worked harder than me? You think that your being ‘naturally gifted’ didn’t earn you anything? Do you really think so highly of yourself?”

“Think highly of myself?” Azula laughed, but Zuko could hear the strain in her voice. “If that’s how you see me, then you don’t know me at all.”

“Well, you seem to think that every nice person has cheated their way to success!”

“Well, you seem to think that everyone who resembles your definition of a bad person should be condemned to be evil for life! Even me!” Both siblings were panting, and Azula seemed surprised that she had yelled. For that matter, so was Zuko. Azula *never* yelled.

Zuko turned back to the board. “Well, maybe some people are born that way. Look at Yue.”

Azula stared at him in disbelief. “ *Yue* ?”

Zuko nodded. “Yue was already arrested for Pakku’s murder. The police must have had good reason. Even though she didn’t kill Chief Song, she’s still a suspect.”

“You can’t be serious! Yue is a teenage girl!”

“What does that have to do with it? *You’ve* been doing awful things to me ever since we were little kids!”

Azula’s eyes widened, but she took a deep breath. “Yue is certainly not having an easy time. She is a teenage girl under a lot of pressure to meet other people’s expectations, and yes, maybe she’ll do anything to meet them. Maybe her father, the murderer, taught her that cruelty and manipulation are the only ways to move through the world. Maybe she’s breaking under the weight of those expectations, and maybe she’ll use that cruelty she’s been taught as an outlet. But it doesn’t mean she always agreed with everything her father does. It doesn’t mean she takes pleasure in other people’s pain. It means she could smile when she’s cruel, because she thinks it’ll pay off later, because that’s what she’s been told her entire life. She’s probably terrified of her father. But it doesn’t mean she was born bad, and she won’t be bad her entire life, even if she was.” The tone of Azula’s voice was light, but her words told another story.

Zuko raised an eyebrow. “Are we still talking about Yue?”

Azula sighed. “I know you hate me. But I don’t want you to think of me as someone who was a monster from the day she was born.” Her eyes wandered to her own reflection in the window. She looked like their mother, realized Zuko. “Believe me, I already had one person who felt that way.”

Zuko sighed. “Azula, I can’t see you as someone nice. Not yet. I’m sorry.” He paused. “But...I can try. I’ll admit I’ve been a little stubborn.”

“You have.”

“But I also need you not to be mad at me. Whatever you think I took from you by being *nice* , I wasn’t trying to. I promise.”

Azula smiled. It was one of the first times he had seen her really smile, and not just smirk at him. “That seems fair.”

The two siblings sat in silence for a while, staring at the clue board. Perhaps for the first time, the air between them didn’t feel thick with tension. It was strange, but it was nice. It certainly made it easier to think.

After a long silence, Azula turned to her brother. “We need some sort of plan. Katara and Sokka may have gone on vacation, but that doesn’t mean that we can leave the investigation for the weekend. People are being slaughtered; the least we can do is try to stop more of this from happening.”

Zuko nodded. “Maybe we should split up. We can cover more ground that way. Maybe one of us will find something new.”

Azula raised an eyebrow. “You want me to go investigate on my own?” Obviously the fact of it didn’t matter, but Zuko wanting her to go off on her own meant more than it seemed to. It meant some small semblance of trust, or at least the knowledge that she didn’t need any protection. Working to prove herself was exhausting, but perhaps it was paying off after all. It was a shame she didn’t really deserve any of his trust. After all this time, she was still lying to him, and it was slowly killing her. Metaphorically.

Zuko stared at her for a second, then nodded. “Look at the board. Every single suspect on here is either a member of the Dai Li, or the White Lotus. If we investigate both groups at the same time, we’re more likely to find something.”

Flickers of doubt rose up in Azula’s mind. “That may be a good plan in theory, but what about reality? After two murders and Yue’s arrest, the White Lotus is going to be more defensive of their mansion than ever. And the Dai Li made it abundantly clear that we are not welcome in their headquarters. If we’re caught in either location, the consequences could potentially be disastrous.”

Zuko smirked at her. “I thought you weren’t scared of anything.”

“I’m not. But risk is probability times consequences. I only take risks when I know I have a plan to minimize the consequences.” Seeing Zuko’s confused expression, she sighed. “You’ve never thought of it that way, have you?”

Zuko shook his head. “It’s usually more like ‘I could gain something important, so I have to try.”

Azula expected herself to make fun of him in some way, but instead found herself smiling. Zuko’s perspective of ‘try absolutely anything and ignore the risks’ was just so... *Zuko* . It was the reason he hadn’t fared so well with their father, but it was also one of the more endearing things about him.

The strategy had gotten him this far. Despite his recklessness, he seemed to be quite an accomplished detective. “All right. We’ll try it your way.”

Zuko’s eyes widened. “Really? No criticism? No complicated plan? No making fun of me for being a reckless idiot?”

“Oh, you’re absolutely acting like a reckless idiot. But it seems to have gotten you this far. In order to succeed, one must learn to try new tactics.”

Zuko continued to look shocked for a few seconds, then nodded. “Okay, then. We’ll split up and investigate the different groups, or at least try.”

Azula gave him a thumbs-up, which felt bizarre, so she stopped. “That’s the plan. But if we get ourselves killed, I’m absolutely blaming you.”

Zuko laughed, and Azula was so surprised that she nearly let it show, but stopped herself. She was walking a fine line between connection and stupidity, after all, and she needed to be careful. “That’s...actually fair.”

Azula turned back to the bulletin board. “All right. The only thing we need to decide now is who’s going to investigate which organization.”

The two siblings stared at the map for a minute, both deep in thought. Azula thought of Ty Lee, of how difficult the White Lotus mansion had been to navigate. She thought of manipulating Long Feng, and of the endless Dai Li soldiers.

Zuko spoke first. “I think I should go to the White Lotus. I can put on a friendly face, and…”

“You? Put on a friendly face?”

“Okay, I can sort of put on a friendly face, and they’ll like that. Plus, the Dai Li don’t respond to that sort of thing, but they do respond to threats and power.” He raised an eyebrow at Azula. “I know you can be really scary when you want to be, but the Dai Li is dangerous. I don’t want to leave you alone with them.” Despite his words, he dug the silver key he’d stolen from Long Feng out of his pocket and handed it to her.

Azula turned and looked at the photos on the map, half of them colored the same shade of green. Despite being about to do something dangerous, she felt strangely calm. The Dai Li may have had secrets, but Azula had uncovered half of them already. Besides, Zuko was right. She *could* be scary when she wanted to. It was an ability she’d possessed since she was a child. “Don’t worry. I think I’m going to be just fine.”

### End Notes

## Chapter 12: In the House of the Enemy, Part One

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko goes off on his own to investigate the White Lotus, but he keeps running into unexpected obstacles.

#### Chapter Notes

TWs: Physical restraint

Be prepared for a lot of descriptions of rooms in this chapter. Happy reading:)

### Text

Zuko’s day started out with a bit of good luck. When he reached the front door of the White Lotus mansion, he found Aang standing there, playing with a bag of marbles and a yo-yo. Seeing Zuko, he waved him over, and Zuko, figuring that it would be easier to get in if he was with Aang, sat down on the grass next to him.

“Can I ask you a question?”

Aang did a forward roll, but landed on his head instead of rolling all the way. Upside-down, he gave Zuko a thumbs-up. “Sure. What’s on your mind?”

Zuko wouldn’t consider Aang his friend, but like most of the White Lotus teenagers, he knew him fairly well, so he didn’t feel bad about asking questions, even if they had nothing to do with the murder. “Every time I’ve seen you, it’s been with a toy, or your pets. Every other fifteen-year-old I know would be on their phone, or playing video games, or whatever fifteen-year-olds who aren’t living with the head of a business empire usually do. Why not you?”

Aang smiled as he did another half-forward roll. “Well, I didn’t know my parents very well. But Bumi did. They were old family friends, so he knew them better than pretty much anyone. Anyway, my parents grew up in a pretty...nontraditional town. Everyone there raised the children together, and they had really strong beliefs about peace, but also about simplicity. They believed in working hard, but also appreciating the simple joys of life.”

“Simple. So no phones, no anything.”

“Right.”

“Why don’t you live there anymore?”

Aang sighed, suddenly looking sad. “The town burned down in a forest fire when I was five. Bumi adopted me, but I promised myself that I’d keep up their traditions as best I could.”

Zuko’s mouth nearly dropped open in surprise. He would never have expected such a happy person to have such a sad childhood. “Aang, I…”

“It’s okay,” Aang smiled again, and it seemed genuine. “That’s a part of my life, and I’m okay with that. But sometimes I wonder what it would have been like to grow up there.”

Zuko nodded. He hadn’t expected to get into such a deep conversation with Aang, but this was what investigating was like. You never knew what the outcome of your ventures would be. It was part of why Zuko liked it. The risk, the unknown, made him feel stronger, like there was nothing in the world to be scared of.

“My mother died when I was nine, you know. It’s not the same as what happened to you, but...sometimes I wonder, too, what life would have been like if she had been there the whole time.”

Aang nodded, then turned back to his marbles and yo-yo. “I guess you don’t want to play marbles with me, huh?” He laughed. Zuko grinned. Aang knew how unusual he was, but he didn’t care. Zuko admired that.

Zuko felt bad leaving Aang behind, but he had no choice. People were dying, after all. “I wish I could, but I...have to get something for my uncle. For the tea shop. He said it was important.”

Aang gave him a thumbs-up. “Nothing more important than tea. Hope you find it!”

“Have fun,” said Zuko quietly as he waved to Aang and entered the house. At least now, he had an excuse for being there, and at least one person who would back him up on it. Probably two if he called his uncle.

It was weird to think that Azula had been here more recently than he had. Zuko must have been to twenty parties in the enormous oak room since he’d moved to Ba Sing Se (the White Lotus, and the Mayor, *loved* parties, after all.) Plus, he’d been to visit his uncle. He didn’t know every room in the house, but he was familiar enough with the central room and the stairs that he knew where to step so that the wood didn’t creak too loudly beneath his feet.

There were six balconies above the main room where Zuko stood, and Zuko hoped to check every single one before he left.

Before going up the stairs, he decided to look into the room right next to them. Zuko had never been in any rooms here besides his Uncle’s three rooms (he had requested his own kitchen, in addition to the bedroom and lounge that every White Lotus member was gifted with), the bathroom, and the main room where the parties were held. As such, every single room was a mystery to him. That made this trip exciting and scary at the same time.

Peeking through the keyhole, Zuko could see what appeared to be a normal gym room. The entire floor was covered in grey mats, and the room was filled with yoga balls, boxes of weights, and various other exercise machines. Through there, Zuko could see another doorway, which led to a pool. Zuko hadn’t even known that the White Lotus *had* a pool.

He was about to turn the knob when a hand grabbed him by the neck and slammed him into the door. Zuko felt panic race through him for a split second, before the hand released him, and he realized that it was Hahn, the annoying one. He would have groaned out loud if Hahn hadn’t been there to hear him. Of all the people he could have run into, it *had* to be Hahn.

“What are you doing here?”

Zuko thought quickly. “I’m looking for something for my uncle’s tea shop. He said he might have left it by the pool.” It was a pretty far-fetched excuse, but Iroh did have a habit of leaving important things in weird places. Plus, Hahn wasn’t exactly the sharpest tool in the shed to begin with.

He seemed to buy it, taking a couple of steps backwards. “There’s nothing by the pool. So stay out of there. That’s *my* gym, no one else’s. Got it?”

Zuko rolled his eyes. Hahn was nothing more than a stuck-up jerk. At least he wasn’t suspicious. That was something.

Zuko began to walk away. “All right then. I guess I’ll...just have to check the upper floors.” Hahn was already typing the code into the lock on the gym door, a lock Zuko hadn’t noticed was there upon first glance. Some detective *he* was. “Bye,” he added halfheartedly, in an attempt to sound sort of normal, before practically running up the stairs to the next floor.

The second floor was the same as the first; door after door that led to rooms Zuko didn’t recognize. This time, he walked halfway around the balcony before he came to another door. He wasn’t sure what it was, but it was made of darker oak than the rest of the doors on that floor. Zuko thought he remembered his uncle telling him that every dark door in the White Lotus mansion led to a study. In retrospect, he wished he’d listened a little harder.

Before he could turn the doorknob, the door flew open, causing Zuko to leap backwards and nearly fall over the side of the balcony. Out of the doorway flew Bumi. Zuko narrowed his eyes at the old ex-wrestler. On the one hand, Bumi was just as much a suspect as everyone else living in the White Lotus mansion. On the other hand, after talking to Aang outside, Zuko didn’t want to suspect him.

This was the problem with long-lasting cases. You got too attached to certain people whom you were supposed to be investigating. It was one of the things Zuko struggled with the most. If Azula ever became a detective (and she was halfway there already, what with how determined she was to work on this case), maybe she wouldn’t have the same problem.

*Then again* , thought Zuko, as Ty Lee’s face appeared in his mind, *maybe she would.*

Bumi ran forward and clapped Zuko so hard on the back that he nearly fell over again. For someone so ancient, the man was *strong* . “Zanzabar! How are you doing today?!”

Zuko gently pulled Bumi’s hand off his shoulder. “It’s Zuko, actually.”

Bumi smacked his hand to his forehead, so hard that he left a mark. “ *That’s* what it was!”

Zuko smiled. Bumi was endearing, at the very least. That was more than he could say for *most* of the White Lotus members. “Well, Bumi, my uncle just left something here that he needed for the tea shop, so I’m just going to check if he left it in that room there, and…”

Before he could finish, Bumi wrapped his arm around Zuko’s shoulders and began dragging him towards the door. “Nonsense! This is my study, you don’t need to look in there! But there *is* a wrestling match on that I’ve been absolutely dying to see! Come in and watch with me! It’ll be great!”

Zuko had to move quickly to get himself out from under Bumi’s arm. “That’s a great offer, but I really need to find this thing for my uncle.” He started off down the hallway. “Maybe another time.” He gave Bumi an awkward wave, and the ex-wrestler waved back enthusiastically.

As Zuko ran down the balcony towards the next set of stairs, he could have sworn he heard Bumi laughing in delight. Maybe the wrestling match was *really* good.

When he got to the third floor, Zuko headed right towards the giant set of doors directly opposite from the stairs. Zuko had never been to this room, but he knew where the doors led: the library.

It took more strength than Zuko expected to push the doors open (was everyone in the White Lotus secretly a world-class weightlifter or something?), but once he did, he wasn’t disappointed.

The library was enormous, so enormous, in fact, that Zuko wondered how it even fit in the mansion. It seemed too big to match the flat exterior of the building. It was at least three stories high, with bookshelves stacked all the way from the floor where Zuko stood to the glass ceiling. Balconies ringed the walls, and Zuko thought he even saw some bookshelves hanging on chains from the ceiling. Before him, bookshelves stretched on for what seemed like forever. Zuko couldn’t even see the other side of the room.

Not knowing where to start, Zuko started pulling random books off the walls and skimming them. His sister had loved books when they were kids, even though his father had only approved of a certain set of books in the first place, but Zuko had never been much of a reader. The characters in the stories always seemed too far away, too unrelatable, untouchable. He’d always preferred writing: even in the strangest setting, the characters all felt like a part of him, because they came from his own mind.

Still, a little more reading might have done him some good now.

He had just finished going through the third bookshelf when he noticed a torch sticking out of the wall at an odd angle. That was another thing about the library; it was lit by torches instead of regular lights. Some people might have called that charming, but it just seemed like a serious fire hazard to him.

This torch looked exactly like the others around the library, but it seemed to be sticking out of the wall at a slightly different angle. Instead of almost sticking straight up, this torch was closer to being parallel to the floor.

Maybe it was just falling out. Zuko reached forward to push it back upwards, but a shout stopped him.

Turning around, he saw the young Professor Zei running towards him, carrying a stack of books and parchment, tripping over his own feet and nearly falling flat on his face with every step. “Wait!” he cried, still running clumsily over before stopping and panting, dropping his books and parchment on the floor. “Young man, do you realize what you’ve just done?”

Bewildered, Zuko shook his head. Professor Zei glared at him. It was the first time he’d ever seen him without a grin or an anxious, forced smile. “That torch is incredibly dangerous! You could have burned yourself! You need to be more careful!”

Zuko let out an internal sigh of relief. “Right, sorry. I just thought it might have been broken.”

Professor Zei shook his head vehemently. “One thing I’ve learned since joining the White Lotus is that absolutely nothing is broken unless we say so.”

Well, that made absolutely no sense at all. “Anyway, I was just looking for, um...a book for my uncle. He said he left it here. I’m just going to see what’s up there, and…”

But Professor Zei was already shaking his head. “I’m sorry, young man, but I technically run the library right now, and your uncle has already passed his limit on overdue books. He’s not allowed to check out any more books until he returns the ones he has!”

Zuko raised an eyebrow. “But this isn’t a public library. My uncle lives here!”

Professor Zei shook his head again. “I’m sorry, but it’s only the White Lotus rules. Now, why don’t you head on home? It’s getting late.”

Zuko checked his watch. It was two in the afternoon, in other words, not late at all. Still, he left the library anyway.

It could have been his eyes playing tricks on him, but as he left, out of the corner of his eye, he thought he saw Zei grab the very torch he’d ordered Zuko not to touch, and put it upright.

On the third balcony, Zuko had to choose a room at random again. This time, it appeared to be some sort of food storage. Zuko thought he remembered his uncle saying something about the kitchen being on the fourth floor at some point, so that made sense.

The entire storage room was colored in black and white. The walls and ceiling were white, and the furniture (counters, refrigerators, freezers, everything) and the tiled floor were black. In the center of the black was one white tile, bearing the insignia of (what else?) a white lotus.

Zuko knelt down on the floor and ran his fingers over the grooves in the white tile. It was artistically impressive, he thought (he didn’t know much about art), but other than that, there didn’t seem to be much in this room worth looking at. Just a lot of refrigerators filled with food, and one that was marked “Hahn’s Grub. Only for the worthy so don’t touch,” in the sloppiest handwriting Zuko had ever seen, including his own, and that was saying a lot.

“May I help you?”

Zuko whirled around to find Piandao standing over him. He looked terrifying with a sword on his back, but he was smiling, offering Zuko a hand to help him off the floor. “Thanks. My uncle just...wanted me to bring him a sandwich for the tea shop. I was looking for the right ingredients.”

Piandao’s eyes narrowed. “That’s odd. I just ran into Professor Zei. He seemed certain that you were looking for a book.

Well, this definitely wasn’t good. “Right! I was! But just as I was about to leave, he called me and said he wanted a sandwich, so I came here!”

Piandao did not look convinced, but nodded. “All right. But the cooks are definitely going to need this room soon, so make it quick. I’d say you have about two minutes.” He was smiling, but his eyes made him look more like he was glaring.

Zuko could tell when he wasn’t welcome. “That’s okay. I can just tell my uncle that I was too late. Nice to see you!”

He walked out of the room as fast as he could without looking suspicious, and once he was sure that Piandao wasn’t watching him, he sprinted down the hallway and up the next flight of stairs. He checked his watch. Three in the afternoon, but Piandao had definitely been suspicious of him. He had three floors left to check, and he was running out of time.

He remembered the next room from Azula’s description; it was the lounge, and she had been right when she had said it must have cost a fortune. This was easily the most expensive-looking room in the house, at least so far. Everything screamed *luxury* . His father would have loved this place, and that only made Zuko hate it even more.

There was a line of books on top of the fireplace, and Zuko saw that one of them was sticking out a little too far, about to fall into the fire. He reached for it, but another hand beat him to it. Turning in surprise, Zuko found Jeong Jeong standing behind him.

“That book belongs to me.”

“Oh. Sorry, I thought it was about to fall into the fire.”

“There is never a need to apologize for stopping destruction.”

It probably said something about the White Lotus that Jeong Jeong *wasn’t* the weirdest person in this mansion. “Well then, if the book isn’t actually falling into the fire, I think I’m going to…”

“Wait.” Jeong Jeong’s voice stopped Zuko in his tracks. “Tell me honestly; what do you think of this room?”

Zuko paused. “Well, I sort of hate it.”

“And why is that?”

Zuko sighed. “It reminds me too much of my father. He always loved to buy expensive things and show them off so that everyone could see how powerful he was. It was never about him, it was about intimidating other people. I guess this room reminds me of that a little too much.”

Jeong Jeong eyed him for a moment, then nodded. “Me too,” he replied, before settling into a chair and opening a book.

It was only after Zuko had left the room and was halfway up the next staircase that he realized that Jeong Jeong was reading a completely different book than the one he had saved from falling into the fireplace. In fact, he had put that book right back where it had been before. In the exact same spot.

By the time he reached the sixth floor, Zuko was starting to get exhausted. It was three forty-five. He’d been here for at least two hours, and he kept running into White Lotus members exactly when he didn’t want to. It was almost as if they all knew why he was there. But that was impossible.

As he walked along the fifth balcony, a door caught his eye. It was strange because, unlike the other wooden doors, all of which were decorated with some ornate carving, this door was flat, and it was the exact same color as the wall. Even more strangely, there was no doorknob.

As he stood and stared at it, the door opened, and Yue walked out. When she noticed Zuko, her eyes grew wide, and she slammed the door shut behind her. She stayed put in front of it, as though she was shielding it from something.

“Oh, hi, Zuko. What are you doing here?”

Zuko debated what to say. Yue was a friend, at least to Katara, but she was acting weird, to be sure. “I’m looking for something for my uncle. He said he left it on this balcony.” He began moving towards the door, but Yue pressed herself even more firmly against it, blocking him.

“I’m sure whatever you’re looking for isn’t in here.”

Zuko raised an eyebrow, and Yue shrank back against the door, clearly nervous. Was this how Azula felt when she was talking to...well, everyone? “You know, a lot of people have told me that today. That what I’m looking for isn’t in this room or that room. Just once, I’d really like to be able to look for myself.” He inched closer, but Yue wouldn’t budge.

“You’re not allowed in here, Zuko. Whatever evidence you’re searching for, it isn’t here, I promise. But you *can’t* go through this door.” She sighed. “If anyone found out I let you in, I’d be in really, really big trouble, okay? I can’t betray the White Lotus. They’re my family. I owe them this.”

Zuko stepped even closer. “Yue, people in this city are dying, *including* members of the White Lotus. You have to understand that. You wouldn’t be betraying them, you’d be helping them.”

Yue shook her head. “ *No one* is allowed behind this door, Zuko. Not even if there’s a killer on the loose.”

“What’s behind this door that’s so horrible if someone finds it.”

Yue sighed. “I don’t know. But the White Lotus...they whisper, sometimes. They tell secrets. They have rules. And those rules...we have to listen to them. *Especially* me. *Please* try to understand.”

Zuko felt his blood boiling. How could anyone put the rules of whoever they lived with above the safety of the people? Above justice? He wanted to like Yue, he wanted to trust her, but he couldn’t. He *didn't* understand.

But Azula would. He had a feeling she would know exactly what Yue was talking about. Maybe that was why he left her alone. Maybe it was because she seemed so distraught. Maybe it was because he knew how much Katara cared about her. Either way, he left the fifth balcony and made his way up to the sixth. It was four in the afternoon.

The seventh floor, and most of the sixth, were made up entirely of bedrooms. Zuko passed a pink one right next to the stairs on the sixth floor that had to belong to Ty Lee, and another one with swords on the walls that had to have been Piandao’s. But by far the biggest room was on the seventh floor. It was practically three times the size of Zuko’s entire apartment, and home to an enormous bed, wardrobe, and desk, all of which appeared to be made of quartz.

This had been Pakku’s bedroom.

Zuko didn’t want to disrupt a dead man’s bedroom, but this was clearly one of the centers of the mansion. If there was any evidence left to be found, it was definitely here.

Unfortunately, there wasn’t much in the room to investigate. Either Pakku had been a very neat person, or most of his possessions had been removed after his death. Both seemed possible. Zuko leafed through a few books on the dresser, and checked under the pillows on the enormous bed, but there was nothing there.

Just as he was about to leave, he felt his foot catch on the blue carpet, and he crashed to the floor. Cursing, he began to get up, but paused when he felt a ridge under his hand. Pulling the rug back, he found a trapdoor beneath his hand, locked with a golden padlock. Immediately, his eyes went to the small golden key sitting on the fireplace.

He grabbed the key, and began to turn it in the lock.

“What are you doing, young man?”

Zuko dropped the key as fast as he could, and whirled around to see Yon Rha standing in the doorway. “I was looking for something for my un…”

“Don’t play games with me, young man! I’ve seen you wandering around this house all day, poking your head into the rooms, and sticking your nose into places that don’t belong to you!” Zuko leaped to his feet, ready to run if he had to. “I don’t know what you’re talking about!” Yon Rha’s eyes flashed, and, faster than Zuko thought the ancient man could even move, he had Zuko by the arm. His grip felt like a stone glove. *Why the hell was every White Lotus member so* *weirdly strong?*

Yon Rha began pulling Zuko across the room, and Zuko, unable to free his arm, had no choice but to follow him. He tried calling for help, but Yon Rha simply laughed.

“This house is enormous, young man! No one can hear you here!”

Zuko gasped for breath as Yon Rha stopped next to a small door and pulled it open, revealing a dark closet. “Why are you doing this?”

Yon Rha glared at him. “So that you learn your lesson! It’s dangerous and disrespectful to go rummaging around in other people’s business!”

And with that, Yon Rha shoved Zuko inside the dark closet, slammed the door, and locked it shut.

### End Notes

## Chapter 13: In the House of the Enemy, Part Two

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula uses her rather unique skillset to investigate the Dai Li, and finds herself working alongside some unlikely allies.

#### Chapter Notes

TWs at the end for this one. Happy reading!

### Text

As Zuko wound his way through the balconies of the White Lotus mansion, Azula, at the same time, was attempting to make her way through the Dai Li headquarters. Getting in hadn’t been too difficult. Well, compared to the load of classes she’d been forced to take in high school, it hadn’t taken too long. Compared to a normal person’s definition, she supposed it had been difficult.

The game had been simple; Azula had found the mansion again easily. There had been two guards, both in police uniforms with green scarves, stationed in front. Walking across the street, Azula had pretended to trip over her own feet and twist her ankle. Being police officers, both of them had rushed over to help her. She had faked a limp all the way to the front door.

Once they had sat her down, Azula examined both of them very carefully, scanning for any weaknesses she could exploit. Had she been able to, she would have done research on both of them prior to her trip, but she hadn’t had that luxury. Eyeing the guard on her left, she noticed a wedding ring on his hand. Looking up, there was a faint smudge of lipstick on his face. So he was still married.

Looking to her right, she saw that the other guard wore no ring, but she could see his phone in his back pocket. It was lighting up with texts from someone named Chit Sang. Squinting, Azula could read the most recent text: *Hey babe, why aren’t you answering? What’s up?* followed by a heart emoji.

So, both guards were romantically involved. Azula could use that. She could see their eyes occasionally darting sideways towards the other. Each time they accidentally made eye contact, their faces would darken, and they would hurriedly look away. *Interesting.*

Azula widened her eyes and let her hair out of its topknot, allowing it to fall down around her shoulders. With her eyes wide and lacking her severe topkot, she just looked like an innocent seventeen-year-old. Exactly the façade she was going for.

She leaned forward, putting her head on her hands, and modifying her voice so that it was slightly higher-pitched, making her sound more like a young, gossiping social butterfly. “So, how long have you two been together?”

Both guards flushed bright red, and looked at each other in a panic. “What?” squawked the left one.

“We’re not together!” cried the right.

“Really?” said Azula, blinking to look more clueless. “There’s just so much tension bubbling between the two of you! I was sure that there was something going on. But wait...are you two exes? Is that it? Or wait...no, you’re both dating other people! Oh wow, that’s hard, I’m so sorry! Gosh, this is such a story, I think I’ll make a post about it the second I get home! My followers will love it, and I…”

“That’s enough!” shouted the guard on the left. “Listen, little girl, I know you’re just excited, but these are our real lives. You don’t know what sort of thing you’re messing with!”

Azula feigned disappointment. “But it would be the best story I ever posted! If I post something this good, maybe the other kids at school will finally like me! They’ve never liked me before! They all think I’m too intense, but with this, I can prove to them how *fun* I am!” Well, *some* of that hadn’t been lies.

The guards looked at each other in desperation. They were clearly running out of things to say to her. “Look,” began the guard on the right, “is there anything else we can do to make this up to you? I’m sure we can find an even *better* story! One the kids will love! What can we do for you?”

Azula tried not to smirk. They fell right into her trap, like flies to the honey. It was almost too easy. They may have been the Dai Li, but Azula had been born and raised a manipulator. They had no idea who they were dealing with. “Hmm, I can’t quite think of anything just yet...”

“Please!” cried the guards in unison. “Do us a favor,” added the one on the right.

Azula pretended to ponder for a moment, but then her eyes lit up. “I know! The kids at school are all scared of this mansion! They think it’s haunted, or some sort of secret government lab! If I could go inside, and make a story about that, they would love it! They’d be so impressed!”

The guards looked at each other, both alarmed. “We’re...really not allowed to do that,” said the one on the left. “We’d be fired if anyone found out.”

Azula put on a resigned smile. “That’s okay. I’ll just use the story about you two.” She got to her feet and pretended to limp down the steps.

“Wait!” cried both guards. The left one ran after her and grabbed her by the arm, panting. “All right, we’ll get you in. But if someone finds you in there, you could be in serious trouble.”

Azula sighed. “I couldn’t risk that. Really, the story about you two is just fine. But thank you for the offer.” She turned and began to walk away again, but the guard on the right stopped her.

“Wait,” he sighed, taking off his scarf. “Put this on. No one will give you a second glance, I promise.”

Azula took it, feigning joy. “Oh my gosh, thank you so much! The other kids are going to *love* this!” Squealing (even though it hurt her voice), she turned and raced inside, quickly shoving Long Feng’s key into her pocket and out of sight after using it. Once she was sure she was out of the guards’ sight, she let her giggly façade fall away.

“Easy prey,” she muttered to herself as she slipped into the dark hallways and let the shadows swallow her. What could she learn while drifting in and out of the darkness?

A lot, it turned out.

The first people she crossed paths with were a pack of guards. Unlike the two at the door, these ones seemed hyper-vigilant, and probably would have scared a normal person, but Azula didn’t let them faze her. Vigilance was, after all, something she could use to her advantage.

Stumbling out of the darkness, she forced a confused look into her eyes, and, pretending to be staring intensely at her feet, ran smack into the lead guard of the pack, falling over onto her back. The guard glared at her, and she wrapped her arms around her knees, pretending to be as small, meek, and terrified as she possibly could.

The guard glared down at her. Azula could see him squaring his shoulders, actively attempting to make himself look more imposing. So he was new in a position of power, then. Good. It would be easier to get information out of him that way.

“Young lady, what do you think you’re doing out of your formation? You know perfectly well that every single guard in this building must stay with their unit at all times.”

From what Azula had gathered, the Dai Li (unlike the White Lotus) was essentially an endless network of nameless guards, none of whom were particularly important. Azula hoped that that was true. “I’m so sorry, Sir. I’m new this week, and I was following my unit, but they disappeared around a corner, and I went the other way, and now I’m here and I’m just so, so sorry! Please don’t report me, I swear it won’t ever happen again!” Because Azula had taken speaking lessons as a very young child to improve her eloquence, speaking quickly had always come easily to her, and she was thankful for it now.

The guard let out a loud (clearly put-on) laugh, and yanked her to her feet. “Ah, fresh blood, then. You think we’d report you to the Mechanist? We’re not stupid enough to go near him!”

Now *there* was something interesting. “The-the mechanist?” Azula made sure to add a slight tremble to her voice. “Who’s that?”

The entire squadron of guards burst out laughing. “Hell if we know!” guffawed the lead guard. “Now go on,” he said, pointing to the right, “the new unit should be that way.” His smile was slightly condescending, and made Azula sort of want to slap him. “Don’t worry about the Mechanist. Stay out of trouble, and you won’t have to ever see him!”

Azula started back down the hall. “But who…”

The lead guard frowned. “You know the Dai Li rules. Never ask too many questions. Now hurry along. If you’re late, I don’t want to be blamed for it.”

Sensing her luck with this group beginning to run out, Azula ran around the corner, and allowed herself to slip into the shadows yet again.

It didn’t take her long to stumble across her next target, and she was in luck, because this woman was hardly older than she was. Given the limited confidence with which she carried herself, and the fact that she was on her own, Azula would wager that she had been a Dai Li member for around a year and was rising through the ranks quickly, but lacked confidence in herself, and probably also faced irritating sexism from her colleagues (because who didn’t, at least at some point?) If Azula could play into that insecurity, perhaps she could learn something more about the Mechanist.

This time, she switched her aura to confident and cocky, and strolled casually around the corner, brushing the woman’s shoulder “by accident” along the way.

The guard turned to her, quickly throwing on an angry exterior, though Azula could easily tell that it was nothing but an act. “Hey! Who do you think you’re talking to?”

Azula laughed, whirling back around and flipping her hair over her shoulder like a mean girl from a high school movie (she thought: she’d never been allowed to see high school movies.)

“Oh, please, you think I care enough to learn your name? I recognize you. You’ve been here for how long, a year? You think you’re hot shit because you managed to get one thing done right and you got a little attention for it. Well *bravo* , but you don’t scare me.” She paused for effect. “In fact, I should report you.”

The woman hugged her arms around her chest. “To the Mechanist? You wouldn’t dare.”

Azula laughed. “Do you even know what he would *do* to you?”

The woman shook her head. “No one does! No one knows anything! Please, just leave me alone!”

*No more information* , thought Azula. *But maybe there’s something else I can find.*

She laughed again. “Leave you alone? Oh, I’ll do better than leave you alone.” She leaned in closer to the woman, shoving her against the wall, being sure to reveal her fingernails, which were filed to a deadly point. “You think the Mechanist is bad? I’ll do something *much* worse.”

The woman’s eyes went as wide as dinner plates. “The Master of Pain? You wouldn’t...you *couldn’t* .”

*Interesting* . Azula released the woman and began to walk away. “Count yourself lucky,” she muttered before disappearing into the shadows once more.

The Mechanist and the Master of Pain. Clearly important figures within the Dai Li organization. What could they possibly be up to?

Unfortunately, the next time she turned the corner, she ran smack dab into Suki, the Dai Li’s child protegé, who was likely to report her instantly to her bosses. Azula knew, because it was exactly what she would have done a year ago if she had found anyone sneaking around her Father’s mansion.

Suki narrowed her eyes at her, and in a flash, had drawn fans with razor-sharp edges out of her belt, and was holding one of them to Azula’s throat. “I remember you. You came with the detective with the scar on his face. *You’re* not supposed to be here.”

Azula studied the girl. She reminded her of herself when she was younger, but there was one major difference. Azula had stopped believing in what her father did a long time ago. She’d simply taken on his beliefs because there had been no other choice. Suki, on the other hand, seemed to genuinely believe that everything the Dai Li was doing was right. Whatever dark secrets were bubbling under the surface, she was unaware of them. So was Azula. If she could convince her to help her, they could work as a team.

She sighed. “You’re right. I’m not supposed to be here,” she grimaced as Suki pressed the fan closer to her neck, “but I don’t want to hurt the Dai Li. I want to help you.”

Suki narrowed her eyes. “You sure have a funny way of showing it.”

Azula winced. “I know, but please just listen to me. The Dai Li is working for an honest cause, you know that.” She actually wasn’t lying. Order in the city *was* an honest cause. “But they are all suspects for these murders. If there are people here who are dishonoring the Dai Li, and using unjust methods, you don’t want them.” She took a deep breath. “I’m not here to destroy the Dai Li, Suki. I’m here to help you pluck the rotten apples out of the tree.”

“Speaking in metaphor isn’t going to convince me.”

“I want the best for the people here who are innocent.”

Suki laughed. “Don’t try that manipulation on me. I live with these people. You think I don’t know what it looks like? I know you don’t give a shit about the people here. I saw the way you looked at me during my interrogation. You think of me as a piece of your little *puzzle* .”

Azula was stunned for a moment, then burst out laughing, smiling. It had been a long time since she’d met a worthy adversary who had enough bite to tell her exactly what they thought of her. It was...refreshing. “All right then, you caught me. I don’t care about the people here, not to the extent that you do. But *you* do care about them. And even if we don’t have the same motivations, we can still work towards the same goal. I think we could help each other, Suki. I could use you as an ally.” She looked the young warrior right in the eyes. “So? Will you help me?”

Suki stared at her for a moment, then nodded, lowering her fan. “If there are people ruining my family, Kyoshi’s legacy...I want to stop them.”

Azula smiled. “I think you and I are going to make a good team.”

“By yourselves?” came a voice from around the corner. Turning around, Azula saw Mai and Toph from the other day emerge. “You don’t really think you’re getting away on your own,” said Mai. Toph grinned, punching her hand with her fist. “You guys are doing some serious rule-breaking, and we want in!”

Suki rubbed the back of her neck anxiously. “Breaking the Dai Li’s rules? For fun? I’m not so sure that’s what I want to do.”

Toph punched her on the shoulder. “Come on, Miss Stick-In-The-Mud! Lighten up!”

Mai nodded. “Yeah. It’ll be more exciting than whatever you do every day.”

Suki’s face reddened with anger. “What I do every day is more important than you realize! I am upholding ancient traditions, which you would know if you actually cared about anyone other than yourself!”

Mai’s eyes narrowed. “You want me to care about your traditions? Then make them actually important.” Her tone was as flat as ever, but her eyes were full of anger, and said everything.

Azula stepped between them. “Look, do the three of you want to help me investigate or not? Every investigation is stronger with more people, but not if their emotional baggage is getting in the way of the case.” Her mind flashed briefly to Zuko in the factory. “If you want to help me, you need to promise that you can push your fighting to the side. *Understood* ?”

The two girls glared at one another for a second, then nodded. Azula smiled. The feeling of assembling a team always gave her an adrenaline rush, not dissimilar to the one she got from solving a puzzle.

She turned, and glanced down the hallway, then at the others. “All right, you three know the way. Let’s start searching.”

The girls went through hallway after hallway. Even Azula couldn’t keep track of the identical shadowy passages in her mind, and soon found herself wondering where she was. She was lucky to have the others with her. They lived here, so they all seemed to have no trouble finding their way around, which made sense. If you had put Azula back in her father’s house, even after a week or so of being away, she would have been able to identify every room, the fastest and most discreet way in and out, and the best places to hide.

After a while, they fell into a sort of quiet rhythm. They would walk in silence, check a room, see that there was nothing there, and continue searching. Occasionally, they would run across a group of guards, but with her green scarf, and in the company of Mai, Toph, and Suki, no one batted an eye at Azula’s presence.

If anything, they got through the packs of guards faster than Azula would have on her own. This was because Toph, Azula was beginning to learn, had quite a sense of humor, and had no qualms about playing up her blindness when it was necessary. With her cane, or with Mai’s occasional verbal cues, she seemed completely able of moving around without any problems, but when they needed to get through a large crowd of guards, it was as though she couldn’t move her legs. Azula had to give her credit for the strategy; it *did* work, and remarkably well at that.

After an hour or two of searching, the four girls paused at a corner. Azula squinted into the darkness, looking for anything suspicious. “Do you think there’s anything down this hallway?”

Suki came up next to her and stared into the darkness. “I’m not sure. It looks suspicious, but we can never be sure.”

Azula nodded. “We should advance very carefully and quietly, and keep our guard up.”

“Guys?” came Mai’s voice from behind them. “There’s actual smoke that looks like it might be poisonous coming out of that closet over there.”

Azula and Suki whirled around, and sure enough, pale yellow gas was seeping out from under the door, and slowly seeping towards them. Azula quickly racked her brain for any knowledge she had managed to retain from advanced high school chemistry. It took a moment, but at last, it clicked. “Don’t go near that!” she cried. “That’s fluorine gas, it’s extremely toxic, and with a concentration that high, we’d all be dead in minutes!”

The girls all leaped backwards as the gas seeped closer, but as suddenly as it had appeared, there was a sound rather like a vacuum sucking air, and the gas disappeared, sucked back under the closet door.

The girls stood in shock, all a little apprehensive about moving another step. Finally, Toph spoke. “Why did the gas disappear like that?”

Suki narrowed her eyes. “Whoever set it loose didn’t want to leave any sort of trace that they were here.”

Azula nodded grimly and, swallowing, made her way towards the closet, hoping that whoever had unleashed the fluorine gas had sucked it all up again. Trying to push away the butterflies in her stomach, she turned the knob and swung the door open, closing her eyes to avoid the gruesome sight she was sure she would find.

A pile of something fell on her, and she shrieked as she lost her balance and fell to the floor. Only after she made sure she wasn’t hurt did she realize that the heavy things covering her felt rather...fleshy.

She opened her eyes. She was lying on the floor, on her back. On top of her, staring her right in the face, were the cold, dead eyes of the two guards who had met her on the steps. They were surrounded by at least fifteen other guards. Every single one of them was already turning stone-cold.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes
