## Chapter 14: The Herb of Death

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Unexpected alliances are made, and Zuko begins to spiral down a dark path. Azula reflects on her past, and finds herself in an unexpected position.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Blood, self-hatred, drinking.

This is a pretty angsty one (if the TWs didn't give that away), but it was super fun to write, so I hope you all enjoy it! Happy reading:)

### Text

Zuko banged on the closet door for so long that his fists bled. He had become numb to the pain about an hour ago (or, he thought. His watch had accidentally smashed when Yon Rha had thrown him into the closet.) His knuckles were full of splinters, both tiny ones that were nearly invisible and enormous ones that Zuko could see even in the dark.

Cutting his hand for what must have been the thousandth time, he slumped down on the closet floor, cursing quietly to himself. He had been stupid coming here, and he should have known all along.

The worst part of it was that he had been *so* close to finding something. Each room had small details out of place, and Zuko *knew* that they were all connected somehow. He had been seconds away from uncovering the truth, but instead, he was stuck here.

Some detective *he* was. What good was almost uncovering huge secrets if he just ended up caught every time? His determination had served him well until now; it meant that he never over-thought things, and never hesitated to protect people who needed it. It enabled him to stay fresh on a case’s trail. But it also put him in more danger. Until now, he had been okay with that. But now, he just felt like a complete idiot.

How was he supposed to protect his sister and his friends, all of whom, it seemed, were trying to help him, when he couldn’t even protect himself? And this wasn’t even the most dangerous situation he would end up in!

But even if he’d already failed, he wasn’t going to give up. He never had before, and he wasn’t going to start now. Not while people were dying all around him. He got to his feet and began banging on the door again, harder and harder, ignoring the pain, ignoring the streams of blood that he could feel running between his fingers and splashing onto the floor. He kept pounding, the ringing in his ears growing louder and louder, but he ignored it and kept pounding. He could feel the very skin coming off his knuckles, but he kept going. He was going to keep going until he was heard.

After about half an hour of pounding on the door and feeling the blood soak his hands, the door suddenly flew open. Zuko wasn’t expecting it to fall away, so he swung his arms forward and fell flat onto the floor.

“Zuko! Oh my stars! What happened to your hands? Are you okay?”

Zuko groaned, finally feeling the pain in his hands that he’d been blocking out for the past few hours. Still, he managed to stumble to his feet and look at his rescuer. “Ty Lee. Sorry if I ruined your night.” He managed a wry smile.

Ty Lee’s eyes were still wide, and she looked incredibly concerned. “Not at all. But what happened to you? Hang on, come to my room, I need to fix your hands.”

Zuko was still in a bit of a daze as Ty Lee dragged him to the sixth floor, where her bedroom was located. Zuko had seen it earlier, and as he would expect, everything inside was some shade of pink. Ty Lee (rather forcefully) shoved him into one of the many pink armchairs.

“I’ll be right back,” she said, and ran out of the room. Zuko wanted to close his eyes because the pink was *so* bright, but Ty Lee was trying to help, so he tried his best. It was the least he could do.

A few minutes later, she was back, followed by Yue, who looked incredibly guilty, and carrying an armful of bandages and a pair of tweezers. She plopped down on the rug across from him, her usual peppy smile gone. Instead, her face was full of worry and authority.

She nodded at him. “Hold out your hands and keep them still.” Zuko sighed. His hands were so awful that he didn’t want anyone else to see them ever again. But Ty Lee was practically glaring at him, so he had no choice.

She was a master at pulling out splinters. There must have been at least thirty in Zuko’s hands, but Ty Lee pulled out every single one in a snap, even the ones that Zuko could barely see with his own eyes. Then she got to work wiping off the bloodstains. His hands were still bleeding, but as she rubbed away the dark red, he had to admit that they looked a lot less messed-up. She took the bandages she was carrying and wrapped them around his hands, so tightly that Zuko almost couldn’t feel any pain at all. Most impressively, she’d done it all in fifteen minutes.

He stared at her. “How did you get so good at that? I didn’t realize the White Lotus taught it.”

“They don’t,” said Yue. Ty Lee nodded.

“Zuko, I work at a circus. Stuff like this happens all the time. We need to all be prepared for this sort of thing.” Her smile returned for the first time. “That should be all better!” She did a backbend and propelled herself over her hands twice to land cross-legged on her bed. Yue came forward, and sat on the pink rug in front of Zuko’s chair. Unlike Ty Lee, Yue was still looking intensely worried. “Zuko, tell me what happened to you.”

Zuko sighed, leaning back in the chair. He didn’t want to admit that he’d messed up...or that he wasn’t always the perfect detective, but Ty Lee and Yue had just helped him. They deserved the truth. “I was investigating the mansion and trying to figure out if the White Lotus was hiding anything that might help me solve these murders. But every time I found something out, someone would come and stop me! It was like everyone knew I was here! And then, when I got to the bedroom on the top floor, I found a trapdoor, but before I could open it, Yon Rha came in and threw me in a closet. He kept saying I needed to ‘learn my lesson.’”

“How long were you in there?” asked Yue.

“I don’t know,” replied Zuko. “About three hours? Maybe more.”

Ty Lee gasped, her eyes like dinner plates. Yue stared at the floor, still looking incredibly guilty. “Zuko, I think I know what they were trying to hide from you. But I promise it has nothing to do with the murders. It’s not dangerous, it’s only a stupid old tradition. If anyone gives you any reason not to believe me later, then I promise to tell you everything. But for now, I know it’s not much, but I’m asking you to *please* trust me.” She stared at him, the pink lights of Ty Lee’s bedroom reflecting in her pale blue eyes. “Can you do that?”

Zuko wasn’t sure what to say. If he knew anything, it was that he couldn’t trust *anyone* . But Katara trusted Yue, and Zuko, as much as he hated to admit it, had come to trust Katara, and Sokka even more. Slowly, he nodded. “All right. I’ll trust you for now. But if I, or anyone else working on this case, is put in danger because of whatever you’re not telling me, you need to tell me. Otherwise, if anyone gets hurt, it will be all your fault.” Yue’s hands were trembling, but for once, Zuko didn’t mind scaring her. It felt earned. “Are we clear?” Yue nodded, still shaking, but looking determined.

The air was silent for a moment, but Ty Lee broke it, leaping off the bed, her peppy smile completely visible once again. “Zuko, I’m *so* sorry that that happened to you. How can I make it up to you?”

Zuko did *not* want to know what ‘make it up to you’ meant coming from someone whose room was *this* pink. “You really don’t have…”

“Great!” squealed Ty Lee, completely ignoring him. “I know an awesome dance place near here! Yue, you in?” Yue nodded apprehensively. Ty Lee grinned. “Amazing! I’ll see if Aang wants to come, too! It’ll be such a good time! Zuko, I promise you, after tonight, today will be nothing but a distant memory.”

Azula, Suki, Toph, and Mai sat in a line on one side of a metal table. On the other side sat Long Feng and Mayor Kuei. Kuei looked somewhat distracted, but Long Feng was glaring at Azula with the force of a thousand angry vipers. Azula glared right back. Long Feng may have been a leader, but he was nothing compared to her.

'&#96;What are you doing here?” he spoke slowly and clearly. “I specifically forbade you and your brother from investigating the Dai Li any longer. Unless you mean to tell me you have broken my, and the Mayor’s, wishes, and therefore broken the law, you must have a very good excuse for why you are here, and why I should not arrest you this instant for the murder eighteen of my soldiers.”

Azula was opening her mouth to come up with some sort of lie, but Suki beat her to it. “Forgive me, sir, but Azula is my friend. She came over this morning to help me train. We found the bodies together, and they had clearly just been killed. She never left my side all morning. She couldn’t have killed them.”

Azula almost stared at Suki in shock, before remembering the precarious position she was in. Long Feng’s eyes widened. Suki was clearly someone he, and the entire Dai Li, trusted greatly. To him, she would never lie on Azula’s behalf, therefore what she was saying must have been true. Still, he was suspicious. “Then why are you wearing a scarf in our colors, if not to fool us into thinking you belong here?”

Toph laughed. “That was my idea! I told Azula she needed to wear less red and more green! We were just having a good time.”

Long Feng’s eyes narrowed. “You’re blind, little girl.”  
Toph planted her hands on her hips. “So?! I have *opinions*!”

Long Feng sighed. “All right, then. All four of you were together. Then please explain to me what you were doing instead of training, and why you were in corridor 267 instead of in the training room downstairs where all three of you were scheduled to be.”

Next to Azula, Suki squirmed uncomfortably. Azula could tell that it hurt her to break the rules in this way. She did feel somewhat bad. After all, it was sort of her fault.

Mai chimed in. “Training is boring. We do it every day. We wanted to try something different. So we went walking around. It was boring, too.”

Long Feng raised an eyebrow. “I see.” He turned to Suki. “Suki, I’m surprised at you. You’re usually so good at rising above the influence of others.” He leaned closer. “I expected better from you.”

Suki stared at her shoes.

Azula sighed. She hated making herself seem weaker than she was, especially in front of adversaries. But she couldn’t let Suki take the fall for this, or else she could lose a very valuable ally. “It was my fault, Sir. I couldn’t handle the training, so Suki decided that it was okay to do something else. She was trying to make me feel better.”

“That’s right,” added Mai. “She was going on and on about trying to uphold the ancient values of loyalty or something.”

Long Feng sighed. “It seems you still have a lot of learning to do, Suki.” Suki lowered her head, not meeting his eyes. He smiled. “But you are on your way to where you need to be. Keep training, perhaps alone for the next few days, and all will be well. Loyalty is an admirable trait…” he glared at Azula, Toph, and Mai, “as long as you are loyal to the right people.”

He sighed, starting to look bored. “Well, it seems that the four of you are innocent. The three of you may return to your training, and *you* ” (he glared at Azula) “should return home as soon as possible.”

“Wait!” cried the Mayor, who had been silent the entire time, springing to his feet. “You’re just going to let them go? I want a word with that one!” he pointed at Azula. “In private.”

Long Feng placed his hand on Kuei’s shoulder. Even from across the room, Azula could tell that he was gripping hard. “Mayor Kuei, that is really unnecessary. I know you’re simply trying to do good for your city, but please, calm yourself and sit back down.” His tone was soft, but Azula didn’t miss the authoritative undertone. His message was clear: *Do as I say* .

“Yeah!” cried Toph, who was already halfway to the door. “Why are you even here, anyway?”

The Mayor looked absolutely bewildered, and glanced nervously at Long Feng, who glared at him. After a moment, he seemed to remember. “Yes!” he cried with obviously false confidence. “I am here because...the events of Ba Sing Se are important, and...Long Feng has encouraged me...I mean, I have decided to take a more active role in them!” He grinned. “Especially the parties!”

Azula could tell that Long Feng absolutely wanted to slap him.

Long Feng turned to the four girls. “That will be all, girls. Please leave me with the Mayor now. We have other people to question.”

The four girls filed out of the room and back into the dark hallway. Even from a few doors down, Azula could still see the pile of corpses spilling out of the closet. For some reason, no one had bothered to remove them.

It was easy to tell that Ty Lee had chosen this place. It looked like the sort of place you would rent out for a thirteen-year-old girl’s birthday party. The tablecloths were white, the bar was surrounded by stools that spun, the flashing lights were rainbow-colored, there were neon palm trees, ice cream cones, and flamingoes covering the walls, and of course, there was a disco ball.

Ty Lee waved to the host, whom she clearly knew, and she, Zuko, Yue, Aang, and Hahn, who had come along for some reason, crammed themselves into a booth. Ty Lee waved at a waiter, and he instantly appeared. Clearly, she knew the people here. Within minutes, the group had drinks in front of them. Ty Lee had ordered a milkshake with so many rainbow sprinkles on it that it hurt Zuko’s eyes. Zuko himself had a glass of wine in front of him. He had acquired a taste for most alcohols since becoming a detective. It was an easy place to drown his failures.

Right now, though, Ty Lee was attempting to cheer him up. She, Yue, and Aang, clearly felt bad for the day’s events. Hahn probably had no idea while they were there, and was more interested in eyeing one of the waitresses, who looked to be about seventeen. His eyes seemed to drift over to her every time she had to bend over slightly to pick up more silverware, due to her tallness. Zuko rolled his eyes. There were too many boys like Hahn in Ba Sing Se, and every single one of them was infuriating.

“Isn’t this place fun?” cried Ty Lee, clearly already on a sugar rush from her milkshake (how much sugar was *in* that thing?) “Who needs evidence when you could have this?” She took another sip. Zuko could have sworn he saw her pupils dilate from the other side of the table.

“Me,” muttered Zuko. He knew that the group was only trying to help him, but he couldn’t help it. He felt like a stormcloud of disappointment and failure. He wanted to be at home with a bottle of bourbon, not here in this pink nightmare.

Yue sighed. “Well, if we can’t cheer you up, maybe we can at least help you with that.”

“What a great idea!” said Ty Lee.

Zuko narrowed his eyes. “What do you mean?”

“I mean,” said Yue, “that you could use some allies inside the White Lotus, so that something like today never happens again.”

Ty Lee’s face lit up. “Yeah! I showed your sister around the mansion! I’d be happy to do more things like that, too!”

Aang nodded. “Me too,” he said.

Zuko sighed as he sipped his wine. “What’s in it for you all?”

Aang thought for a moment, then answered. “The White Lotus is our family, Zuko. We all want to protect them. You’re the one solving this mystery. We want to help with that, however we can.”

Yue nodded in agreement. “All the people we care about are tangled up in this. It’s not just about us, or you. It’s about everyone.”

Ty Lee took a sip of her milkshake and smiled. “Zuko, you guys shouldn’t have to do this alone. We’re useful to you. We can help you whenever you need.”

“All three of us,” added Aang. Hahn was the only one absent from the table. Zuko spotted him making out with the waitress in the corner.

Zuko smiled bitterly, but raised his glass anyway. “Well then, let’s toast to a new friendship!”

The three of them clinked their glasses to his, all smiling. Zuko tried his best to hide the shadows that were creeping into his eyes. Their friendship may have been useful to his case, but he knew he didn’t deserve it.

Once in the hallway, Azula pulled the three other girls into a nearby room. Once she made sure they were alone, she turned to them. “Thank you for helping me in there. Not a lot of people would do that for a semi-stranger.” It was true that she was surprised. In her world, helping anyone, unless they were above you and had the power to order you to do so, was unacceptable, and worthy of severe consequences. To help someone you barely knew was unthinkable.

“My only question is why. None of you want to end up in trouble. Why would you risk yourselves for that?”

The three other girls glanced at one another. Suki spoke first. “Well...what you said before...you were right. I think there may be something going on here. Someone in the Dai Li is ruining the legacy of my family, the legacy that I’ve devoted my whole life to keeping up. I want to catch them, and you’re a detective. I want you on my side, and I want to be on yours. If you’ll let me.”

Mai nodded. “The Dai Li has been smothering us,” she indicated herself and Toph, “since we were born. They’ve never treated us like people.” Suki looked at the ground, clearly hurt. “If they’re up to something…”

“If they’re hurting people, we’re *not* going to let it slide.” Toph rammed her fist into the wall. Azula felt bad for the wall. She felt a smile begin to tug at the corners of her lips.

“So what you’re saying is, you want to help us with this case? Anything we might find, whoever may be guilty? Even if it’s not something you want to see.”

The other girls nodded. Azula smiled. “Good. But if we want to make this work, we need to trust each other. The way we were covering for one another in there...that’s the sort of teamwork that will solve this mystery. But if there’s fighting…” she glanced at Suki and Mai “this will be a *very* short investigation.”

Suki nodded. “We can do that. We want to solve this just as much as you do.”

Azula checked her watch. It was getting late. She should probably head back to the apartment. She smirked as she began to leave, taking Suki with her to ensure that she didn’t get lost. “I think we’re all going to do great things together.”

Despite the blinding lights and the fact that the entire restaurant was an eyesore, Zuko found the hours beginning to slip by. After the alliance had been made, Zuko hadn’t been able to stop the thoughts that kept coming into his head. About failure, and being undeserving of love and other people’s help. About other people being so much better than him that he would only slow them down. About them all turning on him once they realized how weak he was, using him and hurting him and breaking him as he failed them, over and over and over again.

Zuko had gotten pretty good at keeping thoughts like those away. But sometimes they just burrowed into his brain and wouldn’t go away. When he was younger, those thoughts used to explode in fiery outbursts of rage, but he had learned that that called far too much attention to himself. Since moving to Ba Sing Se, he had found another way.

Drinking was easy once you lost track of the number of glasses. You just kept them coming, and everything became a numb blur. You didn’t have to think, or see, or feel. It felt liberating.

Ty Lee looked far away through the spots that had been dancing in his eyes for the last hour. She seemed...what was the word? Worried. He raised his hand, feeling the weight of his arm more than he normally would, and another beer landed in front of him. He drank it, the sickly sweetness of it pouring down his throat. It tasted bad and made his head throb, but he relished the feeling.

“Zuko!” Ty Lee’s voice seemed quiet compared to the pounding inside his head. “Maybe you should stop with the drinks! That really looks like a lot!”

Zuko took another sip of the beer, ignoring her, and nearly gagging on the taste.

“Really,” said Ty Lee. “This is so much, it’ll only make you miserable! Why would you do this to yourself?”

Zuko tipped his head back to swallow the last of the beer. “Because I deserve it,” he mumbled, nearly face-planting onto the table. “Pass me another one.” But Ty Lee refused, pushing herself into his line of vision instead.

“What do you mean you deserve it? What are you talking about?”

Zuko sighed. How could Ty Lee miss something so obvious? “Look at me,” he said, barely aware of the fact that his words were slurring together as he spoke, “I’ve been working on this case for almost a week and people are still dying. What kind of detective does that?”

Ty Lee gave him a pitying smile. “Hey, it’s okay! I’m sure you’ll get everything soon. You just need a little bit more time.”

Zuko groaned, slumping back and almost falling off the stool he was sitting on because he’d forgotten that it wasn’t a chair. “So what? I was never good enough for anything. Not my father, not my sister, and not the people who pretend to be my friends.” The room was beginning to grow dark. Was he blacking out? Had he really drunk that much? “What difference does this make? No matter how hard I try, I’ll never be good enough to protect this city.”

Ty Lee started to say something, but Zuko didn’t hear. The entire room had faded away into blackness and static.

Azula had been curled up on the sofa for hours with her book. She hated to admit it, but she was starting to worry about Zuko. He’d gone to investigate the White Lotus, and she hadn’t heard anything from him at all. It reminded her too much of when they were young and shared a room after their mother had died. He would disappear for hours, and always return beaten and bruised. Azula knew her father well enough not to ask any questions; she didn’t have to.

But, just like when she was growing up, she knew that wherever Zuko may have been, she couldn’t do anything to help him. So she buried herself in her book, shoving her worries to the back of her mind. After a couple of minutes of being unable to focus on reading, she slammed the book back down, irritated.

The anxiety refused to leave her brain and she hated it. She had always been so good at controlling her emotions, pushing them so far into her brain that she never had to think about them, and they never got in her way. How had she developed such an enormous weakness in such a short amount of time?

It felt like she sat staring out the window for hours before there was a knock at the door. Azula had to stop herself from running to open it, but when she did, she found a tired-looking Ty Lee who was in the process of half-carrying Zuko, who was leaning on her shoulder, his eyes completely out of focus and his skin pale. Quickly, Azula grabbed Zuko from the other side, and together, the two girls managed to get him onto the sofa. Azula turned to Ty Lee.

“What happened?”

Ty Lee took a deep breath. “Okay, so Zuko was apparently investigating the White Lotus mansion but then he got locked in a closet because he was discovering too much at least I think that’s why but anyway I found him and I felt really bad so I took him to this dance club I love but then he started drinking like a *ton* of alcohol and I wasn’t expecting it so I didn’t know how to stop him and now he’s really drunk and I’m so sorry!” Her words all came tumbling out in one breath. Azula could see from the dark circles under her eyes that she was exhausted.

“Don’t waste your energy apologizing for someone else’s actions. You can try to protect someone all you want, but in the end, their failures are their own fault.” She was speaking more to herself than to Ty Lee, after remembering their childhood in such detail. She couldn’t even believe what she was saying anymore, not completely. But she *did* believe that Ty Lee had no reason to be sorry.

Ty Lee sighed. “I know, it’s just...I’m tired. When I was growing up, we were sort of all expected to be a unit...you know, because we all looked alike and there were seven of us. So when one of us got in trouble, it was sort of...all our fault. Still kind of working on that.” She paused, seeing Azula’s stunned expression. “Oh my gosh, I’m so sorry! Was that oversharing? I’m working on that, too!”

Azula shook her head. “No, I’m just...amazed. How you can share your past, and your flaws so easily, well, I somewhat envy you.”

Ty Lee nodded. “I just wanted to make sure Zuko got home okay, but...he was saying some stuff that I didn’t really understand. It had something to do with how you two grew up, I think. I guess I was also sort of hoping that you could help him.”

Azula laughed, but she could hear the twinge of regret in her own voice. “I wish. But I...I’m not exactly a ‘helping’ type. Plus, I doubt Zuko wants to even look at me right now. Not while he’s this vulnerable. I’ll just give him some space.”

Ty Lee looked at Zuko for a second, then back to Azula. “Okay. But...you could try to help him. You never know. A little kindness can go a long way.”

A little of *anything* had never been enough for Azula growing up, but she supposed she could try. She turned to Ty Lee. “Thank you for bringing Zuko here. You’re...you’re a really good person. A genuinely good one. I haven’t met a lot of people like you.” In the air, she could feel her fingers tingling. Looking down, she saw that her hand had moved. Her fingers were now only mere inches from Ty Lee’s.

Ty Lee nodded. Her usual huge smile was gone, and replaced by a smaller one that seemed more... *real* somehow. “Anytime, Azula.” Their fingers hung in the air for a second, then, laughing a little awkwardly, Ty Lee slowly drew hers away. “Call me, okay? I’d like to see you again.”

Azula nodded, unable to say anything else. Ty Lee waved to her one last time and disappeared down the stairs, leaving Azula standing in the doorway with her hand still suspended in midair.

She turned to Zuko, who seemed to be staring at the ceiling. His eyes were still glassy, and Azula thought it might be better just to let him sleep. But she couldn’t get Ty Lee’s words out of her brain. So instead, she went and perched on the arm of the sofa.

“You hate the taste of alcohol.”

Zuko stared up at her, his eyes wide and a little out of focus. “No I don’t.” His words were slurred, but Azula had no trouble understanding him.

She sighed. “Yes, you do. You have ever since we were children and went to one of Father’s parties and he made us try champagne. So tell me, why would you drink so much of something you hate?”

Well, this probably wasn’t the kind exterior that Ty Lee had pictured, but it was all Azula could really think of.

“Already told Ty Lee,” mumbled Zuko. “I deserve it.”

Azula’s eyes widened. Of all the answers that Zuko could have possibly given, she had not been expecting that. “And why might that be?”

“Because I’m a failure.” Zuko’s voice was light because of the alcohol, but Azula could hear the emotion underneath. “I’m failing this case, just like I failed everything else. Thought this could be a way out of Father’s life...but I just fail more. I failed Father, failed Mother, I failed you.” His head flopped over the side of the sofa, and Azula had to catch it before he banged it on the floor. “I fail everything.”

Azula sighed, lowering herself onto the rug so that she was sitting on the floor, perpendicular to the arm of the sofa. “Failure is relative, do you know that?”

Zuko stared at her, his eyes still out of focus. “Huh?”

She paused. “I mean that failure is only what you define as failure. You can pretend all you want, but you only think you’re a failure because our father said so.”

“Well *you* only think you’re so great because he said so.” Zuko raised his arm and pointed shakily at her, nearly poking her in the eye. She smiled sadly and stared at the floor.

“Believe me, I’m not so great.”

This seemed to surprise Zuko. “Huh?”

Azula was going to regret this. This much openness, to a person who was so weak they couldn’t even control what they said. Father would have her killed if he knew.

“But Zuko, you were never a failure. All our lives, Father told us a story. A story where manipulation and cruelty were the only way to succeed, where nothing was acceptable except perfection in every skill, and love and compassion were weaknesses.”

“That’s everything you believe.”

Zuko’s words stung, but this wasn’t the time to think about that. “You’re right, it is. Because I let it. But you never did. You were the only one strong enough to *resist* Father. You never let what he said define you. You decided for yourself who you wanted to be, where you wanted to go, what you wanted to do with your life.” She laughed softly. “Sometimes I wish I could have been more like you. Strong enough to be *human* .”

She turned and looked Zuko right in the eyes. “You were never the failure, Zuko. You never failed me. *I* failed *you* . I wasn’t strong enough to protect you from Father, and I was *never* strong enough to resist him.”

She still wasn’t strong enough. Not strong enough to tell him her secret. Her last secret. She wasn’t even strong enough to admit it to herself.

Soft snoring was coming from the sofa. Azula glanced over and realized that Zuko had fallen asleep. He probably wouldn’t remember anything she’d said in the morning.

What did it matter? Would he see her any differently if he did *remember* ? No matter how much she tried to help Zuko, she could never be compassionate or naturally loveable like he was. She was their father’s daughter, and she wished so much sometimes that it wasn’t too late for her. If only.

But spending time with Zuko made her feel like there was still some sort of hope left. Despite his stupidity and recklessness, his tendency to do things like get so drunk that he confessed his darkest secrets to the sister he despised, Azula still felt a connection with him. She was going to do whatever it took to protect him. It was what she should have done a long time ago.

Her desire to protect...was that love? Azula doubted it. She doubted she was even capable of love.

But Zuko was. And she would make sure that he didn’t lose hope in the people who loved him.

Grabbing a blanket from a nearby chair, she threw it over Zuko’s sleeping body as gently as she could, flipped the light switch, and left Zuko lying peacefully in the darkness.

## Chapter 15: Sing a Song of Sixpence

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

As Katara and Sokka return to Ba Sing Se, Zuko deals with the consequences of the previous night, and the group forms a new theory.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Mentions of drinking.

Another chapter is here! Some of you have been writing really lovely comments recently, and it's totally made my day every time, so thank you so much! I hope y'all enjoy this one, too:)

### Text

Zuko woke up with a pounding head, the light of his living room suddenly seeming *really* bright. Groaning, he rolled over on the sofa and almost fell onto the floor. He sat up, trying to blink the brightness out of his eyes. As his vision cleared, he saw Azula perched on the armchair next to him, reading her book. She glanced up.

“Oh, good, you’re awake.” She grabbed the mug of coffee sitting next to her and slid it across the table. “Drink this. It’ll help you feel less like a walking disaster.”

Zuko shoved the coffee away. “Coffee makes me sick. Besides, how would you know?”

Azula laughed. “Please, Zuko, you think I never ever got tangled up in some trouble during high school? I was just exceptional at hiding it.”

Zuko sighed and drank the coffee. It was probably the most bitter thing he had ever tasted in his entire life. “Why is everything so blurry? Ugh, I haven’t felt this shitty in a really long time.” He stretched his arms, trying to keep his tone light and look more confident than he felt.

Azula stared at her shoes. She looked...nervous. Even in his slightly hazy state, Zuko was surprised. He wasn’t used to seeing her that way...well, *ever* .

“Zuko...how much about last night do you remember?”

Fear coursed through Zuko’s veins. What had Azula done? Had she hurt him? His friends? His uncle? What could she have done that she wouldn’t want him to know? What could he have possibly forgotten?

But as he thought, the memories of the night before started coming back to him. Not in complete detail, but he remembered getting drunk, and Ty Lee getting him home, and…

He turned to Azula. “You helped me last night.”

Azula looked away. “Not really. I simply tried to entertain you until you fell asleep.”

More memories were flooding back to Zuko, though he couldn’t quite remember the specifics. “You did help me. You... *talked* to me. You were *honest* with me.” The words felt so strange in his mouth. Hell, he’d spent his whole childhood just muttering the words *Azula always lies* .

Azula’s eyes were wide, and she was fiddling her fingers, just like Zuko sometimes did when he was feeling anxious. “Do you...remember what I said?”

Zuko stretched deep into his brain, but there were places where there was just a black cloud where his memories should have been. “Something about failure, something about resistance, but exactly? No.” He sighed. “Doesn’t seem fair. You probably remember every stupid thing *I* said.”

“I won’t hold it against you.”

Zuko blinked. Even though his sister’s surprising compassion was becoming more and more frequent, it still caught him off guard. “Really?”

“You may not remember, but you didn’t actually say anything that stupid. And what you *did* say…” she laughed softly, “well, I can see where it came from.”

A memory flashed through Zuko’s head. Words that belonged to his sister. *I wasn’t strong enough* *to protect you from Father, and I was never strong enough to resist him.*

Was that how Azula truly saw herself? As weak? As never good enough?

Zuko didn’t really know what to think about that. His head still ached, and he could barely think at all.

But...Azula had helped him, and she hadn’t needed to. It was starting to seem like she really did have some semblance of good in her, however strange it was. Maybe it was worth thinking about more, once he could think clearly again.

Azula was still staring at her shoes. Zuko reached over and tapped her on the wrist, a gesture that made her nearly jump out of her chair.

“Thank you.”

Azula blinked. “Whatever for?”

“For helping me last night when you didn’t have to.”

Azula laughed bitterly. “You *are* giving me shelter. It wasn’t as though I could leave you wallowing in sorrow.” She got up, probably to get herself more coffee, but paused before she could leave the room. “But...I’m glad you’re safe. I don’t know how much of what I said you remember, but those thoughts about failure...they only stop you from achieving your goals. You can’t find justice for others if you’re plagued with self-doubt.”

She disappeared into the other room. Since when did Azula give *advice* ?

Zuko groaned as he went to the kitchen and started sipping tea. Azula had been right about the coffee: it *had* helped. But it was still absolutely disgusting, so Zuko would happily take tea any day.

There was a knock at the door, and both siblings went to answer it. There stood Katara and Sokka, both looking a little tired (probably from the long train ride they’d had.) Katara instantly pulled him into a hug, then moved onto Azula, who accepted the hug but looked absolutely bewildered, standing stiff as a board.

Sokka stayed in the doorway, looking at Zuko rather nervously. Zuko swallowed. Should they hug? Shake hands? High-five? Do that weird pat on the back thing that he’d seen boys doing?

Hesitantly, he opened his arms, and he and Sokka slowly walked towards one another, both sort of wrapping their arms around each other but also not bending their arms either. When they came out of the...whatever it was, Zuko turned and looked Sokka in the eye. Neither of them knew what to say.

It was only Azula and Katara’s giggling from behind them that made Zuko realize that they’d just been staring into each other’s eyes for at least ten seconds, looking like idiots. Zuko hurriedly looked at the floor, laughing nervously. “It’s...good to see you.”

“Yeah,” said Sokka, also nervously, “you too.”

More laughter came from behind him. Zuko turned to the two girls. “Will you two just shut up?”

They did not shut up.

The four of them eventually sat down on the sofa, and began relaying the events of the day before. Zuko realized that he hadn’t known anything about Azula’s adventures with the Dai Li, and was both surprised and not surprised at all that she had managed to make some allies.

Sokka’s mouth dropped open as he told the story of his day in the White Lotus, purposely leaving out the part where he got drunk and made a fool of himself. “Dude! We’re gone for *one day* and you manage to get yourself stuck in the closet?!” He shrugged. “Oh well! Guess we’ll just have to stick around more!” Zuko laughed, even though Sokka’s joke wasn’t actually very funny. Across the coffee table, he saw Azula and Katara make eye contact and giggle again.

Ignoring them, he turned back to Sokka. “So, how was your day with your dad?”

Sokka grinned. “It was good! We haven’t seen him since last summer, so it was nice to be home again!”

Katara smiled, too. “He gave Sokka *combat* lessons.”

Zuko’s eyes widened, impressed. “Really? What does your dad do again?”

Sokka’s face darkened. “He owns our family’s food market, but he used to be in the army when he was younger. That’s how he knows how to fight.”

“So,” interjected Azula, “did you learn a lot?”

Sokka shrugged. “A few things, I guess.”

Azula turned to Katara. “With that spirit of yours, I’m surprised *you* weren’t getting fighting lessons.”

Katara laughed. “I’ve already had them a few times. Nothing much.”

Sokka wiggled his eyebrows. “ *Someone* was too busy preparing for an interview with *Yue* .”

The whole group laughed as Katara’s face darkened at least three shades. “It’s not...that isn’t...ugh!” She couldn’t stop their laughter, but was saved when her phone pinged.

Sokka smirked. “And who might that be?”

Katara’s face was still flushed. “No one,” she muttered. “But...I do need to go, for...reasons completely unrelated to Yue. And I’m taking my interview notebook for...no reason in particular. So...yeah, I’m gonna go now.” Still blushing and clutching her notebook to her chest, Katara practically ran out the door with a panicked “See you later!”

Sokka, still laughing, turned to Azula and Zuko. “She’s going to meet Yue.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “What a brilliant deduction. We wouldn’t have guessed that at *all* .”

Sokka turned to Zuko, who could only shrug. “We *are* detectives.”

Sokka laughed. “Fair enough. But it is nice to see her so happy.” He looked at Zuko. “I’d like to see *you* crack a smile like that for once.”

For some reason, this caused Azula to burst out laughing.

Zuko ignored her and crossed the room to the clue board. “That doesn’t change the fact that we have work to do. With all of these new allies, we have more opportunities to access the White Lotus and Dai Li headquarters. We should use them.” He turned to Sokka and Azula. “Any ideas?”

Azula’s eyes darted towards the Dai Li half of the board. “I didn’t get a chance to investigate the murder scene more closely yesterday before the Dai Li led me away. If I could get back there, maybe I could figure something out. Suki could probably get me in.”

“Hold up,” said Zuko. He still felt bad for leaving her alone with the Dai Li yesterday, and for getting drunk and forcing her to help him. “You’re not going there alone again. The last time we split up like this, I got locked in a closet, and you ended up under a pile of corpses.”

“That was yesterday, Zuko. I do remember.”

“She won’t go alone,” came Sokka’s voice from the other side of the room. “I’m an expert at analyzing murder scenes. I’ll go with her.”

“And what am I supposed to do?” Zuko’s voice came out a little more angry than he’d wanted it to. “Just sit here and wait for you guys?”

“Well…” Sokka looked guilty. “Yeah, I guess.”

Azula met his eyes, and nodded towards the coffee pot on the table. Her message was clear: *you’re* *still a mess.* To be fair, she wasn’t completely wrong. His head was throbbing, but he was used to working with a throbbing head. On the other hand, now that he had all of these allies, he didn’t *have* to anymore. It was an odd feeling.

“We’ll need someone here in case this goes wrong,” said Azula, holding up her phone. “It *is* the Dai Li, after all.”

Zuko sighed, slumping back onto the sofa. He hated feeling useless, especially when his sister and his best friend were out being useful.

Sokka threw him one last guilty glance as they headed out the door.

Katara almost couldn’t believe where she was sitting. Yue’s bedroom was easily the largest bedroom she had ever seen in her entire life. It was also breathtakingly gorgeous; everything was covered in white, pale blue, and silver. Katara was almost worried that she was going to get dirt on something and ruin the entire room. She and Yue were sitting on a plush sofa cushion that was large enough to be a chair. Katara had her notebook and pen at the ready, though she was a little worried about getting ink on the furniture.

Yue looked a little nervous. Katara reached out and placed her hand on her shoulder. “Hey, if you don’t want to do this, you don’t have to.”

Yue offered her a small smile. “I *do* want to do this, Katara. I’ve just never done an interview or anything like this before. That’s all.”

“You’ll be great. I know it.”

Yue’s face darkened a shade. “Thank you.”

Not really knowing where to start, Katara cleared her throat, attempting to sound somewhat professional, but she and Yue just ended up giggling instead.

“So,” Katara began, still laughing, “Yue, how did you end up as part of the White Lotus?”

Yue leaned backwards into the wall. “I was born and raised here. My father was a member, and when he was busy working, Pakku cared for me, and he was a member, too. It was pretty inevitable that I’d grow up to be a member as well.”

Katara nodded. “Are you officially a member yet?”

Yue shook her head. “You have to be initiated by the group and be a devoted citizen to Ba Sing Se and meet a bunch of other criteria. I’m still just a kid to them. But I’ll be a member one day.”

Katara raised an eyebrow. “And do you *want* to be a member?”

Yue nodded, then paused, shook her head, then nodded again. “I guess I do. I mean, there’s nowhere else for me to go. The White Lotus is my home, my family. I have duties to them that I can’t just...not fulfill.”

“Wanting to do something and not having any other options are two different things.” Katara had put her notebook down at this point. She was just worried about her friend.

Yue shrugged. “I guess. I don’t really know. I’ve never *wanted* anything before.” Her gaze drifted upwards and her eyes met Katara’s. “Until now.”

Katara ignored the heat that was quickly rising through her face. “Yue, if living here is making you unhappy, you shouldn’t have to.”

“But it’s not!” cried Yue. “I’m just confused! This is my family, my life! Right here! Just because there are things about it that I don’t like doesn’t mean I should just abandon it!”

Katara dropped her voice. “What about this life don’t you like? Can I help at all?”

Yue sighed. “It’s just...it’s not always easy being on a pedestal. We’re not like the Dai Li, we never try to hide from the spotlight, but because we’re in the spotlight, we just have to be so... *composed* all the time. It’s like we can’t say anything but what’s *perfect* . So nobody ever shows any emotion, and nobody ever talks about anything. Everyone’s always sharing glances and disappearing into random corners of the house. It’s like they’re all hiding something, but none of them are allowed to talk about anything, and I feel that weight, too, I’m not even allowed to be saying what I’m saying right now!” She took a deep breath. “It’s just... *exhausting* .” She glanced up at Katara, who was staring at her in shock. “Oh gosh, I’m sorry! That was way too much information! I didn’t mean to overwhelm…”

She was interrupted as Katara pulled her into a tight hug and didn’t let go.

Suki sighed as she guided Sokka and Azula through the hallways of the Dai Li headquarters. “You know, I offered to help you out, but if you keep coming here every day, you will be in *big* trouble, and I won’t be able to do anything about it.”

Azula sighed. “Look, we just need to get a look at the crime scene, and then we won’t be back for a while. We won’t put you, or ourselves, in danger. I promise.”

Suki sighed. She wanted to protect Kyoshi’s legacy, but she had a feeling that this whole detective business wasn’t going to end well. The Dai Li had more power than any other organization in the world. These teenagers didn’t stand a chance against them.

She didn’t even really know why she was helping them. It would only end badly for her.

Maybe it was because she felt like Kyoshi would want her too.

They came to the head of the corridor where the murder had been committed. “All right,” said Suki. “Here we are. I’m not sure we’ll find anything, but investigate all you like.” She glanced around to make sure no one was following them. “I’m gonna stay here to make sure nobody follows you. The hallway’s a dead end, so you don’t need to worry about anyone coming from the other side.”

Sokka nodded. “Thanks,” he said, as he and Azula disappeared into the hallway. Suki groaned as they walked away. Was she in over her head?

“You are,” said a voice from beside her.

Crap. Had she said that out loud? Or was she just going crazy?

She turned and thrust out her fan, ready to fight, but it was only Mai, standing there and looking bored as usual. She groaned. “What are *you* doing here?”

Mai leaned against the wall. “I’m solving this mystery too. I wanted to see what was going on.”

“Like hell you do. You’re not interested in anything. I don’t even know why you’re here.”

Mai raised an eyebrow. “I may not be crazy, but I like adventure just as much as anyone else.”

“You sure have a funny way of showing it.”

“Right, because acting like a bubbly idiot is so much better.” Mai rolled her eyes. “Why do you get to ask me why I’m here anyway? Why are *you* here? Aren’t you little miss ‘loyal to the Dai Li always and forever?’”

Suki crossed her arms and turned away. “What do you care? You don’t care if I betray the Dai Li. Even though they do nothing but good things for you, you hate them!”

Mai placed her hands on her hips. “You think they do good things for me? How stupid are you? Not everyone gets to be the Dai Li’s princess, you know. Some of us just get pushed to the side and told to stay quiet, with nothing to do.” She paused, noticing how Suki was staring at her. “It’s just really boring,” she added, looking away.

Was what she was saying true? Suki knew that the Dai Li was strict, but they would never treat anyone the way Mai was describing, right?

*Of course not* , she reasoned. This was *Mai* . Mai was never happy about anything. Ever.

“You’re just ungrateful,” spat Suki. “You have no idea how lucky you are.”

“Funny,” muttered Mai. “I was about to say the same to you.”

Sokka glanced over his shoulder as he followed Azula down the hall. “Think she’ll be okay?”

“Suki?” Azula laughed. “I pity anyone who tries to attack her.”

Sokka rubbed the back of his neck nervously. Azula paused, turning to face him. “Okay, what’s wrong?”

Sokka sighed. “I just feel...like I’m in over my head. This is all getting to be so much. You and Zuko could have both been *killed* yesterday. We’re all just teenagers, and we’re getting more and more involved with these murders. I just feel like it’s going to end badly for all of us.”

Azula used her phone as a light to shine further into the darkness as she kept walking. “Honestly? I see your point. But why not us? We’re all smart, determined, clever, none of us are pushovers, and the White Lotus and the Dai Li aren’t manipulating us. There’s no one *better* than us.”

“Easy for you to say.”

Azula whirled around. “What’s that supposed to mean?”

Sokka sighed. “Just that you and Zuko are like...actual detectives, or at least totally act like them, and I’m just a student.” He stared at the floor.

Azula sighed. “Sokka, do you know how I always formed groups when I was forced to do group projects in high school?”

“No?”

Azula placed her hands on her hips. “I didn’t always choose all of the best students in the class. I chose students with a range of specific skills that could help make the project the best that it could be.”

“And your point is?”

Azula sighed. “I swear, you can be just as stupid as my brother. My *point* is, so what if you’re not a detective? The skills that you bring to the table are more important. You can investigate crime scenes, you’re clever and occasionally somewhat funny, and your absurd loyalty to my brother means that he can always count on you. True teams aren’t made of copies of the same person; they’re made of members with a variety of skills that come together to create an impeccable team.”

Sokka blinked. “That’s...actually really good advice. Never pegged you for the advice-giving type.”

“Trust me, I’m not. I’m only telling you the facts that are blatantly obvious but you’re too stupid to see.” She paused, thrusting her hand in front of him. “We’re here.”

They were standing in front of an ordinary looking closet. Sokka hadn’t seen the corpses the day before, but obviously, someone had cleared them all out. Azula began to walk in. “The air shouldn’t be poisonous anymore.”

“ *Shouldn’t* ?!” Sokka did *not* have a good feeling about this, but he followed her anyway. As he entered the closet, a detail on the lock caught his eye. “Azula, look at this.”

She turned and examined the lock. “A gear in the lock. Clever.” She pulled it out and examined it. “I used to use these to play tricks on Zuko growing up. They allow the door to open and shut, but once it’s closed, the gear gets stuck, and the door can only be opened from the outside.”

“Whoever planned this knew what they were doing.”

“Clearly.” Azula shone the light from her phone around the dark closet.

“There,” said Sokka, pointing to an air vent on the wall. “Whoever killed these people must have come in through the vents.”

“That would be incredibly difficult,” mused Azula. “I imagine the vents in this place are a labyrinth, just like the rest of it.”

Sokka felt the thoughts racing through his brain. The gear in the lock, the trip through the vents, the fact that the killer had somehow managed to get their hands on some sort of fluorine gun, and with the other murders, the precision with which the killer had shoved Fung off a balcony, killed Pakku with a thrown knife...it all added up to the same conclusion. “This murder is too elaborate for an amateur. It had to be someone with more experience.”

Azula stared blankly at him. “Such as…”

Sokka snapped his fingers. “Such as an assassin!”

“Let me get this straight,” said Zuko into his phone, as he walked through the streets. “Why do you want me to go to the Mayor’s office? He’s *really* mad at us!”

“What we found could change the direction of the entire investigation,” said Sokka from the other end of the phone. “The police won’t listen to us, but they will listen to the Mayor. We can’t get back fast enough, but Suki said that Long Feng was at the Dai Li headquarters! Maybe you can get to the Mayor before Long Feng starts whispering in his ear again!”

“Got it,” said Zuko, quickly hanging up as he began to sprint. He was only a block away from City Hall, but it was windy enough that his hair and coat were flapping around even before he started to run. By the time he actually *got* to City Hall, he looked like he’d been attacked by a leaf blower. Barely stopping to catch his breath, he raced up the stairs and burst into the Mayor’s office.

Luckily, the Mayor wasn’t in a meeting, but he still looked infuriated. “Young man, what are you doing here? I thought I told you not to come here!”

Zuko doubled over, panting. “I know, Mr. Mayor, but I have important information about the recent murders!”

Kuei leaned back in his chair, giggling. He was *so* weird. “Ooh, and what might that be?”

Zuko was still panting. “Mr. Mayor,” he began.

“Call me Kuei!”

“Kuei, these murders have all been too neat to be performed by someone who’s never killed before! Think about the precision with which Pakku’s killer hit him with a knife, or how Fung’s killer pushed him off a balcony with hardly any struggle! Whoever murdered all of those Dai Li soldiers knew how to get their hands on an *incredibly* dangerous weapon, find their way through the vents of the Dai Li headquarters, and lock a door from the inside only! They were clearly very experienced.”

Kuei leaned forward, his eyebrow raised, his attention clearly sparked. “What exactly do you mean by this?”

Zuko stood up straight. “Mr. Mayor, my friends and I believe that all of these people have been murdered by one killer; an experienced assassin.”

Kuei stroked his chin. “Interesting...a very reasonable conclusion. Yes, that *does* make sense!”

Zuko smiled. “Great! So, if you could just tell the police, then this investigation could finally get going in the right direction, and…”

He was interrupted by the ringing of the phone on Kuei’s desk.

Kuei picked it up. “Hello?” His eyes grew wide. “Long Fe...I mean, no, I do not recognize the person who is calling me.”

Zuko groaned inwardly. This couldn’t be good.  
“No, I absolutely haven’t been listening to those detectives! Whatever gave you that idea?” A pause. “I swear, I wasn’t…” he was interrupted. Then his expression turned fearful. “No, I know the consequences. You don’t need to tell me again.” Another pause. Then, “Thank you for your sage council.” He slowly placed the phone back down on the desk.

Zuko took a deep breath. “As I was saying…”

“Stop.” The Mayor’s voice was cold. “I am lucky that my advisor called when he did. You are not welcome around me, or the Dai Li. Your *theories* are not welcome here.”

“But…”

“I’ve heard enough.” The Mayor tried to push himself off of his chair, but the chair was on wheels, so it rolled out from under him. He slipped and landed flat on top of his desk, squishing his face and raising his hand in the air. “Now, leave City Hall and don’t even think about coming back unless you can bring me a *specific* name.”

Zuko walked out of the office and onto the front steps of City Hall silently, the cold wind still blowing through his hair. It didn’t matter what the Mayor said: Zuko had a lead now. He was going to follow it, and soon, he’d be back in City Hall, with the name of a killer.
