## Chapter 16: Harlequin's Lane

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula, Ty Lee, Sokka, and Zuko take a trip into a dangerous part of town, and encounter more than a few unusual adversaries along the way.

#### Chapter Notes

I'm back! Sorry for being absent the last two days. As you know, I was moving. I missed y'all!

This is one of my favorite chapters, and it's extra long, so hopefully that makes up for the delay a little bit.  
This chapter features a lot of cameos!  
TW: Poison, knives, drinking.  
Happy reading!

### Text

The group woke up the next morning to find that it was pouring rain. For some reason, this seemed to upset Azula greatly, and she kept glaring at the raindrops on the windows while she was drinking her coffee.

“I don’t see the big deal,” said Sokka, who had come over early that morning. “Aren’t you, like, supposed to be super adaptable? Work hard, rain or shine, and all that?”

Ty Lee, whom Zuko had also called that morning, nodded from across the table. Like Zuko, she had declined Azula’s (very strong) coffee in favor of tea. “Sokka’s right, Azula. From what I’ve seen of you, you can succeed in any situation. What’s bothering you?”

Azula’s face flushed as she stared very intensely at the salt and pepper shakers on the table. “I...didn’t pack a raincoat,” she muttered, looking more irritated by the second.

Zuko blinked. “That’s all? Why didn’t you just say so? I have one from a couple of years ago that should fit you.”

“It’s not that,” said Azula, rolling her eyes. “The fact that I wasn’t completely prepared is just pathetic. It’s embarrassing.”

“No it’s not!” chimed in Ty Lee. “Everybody forgets stuff sometimes! I can’t remember the last time I went on a trip and actually remembered everything I needed to pack.”

“Well,” said Azula, sighing as she sipped her coffee, “things were a little different in my house.”

Thankfully, Ty Lee didn’t press her any more, which Zuko was glad about. They had a long day ahead of them, and didn’t have time to rehash any of Azula and Zuko’s...interesting childhood. He was sure they would have *plenty* of time for that later.

He turned to Azula. “Well, I have a raincoat you can borrow if you need one.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “I am *not* wearing any raincoat that *you* give me.”

Thunder crackled outside, and the rain drummed even harder on the windows. Zuko turned and glanced at his sister, who sighed. “I’m going to need more coffee for this.”

Ten minutes later, Azula emerged, her hair out of its topknot for the first time in a while, instead mostly hanging loosely around her shoulders, with a small portion of it sectioned off into a half-ponytail. She wore a trench coat that matched Zuko’s, but instead of brown, it was bright red. The coat fit her like a glove. She actually looked pretty, though Zuko would never tell her that in a million years.

“Wow, Azula!” said Ty Lee, her eyes wide and her face flushed. “You look like a badass detective from some sort of old movie! Only better!”

Azula turned and looked in the mirror. She did not look anywhere near as thrilled as Ty Lee. “I look *ridiculous* .”

“But that red looks so pretty on you!”

“It looks like a costume!” Azula sighed, putting her hands in her pockets. Zuko had never seen her so nervous about what she was wearing. It was strange.

He checked his watch. “The train to the Lower Ring’s leaving soon. We’d better get going.”

As the four of them filed out of the apartment, Zuko grabbed his sister’s wrist. “Hey, what’s the big deal about the coat? You’re all about practicality; I didn’t really think you’d care.”

Azula sighed. “Sorry, Zuko. It was nice of you to lend me your coat. I’m just not used to being unable to control every single thing I wear, and not perfecting every little touch before I go out the door.” She ran her hand through her hair. “I can’t even remember the last time I wore it like this.”

Zuko sighed. “Not that it matters what I say, but...I think you look more like yourself than you have in a while.”

She blinked, then gave him a small smile. “I suppose it isn’t the worst thing in the world.”

“Hey, guys!” called Sokka from the bottom of the steps. “Are you coming?”

After a train ride to the Lower Ring, the four teenagers stood at the end of a cobblestone street, surrounded by tall, narrow buildings that seemed to be falling over. Signs hung haphazardly from several doorways, and smoke was even pouring out of some of the windows. The street was full of people. Even from where she stood, Azula could see some of them carrying guns, swords, knives, all sorts of things. She was grateful for the dagger in her pocket.

“Where are we?” asked Ty Lee, staring openly at every single person who passed them by. Some of them were glaring at her already. Azula felt her grip tighten on the dagger in her pocket.

Zuko turned around. “Welcome to Assassin’s Lane.”

Sokka smirked. “No way.”

“Well, that’s not technically it’s name, but everyone calls it that.”

“I see,” said Azula. “And what is it?”

“Every detective in the city knows about it,” said Zuko. “This is where assassins come to do their business, and to make deals with each other. If it was really an assassin who killed all of those people, they’ll be here.”

Sokka stared at the crowd of assassins. “We should split up,” he said. “We’ll definitely be able to find more people that way.”

Ty Lee fiddled with her braid. “I dunno,” she mumbled. “This seems like the sort of place in a mystery movie where the crew splits up, and then at least one of them gets kidnapped and they all regret splitting up in the first place.”

Azula could practically see Zuko weighing the options in his head: stay safe, or take a risk. Of course, it was Zuko. It was evident what his final choice would be.

Zuko turned to Ty Lee. “You can go with my sister. I’m sure you two are perfectly capable of protecting one another.”

Ty Lee’s eyes drifted over to meet Azula’s, and Azula broke her gaze away and stared at the ground. Friendship with Ty Lee was...confusing, and Azula did not need that while she was investigating a street full of assassins. She would just have to stay focused.

Ty Lee turned to Sokka and Zuko. “But what about you guys? Will you be okay?”

Sokka grinned, awkwardly throwing his arm around Zuko, but pulling it away just as quickly when Zuko’s face turned bright red in response. Azula sighed. *Idiots* . “I think the two of us will be just fine.”

The two pairs set off on opposite sides of the narrow street, and soon, Azula had lost sight of the others altogether.

Zuko was strolling through the crowd like a movie character: quickly and confidently, like he completely belonged in the crowd of assassins. Sokka practically had to run to keep up with him.

“Hey, slow down!”

To Sokka’s relief, Zuko did slow down. “Sorry,” he muttered. “We always walked really fast in my family while I was growing up. Something about the optimization of time and all that. Sometimes I forget.”

Sokka stared at the cobblestones. He never knew what to say when Zuko brought up his family. He didn’t know the whole story; no one did, but he did know that his childhood had been the opposite of pleasant. When Zuko mentioned it, he never knew if it was an invitation to talk more, or maybe the exact opposite.

Zuko tapped him on the shoulder. “Hey, don’t just stand there staring at the ground. You look like a walrus with your mouth open like that.” Realizing what he’d said, he looked away, but Sokka just laughed.

“I’ve always thought of myself as more of the...ferocious intimidating polar bear type.”

A small smile crept up the sides of Zuko’s face. “A polar bear? In your dreams.”

“Hey! I can be *very* intimidating and fear-inducing when I want to be.”

Zuko rolled his eyes, but he was still smiling. “Sure you can.”

“The polar bear is my spirit animal, Zuko! It’s *very* important to me!”

Zuko smirked. “Right. And what’s *my* spirit animal?”

Sokka paused and stared at Zuko for a moment. “A dragon,” he said, the lighter tone disappearing from his voice.

Zuko turned and looked back at him. “You think I'm that scary?”

Sokka looked away. “More like powerful.”

There was a moment of silence before Zuko turned and looked into the nearest building, which was bright orange and did not look particularly intimidating. “Well, let’s see if we’re ferocious and powerful enough to survive this house.”

Sokka smiled. “I have a feeling we are.”

They walked in, and a bell sounded over the door. A man appeared from behind the desk. He was old and wiry, with white hair that stuck out of his ears in triangles, and a triangular white beard. He also wore a strange hat, which was red and floppy, and a smile, which was an odd trait in someone living on Assassin’s Lane.

“Howdy there!” Chirped the man. “The name’s Dock! What can I do for ya?”

Sokka narrowed his eyes, attempting to look professional and intimidating. He had no idea if it was working or not. “That depends. What can you do for other people?”

“Me?” Laughed Dock. “Nothing at all! Nothing important, anyway.”

Zuko pulled a gold coin out of his pocket and began tossing it in the air. “That’s funny. I just happened to have this on me, but only if someone has the right skills.”

This seemed to interest Dock greatly, and he leaned forward. “What sort of skills do you need?”

Sokka caught Zuko’s eye and smirked. He saw what was going on. “Well, that depends. What sort of skills do you have?”

Dock looked around to make sure nobody was watching, then leaned forward. “I work at the docks! I have a boat service that goes by night through the canals of Ba Sing Se! I can get people from ring to ring, and the police are none the wiser.”

Sokka tapped his chin. “Hmmm...not exactly what we’re looking for.” He turned to leave.

“Wait!” cried Dock. “Maybe one of my brothers will have the skills you’re looking for!” He ducked under the table, then reappeared a second later, this time wearing a pale yellow hat. Sokka blinked, surprised.

“Howdy there!” said the man who was probably Dock. “The name’s Xu! My brother says you’re looking for some special skills!”

“That depends,” said Zuko. “What can you do?”

“Well, I sell weapons, of course!” said Xu.

Sokka raised an eyebrow. A weapons seller could have sold the weird fluorine gun to whatever assassin had murdered the Dai Li soldiers. “What *kind* of weapons?”

Xu rummaged beneath the desk and pulled out a tray. On the tray were two butter knives and a fork, all of them rusty and dull. “This kind of weapons!”

Sokka sighed. This was definitely not the guy they were looking for. Whoever had killed the Dai Li soldiers definitely hadn’t used a *fork* .

They both turned to leave, but Xu leaped in front of them before they could leave, holding out one of the rusty butter knives and dropping his voice so that it sounded scarier (at least, that was what he was trying to do.) “Remember that I carry weapons! What you hear on Assassin’s Lane…”

“Stays in Assassin’s Lane,” finished Zuko. “Believe me, I know this place like the back of my hand.” For dramatic effect, he tossed his bangs into the air.

He looked awesome...sort of ridiculous, but definitely awesome.

They left the orange shop and entered the crowd again. “Isn’t this kinda pointless?” said Sokka. “There must be at least five hundred people here, probably more. We’re never going to be able to get through all of them.”

“We just have to follow the crowd,” said Zuko, his eyes darting from person to person, scanning everyone around them. “We’ll find the sort of people we’re looking for.”

Sokka sighed. “If you say so,” and followed him.

Azula and Ty Lee quickly fell into an easy rhythm as they walked down the street. People occasionally came up to them, clearly seeing two young-looking girls and getting the wrong idea. Azula glared at each and every one, and most of them went away after that. If they didn’t, Ty Lee would give them a friendly wave, do a literal backflip, and “accidentally” kick them in the shoulder.

The crowd left them alone after that.

Ty Lee laughed and grabbed Azula’s hand, pulling her down the street. “This is so fun!”

Azula laughed, slightly bewildered. “We’re marching down a street full of murderers and criminals. I can’t see how this is fun.”

“Not that, silly!” Ty Lee pulled her even further. Azula, not used to running on cobblestones, had to struggle to keep up. “I like spending time with you!”

Azula blinked, surprised. Ty Lee had said stuff like this before, but she supposed the real meaning of it hadn’t quite sunk in until now.

Azula hadn’t had friends growing up, hell, she’d barely left the house as a child. The only person she’d ever known who was the ‘friendly’ type was her mother, and her mother had clearly been bothered by something in her from the time she was a child. Her father had loved her, if she met his expectations, but he had never been her friend, he had only loved her as an intelligent business partner, the perfect copy of himself that he’d always wanted to see.

Azula had always assumed that she was naturally built for cutthroat business, and was simply the kind of person that wasn’t meant to have friends. But hearing Ty Lee say she actually liked spending time with her, well...it made her think a lot more than it would have for someone else.

She realized that she’d frozen in the middle of the street, and felt her face flush. Ty Lee was staring at her. “Hey, are you okay?”

Azula fidgeted with her half-ponytail. “Yes, I am. Of course I am. I’m just...not used to hearing stuff like that.” She hoped that would be the end of it, but Ty Lee clearly wasn’t having it.

“What do you mean? That’s just what you say to your friends!”

“Well, I’m not exactly the kind of person who *has* friends!” snapped Azula. In her hurt, her voice came out more bitterly than she had intended. She instantly looked away, blushing and ashamed.

Ty Lee didn’t seem upset, though. Her hand, which had been hanging on its own in the air, slowly drifted towards Azula’s. Azula let out a small gasp of surprise as Ty Lee’s fingers wove themselves in between her own. She looked up into Ty Lee’s eyes. She was smiling. “ *I’m* your friend.”

Azula laughed, not knowing what else to say. “Well, I must say, I can’t really imagine why. In case you haven’t noticed, I don’t exactly make the best conversation partner.”

Ty Lee laughed. “Azula, that’s not what matters. You don’t have to be the perfect friend to be a friend, you just have to try, and to care about the person you’re friends with. And I...I can tell you’re trying. That’s all I care about.”

Azula felt her face grow hot again, but the rain helped cool it off. “Thank you, Ty Lee. I...don’t know how I managed to be so lucky as to have a friend like you.”

Ty Lee smiled. “Believe it or not, I didn’t have a lot of friends growing up.”

Azula’s mouth dropped open. Ty Lee was the epitome of the perfect friend: charming, understanding, bubbly, kind. What more could anyone want? “But that’s impossible! What was *wrong* with everyone?”

Ty Lee’s face turned pink. “Well, everyone always tended to go with my sisters. They were older, better-looking, more talented…”

Azula realized that she was still holding Ty Lee’s hand, and squeezed it tightly, stopping her in the middle of her sentence. “Well, I don’t care what your sisters are like. I know you’re perfect exactly how you are.”

The two girls stood still for a moment, the rain pouring down around them. Azula hadn’t been this raw, this honest, this *imperfect* in...well, since she could remember. But Ty Lee had accepted that, even embraced it. And Azula had been able to do the same.

Whatever was forming between them, Azula couldn’t name it yet, but it felt *real* . More real than anything she’d ever felt before.

Ty Lee smiled at her and began to run again. Their hands still intertwined, they began running down the street, accidentally running into an old man pushing a cart full of round green objects. “My cabbages!” he cried as they ran down the street, through the pouring rain.

As Sokka and Zuko neared the next corner, a boy about their age in a wheelchair rocketed out in front of them. It took Sokka a second, but he soon realized that there were actual rockets on the back of the wheelchair. Well, small rockets.

He was wearing goggles, and, seeing Sokka and Zuko staring at him, he pulled them off, revealing friendly-looking eyes. “Can I help you?”

He looked trustworthy, but he probably wasn’t. Sokka leaned in suspiciously. “Who wants to know?”

“My name’s Teo,” said the boy.

“ *Right* ,” said Sokka, still trying to act guarded and suspicious, even though Teo seemed completely trustworthy to him. “And what’s an innocent-looking teenager named Teo doing in Assassin’s Lane?”

“Oh,” said Teo, laughing slightly. “Nothing revolutionary. My dad’s just been working elsewhere in the city, but usually we set up shop down the street from here. We’re inventors.” He tapped the rockets on the back of his wheelchair. “That’s how I got these!”

“Uh-huh,” muttered Sokka. “And what sort of things do you two *invent* ?” He glanced at Zuko, who was regarding Teo with a serious gaze. What did *that* mean? Stupid detectives and their need to be all *mysterious* all the time.

“Oh, all sorts of things!” said Teo. “Household gadgets, bike attachments, smoke detectors that turn the smoke red…”

“Weapons?”

Teo’s smile didn’t falter. “Sometimes, but we don’t usually sell them. Assassins love our stuff, though, even if it’s not weapons.”

Zuko crossed his arms over his chest, finally coming forward. “Don’t you ever feel guilty about selling your inventions to assassins?”

Teo sighed. “It’s all my father can do to put food on the table. I don’t like it, but...what else is he going to do? Let his family starve?”

Zuko’s eyes widened, and Sokka could see the guilt on his face. Instinctively, he grabbed Zuko’s hand, then, realizing what he’d done, grabbed his wrist instead. “Come on, Zuko. He’s not who we’re looking for. Let’s go.”

Azula stopped short as a shop caught her eye. Most of the other shops on this street seemed run-down, or filthy, or looked like the sort of places where the owners hid corpses in the closet. This one was different; everything in this shop glittered and gleamed. The exterior was painted in a shiny pale green color that Azula had never seen before. Little pieces of gold were embedded into the building’s exterior. Up close, Azula could see that they were pebbles that had been spray-painted. Instead of curtains, strings of silver and gold beads hung from the window panes.

Ty Lee reached out and began toying with the strings of beads, laughing. “These are neat!” she giggled. “They remind me of the beads I used to wear when I was a kid.”

“When I was younger, my father gave me a ruby necklace when I moved up an extra grade in school,” said Azula without much thought.

Ty Lee turned and stared at her. Oh no. Had that been the wrong thing to say? Wasn’t bonding over common experiences supposed to be a thing that people did? Why was this so fucking *difficult* ?

But then Ty Lee laughed. “I’ve got to hand it to you,” she said, still toying with the beads. “There’s definitely no one else like you.”

Before either of them could say anything, a hand reached through the beads. Ty Lee yanked her arm back with a yelp. Azula eyed the curtains suspiciously, then, in one smooth motion, yanked the beads aside, revealing an older woman with enormous earrings and poofy hair who gazed reproachfully at them.

“So, you two dare to disturb the sanctuary of Aunt Wu? A bold choice.”

Azula glanced down at the coat she was wearing. It seemed she had a costume already. All she needed to do now was play the part. “We’re bold people.” She leaned forward, purposely narrowing her eyes, her gaze piercing, her expression cold. “And we have a few questions for you.” She stepped back, casually examining her sharp fingernails, then offered the woman a cruel smile. “That is, if you’re willing to answer.”

“Oh, of course!” said the woman hurriedly. “Welcome to my shop! Feel free to examine anything you like!”

Azula walked in slowly and looked around. She seemed to have entered some sort of a magic shop. There was a bowl in the center of the room that was filled with small bones. There was a small book sitting on one of the counters, which appeared to have various cloud formations listed inside. The counters were also lined with small pots and bottles, containing various face creams and liquids. Ty Lee seemed to take great pleasure in smelling the different bottles, and the woman called Aunt Wu came over and began pointing out various lotions and perfumes.

She seemed to take a genuine liking to the pink-wearing acrobat (and really, Azula couldn’t blame her.) Perhaps that could work in their favor.

She caught Ty Lee’s eye from across the room, and gestured to the bottles, then indicated writing something. Hopefully she would get the message.

“This one smells fantastic!” said Ty Lee, picking up a green bottle that was emitting smoke and most definitely looked poisonous. “What is it?” She held it up to her face to breathe it in, but Aunt Wu snatched it away from her before she had the chance.

“Don’t breathe that in!” she cried.

“Why?” said Azula, coming forward. “What happens if she breathes it in?” She kept her tone accusatory, making it clear that she knew *exactly* what was in that bottle.

Aunt Wu sighed. The two of them had her outmatched, and she knew it. “All right, fine. You caught me. It’s a bottle of poison. That’s what I do. I tell fortunes and make potions, and just to make sure my fortunes come true, I’m not afraid to get my hands a little dirty.” She held up her hands. Azula could see specks of dried blood underneath her nails.

Aunt Wu threw her head back dramatically. She certainly seemed to be the dramatic type. “You’ve caught me. You can do whatever you want to me now.”

Azula saw her hands inching towards the bowl of bones behind her, narrowing her eyes. Ty Lee saw it, too, and quickly moved forward. “Hey, you know what I would really love? You tell fortunes with those bones, right?”

Aunt Wu hesitated, then nodded. Ty Lee clapped excitedly. “Great! How about you tell my fortune?”

“What’s in it for me?”

Azula placed her hand over the bones, twiddling one between her fingers. “If you tell her fortune and stop trying to reach the bones behind your back, we’ll leave here without bothering you anymore, and we won’t tell anyone about your little...magic shop.” She held up the bone between her fingernails, then slowly ground it to dust.

Aunt Wu sighed and beckoned for Ty Lee to sit in front of the bones, which she did happily. Aunt Wu beckoned towards the bowl. “Choose a bone and break it,” she said.

Ty Lee reached for the bone nearest to her. “This one looks like a star!” she said, eagerly breaking it in two. Aunt Wu raised her hands, and pink smoke began to pour from the bone, forming all sorts of shapes in the air that Azula couldn’t understand.

Azula had to hand it to her; this was certainly a complicated and well-maintained façade that she was keeping up.

Aunt Wu’s eyes grew as wide as dinner plates. “I see...a great romance in your future!”

Ty Lee squealed. “Really?”

Aunt Wu nodded. “Yes! I can’t see details, but I see a garden, a dagger, and...a rather brooding personality, but a deeply loyal one, too.” The smoke cleared, and Aunt Wu gave Ty Lee a genuine smile. “You’re a very lucky girl.”

For some reason, Aunt Wu looked over at Azula. Azula looked away, her face flaming. “Well,” she said in an airy tone, “she doesn’t know anyone like that, so it doesn’t matter.”

*Even I can hear the strain in my own voice* , she thought as they left the shop.

They left Teo and disappeared into the crowd again. Sokka turned to his friend. “Hey, are you okay?”

Zuko sighed. “It’s my own fault. Sometimes I forget how hard people have to work just to get by.”

Sokka put his hand on his shoulder, causing them both to freeze in the middle of the street. “Hey, just because someone else has different problems doesn’t mean yours never existed. Everyone’s got something that makes them upset.” His eyes drifted to the scar over Zuko’s left eye. He had never asked how he got it, but he had an inkling. “And...whatever happened to you, you know you can always talk about it. To me, I mean. If you want to. I can listen, I guess, is what I’m trying to say.”

Before Zuko could respond, a tall, muscular man with long hair ran into them. He looked exactly like the kind of assassin that would murder thirteen people. He leaped back angrily, raising his fists. Instinctively, Sokka threw his hands in the air, as a sign that he wasn’t a threat, but the man just grinned and pulled back his fists. “Target practice.”

Sokka yelped and threw his hands up over his head, but Zuko stepped in front of him before the tall man could even move. He stared the muscular assassin in the eye, unafraid. Carefully, Sokka lowered his hands and tried to reach for the boomerang in his bag without anyone noticing. It seemed to work.

“What’s your problem with us?”

The man laughed. “My problem is that you’re standing in the middle of the street, that’s what! Some of us have important business to attend to!”

Zuko kept his gaze level and calm. Sokka’s hand tightened even more around his boomerang. “What sort of business?”

The man laughed. “You mean you haven’t heard of me?” They shook their heads, and he sighed, still looking angry enough to murder them both at any moment. “I am Xin Fu, legendary moneymaker!”

“What does that mean?” piped up Sokka. Xin Fu laughed.

“What does it mean? Why, it means you’ll never go broke around me! All you have to do is place your bet on a match, an injury, even a death, and I’ll make *sure* you win.” There was a dangerous glint in his eye.

Sokka groaned. This guy was strangely terrifying, but probably not the assassin they were looking for. Zuko seemed disappointed, too. “All right, let’s keep going.”

As Zuko turned around, the man rose up behind him, drawing two swords seemingly out of thin air. Sokka didn’t even think, he just jumped forward, ignoring the horrible sound as he smashed Xin Fu over the head.

Zuko turned around, surprised, then looked at Sokka. “Thanks.” Seeing the shock on Sokka’s face, he bent down and carefully felt Xin Fu’s wrist. “He’s alive. And he’ll be *very* mad at you if he wakes up, so it’s time for us to get going.”

Sokka gulped as they left Xin Fu lying in the street and kept following the crowd deeper into the alleyway.

Zuko squinted ahead. “They’re all looking for someone,” he mused, turning to Sokka. “Who could it be?”

Sokka could only offer a shrug in response. He didn’t know the assassins here any better than Zuko did. In fact, he probably knew them even less.

As the day went on (though the sky was so dark, you would never know it), the street began to fill with more and more people. Looking around, Azula could see that each of them had a goal. Each was headed in a specific direction. Some carried enormous weapons and looked like they could slaughter her on the spot, others travelled in packs, laughing. All of them, Azula knew, were dangerous, and absolutely not to be trusted.

The girls stopped in their tracks when a young woman, only a couple of years older than them and *riding the biggest dog that Azula had ever seen* came tearing out of a dark alleyway.

Azula had her ‘detective’ face on in an instant, standing up straight to make herself appear tall and crossing her arms over her chest. “Who might you be? Do you have a *problem* with us?”

The woman slid off the enormous dog, looking unbothered. “No problem with you.” She patted her dog on the nose. “Just looking for someone.”

Azula raised an eyebrow. “You use that *dog* to find people. Right.”

The woman planted her hands on her hips. “Hey, leave Nyla alone. We’re the best hunters there are.” She pulled a silver coin out of her belt and flipped it high in the air, handing it to Azula. “Need someone found? We’re always looking for business. Just show that coin to any shopkeeper on the street. They’ll know where to find me.”

Azula pocketed the coin. Perhaps it could come in handy later. “Thank you, but we don’t need anyone found right now. We’re looking for dangerous assassins. People capable of mass murder.” She raised her gaze to look the woman in the eye. “Say, you don’t know anyone like that do you?”

“I do,” said the woman, leaning back against her dog. “Can’t imagine what two little squirts like you would want with her, though. She’d tear you to pieces.”

“You’d be surprised,” said Ty Lee. “We’re tougher than we look.”

“Yeah, right,” the woman said, rolling her eyes as she climbed back onto her dog. “Hop on. I can take you to her. Maybe she’ll kill some bugs for you.”

Azula rolled her eyes, but accepted the woman’s hand. Ty Lee followed suit. How one dog could fit three people on top, Azula didn’t know. “Hang on a sec,” said the woman. “I don’t travel with strangers. I need names. It’s my only condition.”

“I’m Ty Lee, and this is Azula!” said Ty Lee. “What’s your name?”

“Call me June,” said the woman. She whistled, and soon the dog was carrying them down the dark alleyway.

At last, the crowd reached its gathering point; a dark green pub that, despite the fact that it was only around noon, already had a huge crowd spilling out of it, all of them drinking enormous beers. It made Sokka a little sick just to look at it; sure, he had tried beer at some high school parties like anyone else, but never so much, and never when he still had half a day to get through.

The two exchanged a look, then began pushing their way through the crowd, ducking under peoples’ arms and weaving around different little packs, until at last, they found themselves almost at the very center of the mob.

The cheering crowd had gathered around a group of teenagers that couldn’t be much older than either of them. There were five of them, each carrying a different weapon, and all standing around a wooden table. At the head of the table sat a teenage boy that looked around their age. He had brown hair that looked like a mess but was clearly intentionally sloppy, black eyes with a determined yet mysterious glint to them, and was smoking a cigarette with an *I don’t care* expression on his face.

He grabbed a glass of beer and drank the entire thing in one sip, without the cigarette even falling from his mouth. The crowd burst into cheers.

Sokka crossed his arms over his chest. He didn’t like this guy, whoever he was. He had a shady, attention-seeking air to him. He narrowed his eyes and stared at him suspiciously. One of the other members of the gang, who was possibly the most enormous person Sokka had ever seen, stared back at him, and he quickly looked away.

Zuko, however, smirked and started forward. Sokka grabbed his wrist before he could break out of the crowd. “What are you doing?”

Zuko gently pried his hand off. “I’ve worked with this sort of person before. They’re attention-seeking troublemakers, but as long as you know the right thing to say to them, they’re no trouble.”

Sokka groaned, but he let Zuko pull away his hand. He’d been gripping onto his fingers, and he hadn’t even realized it, which was embarrassing

Zuko broke out of the crowd, and sat down across the table from the boy. The crowd let out a collective gasp.

The boy just smirked. “Well, I see we have a new friend. To what do I owe the pleasure?”

Sokka couldn’t see Zuko’s face, but he could hear him. “That’s for me to know and you to find out. *If* you’ve got the skills.”

The boy leaned back in his chair. “A challenger, huh?” The crowd had gone silent. “Well, then, let’s see what you’ve got.” He slid a glass of beer across the table, as big as his own, and one of his friends placed an equally sized one in front of him. He smirked, exuding confidence. The crowd was watching like a hawk, hanging onto his every movement. “Best out of three.”

“What happens if I win?”

“Whatever you want, within reason.”

“A conversation?”

“Seems fair.”

“And if you win?”

The boy laughed. “Well, whatever *I* want, within reason.”

“And you won’t tell me what that is, will you?”

The boy laughed, throwing his head back and running a hand through his clearly-purposely-messy hair. “Where’s the fun in that?”

Yeah, Sokka *definitely* did not like this guy. He edged around the side of the crowd until he could see both of their faces again. Zuko was wearing a determined stare that Sokka knew very well. Whenever he had a goal, he got that look in his eye. He had never failed to meet one, not that Sokka knew of, anyway.

One of the boy’s friends, a tall, lean boy wearing a hat, showed up on the left with a stopwatch that had seemingly appeared out of thin air. The girl standing next to him took a deep breath and whistled so loudly that Sokka had to cover his ears. Both boys tipped their heads up and began to drink. Sokka was so close that he could see their eyes widening as they struggled to breathe. Both of their eyes were gleaming with determination, one pair with pride, the other with purpose.

Zuko slammed his glass down on the table, and a second later, looking absolutely furious, the other boy did, too. The short girl whistled again, and gestured towards Zuko. The crowd gasped.

The boy’s entire face turned bright red with anger, and he gestured for his friends to bring them two more glasses. Before Sokka could even blink, they were drinking the next round. The boy swallowed the beer so fast that Sokka barely even saw the liquid in the glass before he was slamming it down. The girl whistled again, and gestured towards the boy. The crowd erupted into cheers.

Sokka twiddled his fingers nervously as the short girl laid down the last two glasses. The boy laughed, waving to the crowd with seemingly all the confidence in the world. Zuko, on the other hand, looked like he was about to be sick, but the determined stare that he wore so often was still present in his eyes.

The girl whistled, and Sokka could barely watch as the two of them began to drink, much more slowly than before. Both of them looked to be struggling to swallow. Each second ticked by more and more slowly, and it felt like they were never going to finish.

Until the other boy gasped for air, slamming his glass down on the table with just an inch of beer remaining inside. Zuko smirked as he drained his glass and slammed it down a second later. The crowd stared, openmouthed. The other boy glared at him.

Zuko stood up, making a show of dusting off his coat. “I believe we had a deal.” He beckoned to Sokka, and the other boy beckoned to the girl from the group. The four of them filed into a smaller room in the back of the pub. Zuko closed the door behind them, peering through the keyhole to make sure that no one was watching.

The boy fell back into a chair and threw his legs up onto a table. “All right, stranger. You’ve got guts, I’ll give you that. What’s your deal?”

Zuko smirked as he slid into the chair across from him. “I’m a detective.”

“A private eye,” chimed in Sokka. The title didn’t make any difference, but Sokka thought it sounded cooler.

The boy toyed with the cigarette in his mouth. “A private eye, eh? Got a name, *private eye* ?”

“Depends,’ said Zuko. “ *You* got a name?”

Sokka was half-convinced that he was in the middle of watching some old suspense movie.

The boy laughed. “The name’s Jet.” He gestured to the girl standing next to him. “The whistler over there’s Smellerbee.”

Zuko paused, then held out his hand. Jet took it. “Zuko,” he said. “My partner over there is Sokka.”

Jet raised an eyebrow. “Partner?”

Sokka felt heat rushing to his face. “Not like that!” he said quickly. Zuko raised an eyebrow at him, but said nothing.

Jet rolled his eyes, then turned back to Zuko. “What sort of information are you looking for?” Zuko slid a photo of Pakku across the table, then photos of Fung and Chief Song. “I’m looking for information about these murders. I assume you know something about them.”

Jet nodded, leaning back in his chair. Sokka thought he was going to fall over. “Yeah, I heard about them. Don’t know who did it, though?”

Zuko nodded. “But you and your friends have set up shop here in Assassin’s Lane. Coincidence?” Jet hesitated. “This is off the record, I promise. What has nothing to do with the murders or the people involved is none of my business.”

Jet nodded. “My friends and I, we’re called the Freedom Fighters. Hate the White Lotus and the Dai Li more than anyone else on this planet.”

“Why?”

Jet scoffed. “Why? Because they ruin lives! Because they take all of this city’s money for themselves and waste it in their stupid war! They’re selfish pigs and they deserve to die! Every last one of them.”

Even Sokka, who was better at analyzing corpses than people, could tell that this was personal for Jet. But Zuko said nothing, so Sokka kept his theory to himself.

“And you’re *sure* you had nothing to do with the murders?” Zuko’s face was remarkably emotionless for how normally...fiery he could be. It was strange.

Jet nodded. “We protest, sure. Make signs, sneak in, sometimes we try to scare them a little, but we’ve never killed anybody.” He glanced towards the doorway where his other three friends were. “Most of my friends...they’re just kids. I couldn’t make them go to prison for the rest of their lives.”

“Would you do it?”

Jet raised an eyebrow. “*Would* I? What sort of question is that?! You’re supposed to be a detective, I thought you dealt in facts and evidence, not *woulds* and *what-ifs!* If I were you, I’d be fucking ashamed.” The level of anger in his voice had gone from 0 to 100 in a heartbeat.  
“Hey!” Sokka was surprised at the sound of his own voice. “Whatever trouble you have with the White Lotus and the Dai Li is obviously personal! You’re angry, you’ve said they deserved to die, and you literally live on Assassin’s fucking Lane! We have no reason to trust you! So why don’t you just shut up and answer our questions?”

There was a moment of silence inside the pub, but then Jet laughed. “You’ve both got spirit.” He offered them a cocky grin, and fished a card out of his pocket. “If you’re ever looking for some more... *revolutionary* work, you know where to find me.” He whistled, and his three other friends came through the door. “I think that’s all we’ll be doing today.”

As Sokka and Zuko left the pub, escorted out the door by Jet’s enormous sidekick, Sokka saw Jet throw a nasty glare in their direction before slamming the door shut, leaving them back in the rainy alleyway.  
Sokka turned to Zuko. “He’s *definitely* a suspect, isn’t he?”

Zuko nodded. “This is a street full of assassins, Sokka. *Everyone* here is a suspect.”

Nyla stopped running in front of a dark, dusty shop. Azula could see ancient-looking jewelry sparkling through the smudged windowpane. She and Ty Lee slid off, and June smirked. “I’m not going anywhere. After what you’re about to see, you’re gonna want a quick ride back.”

All of these signs pointed to some horror movie bullshit inside the house. Azula was fifty percent sure they were both going to die.

Still, the detectives always managed to fare well in horror movies. So, Azula put on her ‘mystery solver’ face for the last time (hopefully forever), and they entered the shop.

A bell chimed as they walked through the door. The floorboards of the small, dark, wooden room creaked under Azula’s weight. It was unusually hot in here, and Azula could feel the hairs on the back of her neck standing up with anticipation.

All of a sudden, an old woman emerged out of the darkness. She was the most ancient-looking person Azula had ever seen, even more ancient than any of the members of the White Lotus.

She smiled, looking slightly like a badly-stitched childrens’ doll. “What can I do for you today?”

Azula took a risk, leaning on the doorframe as though she was the most confident person ever to walk the Earth. She stared the woman right in the eyes. “We need someone...gone. Without much of a fuss.”

The woman raised an eyebrow, but seemed unfazed. “I see.” She rummaged around in the jewelry cases for a moment, then emerged seconds later with a ruby-encrusted dagger. “What for?”

Ty Lee chimed in. “It’s a favor for a friend!” Azula was impressed at the facility with which she could lie.

The woman nodded. “A favor like that isn’t going to come easily. It’s going to cost you. *A lot* .”

“Well,” said Azula, toying with a strand of her hair, “we aren’t necessarily sure we need you. What really makes you the best?”

The woman laughed. “Oh, child,” she chuckled, “I’ve accomplished things you would never even dream of. *Could* never even dream of.”

“Could you kill someone in the middle of a crowded event?”

The woman smirked. “Child’s play, if you know the right tricks.”

“In their own home when other people are around?” asked Ty Lee.

“Like taking candy from a baby.”

Azula scanned the woman’s face. She didn’t appear to be lying, but the murders they were describing could also have been any number of kills, not the ones they were trying to solve. Plus, the woman was only saying she *could* do those things. It didn’t necessarily mean she had.

Azula leaned forward so that she was only inches away from the woman’s face. “Prove it,” she hissed in a low, menacing voice.

As Azula began to walk out of the shop, the woman began to laugh a deep, mocking laugh. “You have spirit,” she said at last. “Determination. You’ve got what it takes to succeed. You could even succeed right here.”

In a flash, she moved and yanked the dagger that Azula had been carrying out of her pocket. Azula moved to take it back, but the woman held up the ruby one instead. “This is a work of art. Much better than that cheap knife you undoubtedly stole from someone’s kitchen.” She held it out. “It has been waiting for someone like you.”

Azula paused, then placed the dagger in her pocket. The woman smirked at her. “You’re quite the investigator, it’s true, but you’d be quite the assassin, too.” She winked. “My name is Hama. If you ever need me, I will come to you.”

Azula blinked, and when she opened her eyes, Hama was already gone.

An hour after Zuko had left Jet’s pub, the four detectives sat on the train back to the Middle Ring. Zuko was having a hard time looking Sokka in the eye. Sokka had been so quick to say they weren’t partners *in that way* . Zuko hated that it bothered him as much as it did.

On the other side of the car, Azula looked like her face was catching fire every time she looked at Ty Lee, who kept playfully squeezing her hand. Zuko thought he heard her mutter something like “I’m not brooding and deeply loyal,” which made no sense at all.

After a few minutes of silence, Azula looked up. “So,” she said, leaning back and playing with a strand of her hair, “did you find any new suspects?”

Zuko sighed and nodded. “Too many,” he said. “This city is so full of strange people...it could have been *anyone* . Anyone and everyone.” He groaned, plopping his head in his hands.

Ty Lee nodded as she stared out the window into the pouring rain. “Anyone and everyone,” she muttered, almost to herself. “Yeah, it really could.”
