## Chapter 17: The Call of Wings

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

A new reveal leads the group on another mission in the dead of night, but they're in for a surprise.

#### Chapter Notes

TWs at the end for this chapter! (But MAJOR chapter spoilers in the end notes so read at your own risk.) Happy reading!

### Text

Katara burst out laughing as she threw another pillow across the room at Yue, who grabbed the empty popcorn bowl and used it as a shield. “Aaah!” cried Katara. “I will never vanquish her who possesses the mighty Popcorn Shield!” She threw her hands over her heart and fell backwards onto Yue’s bed.

Yue giggled. “But you have the mighty pillow sword! You’re unstoppable!” She flopped onto one of her bean bag chairs, letting out a dramatic sigh. “I have lost everything.”

Katara made a big show out of setting down the pillow and racing to Yue’s side. “Don’t worry, valiant knight! I won’t let you fall!” She wrapped her arms around Yue’s abdomen and pulled her up.

It wasn’t until Yue’s face was inches from her own that Katara realized just how close she’d pulled her. Blushing, she let go as quickly as she could. Yue laughed nervously and stared at her fuzzy carpet.

“Sorry about that,” muttered Katara.

Yue smiled. “It’s okay. Thank you for coming over. I’ve never had anyone over before.”

“Really?”

Yue nodded. “I didn’t know too many people growing up, so I didn’t exactly have a lot of friends to invite over.”

Katara nodded. “Me neither.”

“Really?” said Yue. “But you’re so friendly! You must have been the most popular girl at your school?”

Katara felt her face darken. “I did have friends. But...my mom died when I was about eight. She was murdered in our house. The kids in my class started thinking it was haunted.” She laughed, but it wasn’t a real laugh. “Kids believe stupid things, you know how it is. But it stuck. Nobody really wanted to come to my house after that.”

Yue was staring at her in shock. “Oh gosh, was that too much? I know it’s sort of creepy, and…”

Yue interrupted by squeezing Katara’s hand, causing her to stop short in the middle of her sentence. “Of course it’s okay, Katara. You can say *anything* to me. I’m just so sorry that happened to you.”

Katara sighed, flopping back onto the beanbag chair. “I know you understand. Probably better than anyone.”

Yue flopped down next to her. “It never feels the same afterwards, does it?”

Katara shook her head. “No. It never does.”

Zuko was woken up early the next morning by someone banging *very loudly* on his bedroom door. Still feeling like he was half-in-half-out of a nightmare, he stumbled out of bed, not even bothering to look at his hair in the mirror (he already knew it was a disaster.)

Azula was standing at his door, about to knock a third time. He raised an eyebrow at her, annoyed but concerned at the same time. “Is something wrong?”

She gestured to the apartment phone on the other side of the living room. “That thing’s been ringing for half an hour. It won’t shut up.”

Zuko groaned, pulling his coat on over his pajamas. “Well, if it was annoying you so much, why didn’t *you* answer it?”

“Well, it’s *your* phone.”

“I never answer my phone,” mumbled Zuko as he slowly walked across the room to pick it up. As the phone kept ringing, Azula tapped her foot impatiently. Zuko walked even slower.

“I think I’m losing my hearing with every second that thing rings.”

“I survived a giant burn on half my face,” snapped Zuko. “I think you can live with a ringing phone.”

Azula looked almost like she’d been slapped, but quickly regained her composure. *Like a fucking* *robot,* thought Zuko. “Fine,” she muttered. “You want to talk about that, talk about it. Do whatever you want, whatever you need. Something I do triggers you? Fine. But you don’t get to use that to criticize me for being *human* .”

Zuko rolled his eyes. “Fine. It’s not like you know what it’s like to really go through something.”

Azula glared at him, but said nothing. “Just answer the fucking phone.”

Zuko stuck out his tongue at her and picked the phone up. “Hello?”

“Finally!” yelled a voice from the other side of the phone. “What the heck, Clue Guy? I’ve been calling you for half an hour!”

“Toph?”

“Give me the phone,” muttered a voice in the background. There was some rustling and shouting on the other end of the line, then “Hi Zuko, it’s Mai, and Toph.” A reluctant pause. “ *And* Suki. We think we might have found something out, that’s why Toph is screaming at you. If you want to come here and figure it out, then come, we don’t care.” She said all of this in her usual flat tone of voice. “But if you’re coming, come quickly. This seems important.” She hung up.

Zuko turned to Azula, whose hair wasn’t yet in her topknot, but other than that seemed completely ready to rush out the door. He looked down at his own pajamas.

“Can you be ready in five minutes?”

A smile spread across Azula’s face. “I thought you’d never ask.”

At the Dai Li headquarters, Suki was an absolute mess. Not that Zuko knew her very well, but when someone who usually seemed pretty tough was slumped against the wall, clutching her knees with tears streaming down her face, he figured that just about qualified as an absolute mess.

Azula turned to Toph, who was practically bouncing up and down with energy. “So? What did you find out?”

Toph leaned in towards them, as though sharing a secret in the schoolyard. “I heard my parents say something this morning,” she whispered. “Something about rushing to a place called *Lake Laogai* .” Juet the name of it sent chills down Zuko’s spine.

“Is that all you have?”

Toph nodded, then shook her head. “Kind of. But they were acting really weird! They were whispering to each other, rushing around, talking about disobedience and discipline, and being in big trouble if they didn’t do something!”

Azula crossed her arms over her chest. “How on Earth did you manage to overhear all of this?” Toph shrugged. “I can’t see. Most people sort of assume that I can’t really hear either.”

“So,” said Zuko. “What are they talking about, then?”

“Some sort of secret hideout,” chimed in Mai. Both siblings turned to her. “It’s the only thing that makes sense. Somewhere they were whispering about, where they go when they’re in big trouble? I’m willing to bet the whole Dai Li knows something. They’re always disappearing for days on end.”

Azula twiddled with a strand of her hair. She was wearing a half-ponytail again. “It does seem like a perfect solution. Say, hypothetically, we go investigate it.” She glanced at Suki. “What’s happening to her?”

“Some sort of identity crisis,” said Mai. “Don’t worry. If we’re going to investigate anything, she’ll be ready to go.” She walked over and sat next to the Dai Li protegé.

Toph looked up at Zuko. “How do you know where this place is?”

“I don’t,” he replied, his mind flashing to the factory from only a few nights ago, though it felt like forever. “But I have a thought.”

Azula pulled out her phone. She clearly had the same idea. “I *think* I know how to get us there.”

Mai sat down next to Suki without a word. The other girl looked up and glared at her. “What are *you* doing here? You’re the *last* person I want to see right now!”

“It’s either me or nobody. Take your pick.”

“Nobody! Easily!”  
“Too bad.”

Suki sighed. “Why won’t you just leave me alone? I need some time to think.”

“What do you need to think about? It was pretty obvious all along that the Dai Li were up to something. I thought it was obvious to you, too.”

“I didn’t want to believe it, okay?” snapped Suki.

“What do you mean?”  
Suki laughed bitterly. “You wouldn’t understand. You hate your parents, so you built your identity on being the opposite of them. But I have no family. No one to base myself off of. All I had was Kyoshi’s legacy, and the Dai Li *made* me into that.” She sighed, blinking back tears. “If the Dai Li is secretly plotting something, or if they’ve been keeping something from me...I don’t really know what to think about myself.”

Mai rolled her eyes. “Don’t be so dramatic,” she said, leaning against the wall. “You’re a person even if the Dai Li has a secret.”

“Not my own person.”

“Sure, you’re your own person. A good person.”

Suki scoffed. “Yeah, right, you hate me. You think I’m a stick-in-the-mud who only knows how to follow the rules.”

“Well, you are.”

To Mai’s surprise, Suki laughed. “Maybe a little.”

Mai let a small smile spread across her face. “But you’re also determined, and you work really hard. And you’re trying to make the world...you know, better. Those things make a *good* person.” Suki was silent. “Are you crying so much that you can’t even listen to me? Is that something crying does?”

Suki shook her head. “No,” she said at last. “I heard you. I was just thinking.”

“You think a lot,” said Mai. “About your identity, about Kyoshi’s legacy and all that. Maybe it’s time to stop overthinking things and just do what you think is good.” She smirked. “That’s what I do.”

“Well,” said Suki, offering her a small smile, “it seemed to work out okay for you.”

“Let me get this straight,” said Katara from the other end of the line. “You two want me to go through the White Lotus until I find someone willing to take a group of teenagers who are investigating a murder into the woods *at night* ?”

“Exactly,” said Azula. “I think I made that perfectly clear. We need someone who grew up here, who knows the woods around the city.”

“This isn’t easy, you know,” said Katara. “The entire White Lotus is preparing some sort of party. They’re impossible to pin down. If I ask the wrong person, I could be in big trouble.”

“Well, don’t do so much poking around that you get yourself *killed* .”

“Hang on,” said Katara. Azula could hear the mischief in her voice. “I never said I wasn’t gonna help.”

“My sister did *what* ?!” squealed Sokka when he arrived at the Dai Li headquarters later that day.

Zuko could see Azula’s clear irritation from all the way across the room. “I thought you were supposed to be the clever one. How many times must I explain this to you? Your sister happened to already be at the White Lotus mansion with her friend, so I asked her to find us someone to take us through the forest, since I figured they would know the area.”

“You should have checked with me first!”

“What is this, the seventeenth century? Do *you* want to go into the dark forest without a guide? By all means, go!” Azula marched off, clearly angry, and started talking to Toph instead.

“Wow,” said Sokka as Zuko came over to join him. “She’s prickly today.”

Zuko winced. “Yeah,” he muttered, “that’s kind of my fault.”

“Want to talk about it?”

“No.” Zuko paused, seeing the hurt look that passed over his friend’s face. “But for the record, I’m not mad at you for asking her to check with you first.”

“You don’t think it was sexist?”  
“Oh, it definitely was. Don’t say stuff like that. But...this is dangerous stuff. She’s your sister, and you don’t want anything bad to happen to her. Ever.” He glanced at Azula, who seemed to be in a better mood since she had started talking to Toph. “I wish I had someone like that.”

“You can,” said Sokka, squeezing his arm gently. “If that’s something you want, I think you can do it. You’re Zuko. You never give up.”

Zuko laughed bitterly, thinking of his argument with his sister that morning. “I’m not so sure.”

Later that day, Azula came over to him. She seemed less prickly than she had been earlier. “Hey,” she said, sliding down onto the floor next to him. “I have something to give you.”

“Oh?”

Azula pulled a silver coin out of her pocket and handed it to Zuko. “A woman on Assassin’s Lane gave this to me. Apparently, she makes a career out of finding missing people. I don’t know when you’ll need this, but you’re a detective, so I can assume you’ll have need of it sometime.” She handed it over. “According to her, you hand this coin over to any shopkeeper on Assassin’s Lane, and this woman will come and help you. At the very least, you can add it to your artifact collection.”

“What artifact collection?”

Azula laughed. “Don’t think I haven’t seen that drawer in your desk with all those little trinkets from your past cases. I can’t make any sense of them, but you take them out every time you need to think, so I can only assume that they must be important.”

Zuko blinked. “I didn’t even realize *I* did that.”

“We all have little habits that we don’t notice.”

“Right. You play with your hair.”

“What?” Azula seemed weirdly shocked. “No I don’t!”

Zuko laughed. “Yes, you do. You’re always toying with whatever strands are hanging down around your face.” He glanced over at her. “You’re doing it right now!”

Hurriedly, Azula pulled her hands out of her hair. “I don’t have any physical habits that I”m unaware of. There was a piece of dust in my hair. I was simply pulling it out.”

With that, she pushed herself up off the floor and walked away.

What had *that* been about?

Azula caught her reflection in a window in one of the hallways that no one was using. She sighed, staring at her face.

She looked like her mother, and she hated it, just like she hated her mother.

Her mother had been *good* , and she had known it. She had always been sweet, and friendly, and gentle, especially towards Zuko. After being taught that this was a weakness, Azula had been bothered by how *happy* it seemed to make her. How could she be weak and still be so *happy* ?

But what had bothered her more was that her mother was *good* , and she had decided that Zuko was good, but never Azula. She had only ever scolded her for doing what Azula had *thought* was strong, for being cold and detached, for the exact same traits that kept Azula safe. Even at her best, Azula had never been good enough for her mother.

And she fucking hated them both for it. Her mother and herself.

She’d never had her mother to tell her *why* she was such a monster, why she didn’t deserve any of her time, or compliments, or affection. She had worked so hard to be perfect, but it hadn’t mattered.

She’d never had her mother to play with her hair. She’d done it once, for some reason, before she’d decided that Zuko was the only one worth her time. It was faint, but Azula still had the memory of her mother’s hands in her hair.

She’d had to substitute for them.

Looking in the window, Azula saw her mother’s face staring back at her. It looked *too* good, *too* perfect. It was unfair that she got to decide what was good and perfect.

Azula threw the curtains over the window so forcefully that she thought she heard the wooden rod supporting them come tearing off the wall.

At six in the evening, Katara arrived at the Dai Li headquarters with Professor Zei in tow. The latter was bubbling with excitement, as usual, but also seemed very confused.

“Back up a minute,” he said to Katara as they entered. “Why am I here again?”  
It was evident that Katara didn’t want to manipulate him, so Azula came forward. She seemed a little shaken, though Zuko couldn’t figure out why, but fine. “We’re solving the murders, Professor. We’re trying to help the White Lotus as best as we can.” She made her eyes big. “That’s what you want, isn’t it?”

“Oh, of course!” said Professor Zei, adjusting his hat and glasses nervously. “That’s all I want! I’m new, I want to help them and prove myself!”

“Sounds like we’re giving you a pretty good chance,” said Azula, with a cold smile. “So, are you up for a little trip to the forest?”

“What?”

Katara looked away guiltily. “We...may not have quite gotten to that.”

Zuko sighed. Oh well. That was what you got for working with nice people. “Okay, quick refresher. We think the Dai Li is hiding something in the forest north of the city. You’re a Professor. You grew up here. You know your way around this forest. We want your help.”

“I’m an Anthropology professor!”

Sokka slammed his fist down on the table. “But you studied Biology in college, right?”

“How on Earth did you…”

“Can you help us or not?”

“I can try!” said Professor Zei hurriedly. “I do know these woods! But I’m not that kind of Biologist! You should know that!”

“Guys!” cried Katara. “We want to help him, not hurt him!” She walked over to the Professor. “Listen, Professor Zei, I know my friends aren’t always the friendliest. But they all have good hearts. They really want to help you, and the White Lotus. The Dai Li could be putting this city, and the White Lotus, in danger, and we want to help them. We’re trying to save our city.” She looked up at Professor Zei, her eyes sparkling. “Will you help us?”

He stared at her for a moment, then nodded. “I would be honored!”

The entire group was soon standing at the north end of the city, following Professor Zei into the dark forest. They were walking in a line. Because she was his new favorite, Katara was walking directly behind Professor Zei, who was chattering excitedly about the different plant species in the forest, and pointing out animal paths and trail markers that they could follow. Azula was walking next to her, and behind them walked Toph, who kept using her cane to whack Katara when she wasn’t looking. Next were Mai and Suki, who actually seemed to be able to have a civil conversation for once, and Sokka and Zuko were the last in line. Zuko kept looking into the treetops. He could have sworn that he kept hearing something rustling in the leaves.

“Hey,” Sokka shook his arm, and Zuko realized that he had stopped walking right in the middle of the path, “everything okay?”

“Yeah,” said Zuko, pushing ahead of Sokka to continue down the path, “I just thought I heard something.”

Sokka nodded. “It *is* creepy out here.” Zuko nodded in agreement, feeling a shiver run down his spine. Suddenly, Sokka stopped in the middle of the path and yelped.

“What’s wrong?”

Sokka was still panting. “Sorry,” he groaned. “Just a bug crawling on my arm.”

Zuko smirked. “You mean the forensics student who analyzes corpses for fun is scared of a little bug?”

“Hey!” laughed Sokka, punching him lightly on the arm. “It’s dark out here! It’s hard to see!”

“Yeah,” muttered Zuko as a gust of wind made the hairs stick up on the back of his neck, “it is.”

“So,” said Mai as she walked next to Suki. “Are you feeling better?”

Suki groaned. “Thanks for the sarcastic comment. You know, earlier today, I actually thought you and I were getting along for once.”

Mai sighed. “No, dumbass, I was being serious.”

Suki blinked. “Really? But you sounded so...sarcastic.”

“This is how I talk,” said Mai. She then raised her voice about five octaves in pitch, making every word dramatic and screeching. “Not everyone has to talk like this!”

Suki burst out laughing. “You never told me you could do impressions!”

Mai smiled. “You never asked.”

Both of them were interrupted by something wooden slammed into their legs. Mai jumped in surprise, and Suki let out a small shriek.

“Hey!” whispered Toph. “Keep it down! Unless you *want* to get us all killed!”

“I’m impressed with how easily you manage to get people on your side,” Azula said to Katara. “It’s quite a rare talent.”

Azula couldn’t see Katara’s face in the dark, but it sounded like she was smiling. “Oh, thanks. I really just...speak from the heart. You know.”

Azula laughed bitterly. “Actually, I don’t.”  
“Really?”  
“Believe me,” sighed Azula. “In my house, you’re only allowed to show your true feelings if it's part of an act.”

“But then...they’re not your true feelings, are they?”

“Exactly.”

They walked in silence for a moment, then Katara said, “I’m sorry.”

“What for?”

“That you had to grow up like that.”

Azula sighed. “Don’t pity me. I was the lucky one. Zuko got the worst of it.”

“Just because the same things didn’t happen to you both doesn’t mean you weren’t hurt.” Katara paused. “I don’t know everything, but...I just think you’re being a little too hard on yourself.”

“Believe me,” muttered Azula. “I’m only thinking of myself in an accurate light.” She kept her tone light and joking, but she believed what she was saying.

“We all think that when we look at ourselves,” said Katara. “I don’t think a lot of us are right.”

They walked in silence for a second, but it was a second too long. Azula grabbed Katara’s wrist, pulling her back.

“Ow! What was that for?”

“Sssh,” whispered Azula. “Think. Who haven’t we heard in a while?”

Katara gasped. “The Professor!”

Azula grabbed her flashlight and shone it on the ground in front of them. At first, there was nothing. Then, she shone it directly in front of their feet, and Katara screamed loudly enough for the birds in the nearby trees in front of them.

Professor Zei hadn’t said anything about plants or birds for at least a minute. This was because he had dropped dead at their feet, his glasses shattered on the ground. He would never utter another word.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

TW: Death, darkness, self-hatred.

I hope you enjoyed that one! I feel like anyone who wears glasses in a murder mystery is automatically condemned to death, especially if they're nerdy, overenthusiastic, and a minor character. Poor Professor Zei. His fate was sealed.  
Anyway, if you've got thoughts, theories, or anything else to say, please leave a comment or come talk to me on Tumblr at @theatergirl06! Hearing your opinions is honestly my favorite thing about publishing this fic!

## Chapter 18: The Witness for the Prosecution

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

After returning from the woods, each member of the group is questioned, but the questionings produce varied results.

#### Chapter Notes

I apologize for any typos in this one. I was very tired when I proofread it.

TW: Corpses, interrogations.

Happy reading!

### Text

Ever the pragmatist, Azula took off after Professor Zei’s death to find some sort of help. As she’d put it “We’re not qualified to transport the corpse of a fully-grown man all the way back into the middle of the city.” Strangely, nobody had worried about her getting lost. There seemed to be a sort of communal understanding that if Azula said she knew what she was doing, she probably knew what she was doing.

The rest of the group was stuck milling around the body. None of them wanted to go any further, because what if who (or what)ever had killed him was still out there, and none of them wanted to leave a dead man’s body alone in the middle of the woods. So they sat and waited.

Suki had been throwing her fans at trees for the past thirty minutes. She claimed it was a way to pass the time, but everyone else could see the beads of sweat on her face, and the panicked look in her eyes. No doubt she was scared, and wanted to ensure that she could protect the group.

In contrast, Mai had climbed up a short tree and was sitting on a branch a few feet off the ground. She was completely still; so still that no one would have known she was there if they hadn’t seen her climb up. Toph was aimlessly poking at Mai’s hanging feet with her cane. She hadn’t spoken a word since the professor’s death.

Katara was kneeling on the ground next to Professor Zei’s body. She was crying, and not just a little. Tears ran down her cheeks without stopping, and she’d been weeping the whole time. She made her sobs as quiet as possible, not wanting to burden anyone else, but she couldn’t help it. Seeing someone, dead at her feet, their eyes cold and unmoving...it reminded her *so* much of her mom. She reached up and grabbed the necklace that her mother had given her, gripping it as tightly as she could.

Sokka walked over after a while and sat next to her in silence. He didn’t need to use words to understand why his sister was crying over the body of an almost-stranger.

Zuko was walking in circles around the group, making sure that no one was closer to the trees than they were to him. Every time he heard a rustle, a snap, even a gust of wind, he stood up straighter, staring deep into the woods. Whoever had killed the professor could still be out there, and Zuko was *not* going to let his friends die because he’d been too irresponsible.

His hands brushed the tiny pistol that he kept in his coat pocket. In general, he wasn’t too thrilled with the idea of people having guns, but when he was investigating murders and walking into the woods in the middle of the night to look for an organization’s secret fortress, he was glad to have some form of self-protection. It felt good to have it now.

It felt like it took a hundred years before shouts and yells started coming through the trees. The whole group rose to their feet and began waving their arms. It almost felt like they were in a haze. Their own voices sounded muffled, and everything seemed to be happening in slow motion.

Azula was the first person to appear, racing ahead of the crowd (which, Katara could now see, mostly consisted of police officers.) She sprinted over, then planted her hands firmly on her knees, trying hard not to show that she was panting. “I’m sorry,” she gasped, “I tried to get help as soon as I could, but when the police showed up, he was with them, and I couldn’t make him go away!”

The police finally emerged out of the darkness, their flashlights lighting up the forest, and the brightness making everyone in the group squint. Some ran behind the group to start gathering up the body for transport, but most stayed on the other side of them, forming a sort of pack that seemed to go on forever. At the head of the crowd was none other than Hahn of the White Lotus. He glared at all of them, while somehow managing to also look immensely proud of himself.

“You’re all coming with us!” he yelled, clearly making an effort to sound more commanding than he actually was. “Don’t leave our sight, because you’re all suspects for the murder of Professor Zei!”

Sokka had seen *way* too much of the waiting room at the police station by this point. The entire group was either pacing nervously or half-asleep on a crummy chair under the fluorescent lighting. Every one of them was exhausted, but none of them were allowed to leave until they’d all been interrogated. And since Hahn insisted on being present for every single one (for some reason, the police were listening to him), that meant that the interrogations were taking a *very* long time.

Suki must have been in the interrogation room for half an hour before she finally came out. She looked a little rattled, and more than a little tired, but her gaze was as steely as ever as she sat down next to Sokka.

“How’d it go?”

Suki shrugged. “Fine, I think. I just told them everything I knew, which isn’t a lot.”

“Then why’d you take so long?”  
Suki laughed. “Oh, you know Hahn. He had to spend twenty minutes talking about all of his theories. He thinks a bear came out of the forest and mauled the professor. Then he started asking me how much I knew about bears, and if I knew how to set them loose.” She giggled. It was the first time that Sokka had seen her (or anyone, for that matter) smile since the professor’s murder.

Sokka smiled. “Yeah, the guy’s a pretty big idiot.”

The door to the interrogation room slammed shut, and Mai walked out. Her face was void of any expression, just like it had been since the murder. She sat at the other end of the room and stared off into space, as though there was no one there.

A police officer poked her head out of the room and gestured to Sokka. “You’re next. Come on in.”

Sokka waved to Suki and entered the interrogation room. Katara had described it to him, but the *dullness* of it, of the chipped wood, the grey floor, the handcuffs bolted to the table, the flickering lights, was something that you had to see for yourself. It was inherently depressing, and Sokka almost felt the strange urge to slump over as he sat down at the table.

He was also exhausted. That could definitely also have had something to do with it.

Hahn and one other police officer were sitting across the table from him. The police officer was scribbling intensely in a notebook, while Hahn was sitting with his hands folded under his chin, looking incredibly smug. Sokka wanted to slap him.

The police officer fumbled with her pen for a second, then glanced up at Sokka. “Your name is Sokka, correct?” Sokka nodded. “Can you tell me if and how you were acquainted with the late Professor Zei?”

Sokka shrugged. “I don’t really know. I knew him, but not really. I mean, I go to the university, so I’d seen him around on campus, and he was in the White Lotus, so I knew who he was, but we’ve never...actually had a conversation or anything.”

“I see,” said the police officer. “And can you tell me what you were doing with Professor Zei, out in the woods north of the city, in the middle of the night?”  
Sokka could feel his heartbeat speeding up, but luckily, the group had agreed on an excuse back in the forest. “We wanted to go on a night hike. Thought it would be an exciting way to spend our vacation.”

“And why was Professor Zei there?”

Sokka really didn’t like lying, but the police and the Dai Li were basically the same thing. They couldn’t tell the truth without risking their lives. “We thought it’d be neat to get him to show us some of the plants in the forest.”

“Yes,” said the officer. “Were you aware that Professor Zei is not a Biology professor?”

Sokka rubbed the back of his neck. Maybe it was something he did when he was nervous, because it felt like he did that a lot. “We were, but one of my friends from school took his class, and said that he also knew a lot about Biology, so we thought we’d ask him anyway.”

“Why ask him and not a real Biologist?”

Sokka had to think quickly. His sleep-deprived brain was practically screaming at him. “Well, my friend’s uncle is in the White Lotus, so Professor Zei was the only person we could contact. You know, since it’s vacation and all.”

The officer nodded, seeming to be finished, so Hahn took that at his opportunity to lean forward, his eyes narrowed to a comical degree. “Sokka…” He held on to the last “uh” syllable of Sokka’s name for *way* too long. “You said you were a student, right?”

Sokka had no idea where this was going. “Yeah, at Ba Sing Se University. I study forensics. Why?”

“Well…” said Hahn. “I just remembered something veeeery important…” he paused dramatically, but didn’t speak for so long that it just felt really weird. “Students hate teachers! More than anything else on Earth!”

“That’s actually not really tr…”  
“That’s why you killed Professor Zei! You’re part of a plot to have the students assassinate all of their teachers!”

Sokka groaned. “Hahn, that’s a ridiculous theory. You have absolutely no evidence! You’re just making it up on the spot!”

Hahn grabbed a page out of the (clearly annoyed) officer’s notebook and began scribbling. “Oh yeah?! Just watch me!”

Sokka groaned and checked his watch. Maybe he could get away with falling asleep if he was discreet about it.

After Sokka left to go into the interrogation room, Suki walked over and sat next to Mai, who was still staring blankly into space. She didn’t really know what to say to the other girl. If she asked about her feelings, she thought Mai might get defensive. But Mai had been a surprisingly good friend today, so she wanted to try. Even if she didn’t always understand Mai’s relationship with emotions.

“So...crazy night, huh?” Suki let out a nervous laugh.  
Mai turned to her, clearly not amused. Beneath her blank stare, there was a deeply depressed look in her eyes that caught Suki off guard. “A man just fell dead at our feet. I think crazy is a bit of an understatement.”

“Yeah, about that…” Well, she couldn’t think of anything to say. She’d just have to wing it, “are you okay?”

Mai rolled her eyes. “I just said a man fell dead at our feet. Of course I’m not okay.”

“Oh.” Suki sounded quiet, even to her own ears. “Do you want to talk about it?”

Mai crossed her arms over her chest and turned away. “No.”

“Okay,” said Suki, still worried. She started toying with one of her fans for a moment, not knowing what else to say.

Sighing, Mai turned around to face her. “Look, it’s not because of you, okay? You got to be the Dai Li’s special protegé and do whatever you wanted because they liked you. I was always being told to shove everything away and shut up, because showing any sort of impoliteness could ruin us. So I don’t like shoving all of my deepest fears onto other people. Forgive me.” She rolled her eyes at the end, her voice oozing sarcasm.  
Suki crossed her arms over her chest. “Okay, I know you’re upset, but I didn’t always have it easy. I had to train and train and train, and always say the right thing, no matter what! I didn’t have a voice either! I *never* did! But that doesn’t mean I can’t talk about stuff that’s bothering me with the people who care about me! I know that, in the end, it’ll turn out better for me if I do.”

Mai rolled her eyes. “You don’t care about me. Just for the record.”

“Fine, believe that if you want to. But you can talk to me anyway.”

Mai sighed. “Suki, there’s nothing to talk about. A man died right in front of all of us.” She put her hand on Suki’s shoulder, surprising Suki so much that she nearly fell out of her chair. “I don’t need what you need in a situation like this. I just need a little time for my brain to work it out, okay?”

Suki nodded. “Okay.”

Mai smirked. “Good. Now, please tell me you have something to *do* . This place is going to kill me with boredom.”

Azula rolled her eyes at the police officer and the irritating teenage gremlin sitting across from her. Personally, she thought it was silly that they were interrogating her at all. Zuko had told her to keep quiet because “these people have a lot of power in the system” but she didn’t even *live* in this city, so what did she care?

The officer took out her notebook and began to write. Next to her, Hahn was toying with a pencil. He was attempting to look cool, but he kept dropping the pencil on the floor, so really, he just looked like an idiot. Azula turned her attention to the police officer, who was also an idiot, probably, but was at least somewhat polite.

“Your name?”

“Azula.”

The officer nodded. Azula could see her write her name down in neat cursive. “Azula, can you tell me how you were affiliated with Professor Zei?”

“I’ve known the man for approximately eight days. Within those eight days, we may have spoken twice.”

Hahn leaned forward, slamming his hands into the table. “You’re lying! I know you know more than you’re letting on!”

Azula rolled her eyes. “I absolutely do not. I assure you, I arrived in this city eight days ago. I couldn’t have known the man for longer than that.”  
“Would you describe your relationship with the professor as positive?” asked the officer.

Azula sighed. The idiocy of these questions was astounding. “More like nonexistent. As I said, we may have spoken twice, at the most.”

“I know you have a motive!” yelled Hahn. “You wanted him dead, I’m sure of it!”

Azula rolled her eyes, leaning back in her chair. “What motive could I possibly have? I’ve barely spoken to the professor for three minutes. I don’t even *live* in this city!”

“That’s what you *say* !” said Hahn. “But I know you’ve been living here for weeks, spying on the professor, and telling no one!”

Azula sighed. “What evidence do you have to support that?” She turned to the officer. “Why do you even listen to him? Did he pay you or something?”

The officer said nothing, but nodded discreetly the second Hahn looked away.

“We have no evidence to support that theory,” said the police officer, who was clearly also fed up with Hahn, “but if you had proof that you’ve been living somewhere else up until eight days ago, that would help us a lot. Is there maybe someone we could call? Someone you’ve been living with? You *are* seventeen, so a parent or guardian, perhaps?”

Azula felt her heart plummet in seconds. This was the one thing she didn’t want to hear. The one lie she’d brought with her to Ba Sing Se. She’d been doing *such* a good job of not thinking about it, getting wrapped up in the investigation. But here it was, knocking at her door.

She swallowed quickly, making sure to keep up her composed expression. “No. I don’t think there’s anyone you can call.”

The police officer frowned and made a note. “Thank you, Azula. That will be all.”

Azula had to work to keep her calm as she left the room. That had been a little too close for her comfort.

How long could she go on hiding this from everyone...from herself, before it all came crashing down?

Zuko found his sister after going over a few questions with Hahn and the police officer. He’d been through enough interrogations to know the drill. The only unusual part had been Hahn insisting that Zuko was secretly a witch and had cast a spell on Professor Zei. He’d asked for a magic demonstration. Obviously, when Zuko hadn’t been able to do any magic, Hahn had accused him of faking it.

“Hey,” he said, sliding into the chairs next to her.

Azula looked up. Like everyone else, she looked exhausted. “What insane theory did Hahn come up with for you?”

“Apparently I’m a witch, and I put a spell on Professor Zei.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “Please. If you were a witch, I’d *definitely* be cursed by now.”

“Hey!” cried Zuko. “That’s...probably true.” He sighed. “Fair enough. What did he come up with for you? Can you secretly manipulate lightning to murder professors?”

Azula burst out laughing. “Wouldn’t that be something,” she mused. “But no. Hahn says I’ve been secretly living in the city and plotting to murder Professor Zei for weeks.”

“Well that’s easy to disprove,” said Zuko. “You could just call Father and get him to tell them that you’ve been living at home.”

Azula looked away. “What’s wrong?” he asked.

She yawned. “Nothing,” she said quickly. “I’m just tired. And Father wasn’t home.”

“Oh well,” said Zuko. “The police do *not* like you, by the way. They think you’re obnoxious.”

“Well, they deserve it,” she muttered. “I’ve only just arrived in this city, and they think that it’s a smart idea to interrogate me for the murder of a man I barely know. The *real* killer could still be out there, and they’re wasting their time with me!”

“Yeah,” said Zuko, “but they’re the police. You don’t want to be on their bad side!”

“What could they do to me?” scoffed Azula. “I don’t even *live* in this city.”

“But they’re allied with the Dai Li,” pointed out Zuko. “They have a lot of power here.”

“Oh, Zuzu,” sighed Azula. “You overestimate them. They have the ability to seem very powerful. But I haven’t actually broken any laws that they know of. They can’t hurt me.”

“If you say so,” said Zuko, knowing that he wasn’t going to convince her otherwise anytime soon.

Katara had barely wiped all of the tears from her eyes by the time she was called into the interrogation room. She felt bad for being such a mess, but every time she closed her eyes, she just saw her mother again. She felt like she was eight years old.

The police officer, who looked just about as worn-out as Katara felt, beckoned her into the interrogation room, and motioned for her to take a seat. Hahn was there, too, looking smug. Katara wanted to slap him.

“Okay, sweetie,” said the police officer. Clearly, Katara wasn’t hiding her tears very well if the police officer was talking to her like *that* . “I’m just going to ask you a few questions, and then we’ll be done. Can you please tell me your name?”

“Katara.”

The officer smiled at her. “Okay, Katara. Can you tell me what sort of relationship you had with Professor Zei?”

Katara nodded. “I didn’t know him very well. I’d helped the White Lotus with a few of their events, so I’d seen him at those, and I’d worked with him a few times, but we never had any long conversations.”

“How would you describe him?”

Katara shrugged. She was aware that she was still crying, but she ignored it. “He was...nice, I guess. He was always enthusiastic about our projects, and never anything but polite to me. But I never got to know him on anything more than a superficial level.

“I see,” said the officer. “Then, if I may ask…”

“Why am I crying?”

The officer blushed awkwardly, and stared at her notebook. “Well...yes.”

Katara managed a weak smile. “It’s all right.” She took a deep breath. “My mother died when I was eight years old. She was murdered. We never found the killer, but...I did find her body.” She took another deep breath, doing her best to speak through her sobs. “Finding Professor Zei’s body...well, it reminds me a little too much of that.”

“Oh,” said the officer, seemingly at a loss for words. “Katara, I’m so sorry.”

“It’s all right.”

“You’re lying.” Hahn’s voice tore through the room like a freezing air current. Katara felt the waves of sadness that were washing over her freeze, and slowly turn to anger. Slowly, feeling like her body was the temple of a thunderstorm, she turned to Hahn, and stared coldly at him. She spoke slowly, each word trembling, barely containing her rage.

“What did you just say?”

Hahn rolled his eyes, leaning back in his chair with a cocky smirk. “You’re lying. You’re clearly just using this sob story of yours to cover your tracks.”

It was like a dam breaking. Katara almost felt like she left her own body as she rose out of her chair, slamming her arms into the table, directly in front of Hahn. But her words were still slow and ice-cold.  
“How dare you?”

Hahn threw up his hands. “Wow, way to overreact.”

Katara felt as though she was going to explode. Not even thinking about it, she reached across the table and grabbed Hahn by the shirt. “How fucking dare you?! I was a *child* , an *eight-year-old* *child* , when I discovered my mother’s body! A *kid* ! And it was my own mother, the most important person in my life! I had to find her, cold and dead, and know that she would never hug me, or...or talk to me, or braid my hair, ever again! I had to come to terms with the fact that I would *never* see her again! I still see her *corpse* every time I close my eyes! And *you.”* Katara slammed Hahn back into his chair, still feeling like there was a storm filling up her body. “You have the *audacity* to tell me that the most traumatic experience of my *life* , of my brother’s, of my *family’s* life, is a *sob story* ? That my *mother’s death* is all about *you* , about fooling *you* ?!” She took a deep breath, but nothing could stop her from yelling. “You’re nothing but a stuck-up, useless, dumb as a fucking rock, rich boy who thinks he’s something important. You give absolutely *nothing good* to this world, and you have *no fucking right* to tell me that *my mother’s* *death* was all for *you* .” She turned away and began to walk out. “If that’s the kind of accusation I’m going to face, I’m not going to answer any more questions from *you* .” She turned to the officer. “If you have any more questions that are actually useful, feel free to ask them later, when *he* is out of my sight.”

She left the interrogation room, slamming the door shut behind her.

The group was gathered on the steps outside of the police station, having been released due to “very little evidence against them.” Toph had fallen asleep on Mai’s shoulder, Suki was leaning on the railing with her eyes half-closed, Sokka was staring at nothing, Azula was sitting on the steps with her head in her hands, and Zuko was pacing lazily, almost coming to a stop every few seconds. Only Katara didn’t look exhausted. Instead, there might as well have been a stormcloud floating above her head. Nobody was brave enough to ask her why.

At last, Zuko managed to get up the energy to stand in front of the group, even though he was yawning. “Listen, everyone.” Everyone looked up at him, most of them looking like they were about to fall asleep right then and there. “We’re all exhausted. We’re not going to get anything else done tonight, so we need to go home and get some sleep. But that doesn’t mean this is over.” He looked around. “The professor’s death may have been a tragedy, but it proves something. I don’t think it’s a coincidence that the professor died when and where he did.”

Azula raised an eyebrow. “So what you’re saying is...it wasn’t a coincidence.”

Zuko nodded. “Far from it. The professor was our way into the woods. Somebody wanted to stop that. Meaning…”

“There’s something out there that somebody *really* doesn’t want us to find.”

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

I hope you all enjoyed that chapter! It was fun to write, especially Katara and Azula's parts. I love those moments when Katara just becomes a tidal wave of anger and raw power(don't worry, it's not the last time you'll see it), and I love Azula just being done with everyone else ("I don't live here.")

If you have thoughts, please leave a comment, or come talk to me on Tumblr at @theatergirl06! Seriously, your opinions really mean so much to me. I'd love to hear them:)

## Chapter 19: The Tuesday Night Club

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

A new development leads the group back to the White Lotus mansion, where they are forced to confront some secrets, emotions, and information.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Mentions of death, unhealthy romantic relationship dynamics.

This one has some fluffy scenes and some angsty scenes. Overall, it was a fun one to write! Happy reading!

### Text

Nobody woke up before noon the next day. Even as he pulled himself out of bed at 12:30, Sokka still felt like he’d only fallen asleep a few minutes ago. Yawning, he made his way to the kitchen, where Katara, who had slept on his sofa since her apartment was further away from the police station, was already up. Without a word, she handed him a cup of coffee.

“You okay?” asked Sokka. “You seemed pretty shaken up last night. And then...I don’t know what happened during your interrogation, but whatever it was didn’t really seem to calm you down.” He laughed, not knowing what else to say.

Katara nodded, taking a sip of her tea and sighing. “I’m okay now. It’s just...seeing Professor Zei’s body reminded me of...well, you know what it reminded me of.”

“I know,” said Sokka. “That’s why I’m asking if you’re okay.” Smiling at Katara, he wrapped his arm around her, pulling her in for a hug. “It’s okay if you’re not, you know. Okay.”

“I will be,” said Katara. “Though if I ever have to see Hahn again, I swear I will *strangle* him.”

Sokka nearly choked on his coffee. Very few things could make Katara angry, but once Katara was angry, she was *really* angry. “Why, what did he do?”

“Oh, just accused me of lying about our mother’s death.” Katara’s tone made it clear that she was still absolutely furious.  
“He *didn’t*.”

Katara rolled her eyes and took another sip of her tea. “You *know* what a jerk he is. He would totally do something like that.”

“I think…” Sokka cut himself off. “Yeah, you’re right. He totally would.” He smirked. “I bet you gave him a real piece of your mind, didn’t you?”

“How did you know?”

Sokka smiled, taking another sip of coffee. “No offense, sister, but you do have some patterns that are a little predictable.”

“Such as?”  
“Such as, when you get angry at someone, they’d better watch out.”

Katara made a big show of flipping her hair and sipping her tea haughtily, like a character from a period drama. “As they should.”

They were interrupted by the sounds of a violin orchestra playing from Sokka’s phone.

Katara smirked, putting her left hand on her hip. “Whose ringtone is *that* ? It sounds like background music from a soap opera or something.”

Sokka tried his best to hide the dark tint that his face had suddenly taken on. “It’s Zuko. He says the four of us are meeting at his apartment in half an hour to try and find another way into the woods.”

“Not Suki, Toph, or Mai?” Katara was interrupted by her own phone. “Nevermind. Suki says the Dai Li is keeping everyone under close watch since the last murder.” Another pinging sound. This time, Sokka saw Katara’s face grow darker as she picked the phone up. “Yue says that it’s the same thing for the White Lotus.”

Sokka scanned himself and Katara up and down. Both of them were still wearing their pajamas. “Think we can get to Zuko’s apartment in half an hour?”

“ *I’m* always on time when I need to be. *You’re* the one who always makes us late!”

“What?! How can you say that?! The complete *opposite* is true!”

Azula hated waiting for other people. Her whole life, she had always worked on her own, doing everything she possibly could with the maximum possible efficiency. It was why she had always hated group projects. You had to depend on other people to finish on time, and do all the tasks correctly. Ninety-nine percent of the time, they either didn’t finish their work, or did all of the work wrong, and then you had to do all of their work in addition to your own, usually at the last minute because your project partner never bothered to tell you that they hadn’t done their work until the night before the project was due.

Suffice to say, Azula had quickly earned a reputation in school for being incredibly bossy, “taking over” group projects, and always doing the entire project herself. It wasn’t even her fault!

Besides not working to the maximum efficiency, Azula hated waiting for other people because she was profoundly not used to doing nothing. She had always been doing *something* ; any minute spent being unproductive was a minute to be ashamed of. She didn’t really know how to sit still and *wait* .

Zuko didn’t seem to have any problem with it, though. He’d brought a book in from his study, and was flipping through it, though it looked almost too heavy to lift from where Azula was sitting. A History of Animation, read the title. It wasn’t something that Azula ever would have chosen to study herself, but she could see why somebody else might find it interesting.

Not knowing what else to do, she picked up the television remote and started flipping through the channels, something she’d never done in her entire life. She wasn’t sure why people would find these shows appealing at all. One of them was about teenagers who looked more like they were thirty, and for some inexplicable reason, owned nightclubs. Another was two adults talking about the ex-wife that they had both married and divorced twice, and another was a cooking show where they had to make cakes that looked like pineapples. The only one that looked slightly interesting was a cartoon that seemed to be about witches who could enchant people with their music, except there was clear romantic tension between the witches. But Azula didn’t understand any of the plot, and she *hated* not understanding things, so she skipped past it to the news. She was about to flip past the news, too, but she caught sight of the headline at the bottom of the screen and paused. “Zuko?”

Her brother looked up from his book. “What?”

Azula gestured to the television screen. “I think you’re going to want to see this.”

Katara was surprised, to say the least, when she and Sokka arrived at Zuko’s apartment, only to have Azula grab them both by the upper arms and yank them into the living room. But once she saw what the siblings were watching, she understood. The four of them simply stared at the television in shock.

Michi, Mai’s mother, was standing in front of several microphones, looking teary-eyed, and holding a baby that Katara assumed was Mai’s younger brother. The headline running across the bottom of the screen read: *Renowned City Council and Dai Li member Ukano found dead.* *Authorities are still investigating.*

“Another murder?” gasped Katara. “So soon?”

Azula nodded grimly. “Seems our assassin has been busy.” She turned up the sound on the TV. “Let’s hear what Michi has to say.”

*“Miss,* ” said a reporter from behind the camera, *“you’ve obviously witnessed a very tragic event.* *How is your Dai Li family coping with this?”*

Michi wiped at her eyes with a handkerchief. *“Well, I won’t lie. It’s been difficult. We were all* *shocked when the news broke that the body was discovered. I think we’re all coping a little bit* *differently. Personally, I’m just trying my best to be strong. For my son and my daughter.”*

“Yeah, right,” scoffed Katara. “Like Mai wants her mother trying to be strong for her.” Azula let out a bitter laugh of agreement.

“ *Can you tell us anything about the circumstances of your husband’s death?”*

*“Well, I don’t know the specifics, since the morgue has been keeping autopsies under wraps in* *light of...recent events.”*

“AKA the string of murders,” said Azula, sipping her coffee.

“B *ut we do know that he was found in an alleyway, and the authorities suspect murder.”*

*“And do you have anyone you may suspect for this crime?”*

Michi’s gaze hardened as she stared into the camera. *“The scum at the White Lotus. I used to try so* *hard to forgive them, but I know they hated my husband, and everything he did. If anyone’s behind* *this, they are.”*

The camera panned away from Michi, revealing a reporter’s face. *“Well, citizens, it seems that the* *police would agree with Miss Michi. Forces arrived at the White Lotus mansion this morning, and* *have been interrogating various members all day. Who knows where this investigation will go* *next? In other news…”*

Azula switched off the television. The group looked around the room, all shocked, glancing at one another. Finally, Katara spoke.

“We *need* to go to the White Lotus mansion. Now.”

The group arrived at the White Lotus mansion to find an enormous van, painted Dai Li green. There was a crowd of officers outside the house, all banging on the door and shouting. Behind the officers was an equally large crowd of television reporters, all of whom were being even louder and more obnoxious than the police officers.

Sokka turned to the rest of the group, a perplexed look on his face. They had ducked behind one of the White Lotus’s many hedges to hide from the crowd, who would undoubtedly be the complete opposite of thrilled to see four teenage detectives messing with their case. “How are we gonna get in there with so many people blocking the door?”

As if to answer his question, there was a loud rustle from the hedge they were standing behind, and a second later, Aang came rolling out of the hedge and onto the ground. He came to the stop in front of the four detectives and stared up at them with a rather grim expression.

He beckoned towards the hedge. “Come with me.”

Sokka glanced at Zuko before following Aang into the hedge. After crawling into the bush, a trapdoor opened in the ground that led to a long stone staircase. At the bottom of the stairs was a stone passageway lined with torches that could only lead into the house.

“Has the White Lotus had this secret passage the whole time?”

Aang nodded. “Yeah. Nobody’s supposed to know it’s here, though, so please don’t tell anyone.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it,” said Sokka. Behind him, Zuko was wearing an expression that made him seem like he was remembering something important. “You okay?”

Zuko nodded. “Yeah, just…” he ran to catch up with Aang. “Aang, are there other secret passages in the mansion?”

Aang twiddled his fingers nervously. “Uh...no. Why would you think that? Of course there aren’t any more.”

Well, the guy may have been sweet, but he was a *terrible* liar. Sokka wondered where the other passages in the White Lotus mansion might have been, and why they had asked a fifteen-year-old to lie about their existence.

It seemed like everybody in this city had some sort of secret. It was honestly pretty exhausting. Life would be a lot easier if everyone would just be honest.

Also if people didn’t murder other people. That would make life a *lot* easier.

After an unusually long walk, considering they had started less than a hundred feet from the house, the group began to climb another set of stone stairs. Unlike the last staircase, which had been straight, this one was spiralling, like the ones inside the mansion. Aang grabbed a torch to lead them up, and Katara, who was the last in line, had to keep running so as not to lose the light due to the staircase’s tight spirals.

When they reached the top, Aang pushed on the stone above him, which revealed itself to be a trapdoor. As they climbed out, the group found themselves in the lower right corner of the White Lotus mansion’s lobby.

The entire group, or at least *almost* the entire group, was milling around. Some were reading, some were holding the doors shut, some were just pacing nervously. Aang, spotting Bumi in the opposite corner, gave the group a wave and raced over to him.

Sokka glanced at the others. “So do we go interrogate people, or…”

Zuko scanned the room. He seemed to think hard for a moment, then he turned to the rest of them. “We split up. Try to get a feel of things. And try not to get ourselves killed.”

The other three of them nodded, and the four of them split off in separate directions, each heading for a different corner of the room. Sokka headed for the doors, where Piandao and Jeong Jeong were pushing hard and trying to hold them shut. Impulsively, Sokka began to push on them, too.

“Why won’t you let the police come in and interview you? Isn’t that sort of suspicious?” The sounds of the crowd outside were so loud that Sokka had to shout just to get the two men to hear him.

Jeong Jeong narrowed his eyes, clearly furious. “These people have the audacity to question our honor, when we have done nothing but good for this city. They simply want someone to blame, in order to continue the cycle of blame and bloodshed. I will not answer to those accusations, and I refuse to participate in a system of that sort.”

Sokka turned to Piandao, who seemed to be the more calm of the two. “And you?”

Piandao sighed. “To tell you the truth, I’m just helping out my friends, for the most part. If the police want to interrogate me on my own, with evidence, they’re welcome to do so, but it feels wrong to accuse an entire organization without concrete proof.”

Those...actually seemed like kind of reasonable explanations. “And you don’t have anything to hide from the police? From anyone?”

Jeong Jeong pushed the door so hard that it slammed completely shut despite the crowd on the other side, causing all three of them to go skidding back a few feet. “The White Lotus is a revered organization with traditions that go back centuries! If we want to keep them from prying eyes, we have the right to do so!”

“So you *are* hiding something!” Sokka was so excited to have discovered something that he was shouting without even realizing it.

Piandao looked around. Even he, who was almost always the epitome of calm, looked slightly anxious. He grabbed Sokka’s shoulders and pulled him in close. “The White Lotus has absolutely nothing to hide, and if we did, we would never share it with an irresponsible nineteen-year-old. Now, please stop asking us questions without a warrant, or else you’re no better in our eyes than those wasps out there.”

Both men turned back to the doors, and wouldn’t speak another word.

After splitting off from the rest of the group, Azula followed Aang across the room, and took a seat next to him and Bumi, who were talking and laughing in hushed voices. She leaned in, trying to catch snippets of their conversation without them realizing that she was eavesdropping. Unfortunately for her, Bumi seemed to sense that she was there right away. Instead of shooing her away, he and Aang both moved aside to make room for her. She tried not to shudder as she lowered herself onto the floor. It had probably (hopefully) been cleaned very recently.

“Thank you.”

Bumi smiled at her. “In times like these, we all need our friends and family more than ever.”

Azula barely knew these people, but she decided that perhaps now wasn’t the time to mention that. “What do you mean ‘times like these?’”

Bumi sighed, his eyes growing misty. “Run-ins with the police never end well for the White Lotus.” He shook his head grimly. “They’ve never liked us, and especially not our attitude towards the rules!” He and Aang both laughed, but seconds later, his expression turned serious again.

“Especially since the Dai Li came along,” added Aang. “We’re just hoping that everything will turn out okay.” He wrapped his arms around Bumi, and Bumi, despite the fact that his gaze was focused on the doors, gently reciprocated the gesture.

Azula was wondering what to say next when a pink blur came flying across the room. She sighed with relief. This would undoubtedly also be confusing and awkward, but it was at least a kind of confusing and awkward that Azula was familiar with. After these past nine days, she had become very familiar with it indeed.

“Azula!” cried Ty Lee, quickly pulling Azula to her feet and wrapping her in a hug, “I’m so glad you’re here!”

“Me too,” said Azula, as Ty Lee released her from the hug. “I hope you’re doing all right. With the police being here, and all.”

“Oh,” said Ty Lee, clearly making an effort to act calm and flipping her braid over her shoulder, something Azula had never seen her do before. Perhaps she did it when she was nervous, “we’re managing. It’s just... *very* tense here.”

Azula knew a little bit about tense houses. She was used to rooms that felt so tense that she felt like she was suffocating. If that was how Ty Lee felt right now, then she couldn’t let that happen. “Well then, we should go outside!” It was only after the words had left her that she realized that she had shouted, and thrust her hand up in the air. How mortifying.

Ty Lee laughed. “I guess a walk in the gardens wouldn’t be the worst idea in the world. You haven’t seen the gardens yet, have you?” Azula shook her head. “Then come on, I’ll show you!”

Azula tried not to show the red spots that appeared on her cheeks the second that Ty Lee grabbed her hand to lead her outside.

The gardens absolutely did not disappoint. They were exactly the sort of gardens Azula would have designed herself, if she had time for such things. Most of them consisted of neatly trimmed hedges that formed rows and squares. Each square housed a different kind of flower, and there were flowers in every color of the rainbow. The whole garden was surrounded by a tall stone wall that was covered in ivy, and at the very center was a glittering fountain that sourced several small streams that flowed through the garden.

Ty Lee led Azula to a spot on the edge of the fountain. She looked so at home in the garden, among the pink roses and the glittering water of the fountain. The garden’s ethereal, random yet perfect beauty reminded Azula a lot of Ty Lee. Ty Lee’s beauty was exactly like that of a garden; mystical, unique, yet breathtaking.

“Hey, are you all right?”

Azula realized that she’d been staring at Ty Lee, and felt her face turn red again, as she looked away. “Of course I’m okay. I’m just glad you got out of there.” She finally managed to turn back to Ty Lee by focusing her eyes on the flowers to her left. “This place is beautiful.”

“Isn’t it?” sighed Ty Lee. “It’s my favorite place in the mansion. Besides my room, it’s where I feel the most…”

“Free?”

Ty Lee nodded. “How did you know?”

Azula sighed. “I grew up with a lot of tense rooms and strict rules. Places that were all my own helped a lot.”

Ty Lee frowned, leaning back. “Look, Azula, I don’t know everything about how you grew up, but I’m just sorry that you went through...whatever it was. It sounds hard.”

“Says the girl whose house is currently swarming with police.”

Ty Lee laughed. “Fair enough.” She turned and looked at Azula. “But really, if you ever want somewhere to talk about it...you’ll always be safe here.”

“Nonsense,” said Azula. “You just said this garden is where you feel free. I couldn’t take that away from you.”

Ty Lee reached over and took Azula’s hands. Azula had to force herself not to look away as her face reddened for the thousandth time. “Azula, the garden is my space. I can do what I want with it, and I can fill it with whatever makes me happy. You’re my *friend* . You could never do that to me.”

About eight hundred emotions were racing through Azula’s mind. Here was someone...someone bright, and warm, and amazing, and she was saying that Azula made her *happy* . She *saw* something in Azula, somehow, that made her *happy* .

Maybe it was temporary insanity, or an impulse, or sleep deprivation, but Azula said it anyway.

“Say, Ty Lee...would you ever want to do something with me? I know we’re doing something right now, but see...what I meant was, well, getting to know you has been so lovely, and…”

“Like a date?” Ty Lee’s face flushed pink. Azula could feel her heart beating inside her chest. Still, she managed a nod. Ty Lee smiled.

“I would love to.”

After last night, Katara wasn’t in the mood to talk to anyone. She stormed across the room and leaned on a pillar instead, surveying the crowd around her. There was an air of tension in the room, to be sure, but Katara didn’t mind. It felt a little bit like a stormcloud, something that matched Katara’s current mood absolutely perfectly.

“What brings you here?” asked an ancient voice from next to her. Surprised, Katara turned to see Yon Rha leaning on the other side of the pillar.

“Oh,” she said, toying with her hair and laughing awkwardly. What lie was she supposed to tell? “I’m...uh...here to see Yue!” Well, it was a half-truth. She would never turn down seeing Yue.

Yon Rha raised an eyebrow. “I believe Yue is busy today. She has important engagements to attend to.”

Katara narrowed her eyes. She was *not* going to leave her friend alone at some White Lotus thing, not after Yue had confessed to her about feeling pressure and the weight of everyone’s expectations on her all the time. She would do everything she could to support her, especially on a day like this.

She turned to Yon Rha. “Listen, I know you’re all stressed, but I need you to take me to Yue. Please.”

Yon Rha threw his hands up in the air. “Who am I to separate two people who are close to one another? But I should warn you...you may not like what you find.”

“What could Yue be doing that I wouldn’t like? She’s my friend, not an extension of me. It doesn’t matter what she does.”

“If you say so,” said Yon Rha, opening the door to a hallway. “Follow me.”

After a few feet, they made a right, into a hallway made entirely of some sort of purple gemstone. Katara found herself staring in awe at the glittering walls. She could even see her own reflection if she looked at the hallway from the right angle. It looked distorted, and she laughed.

Yon Rha stopped abruptly in front of a small door, painted with a four-leaf green clover. “They’re in there?”  
“Who’s *they*?”

Yon Rha sighed, looking nervous. “See for yourself.”

Katara opened the door, then dropped the notebook and pen she was carrying in shock. The door opened to a small, wooden room, hardly bigger than a closet. Inside the room stood Hahn and Yue. They were kissing.

It felt like an eternity before Katara’s pen finally hit the ground, another eternity before Katara finally managed to summon words. “Yue?”

Yue caught sight of her, and quickly broke away from Hahn. “Katara! I...I promise, it’s not what you think!”

Rage, sadness, and confusion all swirled around inside Katara’s mind like one giant whirlpool. She could feel tears welling up in her eyes. “What are you doing?”

Hahn stepped forward, wearing that same obnoxious smirk. “You mean you don’t know? Oh, Liar Girl. I thought you were smarter than that.”

Katara felt her fists clench. Regardless of her feelings about Yue, she knew *exactly* how she felt about Hahn. “Explain. *Now* .”

Hahn made a big show of throwing his arm around Yue’s shoulders. Yue tried to pull away from him, but he pulled her close and held her tight. “This girl right here is gonna be my future wife! We’re getting married, baby!”

It took a few seconds before the words finally sank into Katara’s mind. She could feel the storm welling up inside her body. She turned to Yon Rha. “What does he mean?” She hated how her own voice shook.

Yon Rha nodded, smiling, unaware of Katara’s tears. “These two are the future of the White Lotus.”

“Yue,” Katara could barely manage a whisper as she turned to face the girl she’d thought was her friend, maybe even more, “tell me it isn’t true.”

Yue looked away, tears falling from her eyes, her lower lip trembling. “It’s true, Katara,” she said at last, her eyes shining. “I’m engaged.”

Zuko took the group’s splitting up as an excuse to quickly dash up the stairs and out of sight. Aang had basically confirmed that there were more secret passages in the White Lotus mansion, and Zuko had a hunch that he knew where one of them was.

When he got to the third floor, he found himself outside the giant doors of the library for the second time. What he didn’t expect to find was his uncle blocking his way.

“Zuko, I’m begging you. The White Lotus is more dangerous than you might think. There are secrets buried in this mansion that I wouldn’t wish on anyone. For your own safety, please stay away.”

Zuko stood tall. He’d always been stubborn, and he wasn’t going to stop now, not when people’s lives were on the line. Not even for his uncle. “Uncle, I’m sorry. But I need to find out everything I can if I’m going to stop more people from getting killed. This threat is *real* . People are *dying* . *You* hired me to take this case, so *please* , let me solve it.”

Iroh stared at him for a second, then let him pass with a small smile, pressing a finger to his lips.

Zuko sprinted through the library to the crooked torch he remembered from a few days ago. This time, he yanked on it without any hesitation. As he pulled, he felt something creak, and the bookshelf directly to his right spun sideways, revealing a stone passageway nearly identical to the one they’d used to enter the mansion.

Not missing a beat, still gasping for air, he ran down the passageway as fast as he could. He was vaguely aware that he turned left at some point, and that he was going down, but other than that, he just ran. He had no idea how far.

At last, he reached the end of the passage; a circular chamber lined with torches, with a wooden chest in the center.

Yanking on the lid as hard as he could, Zuko managed to pry it open and grab the paper inside. Too full of adrenaline to wait, he rolled the paper open and held it up to the torchlight.

It was a map, showing a route to the East of the city, ending in a red X with a small note saying “Show no one, tell no one. Secrets must stay buried.”

Zuko let out a gasp, trying to process what he was seeing. A map, a secret location, something the White Lotus didn’t want anyone to find…

Could the White Lotus have some sort of secret fortress outside the city, just like the Dai Li?
