## Chapter 20: Philomel Cottage

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

A trip into the Eastern woods brings Zuko, Sokka, Katara, and Azula on a trip down memory lane.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Flashbacks, corpses, death, burning, child abuse, self-hatred.

Sorry this is being posted so soon after the last chapter! I usually like to allow a little more time, but that didn't happen today, so y'all are getting two chapters one hour after the other. Oh well!

As the summary and TWs might have given away, this one's pretty angsty. Enjoy:)

### Text

Azula used her phone to light up the map that Zuko had brought out of the library. The four of them had crowded into a small closet on the second floor to avoid being spotted, and unfortunately, there was no light inside.

“I don’t believe this,” said Katara. “Another secret fortress?”

“Seems like *everyone* around here has some sort of secret,” said Sokka. Azula laughed, and even in the dark, she could see the whole group turn to stare at her.

“ *Everyone* has secrets,” she said. “Only a fool would believe otherwise.” If only she could share her own.

“Not the point,” said Zuko, turning back to the map. “We need to get to this place before the White Lotus realizes that their map is missing.”

“We need to do more than that,” said Azula. “We need to make sure that neither the White Lotus nor the Dai Li messes this up. We don’t want a repeat of the last time we all went into the woods.”

“We can probably make it out of here without being spotted, especially if we get someone to cause a distraction,” said Sokka. “But what about the Dai Li? They could be following us.”

Azula pulled her phone away from the map and typed a text to Suki. She received a response within seconds. “Not if we have allies who know how to avoid them.” She showed the rest of the group her screen. “I think we’ll be just fine with her and Mai around.”

“Okay, then,” said Katara, opening the door a crack and peering out. “That doesn’t solve the problem of getting out of here.”

“Need a hand?” said a voice from the other side of the door. Katara gasped and swung it open, nearly slamming it right into Aang, Ty Lee, and Yue, who were standing outside, all of them smiling.

“We can get you out of here,” said Yue. “Just use the way you came in.”

“No one’ll see you,” added Aang.

Ty Lee smirked, the first smirk Azula had ever seen from her, and looked directly at Azula, who was pretty sure she looked like a tomato, and had never been more glad for the absence of a mirror. “We can be *very* distracting when we need to be.”

Forty-five minutes later, the group was standing on the Eastern edge of the city, now accompanied by Mai and Suki, both of whom had been more than happy to get out of the house.

“They were keeping us under lock and key,” Suki said. “It was suffocating. I couldn’t even train without someone watching me.”

“It was boring,” Mai added. “You couldn’t do *anything* fun with those vultures looking over your shoulder all the time.”

“How did you manage to get out here, then?” asked Katara as they began walking into the woods, following Zuko, who had the map, and Sokka, who was apparently really good at reading maps.

Mai smirked. “Toph lent us a hand,” she said. “When the youngest member of your group, who also happens to be blind, appears to be having a fit because her peas weren’t cooked enough, you’d be surprised what you can get away with.”

“I’ll bet she had a fun time with *that* ,” said Katara, smirking at the thought.

“ *Had* ?” said Suki. “She’s probably still screaming now!”

All three girls burst into laughter, earning them a glare from Azula, who, Katara noted, had coiled her hair into a topknot again. She thought Azula looked better with her hair half-up-half-down, but she wasn’t going to say anything. She ran a few feet, and fell into step beside the amateur detective.

“Do you...know when you’ll need to go home?”

Azula shook her head. “I’m technically on October vacation until the beginning of November, but my father gave me permission to stay away for as long as I wanted. Said I needed ‘real world experience’ and that anything I missed could easily be supplemented with private tutors and doubling my classes.” She turned and looked at Katara. “What about you? Don’t you have to go back to school?”

Katara shook her head. “My school has a thing for seventeen and eighteen-year-olds where you can take a semester to do ‘career based learning’ if you finish your credits early. That’s what I’m doing with the Ba Sing Se Journal.”

“Have you enjoyed interning for them?”

Katara sighed. “I guess. I don’t do much. The government in this city puts a lot of restrictions on what people are allowed to write. I started interning in journalism because I thought I’d be able to reveal the truth to the general public and, you know, help people, but mostly I’ve been sorting files and running back and forth, helping people go through the town archives. Even the actual reporters don’t do much. They just use the template the government gives them.”

“Maybe it’s time to start your own news source if you’re unhappy with the current ones.”

“I wish, but I’m too young to do anything like that.”

“Nonsense,” said Azula. “My father’s been training me to run a business empire ever since I was a child.”

Katara raised an eyebrow. “That’s...a lot of pressure to put on someone.”

“Well, I displayed a lot of the necessary traits early on, so it only made sense.”

“Necessary traits like what?”

Azula sighed. “Well, if you must know, traits like high intelligence, perception, pragmatism,” she looked uncomfortable for a moment, staring at her shoes, “and ruthlessness.”

Katara was surprised when a harsh laugh escaped her. “Well, I’m sorry, but those are messed-up traits to pin on a child!”

“It was only the truth.”

“Who cares? We all have tons of different traits when we’re little! It’s messed-up to take some small aspect of a child and exploit it until they’re convinced it’s all they ever get to be!”

“I never thought of that,” said Azula, grabbing Katara’s wrist to stop her from tripping over a root. “But that doesn’t mean that I wasn’t an unusual child.”

Katara smiled. “Knowing you, I wouldn’t imagine that you were ever anything else. All I’m saying is...you don’t have to only be those things because your father told you that that’s what you were.”

Azula was silent. Katara wished she knew what she was thinking. Like Zuko, her new friend clearly didn’t want to share everything. Katara could respect that, but she hoped that Azula knew that she was here if she ever wanted to share more.

Up ahead, Zuko and Sokka came to a stop, and beckoned to the rest of the group to come forward. The narrow path had come to a clearing, surrounded by about twelve tall, wide trees, all of which were clearly the same species, and had probably been planted intentionally. The only tree out of place was a tree that had been cut down, which was partly covering the path the group was on. It was clearly supposed to block trespassers (like them) from entering the clearing.

The cottage in the middle of the clearing couldn’t have been built by anyone other than the White Lotus. It was made of pure white marble, and despite the fact that it was technically a cottage, it looked rather grand, with a smaller part that looked to be a front hall, and a larger part in the back. There was a white, round, stained-glass window above the door that took the shape of (what else?) a lotus flower.

Instinctively, the group ducked behind the trees on either side of the trail. Katara found herself next to Azula, behind a tree to the right of the cottage door.

“Somebody needs to go in and make sure no one’s there,” whispered Sokka from Katara’s right. To her left, on the other side of the trail, Suki nodded. It took Katara a moment, but she soon felt Azula, Zuko, Suki, and Mai’s eyes on her.

“Why is everyone looking at *me* ?”

Suki shrugged. “We need to send someone in who’s believable. You can say that you’re getting something for Yue.

Katara thought of Yue’s engagement, her lies, and felt her blood boil. She cared about her friend, but was also completely furious at her. She didn’t know what to think.

“I don’t want to talk about her right now!” she hissed.

Azula rolled her eyes. “It doesn’t matter whether your sentiment is genuine or not,” she whispered. “As long as anyone you may run into believes you.”

“I’m not going to use my friendship to lie to people!”

Azula sighed. “Katara, do you want to stop these murders or not?”

“Of course I do!”

“Then we need to do what’s necessary! When you’re in dangerous situations like this, you can’t afford to be morally perfect all the time! Even if you want to.”

“It doesn’t make you a bad person,” said Zuko, who clearly understood her better than Azula did right now. “We’ve all had to make sacrifices when we’re fighting for what’s right.”

Katara sighed. She didn’t like this, but what choice did she have? “All right, fine. I’ll go. And if I see anyone, I’ll lie.”

Sokka reached over and squeezed her arm. “I’ll go with you,” he said, smiling. “You can say you needed my help to get through the woods.”

Katara rolled her eyes as the two siblings made their way towards the cottage. “That could *not* be more untrue.”

Zuko didn’t realize he was drumming impatiently on the tree until Azula reached over and slapped him.

“Ow!”

“If you keep drumming on that tree like you’re in high school band rehearsal, it will be heard for miles around, and we will all be apprehended and possibly murdered.”

“Wow,” said Mai from the other side of the path, “your thoughts are even darker than I thought.”

“You’re one to talk.”

Mai was about to say something back, but they were interrupted by a clatter from the cottage. Turning, the four of them peered through the trees. A few seconds later, the door opened, and Sokka and Katara popped their heads out, beckoning to the rest of them. Zuko started towards the house, but Azula grabbed his arm before he could go any further. “Wait. We should get someone to stay out here in case someone else shows up.”

“Good idea,” said Suki, drawing a fan from her pocket. “I’ll stay here. The rest of you can go on in.”

“Hold on,” said Mai, turning to Suki. “Are you trying to get rid of me?”

“No, I just…”

“No one should be out here alone.” Mai took a seat on the fallen log, and turned to the two remaining siblings. “You two go into that dusty hellhole and let me know if you find anything interesting. I’ll make sure Princess over here doesn’t get into too much trouble.”

“I don’t need any protection!”  
“Sure you don’t,” said Mai with a smirk. She turned back to Zuko. “Seriously. Go in before somebody else gets here. We didn’t come all the way into the woods for nothing.”

Zuko nodded, and he and Azula edged their way towards the house, where Sokka was already waiting in the doorway. “Hurry up!” he whispered. “Who knows how long we have?”

“Did you find anything?” asked Azula as they reached the door.

Katara appeared next to her brother in the doorway, nodding. “You two are going to want to see this.”

Zuko wasn’t exactly sure what he’d been expecting, but this definitely wasn’t it. Usually, at least in movies, these sorts of secret fortresses were dark, probably filled with cobwebs, and a bunch of really old artifacts that were stacked so high that it was sort of like a maze. This cottage was the exact opposite of that; everything inside was white, grey, or silver. Sunlight streamed through the window, making the whole room seem like it was glowing, and the floor was bare, except for an enormous number of filing cabinets lining the walls. Katara and Sokka had opened one, and were spreading out its files on the floor.

“Filing cabinets?” mused Azula. “An interesting thing to hide.”

“It means they have information here that they don’t want us to find,” said Zuko. He turned to Sokka and Katara. “Did you find anything that looked a little out of place?”

“A little?” Sokka scoffed. “Buddy, we found more than that.”

Katara nodded. “Come look at this.”

The siblings knelt down around the pile of files. Zuko picked them up and began to leaf through them.

Each file contained a photo of somebody, and several pieces of information about them. “Who are these people?” asked Azula, who was flipping through files at an alarming speed. “People allied with the White Lotus?” She held up the file she was holding. “I think this is the man who runs the circus where Ty Lee works.”

“That’s what we thought, too,” said Sokka. “Then we found this.” He held up another file. Inside of it was a picture of Long Feng.

“Okay, then,” said Zuko. “Allies and enemies. Kind of creepy, but I guess it makes sense.”

“I don’t think so,” said Katara. “Look at how many cabinets there are.” She got up and started opening the file cabinet doors. Each cabinet was completely full. “The White Lotus couldn’t possibly have *this* many allies and enemies.”

“Then what?” said Azula, pulling another file from a random cabinet. As she did, a photograph came fluttering out. Katara’s face stared up at them.

Clearly freaked out, Katara raced over and picked up the photograph, her hand running over her face as though she couldn’t believe that it was the same face as the one in the picture. “What am *I* doing here? I barely *know* the White Lotus!”

Zuko picked up another file. This one had a photograph of Chan, the idiot who co-owned a bar. He had no relationship to the White Lotus at all, at least not that Zuko knew of. “I don’t think it’s personal, Katara,” he said, looking up at the others. “I think the White Lotus has a file on everyone in the city.”

The group stood in silence for a moment until Sokka picked up a file, flipping it open. “That’s not all. Look what kind of information they keep in here.” He turned the file outwards so that the rest of the group could see it. “There’s name, age, profession, all that normalish stuff, but look at this.” He began reading the file out loud. “What we are owed, why they threaten our principles.” He shuddered. “Sounds like the White Lotus is watching people more closely than we thought.”

Azula was still thumbing through files at a rapid rate. “Seems like more than half the entrepreneurs in this city owe the White Lotus some amount of money. It’s really astounding. And from the looks of it, they could pay them back, but the White Lotus won’t let them. It says here ‘Keep debt. Use for future influence.’”

“That’s not the worst of it,” said Katara. “Everyone who so much mentions order, or rules, is written up in here.” She began to read, too. “Why they threaten our principles: Mentioned the benefits of laws in an offhand comment to their class at school.” She looked up, her eyes wide. “This person was a *teacher* !”

“This is insane,” said Sokka. “What do we do with this?”

“We go through more files,” said Zuko. “As many as we can. And we take pictures.” He held up his phone. “Anything that looks incriminating, we photograph.”

“And then?” asked Katara.

Zuko sighed. “I don’t know. But it’s a start.”

The four teenagers each went to a different corner of the room and began skimming through files. Soon, stacks were forming next to all of them, and even though reading the files had been Zuko’s idea, he could feel his eyes beginning to glaze over already.

That is, until he stopped on a file with a *very* familiar face.

It wasn’t that Zuko hadn’t seen pictures and videos of his father on the news since he’d run away two years ago. Hell, he saw something resembling his father’s face every single time he looked in the mirror. But seeing him so close, so solid in Zuko’s hands, even just in a photograph, made every single one of Zuko’s senses go on high alert. Adrenaline coursed through Zuko’s body, and it was as if he was right back home all over again.

*Zuko was seventeen years old, and had just graduated high school. He was supposed to go to the* *elite Agni University next fall. That was what his father had wanted for him ever since he was a* *child. He may have been a failure, but by some miracle, he’d gotten in.*

*And he was about to throw that all away.*

*It was a dark and stormy night as Zuko threw his phone, a few clothes, and a photograph of him* *and his mother into a backpack. It had taken two years of reconnecting with his uncle, but Zuko* *was finally ready to refuse the life his father had planned for him. He was ready to leave his* *father.*

*Thunder crashed outside, making it easier for Zuko to sneak as quietly as he could down the* *creaking stairs. He didn’t bother leaving a note, not even for Azula. If she’d cared at all, he would* *have. But he knew she would be glad to have him gone; after all, her purpose in life seemed to be to* *carry out her father’s will and mock Zuko constantly.*

*He wouldn’t miss this place. Not the constant fear that he was about to be punished, not the* *mockery, not the impossible standards, and not the smashing clay that echoed through the house* *more and more often ever since their mother had died, eight years ago now.*

*As he was about to slip out one of the side doors, a light came on. Zuko whirled around to find his* *father sitting in a large, red armchair. He was smoking a cigarette, something he never did. Zuko* *knew the cigarette was purely for effect, but he got chills down his spine all the same.*

*He couldn’t keep living in fear like this. That was why he was leaving.*

*“Going somewhere?” His father’s voice was like cold oil, oozing from his lips, wafting through* *the room like a chill in the air.*

*There was no point in lying. Zuko drew his shoulders back and stood tall. “Yes. I’m leaving earlier* *than I planned. And I’m not coming back. I’m not going to Agni University. I’m not going to live* *under your thumb anymore.”*

*His father laughed. “It’s funny that you think you have a choice. You were born ‘under my thumb’* *as you say, and you are far too weak to fight me.”*

*“Maybe so,” shot back Zuko. “But I’m not too weak to say that I don’t want to live like this* *anymore. I am your son, and you don’t even treat me like a living creature. I deserve more than* *this.”*

*“I gave you everything,” hissed his father with venom in his voice. “What more could you possibly* *want?”*

*“Anything,” snapped Zuko. “Anything is better than feeling unsafe in my own house. No human* *being should have to live like that.” He looked his father right in the eyes. “You’re a monster. No* *one deserves you.”*

*In a flash, Ozai moved across the room and grabbed Zuko by the arm. In a flash, he had taken the* *still-burning cigarette and pressed it into Zuko’s arm. Zuko felt the pain shoot through him, and* *tears prick at the edges of his eyes, but he didn’t scream. His tolerance for pain was way beyond a* *cigarette.*

*Ozai was gripping his arm so tightly that Zuko was starting to feel numbness in his left hand. He* *fought as hard as he could, but couldn’t free himself.*

*“This is what you’re afraid of?” hissed Ozai. “This is what’s so monstrous to you? I live to teach* *you respect, for our family and for me. If you cannot understand that, that is your failure.” He* *drove the cigarette harder into Zuko’s arm. “And you will pay for it.”*

*Before he knew what he was doing, Zuko swung his arm up and slapped Ozai in the face. He was* *so startled that he stumbled back, allowing Zuko to race to the doorway and slam the door behind* *him. He began to run through the pouring rain, into the dark. He had little money and only a* *vague plan, but he knew he couldn’t go back.*

*“Goodbye Father,” he muttered to no one, as he ran into the dark.*

Sokka saw Zuko staring off into nothing, and waved his hand in front of his face. “Hey, you okay?”

Zuko blinked. “Yeah, totally. I just...got lost in thought.”

Sokka caught sight of the photo Zuko was holding. “Is that your dad?”

Zuko nodded. “Unfortunately.”

“Yeah, he doesn’t look like a friendly guy.” Sokka took a seat on the floor next to Zuko. “What does the White Lotus say about him?”

“Um…” Zuko glanced at the file. “That he owes them nothing, is selfish and power-hungry, and definitely a potential threat to the freedom of others, but that his son lives with one of their members, and could potentially be used as a bargaining chip.” He laughed bitterly. “Well, that isn’t true. My father couldn’t care less about me.” His gaze travelled across the room to Azula. “He cared about her, though.” For just a second, his gaze grew wistful.

“Hey,” said Sokka, putting his arm around Zuko before he could really think about it too much, “I care about you. Who cares what that idiot thought?”

Was Zuko *blushing* ? Sokka must have been imagining it. *He* was blushing, that was for sure.

Oh crap. They were staring at each other. What should he say? He couldn’t think of anything!

Thankfully, Zuko spotted something in the files. “Hey, this guy looks like you and Katara.” He pulled it out and showed Sokka the picture.

“Oh yeah,” said Sokka with a small laugh. “That’s our dad. I always forget you haven’t met him.”

“What’s he like?”

Sokka thought for a moment. “He’s...strong. When our mom died, he took on double the shifts at the market...that’s what our family owns. We almost never saw him, but every time we did, he always took the time to show us that he loved us.”

“He sounds great.”

“Yeah,” said Sokka. “He really is.”

*Sokka was ten years old, sitting in the kitchen, working on his math homework. Since their* *mother’s death and the drop in their family’s income, they had moved to an apartment in a* *different town from the food market. His dad came in, back from the hour-and-a-half long train* *ride that he took to get to the market.*

*“Hey, Dad,” said Sokka. “Why don’t you get a job closer to home? That way, we’ll get to see you* *more.”*

*His dad smiled at him, and sat down next to him at the counter. “Sokka, let me tell you something.* *There are going to be certain things in life that you decide are the most important things. Things* *that, even if we’re the most logical, practical people, we’ll put above absolutely anything else* *because those are the things close to your heart. The ones you care about the most. For me, that’s* *the store. It belonged to my wife’s family, and I loved...love my wife more than anything in the* *world. It’s important to me that I keep the store going. For her.” He gave Sokka a pat on the* *shoulder. “I’ll need you to take care of the house when I’m at work. Protect it as best as you can.”*

*“With me here, nothing like what happened to Mom will ever happen again,” promised Sokka.* *“I’ll make sure of it!”*

*His dad smiled softly. “I have no doubt.” He yawned, clearly exhausted. “I’m going to bed for the* *night. But Sokka?”*

*“Yeah?”*

*“Never forget those important things.”*

“Sokka? Everything okay?”

Sokka blinked. He didn’t know why he’d remembered that moment so suddenly and so clearly, but it was good advice. *Never forget those important things.*

He turned and looked at Zuko, who was still staring at him, concerned. *Things that, even if we’re* *the most logical, practical people, we’ll put above absolutely anything else because those are the* *things close to your heart.*

“Yeah, everything’s totally fine.”

Katara smirked as she caught sight of her brother making googly eyes at Zuko on the other side of the room, then turned back to the files that she and Azula were sorting through.

“How much longer do you give them?” asked Azula.

“Huh?”

Azula smiled mischievously. “You know, Pining Idiots number One and Two over there. How much longer do you think they’re going to keep going on like this?”

Katara laughed. “Oh, they’ve been at this for *months* . I give them another six weeks, at least.”

“Really?” mused Azula. “I say they’ll figure it out within a week of this case being finished.” “What if the case takes five weeks or longer?”

“It won’t. Not with all of us working on it.”

“All right, then,” said Katara, smiling slyly. “Want to bet on that?”

Azula grinned. It was one of the first full-on grins Katara had seen from her. “You’ve got yourself a deal. Whoever wins has to buy the other one a drink.”

“Oh,” said Katara uncomfortably, “I actually don’t drink.”

Azula laughed. “Not *that* sort of drink. You think I would do that to myself? I meant the other kind of horrible drink. You know, those insanely sugary iced teas that I’m positive you love.”

“Oh,” giggled Katara. “Then in that case, we’ve got a deal.” She reached out and made a big show out of shaking Azula’s hand.

“A pleasure doing business with you.”

Still laughing to herself, Katara turned back to her files, then froze. Her mom’s face was staring back at her. It looked like her brother’s, but she recognized the fierce gaze that Katara herself saw every time she looked in the mirror.

She looked so beautiful in the photo. It had clearly been taken without her permission (a fact that made Katara want to murder every single White Lotus member right then and there), but she was in the middle of laughing, and looked the happiest that Katara had ever seen her.

Not that her mom had been unhappy. On the contrary, she had always been a beacon of warmth, joy, light, and love, right up until the very end of her life. She had thrown herself into helping those around her, and loved everyone with passion, wholeheartedly.

Katara missed her so much. Her mom had *understood* her. Her simultaneous desire to heal the world, and fight the wrongs in it with every inch of her body. Her mom was the only person Katara had ever met who truly understood that.

She could still remember the day she died as though it was yesterday. Hell, it flashed through her mind every time she closed her eyes for too long.

*Katara laughed as her mom chased her through the house. She was eight years old, and didn’t* *want to go to bed. Sokka, two years older, was out late working at the store with their father, so* *Katara and her mom were all alone.*

*Katara skidded on the floor in her socks, and her mom scooped her into her arms. She was almost* *too big to be scooped up, but her mom always managed it anyway. It was like the space in her* *mom’s arms had been made just for her. She always fit perfectly.*

*“All right, little warrior. It’s bedtime for you.”*

*“But Mom!”*

*“Sssh,” her mom whispered, pressing her finger to her lips. “Even the strongest, bravest, most* *wild girls need to sleep.”*

*Katara sighed, forcing her lips into an exaggerated pout. “Fiiiine.” She pretended to go limp in her* *mom’s arms. “I’m asleep now.”*

*Her mom laughed softly. “Your eyes are open, darling.” She leaned down and gave Katara a* *gentle kiss on the forehead. Katara laughed, and began to close her eyes.*

*There was a crash from somewhere in the back of the house. Katara screamed, but her mom* *clapped her hand over her mouth, pressing her finger to her lips again. This time, all of the* *playfulness was gone from her expression. They stood in silence for a moment, and then, to their* *horror, the floorboards began to creak with footsteps.*

*Her mom grabbed a lamp off one of the tables. Her voice was quiet, but full of conviction. “Katara,* *I need you to do absolutely everything I say. Can you do that?”*

*Katara nodded, fear and adrenaline coursing through her veins. “Yes, Mom.”*

*“Good.” Her mom turned back to her for a second, looking right into her eyes. “I need you to go* *upstairs and hide in the closet. Like we do during Hide and Seek. Lock the door behind you, and* *don’t make any noise. Don’t even breathe loudly, if you can. Do not come out until Dad, Sokka, or* *I tell you it’s okay. Do you understand?” Katara nodded, eyes wide. “Good. Now run upstairs, as* *fast as you can. I love you so much.” Her mom planted one last kiss on her forehead before* *motioning Katara up the stairs.*

*Katara didn’t think she’d ever run as fast as she ran to get to the closet. She sat in the dark for* *what felt like eternity. She was alone and helpless, couldn’t see, could barely hear anything, except* *some crashing, and once, a horrible scream that almost made Katara scream, too. She felt tears* *pouring down her cheeks, but dared not call attention to herself, so she sobbed quietly, in the dark* *closet.*

*It felt like hours before she came out. She had no idea how long it really was, but once she hadn’t* *heard any sounds for a while, she couldn’t take it anymore. She opened the closet door and tiptoed* *down the stairs. When she got to the bottom, she froze, shaking.*

*At the bottom of the stairs lay her mom. Her eyes were closed. Katara knelt down and began* *shaking her, wondering why she wouldn’t wake up. Why was she so cold? And why was the floor* *around her stained with red? Why was the red seeping into Katara’s blue pajamas?*

*Katara didn’t realize it for a couple of minutes, but when she did, she cried more than she’d ever* *cried in her life.*

Even remembering the day made tears spring to Katara’s eyes. She would never forget how *terrified* she had been that day. How helpless she had felt.

But that was why she solved mysteries like this. So that she could take her fate into her own hands, spread truth and justice, and never be that helpless little girl ever again.

Azula was doing her best not to scoff at the sight of Katara looking at a photograph of her mother and crying. Crying was the largest show of weakness that Azula could think of. Why would anyone waste it on their *mother* ?

Well, perhaps Zuko would. Perhaps that was just something that ordinary people did.

Azula turned back to the files, attempting to throw herself into the calming sound of paper rustling, but instead, she found her own mother’s face looking at her. It was almost like looking in a mirror, but her mother’s smile had a softness to it that Azula couldn’t recreate if she tried.

Then again, there were a lot of things that she hadn’t been able to do for her mother. Apparently, *perfect* wasn’t good enough for her.

*Azula was five years old, laughing and running after Zuko through the gardens of their house. She* *was catching up to him, and then she tapped him on the back. Her father’s voice echoed through* *her head. “Show them all who’s in control,” it said, lingering in her mind long after her brain had* *processed the words.*

*Azula shoved Zuko to the ground, laughing. She had done it. “My little power-hungry monster,” he* *would say, ruffling her hair. Monster was a pet name he had for her, something that was all her* *own. It meant she was special, deserving of praise.*

*“Azula!” her mother’s voice echoed through the gardens, and she felt a hand clasp itself around* *her arm. “We don’t shove people like that! How could you do that to your brother?”*

*Azula looked down at Zuko. He was crying. Father said that crying was a sign of weakness, and* *that your enemies preyed on it. “I’m just teaching Zuko who’s in control,” she said. “He should be* *thankful. Now he knows.”*

*Her mother looked absolutely furious, though Azula didn’t know why. “Young lady,” she said, her* *voice shaking, “you do not control anything. You are a five-year-old girl, and you are still very* *young. There’s a lot you don’t know about the world.” She released her. “Now, go play by yourself* *for a while. Think about what you did.”*

*Azula sighed as she walked over to another corner of the garden. It was the first time anyone had* *ever questioned her, told her that she couldn’t do something. And she hated it.*

*Azula was six years old, and attending her grandfather’s funeral. He had owned Sozin Enterprises* *before her father, and he had always had it out for her father. She smiled as his body was lowered* *into the ground, proud to be her father’s daughter at the dawn of his new empire.*

*Her father refused to catch her eye across the room and smile at her, even though he’d talked of* *nothing but Grandfather’s death for weeks. She hated seeing him be so cold. It made her feel all* *alone. He was all she had; Zuko hated her for being better than him, and Mother always sided with* *Zuko. It made her feel as though she’d become undeserving of his love.*

*She tried her best to get his attention. She sidled up near him, taking Zuko with her. “Are you sad* *about Grandfather?” asked Zuko. He looked nervous. Azula understood why. Father didn’t like* *Zuko. It wasn’t safe for Zuko around him. If Azula wasn’t naturally so intelligent and cunning like* *her father, she wouldn’t be safe either.*

*“No,” she said, making sure her Father could hear her. Maybe, if he heard her restate their* *opinions, he would see how much she cared. “Grandfather was getting too old for his job anyway.* *Someone was going to end up replacing him soon. And it’ll be much better for the company this* *way.”*

*“Young lady!” came her mother’s voice from behind her. “How could you possibly say that? This* *is a funeral!”*

*Why did no one ever want to hear the truth? Father had no problem with the truth. “It’s only the* *truth!”*

*Her mother sighed. “Have you no sense of humanity, of...how people act?!”*

*What did her mother mean? She knew exactly how people acted. She was already learning how to* *pick out their weaknesses and use them for own gain. She already knew that she was talented, and* *that people weaker than she was didn’t like that. “Of course I do, Mom.” She put extra sweetness* *into the last word, just for good measure.*

*As she walked off, she heard the words her mother uttered to herself. “What is wrong with that* *child?”*

*Azula ignored the pains in her chest as she heard those words. How could her mother think there* *was something wrong with her? She was perfect.*

*Was there something about Azula that meant that, no matter how perfect she was, her mother* *would never want her?*

*Azula was seven, and doing something she never thought she’d do. She was betraying her father’s* *trust. She had overheard him mumbling to one of his business associates, something about Sozin* *Enterprises heads only being allowed to have one heir. She had only heard the words ‘kill the son’* *before fleeing back to Zuko’s room.*

*She didn’t want Zuko dead. She hated him for taking her mother from her, and she thought that he* *was a weakling, to be sure, but he also brought out a side of her that felt warmer, in a good way.* *He was the only person that did that.*

*Plus, if she was being honest, she didn’t want to be alone with her father. For some reason.*

*Zuko wouldn’t believe her. She tried as hard as she could to tell him, but he would never listen to* *her. It was that same part of her, whatever it was, that Mother hated so much. The part that was* *never afraid to show people who was really in control, who was stronger, to mock and belittle, to* *tell the truth, even when people didn’t want to hear it.*

*Zuko said she was sick. Was that really how he thought of her?*

*Another arm grabbed her around the waist, pulling her outside. “It’s time for a talk.”*

*Azula’s mother spun her around. “What’s going on?”*

*Azula laughed. “Father’s going to kill Zuko. Something about the company only having one heir. I* *tried to warn him, but he won’t listen to me.” She crossed her arms over her chest. “He hates me* *now. Just like you do.”*

*Her mother sighed. “Azula, why are you laughing?” Her tone was rather cold and detached.* *Ironically, it sounded like Father’s.*

*Azula blinked. She hadn’t been expecting that question. “Father always laughs when he does* *things like this. He says it’s a way of showing your power.”*

*Her mother gave her a pitying smile. “Azula, have you ever considered that life is about more than* *power? It’s about love.”*

*She should talk. It wasn’t as though she’d ever had enough love to go around. “Love isn’t for me,* *Mother. Love is for fools.”*

*Her mother sighed. Something dangerous was flashing in her eyes. She leaned in and kissed Azula* *on the forehead, the first time she’d done it in years.*

*“Azula, I’ll never understand you, but please, protect your brother as best as you can. This world* *has not been kind to him.”*

*She disappeared into the darkness.*

*And she never came back.*

Even now, as the memory came back to her, Azula felt her fists clench. The world hadn’t been kind to *her* , either. It had made her a monster, given her the impossible task of protecting Zuko against her father. But had her mother ever cared? No.

*It didn’t matter* , Azula told herself, tearing her mother’s photo in two where no one could see. She was solving a mystery. She didn’t have time to think about her mother. Not now, and not ever. “I’m bored,” said Mai, leaning against the tree. “I wonder what they’re doing in there.”

“You’re the one who volunteered to stay out here! I was fine on my own!”

“Yeah, well,” mumbled Mai, “I wanted to make sure you didn’t get yourself killed.”

Suki smiled, feeling a small blush rise to her cheeks. She gave Mai a playful punch on the arm. “Hey, you *do* care about me!”

“No I don't!” said Mai, rolling her eyes, though her face was flushing slightly, too. “I think you’re a boring stick-in-the-mud who’s having an identity crisis and hanging out with the rebellious girl as a way to cope.”

Suki felt the smile drop off her face. “You don’t actually think I feel that way, do you?”

“No. Yes. I don’t know,” said Mai, shrugging. “Usually, when people want to be my friends, it’s because they want something from me. My family likes to use me to make them look nice. Other kids usually want something to do with money, or to look cool. Whatever. I’m not mad or anything. I’m used to it.” She looked away.

Suki paused, then slid her hand over and squeezed Mai’s arm gently. “Well, I like you because you’re a good friend. Yeah, you’re exciting and I’ve done a ton of things I’d never do because of you, but even without the mystery, I’d still be your friend.”

Mai looked at her, as close to stunned as Suki had ever seen Mai allow herself to be. “You’re not lying? If you’re lying, I will pick off every one of your fingernails one by one.”

“I’m not lying,” said Suki. Then, she let out a small giggle. “But I’d like to see you try.” She wiggled her eyebrows dramatically, and Mai laughed.

Rustling further up the path caused them both to fall silent.

After a loud whistle from outside, the group frantically reassembled the files, throwing them back into the cabinets and hoping that they would be in almost alphabetical order. Katara pocketed the photo of her mother before she left. That sort of memory didn’t belong to the White Lotus. She thought she saw Azula shove something in her pocket, too, but couldn’t be sure.

The group raced outside, and Suki and Mai yanked them into the trees just as Jeong Jeong and Piandao emerged, heading towards the cottage, and closing the door behind them.

The whole group took one last look at the cottage, then began to run back up the path, hoping that whatever Jeong Jeong and Piandao were up to would take a long time.

They didn’t stop running until they were back on the train. Katara was seated next to Zuko, who had taken a couple of files, and was now reading through them.

“You okay?”

Zuko nodded. There was a familiar fiery determination in his eyes. “Yeah. I just need to get to the White Lotus.” He turned and stared out the window at the city flying by. “I need to ask my uncle some questions.”

## Chapter 21: Miss Marple Tells a Story

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko looks for answers, Azula becomes unsure of her feelings, and Katara makes her own feelings clear.

#### Chapter Notes

This chapter marks the halfway point of this fic! I can’t believe so much has been posted already. I can’t believe I even WROTE this much! Thanks so much to everyone who’s read this far! You all are amazing and deserve a medal!

I basically need to spend every last second of this month writing if I want to finish this fic on time. Wish me luck!

TW: Injury, self-hatred, mentions of mass killings.

### Text

Zuko hadn’t felt like this since he was running away from his father. It was like he was walking through a tunnel, and everything other than him, the path in front of him, and his end goal, had dissolved into black nothingness. He could vaguely hear the voices of everyone around him, but he couldn’t make out their words, nor did he care what they were saying. All he could feel were his fingers clenched around the files in his hands.

How could his uncle *lie* to him? Iroh was supposed to be the *good* family member, the one Zuko could always count on to love unconditionally, to help when it was needed, and to be *honest* . He was the first person Zuko had trusted after being manipulated by everyone around him his whole life. How could he have *done* this?

The train dropped them off in the Upper Ring, and as Zuko walked towards the White Lotus mansion, he barely registered how far he went, or how long it took. Cars and buses honked loudly as he crossed streets without looking, but he ignored them and kept walking. He might have been crying, but if he was, he couldn’t feel it. He felt angry, betrayed, and somehow numb, but not sad.

Somebody nearby called his name, but it faded into the background with the rest of the blackness. Everything sounded fuzzy, like he was underwater.

He was finally trying to trust people, and one of the people closest to him had been hiding something important from him the whole time.

The White Lotus mansion loomed out of the darkness, seeming to come out of nowhere. Zuko couldn’t even remember how he’d gotten there from the train station. It was daytime, but storm clouds were beginning to fill the sky, and it was the afternoon, which meant that the police were gone. Maybe they’d finished asking everything they needed to ask.

That was fine with Zuko. It meant that *he* got to ask the questions. And he wasn’t leaving until he got answers.

The gate of the mansion seemed to open magically for him, and the tunnel that Zuko was walking through grew narrower and narrower as he stormed towards the enormous old oak doors. Not caring how heavy they were, he threw his hands forward and shoved on the doors with all his might. Somehow, they opened, and Zuko kept walking into the lobby. The tunnel fell away, but everything in his line of vision remained blurry, like a camera that was out of focus. When he spotted his uncle on the other side of the room, his eyes zoomed in on his face, and everything but him became black. Zuko walked over, each step sounding like a drum, shaking with rage. His uncle spotted him, and his eyes widened.

“Zuko, what…”

Zuko held up the files in response, still shaking, nearly ripping them with how tight he was holding on.

Iroh’s eyes seemed to grow heavier with understanding. He nodded grimly. “Come with me,” he said, beckoning towards a lounge off to the side of the main room.

Zuko hesitated. What if this was some sort of trap?

But it was his uncle. And Zuko needed answers, now.

He followed Iroh into the lounge and closed the door behind them.

The rest of the group was milling around the front hall of the White Lotus mansion. After Zuko had practically sprinted across the city in his stormcloud-like rage, it was all they could do just to keep up with him.

Suki and Mai were standing awkwardly in a corner. It was evident that neither of them knew what to do with themselves. After all, they were standing at the center of the headquarters of their greatest enemy. Azula had showed up on Zuko’s doorstep nine days ago, so she understood the sentiment. Mai looked excited (well, as excited as Mai could look), and was no doubt pleased with how much this was going to piss off her parents, but Suki, who probably associated herself with the Dai Li more than Mai ever had, looked like a fish out of water.

Sokka was sitting on the steps and staring into space, and Katara was pointedly looking away from Yue every time she came near her. *Interesting* . Azula had pegged Katara and Yue as close friends with something more bubbling just under the surface. She’d hardly seen them happier than when they were together, or thinking about one another. For Katara to be avoiding Yue, something drastic must have happened.

Speaking of friends with something more (maybe. Hopefully? Who knew?), Azula began to scan the room, definitely *not* searching for a certain pink-clad acrobat.

“Azula!”

Azula nearly jumped into the air, then quickly recovered. Ty Lee had snuck up on her, something few people managed to do. She turned around, working hard to hide her surprise. “Ty Lee.” She had no idea whether to make her tone formal, or friendly, or neither. This was all incredibly confusing, and Azula hated it. And liked it. Nothing made sense. “It’s...good to see you.” She could hear the flatness in her own voice, and wanted to kick herself.

“You, too,” said Ty Lee. “Hey, listen, I know we talked this morning, but if you’re not off solving a mystery, I was wondering if you were free...now? We could go on that...date we talked about, if you wanted.” Ty Lee was blushing, and Azula couldn’t help but think that she looked adorable when she blushed.

Azula glanced at the door where Zuko and Iroh had vanished. It seemed like they wouldn’t be coming back for a while.

“I think this afternoon is wide open.”

Katara was pacing back and forth across the room for the tenth time when a hand grabbed her arm. Katara did her best to pull away, but the hand grabbed her again. Angry, she turned to face Yue, who was staring at her with wide, apologetic eyes. Katara did her best to ignore how pretty her eyes were. It made her feel even worse.

“Katara, please, I just want to talk!”

“I don’t want to talk to you!” Katara wrenched her arm away and began to walk towards Sokka.

“I never wanted to hurt you!”

“Well, you did!” Katara shouted, whirling around. “I did everything in my power to help you, and you lied to me! You tricked me into believing you cared about me!”

“I do care about you,” said Yue quietly. “I didn’t get a chance to explain before, but please, just hear me out. After that, you can ignore me all you want. You never have to speak to me again.”

Katara felt something like lightning racing down her spine. Anger, betrayal, and hurt combined into one deadly spark. But she nodded anyway, and she and Yue sat down, hidden on one of the spiral staircases.

“Explain,” said Katara. She could hear the coldness in her voice, so unusual for her, but she didn’t care.

Yue sighed. “I’m engaged to Hahn. I lied to you about that, and I’m sorry. But I don’t love him. He’s a horrible person, and I never wanted to get engaged to him.”

“Right,” said Katara, rolling her eyes. “You got engaged to someone you hate. So believable.”

“It’s the truth,” said Yue. “I got engaged to him because Pakku, my father, and the entire White Lotus expected it of me. I owe the White Lotus everything, and they, in return, have things they need me to do. I don’t have the option of disappointing them.”

Katara’s eyes widened. “That’s why the police accused you of killing Pakku,” she realized. “They thought you killed him to get out of your marriage.”

Yue nodded.

Katara had a thousand questions. But she settled for the one that mattered the most. “What about me? Why did you lie to me?” She still felt angry, and betrayed, but she didn’t have the heart to be cold anymore. Not while Yue was so heartbroken.

Yue sighed. “I wanted to tell you. I really did. But I could never find the right moment. I guess...I didn’t want to tell you because I...I thought I felt something. Between us. And I thought that if I didn’t mention my engagement, it could just...happen.”

Almost unintentionally, Katara slipped her hand into Yue’s. Yue was crying, and Katara felt tears falling from her own eyes, too. “Yue, there *was* something between us. But you should have told me the truth.”

Yue sighed. “I’m sorry.”

“I know you are.”

There was a moment of silence. “What now?” asked Katara. “Pakku’s...gone. You don’t have to do what he says anymore.”

“Yes, I do,” said Yue. “It’s not just him. The entire White Lotus gained control over my life the second they took me in. I owe them this.”

“But you don’t!” cried Katara. “Yue, I like you! A lot! But I like the *real* you! The you that knows she’s a person and not just the White Lotus’s puppet!”

“I’m not a puppet,” said Yue. “I’m someone who has obligations to fulfill.”

“So what does that mean for us?” said Katara. “Are you not allowed to see me now?”

“No!” cried Yue. She reached her hand out for Katara. “We...we can still do this. As long as the White Lotus doesn’t find out.”

Katara could barely manage to do it, but she pulled her hand away. “No,” she said, standing up. “I’m happy to be your friend, Yue. In fact, few things would make me happier, but I can’t be more than that. Not if I have to be a secret while you get married.” She began to walk down the stairs, then paused, turning back. “If you’re ever ready, I’ll be here.”

She walked down the rest of the steps without looking back.

Zuko took a seat behind the desk in the lounge before his uncle could get there, throwing his feet up and sliding the files across the wooden surface. He didn’t want to give him any illusions about who was in charge. He wondered if this was part of how Azula thought sometimes.

“Explain everything. Now.”

“Zuko, there are things you won't understa…”

“I don’t care.” Zuko’s voice felt like ice, even in his own throat. “People are *dying* , Uncle. If I’m going to stop this, I need to know everything. I thought I made this clear.”

“These files are not relevant to…”

“You don’t get to decide what’s relevant!” cried Zuko. “I’m the one you hired to investigate this! I decide what’s relevant, and I say it’s relevant that the White Lotus has been secretly keeping files on every person in the city, along with how you can control them and how much of a *threat* they are! So explain this.” He slammed his fist on the desk. He felt a splinter pierce his hand, and blood flow over his knuckle, but he didn’t care. “Right now.”

Iroh sighed. “Freedom comes with a price, Zuko.”

“Don’t be cryptic. I know you’re avoiding my questions.”

Iroh sighed again. “The White Lotus is a...complicated organization. More complicated than it seems. We fight for freedom in this city. We support local businesses and cultural displays, so that everyone can express themselves however they wish. But not everyone wants to be free. People will turn so naturally to oppression, and that’s where the files come in.” He grabbed one of the files off the desk and studied it. “We invest a lot of money in other people, but we need to make sure they put it to good use. That’s what the files are for. If they misuse their power, we can...remind them of it.” Iroh looked away.

“So what you’re saying is that you control other organizations to stop them from being controlling. Do you realize how hypocritical that is?”

Iroh shrugged. “Someone has to pay the price, Zuko. It’s better if it’s a group of people with good intentions who value art, freedom, and love.”

“I can hear the shame in your voice,” Zuko spat, glaring at his uncle. “You don’t even believe what you’re saying.”

“Suit yourself,” said Iroh. “I’m only telling you the truth. Whether or not you choose to believe it is up to you.”

“Why are you all so obsessed with freedom?” said Zuko. “Aren’t there more important things? Like responsibility, or justice?”

Iroh sighed. “The White Lotus is a complicated organization, filled with...complicated members. We all have things we’ve done, or things that have happened to us, things we’d rather hide. We want to better the city, but if these secrets were brought out, as they would be in an ‘orderly’ world, we would be unable to help the city in the way we want to.”

Zuko was shaking with anger again. “You’re all sick,” he hissed. “You’re using your money and power to hide from your past mistakes? How does that make you worthy of protecting this city?”

Iroh sighed. “No one is worthy. But we choose to accept that responsibility, because we have all lived long enough to bear it.”

“And do you know each other’s secrets?”

“No,” Iroh admitted. “We write them down when we are initiated, as a sign of accepting the past and moving on, and then we lock them in a box where we never have to look at them again.”

“So you don’t even know what everyone else did?” asked Zuko. Iroh shook his head. “Uncle! You could be living with serial killers and not even know it!”

“I trust the rest of the White Lotus with my life,” said Iroh. “And I trust you, too. I trust that you will uncover whoever is committing these atrocities.”

“Fine,” said Zuko, still furious, “if you trust me so much, tell me *your* secret.”

Iroh sighed. “The Dai Li is a young organization, but not younger than I am. They existed in the city when I was a young adult. I was foolish then, full of fire and rebellion. I wanted to burn the order and oppression that resembled that of my family to the ground. I did everything I could to stop them. I set headquarters on fire, threw bombs…” he sighed, tears falling from his eyes, “I probably killed dozens, maybe over a hundred people. Even my own son was killed.” He looked up at Zuko. “That is what caused me to stop, and join the White Lotus instead. Here, I can put the past behind me, and change the city for the better. Can’t you at least try to understand?”

Zuko looked away. “Almost everyone deserves a second chance if they truly want to change,” he said at last. “But you’re all using your power and money to run from the past and control others. I don’t know how that makes you any better than you were before.”

Iroh had no answer for him.

Azula stared at the pink, dripping, sugary strangeness sitting in a cup in her hands. She knew what it was, of course. It was ice cream. But Azula had never eaten ice cream before. Her father had always told her that food was a necessity, and eating anything other than the necessary nutrition was frivolous and a waste of your time and your health. The only exception Azula had ever made to that rule was coffee, which had allowed her to run on less sleep, and thus be more productive. This wasn’t like that.

“Hurry up and eat it, silly!” giggled Ty Lee. “It’ll melt if you don’t.”

Azula stared at the pink mass sitting in her cup. Gingerly, she picked up her spoon and poked at it. It felt edible.

“Oh my stars,” said Ty Lee, her eyes widening. “You’ve never eaten ice cream before, have you?”

Azula sighed. “I think I’m getting worse at hiding the parts of me I don’t like. I apologize.”

Ty Lee blinked. “Don’t apologize! That’s the point of friends. They love all of you: the good and the bad! And as long as you’re not hurting me, I don’t care that not everything about you is perfect. Plus, it’s kind of cute that you’ve never had ice cream before.”

Azula smiled at Ty Lee. Maybe having someone so...accepting around would be good for her.

Or maybe it just made her weaker. Azula could feel herself growing weaker by the day, and she couldn’t stop it.

But was it so bad when it made her feel *this* happy? Azula didn’t know.

She took a deep breath, scooped the pink goo out of her cup, and popped it into her mouth. She let it slide over her tongue. It was cold and creamy, and the texture was pleasant. It was sweet, but not overly so. It tasted of strawberries and sugar, and the pink color reminded her of Ty Lee.

It was possibly the most amazing thing Azula had ever tasted. She couldn’t stop the smile that spread over her face.

Ty Lee laughed. “It’s amazing, isn’t it?” She had already finished her own ice cream, and was now chomping on her cone.

“All right, fine, I admit it.” Azula looked at Ty Lee and laughed.

Ty Lee looked back at her. “What?”

“Nothing, it’s just that…” Azula couldn’t stop giggling. It was so unusual for her. “You have ice cream on your nose.”

Ty Lee took a look at her reflection on her phone, and burst out laughing. Azula didn’t realize she was staring until it was too late. “What?” asked Ty Lee, still giggling.

“You have a beautiful laugh.” The words were out of Azula’s mouth before she could stop them. “What I mean is...you’re beautiful. All of you.”

How *stupid* . How was she supposed to solve murders if she was turning into a mess like *this* ?

Ty Lee’s cheeks turned a deep red, and she stared at Azula, her eyes wide. They were frozen on the stone wall where they sat, their hands and faces mere centimeters apart. Azula could feel Ty Lee’s breathing, and her own heartbeat.

*What is wrong with that child?* Her mother’s voice came piercing through her mind, followed by her father’s. *My little power-hungry monster.*

What was she *doing* , letting someone get so close to her? She was *dangerous* , and not only that, she was *in danger* ! Her own mother had thought she was a monster, her father had noticed how dangerous she was when she was just a child, and her own brother couldn’t understand when she was trying to help him because he hated her so much.

She didn’t know how to be a good *person* , let alone...whatever she and Ty Lee were becoming. All she knew how to do was build up walls and manipulate everyone around her, and Ty Lee was making that go away, too. Soon there would be nothing left. Nothing but the monster her mother had scorned.

Ty Lee was a light in the darkness. She was good, and *happy* . She deserved better than a monster.

Azula pulled away, trying her best to ignore the hurt on Ty Lee’s face. It was better to stop now, before Ty Lee got too invested in the person that Azula wasn’t, the one she somehow thought Azula was. “I can’t do this. Not me, not you, not now.” She forced herself to look Ty Lee right in the eye. She was crying, and it took every muscle in Azula’s body not to cry, too. “I’m sorry.”

She turned and, even though it made her weak, raced out of the park. She could have walked and kept her cool, but she wanted to get out of there before Ty Lee could see her start to cry.

Sokka had just wandered into the library, and was looking for books on how to analyze a corpse. He hadn’t studied since Pakku’s murder, and even though he was getting a lot of...hands-on experience, he still had tests once the break was over, a week or so into November.

He had just gotten to the right section when there was a crash, followed by a scream. Sokka heard footsteps all around him as everyone in the mansion rushed towards the noises. Sighing, Sokka raced after them, hoping with everything he had that no one else was dead, and that Katara and Zuko were both safe.

The entire White Lotus, plus Zuko, Mai, Suki, and Katara, were all crowded around a corner of the first floor, where Aang was sitting on the floor, looking visibly shocked. The scream, Sokka realized, had come from him.

Sitting next to Aang on the floor was Bumi. He looked frazzled, and (to Sokka’s dismay) his head was bleeding, but he was alive.

Zuko knelt down next to them. He was clearly still angry about something, but he looked worried, too. “What happened?”

Aang still looked as though he’d seen a ghost. “Someone hit Bumi!”

Zuko turned to Bumi. “Is this true?”

Bumi nodded. “I didn’t see much, but I saw a shadow come through that window over there!” He pointed to a window that was completely closed. “Fastest thing I’ve ever seen, and I was a wrestler! Then they picked up that vase…” he pointed to a vase that was smashed on the floor next to him, “and hit me on the head!” He laughed. “Stroke of luck, eh?”

Despite his laughter, nobody else in the group was smiling. Sokka picked up a shard of the vase. It was incredibly thick and heavy, and even though it was only a shard, Sokka had trouble lifting it with one hand.

“Do you think this was an attempted murder?” asked Aang, his eyes wide and full of tears.

Sokka hated to hurt the kid, but he wasn’t going to lie. “Yeah, Aang, I think it was.” He turned back to Bumi and the smashed vase on the floor. “He’s lucky to be alive.”

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

I hope you all enjoyed that chapter! This was a pretty tame one, so I threw in some relationship drama to make up for it:)

## Chapter 22: Wireless

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

In the aftermath of the latest attack, everyone is left to stew in their own feelings, and the result is not pleasant.

#### Chapter Notes

Enjoy one more low-key chapter before you get some plot in the next one!

So far, writing a chapter a day is HARD but satisfying!

TW: Mentions of forest fires and mass deaths.

### Text

At Sokka’s words, Aang’s eyes grew wide and filled with tears. He jumped to his feet and raced out of the room, almost knocking Hahn over in the process. Personally, Zuko sort of wished that he *had* knocked Hahn over.

Looking more than a little guilty, Sokka used the path that Aang had cut through the crowd to run after him. Zuko started to follow, but Katara put her hand on his shoulder, and he stopped.

“I don’t think they want any more visitors to be here any longer than they need to.”

Zuko looked around. The entire White Lotus was crowded around Bumi. Even though Zuko’s feelings about the group were now *very* mixed, he did respect what seemed to be their genuine commitment to one another.

Piandao stood up and faced Zuko, Katara, Hahn, and Yue. “The White Lotus needs to have a word in private. Anyone who lives here, please give us some space. Anyone who doesn’t…” his gaze lingered on Zuko and Katara “please go home.”

Zuko sighed as he and Katara left the mansion. After the adrenaline of searching for answers on the White Lotus, and finally getting them, he felt as though every last drop of energy had been drained from his body. Where he had felt fierce anger and conviction, he now felt...empty. He had found answers, but not the ones he needed. They were still no closer to solving the murders.

“Zuko?” Katara’s voice came from his right. She looked concerned. “Are you okay?”

He doubted she would believe him, but he didn’t care. “I’m fine. Let’s just go home.”

Sokka found Aang in one of the side yards, petting the most enormous dog that Sokka had ever seen. Being careful not to sit on the dog’s tail, Sokka slowly lowered himself down into the grass and took a seat next to him.

“Mind if I join you?”

Aang shook his head. Seeing him this quiet was so *weird* .

The giant dog walked over and licked Sokka on the face before he could get out of the way. Sokka shrieked and fell back onto the grass, where the dog got on top of him and started licking him again. “Aah! Get it off, get it off!”

Aang let out a soft laugh, and smiled a little. “This is my dog, Appa. I’ve had him for as long as I can remember.”

“Well, can you please use your lifelong friendship to *get him off of me* ?” Seeing the slight hurt on Aang’s face, Sokka sighed, going limp in the grass. “I didn’t mean that,” he said reluctantly. “I’m sure you two have a very...meaningful friendship.” Sokka had never been much of an animal person, so he had to practically force the words out of his own mouth.

Aang kept smiling as he waved the dog off of Sokka, who sat up, feeling a little like he’d been hit by a truck, but Aang’s smile was sad. He was still crying, Sokka realized.

“Hey, I’m sorry if what I said in there scared you.”

“It’s okay.”

“No, it’s not. You’re not investigating this, and I shouldn’t have forced you into all the scary stuff like that.”

Aang sighed. “But it was never *you* who forced me into it. This whole thing is terrifying! My family’s been *dying* , one by one, and everyone’s been treating it like a game! I thought if I stayed happy, and just pretended like everything was okay, and never hurt anyone, then this would all just...pass me by! But it hasn’t! It’s only getting worse, and Bumi, the closest thing I have to a real family, was almost *murdered* ! I don’t know how you can all talk about this stuff so easily! It’s so *awful* !” He placed his head between his knees.

“You’re right,” said Sokka after a moment.

“I am?”

Sokka nodded. “The truth is, when we work with stuff like this, sometimes it’s easy to forget how *real* it all is. We get so caught up in the clues and the puzzle that we forget that real people are involved, and we forget about the people important to them.” He glanced at Aang. “Their family.” He put his hand on Aang’s shoulder. “That’s why we need people like you to remind us sometimes of why we do this. We do this to stop people, real people, from getting hurt.” His mother’s face flashed through his memory. “Because every time another person dies, it’s a whole group of people who have to deal with the consequences.” He sighed. “I’m sorry you have to deal with all of this, Aang. But we’re not going to forget how important this is. We’re going to figure out who’s doing this, and put a stop to these murders before anyone else gets hurt.”

Aang smiled at him, then sighed, twirling a blade of grass between his fingers. “It’s just…seeing my family die is reminding me so much of the last time I saw my family die.”

Sokka’s eyes widened. “What do you mean?”

Aang turned to face him. “I grew up in a really tight-knit town. But when I was five, it burned down while I was away. I lost my entire family that day. I just...don’t want to lose them again.” Sokka sighed, gently (if a little awkwardly) putting his arm around Aang. “My mother died when I was ten. I know nothing can ever make you get over losing your family like that. It’s never the same.” Aang nodded. “But we *can* do everything in our power to protect our new families. You’re doing that, Aang. You’re here to remind us of what really matters when we need it. And by doing that, you’re helping us save your new family.”

Aang smiled. It was still a small smile, but it wasn’t forced. “Thanks, Sokka.”

“Anytime.” Sokka stood and got up to leave, but Appa leapt on him and knocked him to the ground. Aang laughed, then gently pulled Appa back, allowing Sokka to stand up and start walking away.

“Sokka?”

“Yeah?”

“I hope neither of us has to lose anyone else.”

Sokka sighed, thinking of Katara and Zuko. “Me too, Aang. Me too.”

Zuko and Katara arrived back at the house to find Azula curled up on the sofa and doing something Zuko had never seen her do before in his life; rereading a book.

“What are you doing?”

Azula looked up, glaring at him. Katara muttered something about needing a glass of water and walked into the kitchen. Zuko turned back to his sister, who had placed her book on the coffee table and now had her arms crossed over her chest. “What do you mean *what am I doing* ?”

Zuko sighed, annoyed, and sat down on the arm of the sofa. Azula began prodding him with her feet, but he ignored it. “You’re *rereading* a book. A *romance novel* . I’ve never seen you reread anything in your life, unless it was for school.”

“Well, perhaps I was forced to adjust to the lack of books in your apartment.”

“Azula, there’s literally a bookstore less than a block away from here.”

Azula sighed. “Fine, I’m rereading something. Who cares? Maybe I just enjoyed it very much.”

Zuko took a closer look. Her hair was back in a topknot, and...were her eyes *red* ? “I would *maybe* believe that if you didn’t look absolutely miserable.” He thought for a moment. “I saw you leaving the White Lotus with Ty Lee. Does this have something to do with that?”

Azula, who hadn’t stopped poking him with her feet, angrily jabbed him with her right one. “Maybe it’s absolutely none of your business!” She picked the book up and turned the page so hard that Zuko heard paper tearing.

“Didn’t Ty Lee give you that book?”

Azula said nothing, instead forcefully turning the pages and pointedly looking away from him.

Zuko sighed. “Azula, I’m not going away until you answer.”

Azula groaned, sitting up and tossing the book at him. Luckily, it was a paperback. “Yes, it just so happens that Ty Lee gave me this book. That has absolutely nothing to do with why you think I look miserable. I’m just tired.” She glared at him one last time, then curled up into a ball and lay down again, pointedly looking away from him.

Suddenly hit with another wave of exhaustion, Zuko slumped down on the sofa next to her. It was so *draining* to work endlessly on a case and feel like you were never going to solve it. It felt like you were climbing a never-ending staircase, and no matter how high you climbed, you would never be enough.

“Is it too much to ask for three inches of space?” snapped Azula.

“I’m not here to fight,” mumbled Zuko, still feeling exhausted. “Mind if I join you?” He rolled over so that he was hanging upside-down off the edge of the sofa. It was a position he’d loved ever since he was a kid.

Azula wrapped her arms around her knees and squeezed herself into a corner of the sofa, rolling her eyes. “I don’t see how this is fair. You do nothing but brood and stew constantly in your own angst, yet the one time I want to do the same, you won’t leave me alone.”

“So you admit you’re brooding.”

“I can do it *once* ! You do it *every day* !”

“No I don’t,” Zuko mumbled, still tired.  
“My evidence says otherwise.”

“Look, can you just tell me what’s bothering you?”  
“Why do you even want to know? It has absolutely nothing to do with you.”

“You live with me. I’m concerned.”

“You’re not concerned. You sound like a robot when you say that.”

“Fine, I just want to know because I want to know. Is that enough of an explanation for you?”

Azula side-eyed him from her corner of the sofa. “Fine. I’ll tell you what’s bothering me, if only to get you to shut up, but in exchange, you have to tell me what’s bothering you.”

“Fine. You’re first.”

“Why?”

“Because I said so, and I’m tired.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “You’re acting like a five-year-old, you know that?”

“Just tell me what’s going on.”

“Fine.” Azula’s tone was void of any emotion. “I had to let someone go. Someone that I...felt rather sentimental towards.”

“You mean Ty Lee?” Zuko swung upwards and grabbed the back of the sofa so that he could look Azula in the eye. “But she likes you. Even you can see that.”

“I’m well aware,” sighed Azula. “At least, I think I am. That’s why I had to let her go.”

“You’re not making any sense.”

Azula pulled her knees closer to her chest. “You wouldn’t understand,” she muttered, burying her head in her knees. Then, she propped her head on her hands in order to look up. “But I told you what was bothering me. Now it’s your turn.”

“I don’t think you exactly told me everything.”

“That wasn’t specified in our deal. Now hold up your end.”

Zuko groaned. “Fine. I hate that we’ve been working on this case for almost two weeks, and all we have are a shit ton of suspects and no idea which one of them is guilty. It feels like we’ll never solve it.”

“We will,” murmured Azula, who now seemed to be half-asleep on the arm of the sofa. “With all of us working on it, our chances are very high. It’ll just take some time.”

“Every second we don’t solve this case, someone could be dying, and it’s our fault.”

“But in the end, we’ll catch the killer, and the amount of people saved will outweigh the costs.”

“That doesn’t mean that people aren’t going to die.”

“I never said that. But they all have a significantly higher probability of not dying if we try than if we don’t.”

“I’m failing them.”  
“No you aren’t,” Azula said sharply. “You’re helping them when no one else will.”

“But I’m not succeeding.”

“They don’t care. They’ll all love you just for *trying* .” Her tone was slightly bitter, but Zuko couldn’t quite figure out why.

“What am I supposed to *do* ? I can’t leave all of these people with a killer on the loose.”

“Figure out a logical next step. Aren’t you supposed to be a detective?”

“What does that have to do with anything?”

“I’m only saying that you should be able to find a solution.”

“Don’t talk to me about what I *should* do,” groaned Zuko.

“All right!” came a shout. Both siblings turned and saw Katara standing on the other side of the room, holding a glass of water and looking incredibly irritated. “Enough whining, both of you! Either decide that you’re going to be miserable forever or just get up and *do* something about it!” She gestured towards the clue board on the table. “Look! You have a whole bulletin board full of clues! Right there! Use it!”

Zuko sighed. “You don’t understand, Katara,” he said. “Getting up and doing something can be really hard sometimes.”

Katara’s face softened. “I know it can. But there are people counting on you. Like you said. And we *can’t* let them down.” She turned towards Azula, but continued talking to both of them. “I know what it’s like to feel hopeless, or alone, or to get my heart broken. But I also know what’s really important to me, and who I can always count on. When life gets hard, I lean on that. And I always find it in me to keep going. If I can do it, I know you can, too.”

Zuko hated that she was right, and from the look on Azula’s face, so did she, but they both pulled themselves off of the sofa and walked over to the clue board. Katara took a sip of her water, and as she did, she looked a little bit like a movie heroine. Honestly, Katara would make a pretty kickass superhero.

He spent what felt like hours staring at the clue board. He looked back and forth between the White Lotus and the Dai Li, trying to find some sort of link, something that stuck out to him, something that he could take and build upon.

At last, he felt the wheels in his brain click into place. He turned to Azula and Katara, smiling for the first time in a while.

“What is it?” asked Azula. “Did you figure out your next steps?’

“I think I did,” said Zuko. “The reason we can’t zero in on any suspects is because everyone is so suspicious!”

Azula and Katara both laughed, though Azula’s laugh was meaner. “You’ll have to be a little more specific,” said Katara with a sympathetic smile.

“I’m saying that these organizations, and the people in them, are all hiding something. It could be the murders, but it could be something else entirely. If we find out the other secrets…”

“Then that will clear our pathway to discovering the murderers!” cried Azula. “Of course! It makes perfect sense!”

“But how exactly do we do that?” asked Katara. “There are so many things to look at.”

Zuko turned to the board, and smiled as he saw Professor Zei’s photo. Pulling it off, he turned and showed it to the others. “We never got to go into the woods north of the city.”

Katara’s eyes widened. “Zuko, that’s really dangerous. The last time we tried it, someone *died* . Should we risk that again?”

“It’s the only way,” replied Zuko. “So call Sokka, Suki, and Mai. Get as much rest as you can before tonight.” He threw the photo away, and turned his gaze to the Dai Li half of the board. “We’re going to find Lake Laogai.”

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes
