## Chapter 23: The House of Lurking Death

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Filled with a newfound determination and purpose, the group sets out for Lake Laogai with the help of an unexpected ally, but danger lurks just over their shoulders at every turn.

#### Chapter Notes

TWs at the end (but beware of spoilers!)

This was one of my absolute favorite chapters that I've written so far! It's a little long, but hopefully it'll be worth it. Happy reading!

### Text

When Mai and Suki arrived at the edge of town that evening, they brought an unexpected guest. Zuko recognized her as Joo Dee, the secretary at the police station. She, like the rest of the group, was dressed in dark colors, and looked anxious.

Azula narrowed her eyes. “What is she doing here? We hardly know this woman.”

Joo Dee threw up her hands. “Please, I want to help you. I may work for the Dai Li, but I overheard Mai and Suki talking about your plans, and what you’re about to do is extremely dangerous. As a servant of the city, it’s my job to keep you safe.”

“By concealing information from us?” Azula crossed her arms over her chest. “As if we’d fall for that.”

Joo Dee shook her head. “I’m not going to conceal anything from you, I promise. I’ll take you to Lake Laogai, I’ll get you in safely, and I’ll show you everything that’s there. I swear on my life.”

Zuko nodded, turning to the rest of the group. “Joo Dee, I think we need a moment to talk about this.”

Joo Dee nodded. “Of course. I understand completely.”

The group formed a circle. Zuko glanced at the rest of them, all of whom looked somewhere between scared and determined. “What do you all think? I'm willing to risk this, but I’m not putting any of you into a situation where you don’t want to be.”

“I don’t trust her,” said Azula. “She barely knows us. Why would she want to help us? It doesn’t add up.”

“Kind of ironic coming from the girl who came to the city and jumped right into a murder investigation,” said Katara. “I think we should give her a chance. She can help us, that’s for sure.” “But she could betray us,” said Sokka. “At any second. She may have information we need, but if she calls the Dai Li to follow us, then it’s not worth it.”

Zuko glanced at Suki and Mai. “She came with you two. What do you think?”

Suki groaned. “We’re so sorry, everyone. We didn’t mean to bring her, but she overheard us, and it was either bring her and risk it, go with her knowing about it and risk her telling the Dai Li, or not go at all. We thought the best option was to take her with us.”

Zuko nodded. “It’s a risk I’m willing to take.” He turned to Sokka and Azula, the skeptics. “Are you okay with this?”

Sokka sighed. “I just don’t want anyone to get hurt, that’s all.”

Before he could overthink it, Zuko reached forward and took his hands. “I promise you that I will do every single thing in my power to stop anyone from getting hurt. But this is our only chance at finding this information. And I need your help.”

The feeling of holding hands with Sokka finally caught up to him, and he quickly stepped back, trying not to trip over his own feet.

Sokka sighed. “I’m not going to leave you behind. Just...let’s all be careful, okay?”

“Always.” Zuko took a deep breath, then turned to his sister. “Azula?”

Azula looked away for a moment, then sighed. “I’ll do what needs to be done,” she said at last. “But if she betrays us…”

“You can tell me off all you want when we’re dead.”

“You will experience eternal torture.”

The group broke their circle and turned back to Joo Dee. Zuko stepped forward. “You can come with us. But if you break your promise…”

Joo Dee smiled. “I wouldn’t dream of it.”

The dark forest sent chills down Katara’s spine, despite her best attempts to block her fear. It reminded her *so* *much* of Professor Zei’s death, hell, it was almost the same path they’d taken then. She could almost hear his voice, his footsteps, feel his body at her feet. It was all too much death, too much pain, too much hurt.

She was going to stop it tonight. At least a part of it. Katara had never been the type to sit by and watch while people got hurt. So she clenched her fists and kept walking.

Suki came up next to her. Up ahead of them, Mai and Sokka were talking to Joo Dee, and behind them, Zuko and Azula were walking side by side. Even though they weren’t talking, the image of them walking together struck Katara nonetheless. It didn’t seem like something they would have done when Azula first arrived.

She hoped things worked out for them. After everything the two of them had been through growing up, they both deserved a friend who understood what it had really been like.

“You okay?” asked Suki. Katara looked down, and realized just how tightly her fists had been clenched.

“Yeah, I am. I’m just a little…”

“Nervous? Why would breaking into the secret fortress of an organization who probably has the power to kill you make you nervous?”

Katara let out a small laugh. “You have a point.”

“Seriously, though,” said Suki. “I’ve been training with the Dai Li my whole life. They’re not exactly the warm and fuzzy type. But...you just have to use the energy from your fear to keep going. You need to accept it, and understand that it won’t stop you.”

“That’s good advice,” said Katara. “Thanks.”

“You’re welcome. Not that you need it,” added Suki. “From what I can tell, you’re one of the bravest people here.”

“Really?”

“Sure. Blocking out your fears is one thing, but it’s a lot harder to feel them fully and keep going anyway.”

“Well, the same goes for you. I’ve never seen fear stop you.”

Suki’s face turned a light shade of red, and Katara saw her eyes dart over towards Mai. “I wouldn’t say that.”

“Oh?” Katara made sure not to stare at the girl with the buns in her hair. “Is there a story there?”

“Not really,” sighed Suki. “Just some new feelings that I’m not sure I understand. I want to talk about them with her, but…”

“You’re scared?”

Suki sighed. “Yeah, kind of. I mean, this is Mai we’re talking about. She doesn’t like to talk about feelings or anything like that. I’m worried that I’ll lose her if I try and talk to her about it.”

Katara glanced up ahead at Mai. “I think you should talk to her. Even if she doesn’t feel the same way...whatever it is that you’re feeling...she’ll probably respect you for talking to her about it. And if she doesn’t, then she’s probably not the kind of person you’d want as a friend in the first place.”

Suki sighed. “I’ve never had a friend like her before. I...don’t really know what to do.”

Katara smiled at her. “I know it’s corny, but I would just follow your heart. Whatever happens next will happen, but it’s always a good place to start.” If only she could do the same.

Before Suki could respond, Joo Dee, in the front, threw out her arm, and the group came to a halt. Even in the darkness, Katara could make out the outline of a door carved into one of the huge trees. “We’re here.”

As they descended down a spiral staircase that seemed to go on for miles, all Mai could think of was how *Dai Li-like* this place was. It was damp, and dark, and depressing. There were cobwebs in every corner, and the torches on the walls were covered with a sort of stone that made everything glow green. She could see why it was called *Lake Laogai* . It really felt like they were underwater.

The stairs bottomed out into a huge chamber with about seven or eight passages leading off in different directions. Mai couldn’t see down each one, but from where she was standing, they looked pitch-black.

“We’ll never get through all of these in one night,” said Sokka. “Guys, I hate to say this, but do we need to split up?”

“Are you insane?” said Azula. “If we weren’t already about to get ourselves killed, you’ve just ensured it.”

“He may be right, though,” said Suki. “I don’t like it either. None of us do. But we’re racing against the clock here. We only have a few hours to get as much information out of this place as we can.”

Mai sighed. She hated that they were even here. She wished they could have gone somewhere *away* from the Dai Li. At least she was free here. But this place gave her the creeps. The sooner they got out of there, the better. “I don’t think we have another choice.”

“All right,” said Zuko, stepping in front of the group. “We’ll go in three groups of two. No one is going off on their own.” He turned to Joo Dee. “Is there another exit, or is this the only one.”

“There’s another one,” said Joo Dee. “Follow the darker green torches and you’ll find it. I’ll meet you there.”

“All right,” said Zuko. “Don’t leave without absolutely everyone. Understand?” Joo Dee nodded. Zuko turned back to the group. “Okay. Everyone, grab a partner. Don’t let them out of your sight, make sure they get out of here safely. From this point forward, they are your responsibility.”

Mai found herself next to Suki, who for some reason was avoiding her gaze, and the two of them set off down one of the tunnels to the left. Luckily (or not) this side of the fortress seemed to be mostly empty, at least for the moment.

Suki peered through one of the doors. “This looks like a weird, creepy gym or something. It must be where they train their guards.”

“I thought they trained their guards at the police station.”

Suki sighed. “I guess they lied. Seems like they lied to me about a lot.”

“You know that doesn’t say anything about you, right?”

“I know. I just wished I hadn’t been stupid enough to fall for it.”

“Hey, I didn't know about this either.”

“But you knew they were evil.” Suki sighed, pausing in the middle of the stone tunnel. “Do you...think I’m evil, too?”

“What? Are you stupid? No.” Suki frowned even more, and Mai sighed. “I didn’t mean it like *that* . Yeah, you annoyed me. I thought you were boring, and a stick-in-the-mud, and probably a pushover too, and annoyingly talented. But now I know that only one of those things is true. We’re friends.” She gave Suki a small smile as they turned a corner past a dark green torch.

Suki’s face grew slightly red, and Mai was pretty sure it wasn’t from the green torchlight. “...Just friends?” she asked after a moment.

Mai felt heat rush to her face. The fact was, she didn’t know the answer. She thought she might feel...the feelings that Suki was talking about, but she was so used to ignoring her feelings that she wasn’t very good at identifying them. She didn’t want to give Suki the wrong idea, but she didn’t want to hurt her, either.

“I don’t know,” she said after a while. “I’m sorry that’s all I can say.”

“It’s okay,” said Suki with a smile. They came to another fork in the path, and turned right past the dark green torch. “Let’s just get out of this creepy place as soon as we can.”

“I still think we’re very likely to die down here,” Azula pointed out as she and Zuko took a passage to the right of the entrance. “I’m actually working on calculating the probability, and…”

“Since when are you afraid?” snapped Zuko. His harsh tone caught Azula off guard. Perhaps her constant reminders of the danger were...slightly more irritating than she had initially thought. He sighed. “Sorry. I just don’t need to be reminded that we’re going to die every two seconds.”

Azula groaned. “I’m sorry too,” she admitted. Not something she said very often. It felt strange. “I just...wanted to make sure you knew what you were getting into. You can be..reckless, and I can’t always protect you. I wanted to try. Obviously, it didn’t go so well.”

Zuko paused. Azula couldn’t quite read his expression, but it seemed like he hadn’t been expecting her response. Finally, he turned back to her. “I...appreciate that. But I don’t need your protection, just like you say you don’t need mine.” He turned and began walking again. “I’ve done just fine without it.”

The bitter undertone of his words didn’t escape her, but Azula ignored it. She could still be the perfect detective without trying to protect him. There was always another way.

She turned her attention to the doors that they were passing by, and it struck her that they weren’t doors at all. They were…

“Zuko!” she hissed. “Come look at this.”

He shone a small flashlight on the doorway to their left, which was covered not by a door, but by thick, metal bars. He shone the light down the tunnel. Every door was the same.

“This is a prison,” said Azula, moving closer to the bars. She could now see the silhouette of someone sleeping behind them. “I wonder what all of these people did to end up here?”

“This is illegal, isn’t it?”

“Why are you asking me?”

“You’re the one who read all of those law books, aren’t you?”

Azula looked closer into the cell. “Whoever’s in there is chained up incredibly tightly. Those aren’t humane conditions. That isn’t legal here, but the Dai Li’s allied with the police. I would bet that they know about it, and are ignoring it.”

“It’s awful.”

There was a clattering from further down the hall, and the siblings glanced at each other. Zuko grabbed Azula by the arm and pulled her down the hall, into an empty cell with an open door. Here, no light shone on them. Azula couldn’t even see her own arms. But they could see the tunnel perfectly.

A man, tall and muscular with horrible sideburns and his hair pulled back into a bun, was making his way through the prison. Azula gasped as she caught sight of his face in full, then quickly clapped her hands over her mouth. He turned slowly in their direction, and the siblings held their breath. Azula could feel her heart beating inside her chest.

He shone his flashlight into the empty cell, and Azula hurriedly flattened herself against the wall. Zuko did the same. The light stayed for a moment, then left the cell as he continued down the hall. Azula wanted to sigh in relief, but didn’t dare. She tapped Zuko on the shoulder, and leaned in so that she could whisper as quietly as possible.

“That man’s name is Zhao. I remember him; he worked with our father once, years ago. We were children.”

Zuko nodded, but said nothing. They both stared into the tunnel, getting as close to the light as they could without being seen.

Down the hall, Zhao had grabbed one of the sleeping prisoners out of their cells, and had them pinned against the wall. If she squinted, Azula could see what Zhao was holding to their throat; a cigarette. *It must burn* , Azula realized.

“Tell me,” demanded Zhao. His voice was soft and slithery, like oil. “What do you know about insurgent activity in Assassin’s Lane?” He wrapped his other hand around the left side of the person’s face, letting his fingernails scratch their skin.

“Nothing!” said the prisoner, their voice trembling. “I swear! Please, don’t hurt me!”

In response, Zhao dug his fingernails into the prisoner’s cheek, and twisted the cigarette in their neck. The person shrieked, and went limp against the wall. Zhao just smiled coldly. “Don’t hurt you? But I’m the *Master of Pain* , after all. That would be denying my purpose.”

Azula leaned in again. “I heard about him while I was investigating the Dai Li. They’re all terrified of him!”

Zuko nodded grimly. “I can see why,” he whispered back.

“I swear!” cried the prisoner. “I live near Assassin’s Lane, it’s true! But I never go there!”

“What a shame,” mused Zhao. “If you had any valuable information for me, I could have let you go. But since you’re so resistant, it seems I’ll just have to…” he ripped the cigarette out of the prisoner’s neck. Azula could see the burn even from where she stood. Zhao took a match and lit the cigarette so that the tip was still flaming. He drove it back into the prisoner’s neck, even harder than before. “ *Keep at it* .”

The prisoner screamed so loudly that Azula thought everyone underground must have heard it. Zhao shifted so that Azula couldn’t see the prisoner’s face anymore from where she was standing, but she saw the prisoner’s body go limp. They weren’t dead; even while they were unconscious, Azula could still hear them gasping for air.

Zhao flung them back into their cell and continued down the tunnel. Azula could hear his laughter long after the echoes of his footsteps had vanished completely.

Hesitantly, she and Zuko crawled out of the empty cell, and began creeping down the tunnel, thankfully in the opposite direction from Zhao. As they walked, Azula turned back to Zuko. She dared not speak any louder than a whisper.

“What do you think they’re using a secret prison-slash-torture chamber for?”

“The same thing they’re always working for,” replied Zuko, also whispering. “Control.”

The central passage that Katara and Sokka were walking down seemed to be glowing brighter than the others. There were more torches here than there had been in the entrance, and the further down the tunnel they got, the closer together the torches became.

The passage was lined with shelves. There were very few doors, and the ones that there were were marked with signs reading *danger* and *keep out* ! Haphazard shards of glass, tools, and occasional rolling carts were scattered all the way down the tunnel.

“What is this place?” asked Katara, her eyes wide, looking around as she stepped over a broken glass bottle. Something about the tunnel looked slightly familiar to Sokka, but he couldn’t quite put his finger on it.

“I don’t know.”

There was a clanking from further down the hall. Frantically, Sokka grabbed Katara and leaped onto one of the carts. Both siblings wrapped their arms around their knees and curled up as tightly as possible. Sokka could feel Katara’s breath on his shoulder, and his heartbeat getting faster as the clanking grew closer.

The man who walked by looked like one of Sokka’s science professors, but weirder. He had an enormous tuft of black hair, but absolutely none on the very top of his head, and there were chunks missing from both his eyebrows. He wore a lab coat, which hung askew on his bony shoulders and was covered in dark smears. In his right hand, he held a beaker full of a glowing blue substance. Sokka remembered Zuko saying something about a glowing blue substance being made at the Dai Li’s factory, so he figured that this was the same thing.  
The man reached into his pocket. Sokka immediately tensed up, but relaxed again when he realized that it was only a tape recorder. The man clicked the top of it, and began speaking.

“Day 1 of practical trials of serum number 45. This serum has been rather...inconsistent in previous trials, but I believe I have managed to manipulate it to produce the desired effects. We have yet to test the serum on human subjects, but we have gathered a multitude of potentials, and with the serum being produced en masse, I have no doubt that the trials will be a huge success. If we pull this off, it could be revolutionary!” The man seemed overwhelmed by his excitement for a moment, then gathered himself and continued muttering into the tape recorder as he continued past Katara and Sokka towards the entrance. “The prisoners...I mean, willing subjects, seem to have taken a slight dislike to me. They never even use my name, they only call me ‘The Mechanist.’ Actually, everyone in the Dai Li does that. Perhaps I can make a note with Long Feng to put something in my contract to fix it.” The rest of his words were lost as he moved out of Sokka’s range of hearing.

Careful not to make any loud noises, the siblings crawled out of the cart. A gust of wind blew through the tunnel, making Sokka’s teeth chatter. “If this creepy place is also some sort of experimental drug testing center, then we need to get out of here *fast* . Come on, we’d better get going.”

Katara didn’t argue with him, and they set off towards the exit.

Katara was more than ready to be out of Lake Laogai when they arrived at the final round room. To her relief, Zuko, Azula, Suki, and Mai had all made it there safely, and they all looked unharmed. Joo Dee was also standing at the head of the room with her back to them.

Zuko turned to Sokka and Katara. “Did you guys find anything?”

Sokka nodded. “You wouldn’t believe what we found. You?”

“You could say we saw some things we weren’t expecting.”

“Well, that’s good, isn’t it?” chimed in Katara. “We have new information that you guys can use.”

“It’s great!” said Sokka. “And see, Azula? We split up and we didn’t die! We’re all still here!”

Zuko nodded, then turned to face Joo Dee. “Joo Dee, thank you for helping us. We may have made big steps in solving these murders. We’re ready to leave now.”

Joo Dee stayed with her back to them, but said nothing. Katara felt her heart begin to beat a little faster. Was something wrong?

“Joo Dee?” asked Zuko, hesitantly stepping forward. “Did you hear me? I said we’re ready to leave now.”

Very slowly, Joo Dee turned around. Her sincere expression from earlier was gone, and replaced by an enormous, false, *terrifying* grin. Katara nearly let out a scream, but stopped herself. When Joo Dee spoke, her voice was emotionless and robotic.

“I’m afraid there *is* no exit in this room. There never was.”

Guards suddenly came pouring out of every passageway, filling the room faster than Katara could even process. More and more of them came in with each second. Katara could see the passageways; they were full of guards, but they were their only chance.

Katara wasn’t sure which one of them yelled, but she heard a voice through the crowd.

“Run!”

The group took off sprinting down different passages. Azula had lost track completely of where she was going, and where everyone else was, despite her best attempts. She just ran, pushing past guards before they saw her coming, using her small size to duck under arms and around corners without being caught. She grabbed a whip from one of the passing guards, and began brandishing it as she ran, trying to keep any guards away from her. She could feel them on her heels and up ahead, but she didn’t stop running. Her father had taught her long ago that impossible odds were never a reason to give up.

She raced around a corner and slammed into Zhao, the Master of Pain. She fell backwards and hit the floor hard, trying not to wince in pain. He smiled down at her, his cruelty on full display. She smiled coldly up at him. If she could just ignore her rapidly beating, adrenaline-fuelled heart, maybe she could pull this off.

“Well, well, well…” Zhao grabbed Azula’s arm and pulled her to her feet, but he didn’t let go, “what have we here?”

Trying to think while every inch of her body was pulsing with adrenaline was difficult, to say the least. Still, Azula kept her gaze level and confident. “Your worst nightmare.”

Zhao laughed. It was a loud, full laugh for someone with such a slick, slippery voice. “Is that so?”

Azula smirked. This man preyed on fear. If she could push hers away, perhaps she could succeed against him, at least for the moment. “I wouldn’t believe it either, if I were you. But that’s your mistake.” Slowly, gripping it tightly, she used her free hand to grab her dagger out of her boot. She was *incredibly* thankful to have brought it. “I may not be the Master of Pain, but I know who you are. I know every little thing about the White Lotus *and* the Dai Li.” She laughed. “Since I came to this city, I’ve done nothing but investigate you all, and you wouldn’t believe what I’ve seen.” She leaned in, hating every second that her face was close to his. “I even know your weakness.”

To her dismay, Zhao laughed again, and only gripped her arm tighter. “Nice try, Little Charmer. You may know a lot about this city, but I *have* no weaknesses.” He started pulling her down the tunnel. “You’re coming with me.”

Azula had been dragged around by her father enough times to know how to get out of tight holds like this one. As Zhao pulled her into another passageway, she spotted a round room at the other end. *The exit.*

Using her free hand, she swung her arm around and drove the handle of her dagger into Zhao’s arm. She’d been attempting to use the blade, but this would work, too. She pushed it in harder and harder, enough to leave a bruise, until she felt his grip on her arm weaken. The second she did, she pocketed her dagger, swung backwards into the air, and used her momentum to dash forward, prying his weakened arm off her own. With every ounce of her strength, she dashed down the tunnel towards the stairs, but Zhao’s words did not escape her ears, spoken in his chilling, oily voice.

“You’ll pay for this, Little Charmer. Your time is coming soon. I promise.”

Suki was lucky enough to find herself in an empty passage, without any guards to push through, but she could hear their footsteps behind her. She pulled out her fan as she ran, ready to leap into a fight at any moment. She would be in *huge* trouble if she were caught. If she escaped, maybe she could lie, at least enough to keep herself out of danger. She didn’t know what the Dai Li did to the people down here, but they had lied enough. She could never trust them again, and she knew that getting caught would have devastating consequences.

She reached a fork in the tunnel, and, even though her brain was screaming at her not to, paused for a fraction of a second before turning left. She sprinted even faster, faster and faster, as fast as she could physically run.

All of a sudden, something rolled under her left foot. Her legs flew out from under her, and she went smashing into one of the tunnel walls. She didn’t think anything was broken, but she was unable to do anything but lie still, dazed. The tunnel was blurry, and it was starting to come into focus, but not fast enough.

Guards swarmed around her, scooping her up and beginning to carry her back down the tunnel. As feeling began to return to her body, she began to twist and kick, struggling to free herself, but they just crowded around her, gripping her tighter and tighter until she couldn’t even see the tunnel through the mass of guards.

She ignored the tears in her eyes at the thought of what they would do to her. She had to be strong, and she needed to stay calm if she was to survive this.

All of a sudden, one of the guards shrieked, then another, and they began to fall away. The second she could, Suki threw her legs out and kicked as hard as she possibly could. The guards holding her let her fall, and she was running away as soon as she hit the floor.

At the head of the tunnel, Suki could see the stairs, only five hundred steps or so away. She turned back to see what had pulled the guards off of her, and screamed.

Mai was standing at the other end of the tunnel, throwing knives at the guards. She wore a determined glare that Suki had never seen on her before. The guards got closer and closer to her. She was outnumbered, but she kept fighting. The more knives she threw, the angrier the guards got, and the closer to her they swarmed.

Suki began sprinting down the tunnel to help. “What are you doing?!” she cried.

Mai smirked. “What does it look like, Princess?” She threw a guard off of her as she shouted, but they were beginning to overpower her. “I’m saving your neck! Now get out of here before I can’t save either of us!”

“But they could kill you!”

As the guards piled on top of her, the last thing Mai gave Suki was a small, genuine smile. “Eh, the Dai Li never liked me anyway. Now get out of here!”

The guards and Mai vanished around the corner, leaving Suki standing in the middle of the stone tunnel. She felt tears in her eyes, and fury coursing through her. Fury at the guards.

She began to sprint after them, but a hand grabbed her wrist. She whirled around angrily, ready to fight, but it was only Azula, looking as exhausted as Suki felt.

“What happened?”

Suki had to gasp for air. “They...they took Mai. She saved me, and I let them take her.” She was furious at the Dai Li, at the guards, and at herself. The person she *cared about* was gone, and it was all her fault. She tried to sprint back down the hallway, but Azula held her tight.

“Look,” said Azula, annoyingly calmly, “Mai sacrificed herself so that you could get out of here. If we leave now, you have a chance at saving her. But if you follow her, you’ll only get captured, and then you won’t be able to save her *and* her sacrifice will be in vain. Is that what you want?”

“I can’t just leave her here!”

Azula wrapped her arms around her and began dragging her towards the exit. For someone so tiny, she was strong. “I know it isn’t fair. But we don’t have a choice. We need to get out of here *now* !”

Suki blinked back her tears and fought every inch of the way as Azula dragged her towards the stairs.

Zuko was the first of the group to reach the stairs, and he fought guard after guard, trying his best to keep the exit open for his group. He lost track of how many people he knocked down, how many punches and kicks he threw, how much blood was spilled on the stone floor. He refused to stop fighting until his friends all escaped. He *wouldn’t* abandon them here. Not in a million years.

He felt relief rush through him when Sokka came careening out of the left hand tunnel. He had about five guards right on his heels, but at least he’d made it this far. As he ran, he threw his boomerang over his shoulder, and it swung back around, hitting two of the guards in the head before it flew back to Sokka’s hand. Sokka sprinted towards the stairs, and Zuko held out his hand and swung him around to give him more momentum.

“What about you?” yelled Sokka as the momentum from the swing propelled him up.

“I’ll be fine,” yelled Zuko. “I need to make sure everyone gets out of here, but just *run* !”

Sokka looked pained for a moment, but seeing Zuko’s glare, he turned and raced up the stairs, out of the fortress and into the woods.

Katara was next, only a minute or so later. She came out of the central tunnel, covered in some sort of purple goo, as though she’d run through a child’s slime factory, but other than that, she looked unharmed. She had only three guards on her tail, and as she ran, she pulled a chunk of purple goop out of her hair and threw it behind her. It hid one guard directly in the face before falling to the floor and causing another one to slip.

Zuko reached out his hand to swing her around and up the stairs.

“I’m not leaving everyone!” she cried as she was propelled upwards.

“Me neither! That’s why I’m staying here!”

Unlike her brother, she screeched to a halt and ran down to stand next to Zuko. “I’m *not* leaving the rest of us down here. Nothing you do or say could make me.”

Zuko knew better than to argue with Katara when she got that determined, stormy expression on her face.

For the next ten minutes, everything seemed to move in slow motion. Guards came to try and apprehend them, but Zuko and Katara drove them away every time. Zuko could see his own worry reflected in Katara’s face, but he didn’t let it show. If the other three had been caught because they were trying to help *him* …

He couldn’t think about that. It would only make him lose the fight.

After what felt like forever, Azula and Suki finally emerged from the tunnel. Azula was dragging Suki, who was struggling and fighting her. Katara instantly raced down the stairs to help, punching a guard off the railing as she went.

“What happened?”

Azula’s expression was grim. “Mai sacrificed herself to save Suki. And if we don’t want that sacrifice to be in vain, we need to get out of here *now* .”

Suki nodded, prying herself from Azula’s grip and looking towards the exit with steely determination. She was crying.

The four of them sprinted up the stairs and into the woods. They didn’t stop running until the city lights came into view again.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

TW: Burning, physical torture, abduction.

I really really hope y'all enjoyed that one! I had so much fun writing it, especially the climactic scene with Mai and Suki (and Azula.) PLEASE leave a comment if you have something to say, because I'd really love to hear your thoughts on this one.

## Chapter 24: The Double Clue

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Discouraged by the events at Lake Laogai, the group splits off in rather odd directions, and discovers several surprising pieces of information.

#### Chapter Notes

Sorry for the brief hiatus between the last chapter and this one! I've been having a bit of a hard time getting motivated to reread and post, but I'm trying to improve, so please bear with me!

TW: Heights, knives, threats.

Happy reading!

### Text

After the events of the previous night, Suki had retreated back to the Dai Li mansion without a word. No one had seen or heard from her since morning, except a quick text saying that Toph had vouched for her, and that she wasn’t in any sort of danger.

Katara was worried about her, but she was worried about so many other things that it was hard to focus on that. She was worried about Suki, she was worried about Mai, she was worried about whatever experiments the Dai Li was carrying out in secret, she was worried about the innocent citizens who had been taken prisoner, she was worried about everyone who seemed to be in danger from these murders, and (rather selfishly) she was worried about herself and her friends, and the danger that seemed to be catching up to them.

The four of them (Katara, Zuko, Sokka, and Azula) had all crashed at Zuko’s place after the trip to Lake Laogai, Katara and Sokka’s apartments being further away. Katara didn’t know about the rest of them, but she, sprawled out on a couple of pillows that they had put on Azula’s floor, hadn’t been able to sleep. Every time she closed her eyes, all she could picture was running down dark passages while Dai Li soldiers crowded around her. At last, she’d drifted off around five in the morning, out of pure exhaustion.

As she wandered into the kitchen, around noon, she found the other three already there. Zuko handed her a cup of tea, and she sipped it gratefully, feeling the caffeine slowly work its way through her system. Katara wasn’t usually much for caffeinated tea (she usually preferred fruit teas), but she’d been using it recently to make up for her late nights. It probably wasn’t the best idea, but what else could she do?

There was a sort of silent fog hanging over the kitchen, except for the rain drumming on the windows. Maybe nobody wanted to speak about last night because talking about it would make it all seem too real. Katara couldn’t even bring herself to mention Mai’s name.

Plus, Sokka and Zuko were avoiding making eye contact with each other, and had been ever since both of them had pointedly refused to share a bedroom the night before. Katara got the sense that both of them were hurt by the other, but would never admit it because they either didn’t quite understand why, or did and thought it was hopeless. She wasn’t worried, though. They may have been idiots when it came to each other, but they’d come around eventually.

At last, Azula spoke. Of all of them, she seemed the least rattled by the events of the night before. Sure, she looked a little tired, but she was Azula. In the short time Katara had known her, she’d learned that Azula rarely, if ever, let herself get rattled by *anything* .

“What are we supposed to do now?”

The kitchen fell silent again. None of them had an answer.

Katara swallowed. “We can’t stop going. I know we’re all scared after last night…” her eyes wandered over to Azula &#96;&#96;even if we don’t want to talk about it, but we need to stay motivated, especially now that we know just how many people need our help.”

Zuko nodded. “We can’t let the Dai Li get away with this.”

“But we can’t go to the police right now!” chimed in Sokka, still actively trying not to look at Zuko. It wasn’t working. “The Dai Li and the police are one and the same. Since we escaped, we can all claim that we never went to Lake Laogai. But if we confess, they’ll just arrest us. We can’t afford that.”

“Then who do we tell?” said Azula. “Not the mayor, not the White Lotus. There’s no one with any sort of political power in this city who can help us.”

“There *are* police officers who aren’t part of the Dai Li,” said Zuko, “but we have no way of knowing who they are.”

“So we’re stuck,” Azula said bitterly, taking another sip of her coffee.

“Not necessarily!” said Katara. “Just because we’re in a tricky position right now in regards to the Dai Li doesn’t mean we can’t keep working. I know you all want to solve this just as much as I do. Don’t give up on yourselves after one setback. I know we’re all better than that.”

After a moment of silence, Azula turned to Sokka. “Your sister has a thing for speeches, doesn’t she?”

Sokka shrugged. “At least they’re good ones!”

“She has a point, though,” said Zuko, beginning to pace back and forth, tapping his fingers to his chin. It was one of his habits that made him look like a fictional character. “If we can think of other areas that we didn’t have as much time to investigate, the Dai Li’s attention is going to be entirely on Lake Laogai right now. This might be a good opportunity.”

“Well,” said Azula, pouring herself another cup of coffee, “you know I’m all about seizing a good opportunity.”

“Well, what can we think of?” said Katara. “There has to be *something* .”

“Actually,” said Sokka, an idea seeming to come to him, “I think there is.” He turned to Azula. “Remember when we went to the morgue and deduced that Chief Song was killed for revenge?” Azula nodded. Katara remembered it, too, even though she hadn’t been there. It was strange; that day felt like a lifetime ago, but it hadn’t even been two weeks.

“Well, I’ve been thinking, all of the other bodies should be there, too. If we could get a look at all of them, or at least some of them, maybe we could come to some sort of conclusion.”

“That’s a great idea,” said Zuko, with a slight edge of bitterness to his voice. “You two make a really great team.”

Azula’s eyes darted from her brother to Katara. “Wow... not that I wouldn’t be thrilled to look at more corpses, but I actually have another *important* investigation to do, and it’s critical that I do it today.” She pointed at Katara. “Katara’s coming with me. Right, Katara?”

Katara usually didn’t condone lying, but she wasn’t going to argue with this. She nodded. “It’s very important. We’re *so* sorry.” She widened her eyes, pretending that an idea had struck her. “But hey, why don’t *you two* go to the morgue together? It’s always good to bring backup!”

The two of them looked away from each other awkwardly. Katara sighed. “Guys, don’t be ridiculous. You are not going to the morgue by yourself. Azula and I are busy. There is only *one* option.”

Zuko sighed, and let his eyes wander over towards Sokka for the first time all morning. “Fine,” he said at last. Sokka nodded, a small smile creeping up the sides of his face. He was trying hard not to smile, but it was a lost cause.

As the two boys left the apartment, Katara turned to Azula. “A morgue. Can’t get much more romantic than that, I suppose.”

“I do my best.”

“Well,” said Katara, “what *are* we going to do while they’re on their date at the morgue?”

Azula smirked, pulling out a ruby-encrusted dagger from the pocket of her skirt. Combined with her blood-red top, black boots with studded straps, and the fact that her hair was in a *perfect* high ponytail that day, she looked like she could kill you at any moment.

“I wasn’t lying about having investigations to do. I saw a few things in Assassin’s Lane that I’d like to examine again. Some of them are too talented to overlook.”

Katara sighed. “Well, I hope you have room for one more, because I’m going to be bored to death if I’m here alone all day.”

Azula smiled, applying a lipstick that was the same blood-red color as her top. “Oh, I was counting on it.”

Sokka and Zuko had more trouble breaking into the morgue than the last time Sokka had been there. It was daytime, so the morgue was technically open, meaning that there were more people there, but at the same time, neither of them could fit into the vent that Azula had used to get in last time. They were both too tall.

“Well,” said Sokka, “looks like this plan was a bust. Let’s just go home and forget…”

“Wait,” said Zuko, grabbing his hand and causing Sokka’s face to turn two shades darker, and making him almost trip over his own feet, “I don’t want to fight like this. What...why are you angry with me? If nothing else, you owe me an explanation.”

Sokka sighed. He *wasn’t* angry with Zuko; he was hurt. He was hurt because Zuko had seemed repulsed at the idea of sharing a bedroom with him, and he was hurt because he knew that his friend would never return his feelings. He wasn’t usually one for drama, or getting upset over little things, but he couldn’t help it. He was hurt, and didn’t know what to do about it.

Of course, Zuko didn’t, and *couldn’t* know any of that. So he lied, even though he hated lying to Zuko. “I’m not angry with you, Zuko. I’m just frustrated with this case, and I’m tired.”

The look in Zuko’s eyes told Sokka that he didn’t believe him, but he seemed to accept the explanation anyway, and turned back to the morgue. “That doesn’t solve the problem of getting in here.”

Seeing a piece of rope hanging out a second-floor window, and with his mind on the subject of...things, Sokka felt a lightbulb go off in his brain. “Maybe it does.” He gestured to the rope. “If I stand on your shoulders, I could probably jump up there. Then I could lower the rope, and pull you up.”

“That sounds like an incredibly risky plan. Downright stupid, actually.” But Zuko was smiling.

Sokka smiled back. “Stupid enough to work?”

Zuko sighed, rolling his eyes. “Probably.”

It took ten minutes of poking, awkward fumbling, Sokka feeling like his body temperature had just permanently changed, and falling over a lot, for Zuko to finally be able to lift Sokka onto his shoulders. He was still six inches or so below the window, even standing on his toes and reaching his hand up as high as he could.

Fear coursed through his body. It was mild compared to the fear he’d felt the night before, but it was still fear. He looked at Zuko, trying his best not to focus on how far his head was from the ground. “If I fall to my death, catch me!” he joked.

Zuko looked back up at him. There was no joke on his face. “Promise,” he replied with a small smile.

Somewhere inside of Sokka, it registered that Zuko *meant* it. If Sokka fell, he would stop at nothing to catch him.

So he took a deep breath and jumped. For one horrible moment, his hands flailed in the air as he grasped frantically for nothing, but his fingers soon wrapped around the edge of the windowsill. He didn’t have the best finger strength in the world, but he held on for dear life.

Now, however, he had another problem. He had gotten to the windowsill, technically, but he was still stuck hanging in midair.

“What are you waiting for?” called Zuko from the ground.

Oh, this was *so* embarrassing. Sokka was lucky that Katara wasn’t here, or she would have had a field day with this. On the other hand, having Zuko here wasn’t exactly better. “I...uh...may not have thought this far.”

“What do you mean?”

Sokka sighed. “I...uh...didn’t really think about the ‘pulling myself up by my arms’ part.”

There was silence. Then, “You mean to tell me that you study dead bodies for fun, spent last night running for your life from at least a hundred Dai Li soldiers, and you don’t think you can do one pull-up?”

“I don’t think, I *know* .”

“Don’t be stupid.” Zuko’s voice was slightly harsher than it normally was, but Sokka could practically hear the good intentions behind it. “Sokka, you’re a *detective* .”

“Not officially!”

“Who cares? You solve murders, you’re smart and you make good plans. You’re one of the best allies anyone could ask for. I think...I *know* you can do this.”

Sokka took a deep breath and pulled with every muscle in his body. His arms felt like they were on fire, and he felt like he would fall at any second, but he kept pushing, until, with a final burst of momentum, he swung himself up onto the windowsill, gasping for breath.

“I don’t think I’ll ever use my arms again!” he called down to Zuko, who was smiling up at him.

“Well, you need them right about now,” replied Zuko. “Unless you want to just leave me down here.”

Sokka felt his face flush. He’d forgotten. Quickly, he lowered the rope and held it tight, but to his surprise, he barely needed to pull it. Zuko scaled the wall without much trouble. It was *really* impressive.

When Zuko got to the top, Sokka realized he was staring, and quickly looked away, trying his hardest not to blush. “Where did you learn how to do that?”

Zuko shrugged. “I climbed up and down the side of my house a lot growing up.”

Sokka groaned. “You can do *that* and I can barely do one pull-up. Remind me why you want me around, again?” He kept his tone light, but he knew that he really meant it.

Zuko paused. He could probably also tell that he really meant it. Well, that was mortifying. “Are you serious?”

Against his better judgement, Sokka nodded.

Zuko reached forward and took his hands, which only made Sokka feel a little bit dizzy. He couldn’t blame Zuko, though. He didn’t know what Sokka felt, and Sokka was going to do everything in his power to keep it that way. “Sokka, you’re...you’re the best friend I’ve ever had. You’re smart, and you’re funny, and you’re...important.” Zuko looked away awkwardly. “Even if it took me a little too long to open up to you...you’re kind of like my family now. I wouldn’t want to do this case without you.”

Sokka thought his heart might fall out of his body, it was beating so fast. But he tried to play it cool, anyway, pulling his hands away and putting on a cocky smile. “Well, then, if we want to look at those bodies, we’d better get going.” He started walking down the hallway.

“Wait,” said Zuko, pulling him in the opposite direction, “aren’t there files on these bodies? Maybe we could start there.”

“Oh,” said Sokka softly, “yeah, that actually makes a lot more sense.”

They were lucky that the hallway was deserted, because they would have had a very hard time hiding if they’d needed to. As far as Sokka could tell, the hallway was completely empty of any furniture or things to hide behind.

There was no way of knowing whether or not there was anybody inside the office, so Sokka was about to suggest listening at the door when Zuko ran forward and kicked it open, sending it slamming into the wall. Well, hopefully there was nobody else in the building.

Sokka locked the door behind them, just in case. Zuko was already down on his knees, tearing through the file cabinet. Sometimes Sokka forgot how *fast* Zuko could go, especially when he felt like he’d lost something. It only made him want to win even more.

“Look at these,” said Zuko, spreading the six files out on the floor. “Can you make any sense out of any of this stuff?”

Sokka knelt down and began looking through the files. There were six of them now, a thought that made him sick to his stomach all on its own: Pakku, Fung, Chief Song, the group of Dai Li guards, Professor Zei, and now Ukano.

“Hmm,” he mumbled to himself as he flipped through the files, “this is a little strange.”

“What is it?” asked Zuko, leaning over his shoulder. “Did you find a pattern?”

“That’s the thing,” said Sokka. “Pakku was stabbed with knives that someone threw. Fung, by the looks of it, was thrown off a balcony. Chief Song was slashed to death, and those Dai Li soldiers were poisoned. According to Professor Zei’s autopsy, he was killed by some sort of slow-acting poison, but no one knows what kind or how slow, and Ukano was somehow...frozen to death and found in an alleyway.” He closed the files, and turned to look at Zuko.

“So what this means is…” Zuko began.

“There *is* no pattern, no sort of common thread” finished Sokka. “None at all.”

Azula realized that Katara was staring at her as they took the train down towards Assassin’s Lane. She tried to ignore it, because Katara wasn’t normally the type to stare, and both of them were still tired from the previous night, but eventually, her irritation got the better of her.

“ *What* is so fascinating that your eyes keep wandering in my direction?”

Katara blinked. “I’m sorry. It’s just...you’re wearing Zuko’s red coat again.”

It was true. Azula had donned the red trench coat for a second time, and she had done so for two reasons. “It’s raining.”

“And…”

Azula sighed. “ *And* I made an impression the last time that I was here, and it seemed to serve me well. I don’t want to lose that.” She turned to face Katara completely. “Hang on a second, have you ever been here before?”

Katara nodded. “Once. When I was younger I…” she looked away “I came here looking for my mother’s killer.”

“Did you find them?” The words were out of Azula’s mouth before she could really think about them. If her mother were here, she would chide her for being insensitive. *But why did she care* *what her mother thought?*

Katara sighed. “Obviously not, but if I’m being honest, I never really got the idea out of my head.” She glanced up. “Don’t tell my brother that.”

“Wouldn’t dream of it,” replied Azula. “And who knows? Maybe you’ll have some good luck today.”

“We could use some good luck,” sighed Katara as they exited the train into the Lower Ring, and began walking towards Assassin’s Lane. “After last night, that is.” She paused. “Are you okay? After last night, I mean.”

Azula shrugged. She didn’t feel as panicked as everyone else seemed, and she wasn’t sure how to interpret that. “I’m exhausted, obviously. And of course, I don’t want anything bad to happen to Mai.”

“But aren’t you *scared* ?”

“Of what?”

Katara shivered. “I don’t know, the Dai Li, maybe?”

As they turned into Assassin’s Lane and began to walk down the cobblestone street, Azula thought carefully about what she wanted to say. “I suppose I see it this way. The Dai Li have no more power or knowledge than they did before. They have the same resources, and they know that we’re investigating the case, just as they did before last night. They’re not going to suddenly attack us, because nothing has really changed, not in that regard, anyway.” Azula toyed with a strand of hair from her ponytail. “Now, where is that woman? Perhaps I should have been more skeptical of her cryptic promises.”

“But aren’t you worried about Mai?” said Katara, jogging a few steps to catch up with her. Azula hadn’t even realized that she’d been speedwalking. “I mean...she could be dead, and here we are, not helping.” She looked down, and Azula realized she was feeling *guilty* .

“Obviously, I don’t *want* anything bad to happen to her,” replied Azula. “But I don’t feel any guilt. Mai knew the risks of the trip when she agreed to come, and if we want to help her, we need to wait until they aren’t expecting us. Otherwise, we’ll ruin everything she sacrificed herself for.”

“But she could be *dead* already!” Katara shouted, not realizing she was shouting.

Azula put a finger to her lips. In that pose, with her red lipstick and red coat, she felt even more like a character from a murder movie. “Sssh. And if she’s already dead, then there’s nothing we can do now anyway. We need to be patient.”

“But you don’t think we failed her?”

“Of *course* we failed her.” Azula’s tone was bitter, so much so that it surprised even herself. “But failure is meant to be something to avoid at all costs, and when it comes, that only makes us work harder.” She turned and placed one hand on Katara’s shoulder. The other hand was still clutching the ruby dagger in her pocket. “Now, the Dai Li will *never* get their hands on one of us again.” “You’re awfully confident,” said a voice from the side alley they were passing by. Azula and Katara whirled around, and found themselves face to face with Hama, who smirked and beckoned them into the dark side street. She gestured to Katara. “I see you’ve brought a new friend.”

Azula placed her hand on her hip, and made sure that she looked as confident and threatening as physically possible. “Don’t worry, you can trust her. I only associate with the strongest.”

She could see Katara trying not to roll her eyes, and shot her a glare.

Hama smiled that same, children’s-doll-like smile. “Well, welcome to Assassin’s Lane. I see you’re looking for me. But tell me, why should I listen to either of you?”

“We are,” said Azula. “And you should listen to us because…”

“Because it’s the right thing to do,” said Katara. “Our friends are in danger. We *need* to help them. We... *I* won’t leave them alone.”

“Interesting,” said Hama. “A compassionate spirit. We don’t get a lot of these around here.” She leaned forward and took Katara’s hands in her own. “You are *such* a strong soul, child. I can see it in your eyes; your desire to protect your friends: your love, your loyalty, your *ferocity* .” She gestured to Azula. “Your friend here is like a lightning bolt: intense, dangerous, precise, even deadly, but child, you remind me of myself when I was younger. We are entire storms.” Delicately, she pulled a ring off her finger. It was silver, like Azula’s dagger, but embedded with a small blue stone. A Star Sapphire, Azula thought it was called. She slid the ring onto Katara’s hand. “Take this.”

“What for?”

Hama smiled. “It’s like your friend’s dagger. A reminder of your greatest strengths.”

Well, it was certainly a kind gesture. Too bad it was almost certainly some sort of façade. Most everything was, after all. “All right,” interjected Azula. “Enough stalling.” She pulled the dagger out and began twirling it around, making sure to keep a tight grip on it. “Who are you, and why do you kill?”

Hama laughed. “Well, if it’s *that* you want to know, you should have just asked.”

Katara folded her arms across her chest. “We did ask. Now we’re waiting for answers.”

Hama laughed. “You have spirit. Just like your friend.” She leaned forward, her eyes glinting. “If you ever wanted, you could find a place here.”

Katara didn’t waver. “Enough stalling.”

Hama sighed. “You may think me ruthless, but everything I do has a reason.”

“Everyone says that,” said Azula.

“And it’s true. Everyone *does* have a reason. But my reasons are the right ones.”

“Elaborate.”

Hama stared into the alleyway. Azula could tell that her mind was taking a sort of trip back in time. “I’m sure you’re aware of those who have immense amounts of privilege in this city. Those who have endless power, and who abuse it every time they’re given the chance.”

Katara raised an eyebrow. “You mean the White Lotus and the Dai Li.”

“Them, and anyone who aids them in their quest for power.” Hama looked up. “That power belongs to no one, *especially* not them.”

“If not for power,” interjected Azula, “then why *do* you kill?”

“Your friend will understand,” replied Hama. “I can tell from the look in her eyes. She’s lost someone she loves, and not naturally. Someone *took* them from her.”

Katara placed a hand to her throat. Azula had noticed before that she always wore the same necklace. “My mother…”

Hama sighed. “When I was a young girl, the White Lotus and the Dai Li were far more violent. There used to be battles, raids, flames, and death. They didn’t care who they hurt, only that they could defeat one another. But they came after my family. We were ancient artists who refused to give our art to either of them, and they didn’t like that.” She looked at the ground, tears pricking at the corners of her eyes. “They murdered my entire family, and all of our friends. Now there are none of us left, and they didn’t even *care* .” She looked up, her eyes full of determination. “And I have devoted my entire life to making sure that never happens again.”

Katara’s eyes were wide and sparkling. Azula took the dagger in her hands and stared at her reflection in the gems. This woman was a murderer, but her motives were nothing if not heroic. What did that say about her? About Katara? About Azula?

By the time Azula looked up from her dagger, Hama was gone.

“Are you all right?” asked Azula as they walked out of the alleyway and back onto Assassin’s Lane. “I know that this brings up some...memories for you.”

Katara blinked, surprised to see Azula asking such a question. “Yeah, I’m fine. It just...takes me back, you know?”

Azula nodded. “Actually, I think I know better than you might think.”

Katara raised an eyebrow, a memory drifting back into her mind. “Zuko...he said that your mother died when you were kids.” She looked up. “Did you ever find out what happened to her?”

Azula sighed, looking away. “Believe me, my relationship with my mother was nothing like yours.” There was a long-held bitterness in her voice as she spoke. “And I think that Zuko and I both know *exactly* what happened to her.” She sighed. “He just could never prove it.”

Katara wanted to know more, but she could feel Azula growing pricklier by the second, so she decided to stop prodding for the moment. Maybe she could ask again another day. For now, the afternoon was starting to slip away. It was time to head home.

As they walked down the street, Azula quite literally ran smack-dab into a tall boy who couldn’t be much older than Zuko or Sokka. As he turned around, Katara caught sight of the cigarette in his mouth.

Evidently, Azula understood something about this boy that Katara didn’t, because there was a glint of recognition in the other girl’s eyes when she looked at him.

“Watch where you’re going, bitches!” The boy seemed fiery, to be sure.

Katara felt anger rising through her body. She *hated* rude people, especially people who were rude to complete strangers who hadn’t done anything wrong. “Don’t talk to us that way! We haven’t done anything to you!”

The boy laughed. “Those are bold words, coming from a tiny little thing like you. Don’t you know who I am?”  
“We do.” Azula’s voice was chilling, completely void of any emotion. “You’re Jet. You pretend you run this place, and you talk a big game, but everyone knows that’s a lie.”

The boy named Jet narrowed his eyes, and stepped closer to them. “How do you know my name? What the *fuck* do you think you’re playing at?”

Azula laughed, a cold, cruel laugh. “Don’t be so quick to imagine the worst. My brother met you.” She toyed with a strand of her hair. “You might remember him. He beat you in a drinking competition, which, to be honest, is pretty pathetic for you, because my brother can’t hold his alcohol to save his life.” Her tone had become more playful, but Katara didn’t miss the threatening undercurrents. Seeing Azula being purposely horrifying like this was both thrilling and awful at the same time.

Jet laughed. He, too, was now putting on a threatening exterior. “Yeah, I remember your brother. He gave me a little surprise for a second, but I showed him who’s boss.” He leaned towards them. “Kind of like I’m about to do to you.”

Azula showed no reaction to the threat, simply laughing again, pulling out her dagger, and toying with it. “You can try, if you like. But whatever my brother did to surprise you…” she leaned towards him this time, her eyes blazing, “I am *infinitely* more determined *and* scarier.” She drew back. “So, if you have any sort of information, I suggest you tell us now. Before this gets...messy.”

“I don’t know what kind of information you want.”

Azula’s eyes flashed again. “Don’t bother lying to us.” She stepped forward, pointing her dagger.

Jet groaned. “Fine. You want information? I’ll give you information. The White Lotus and the Dai Li are some of the worst people ever to walk the Earth. My family did *nothing* to them, except living in the Lower Ring. But do you want to know what the Dai Li did to us? They whispered in the Mayor’s ear and told him to raise our taxes. And the White Lotus? Didn’t lift a *finger* to help us.” His fists were clenched, and his voice was getting more and more furious. “My family became homeless, and then my parents *starved* , because of those assholes.” He gave Azula’s arm a shove. “Take that dagger the Puppetmaster gave you and shove it up your ass. If you’re working for the White Lotus or the Dai Li, you have no business being here.” He turned and began to disappear into the crowd.

“And if we’re not?” asked Katara.  
Jet turned back so that Katara could only see half of his face. “Then it’s none of your business anyway.”

At last, Katara and Azula reached the end of Assassin’s Lane. As they boarded the train, Katara turned to her friend. “Do you think he’s guilty?”

Azula studied her nails. “I certainly think it’s possible. Do you?”

Katara shrugged. “He could be. But so could a lot of other people.”

“Like Hama.”

Katara fiddled nervously with her hair. “Hama’s different. She’s lost someone. A lot of someones, actually.”

“So has Jet. So have most of us, at this point. What makes her different?”

“She just...is,” replied Katara. “I can’t hate her. Even if she *did* kill them. She feels too...human.”

“Jet *did* call her the Puppetmaster, though. Interesting.”

“I’m not sure what to make of that,” replied Katara. “I’m not sure what to make of any of this.”

“By the way,” Zuko said to Azula as she re-entered his apartment, “the White Lotus is having a party tonight. We’re all invited.”

Azula sighed, throwing herself down onto the couch. Zuko was seated by the clue board, writing down causes of death over and over again in his notebook. It didn’t help. “ *Must* I go? Fancy parties can be so useless.”

Zuko nodded, and Azula rolled her eyes. “Look, I don’t want to go either, but we sort of have to if we don’t want the White Lotus to hate us. Plus, there could be important information there.”

“I suppose,” said Azula. She picked up her novel and began to read, and Zuko turned back to his notebook.

“Zuko?”

Zuko put the notebook down and turned to face the sofa. “Yeah?”

“What do you think makes a person good?”

Zuko didn’t really know how to answer that. “I don’t know. Trying to be good, I guess. That’s what I do.”

“Do you think you’re good?” Azula’s question was blunt, but it didn’t bother Zuko.

Zuko thought for a moment, then nodded. “I ran away from home to pursue a life in the city, chasing justice. I know I’m not perfect, but...yeah.” He didn’t really know how to finish. “What made you ask?”

“Just some people I met today,” mused Azula. “They were...well, I'm not sure what they were. They were the sort of people who could have been heroes, if given the chance.”

“But they weren’t?”

Azula shook her head. “It’s strange to see. People who could have been heroes.” She looked up at him. “I suppose that’s part of what makes you unique. One could argue that no one gave you the chance to be a hero, so you carved it for yourself. That’s rather admirable.”

Zuko blinked. He couldn’t remember Azula complimenting him...well, ever. “Thanks.”

She nodded and turned back to her book.

“Azula?”

She put the book down. “Yes?”

“Do you think you could have been a hero? In another life?”

Azula paused for a brief moment, then shook her head, laughing slightly. “Just because some people made themselves heroes doesn’t mean we all can.” Her expression turned serious. “But I do have positive traits. Like anyone.”

“What do you think you are, then?” asked Zuko. “Do you think you’re good?”

Azula didn’t answer. She waited for so long that Zuko was beginning to think she wouldn’t answer at all.

“I suppose I have to constantly work with the good and bad in me. Like most of us.”

“How’s that going for you?” Zuko hadn’t meant it as a joke, but surprisingly, Azula laughed, before her expression turned serious again.

“I suppose we’ll have to wait and see.”
