## Chapter 27: The Girl in the Train

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

In light of the group's most recent discovery, Katara finds herself on a ruthless hunt for justice. Meanwhile, Azula goes toe to toe with Hama in a bid for answers.

#### Chapter Notes

TWs at the end for this one!

This is an intense one, but writing it felt so satisfying. It was a chapter that was full of so many charged emotions that writing them all down felt...cathartic, in a way, even though I didn't have the same experiences that the characters have here.  
Anyway, happy reading!

### Text

Katara couldn’t see. She knew the world around her still existed, but all of it had faded into darkness, replaced with flashing images of her mother’s body, stained with red, cold on the wooden floor. Her dark hair, exactly like Katara’s, now a matted mess, soaked with blood. Her blue eyes, usually so full of warmth and love, staring at the ceiling, completely cold and empty.

Her mother hadn’t just died; she had been *murdered* . *Stolen* from Katara and Sokka and every other person who had loved her. She had been good, and kind, and beloved, and someone had ripped her life away from her, right in front of Katara’s eyes.

Now, Katara saw the image of a man standing over the body. Her mother hadn’t just been killed by someone, she’d been murdered by Yon Rha. Someone Katara knew. He had gone through the archives with her, talked to her at parties. He’d spoken to her as though everything was normal, when all along, he’d stolen the most important person in her life away from her.

*He was a cold-blooded fucking monster.*

“Katara?” Suki’s voice sounded far away and static-y, as though she was talking to her over a walkie-talkie that was running out of battery. “Katara, talk to me.”

But Katara was done talking. She’d talked to so many people about her mother’s murder, poured her heart out to them. All this time, she’d felt it as something from her past, something that was finished, finite. And it had brought her nothing. It hadn’t brought her mother justice.

But now, it wasn’t something that was over anymore. That monster was still out there, and talking about her feelings wasn’t going to avenge her mother, and it wasn’t going to save the rest of Ba Sing Se from the murderer hiding in their midst.

Her mother’s face was so large in her mind that Katara barely felt her own movements, barely felt herself swing off the tree branch and begin sprinting through the forest, so quickly that Suki and Mai couldn’t catch up to her. Their shouts cut through the trees, but Katara heard nothing but faraway echoes on the wind.

She had more important things to do.

Azula could hear her brother outside, talking hurriedly with Sokka on the phone. Whatever Katara was up to, it couldn’t be good, and even though she could barely hear him, it was easy to tell how worried Sokka was. Zuko sounded worried, too, and Azula couldn’t help but think that it was sort of nice that he was worried about his friend. Of course, worrying too much about others made you vulnerable in a million different ways, so Azula generally tried to avoid it, but she was starting to see the appeal. Especially when she watched Zuko, Katara, and Sokka. There was something special about true friends that made teams significantly stronger, something Azula wished she could understand.

She didn’t understand, not yet, but she was getting there.

But for the moment, friendship was not what she was focusing on. She turned and faced Hama, who was still sitting across the table from her, looking smug.

“I see you thought you’d have better luck with me alone, but you’re wrong. You won’t.”

Azula leaned back in her chair. She was trying to maintain a portion of the detective façade she often maintained on Assassin’s Lane. It had worked then. “And why is that?”

Hama laughed. “Because you’re not fighting for anything. You have a determination, a spark inside you. That much is clear. But you don’t have a *reason* .” She smirked. “Not like your friend who’s about to kill someone.” Seeing Azula raise an eyebrow, she laughed again. “The walls are thinner than you think.”

“I may be wrong about the walls,” said Azula, “but you’re wrong about me. My goal is absolute perfection in whatever situation I’m in. Whether that be being the perfect student, or the perfect daughter…” she narrowed her eyes “or the perfect detective.”

“But *why* ?” cried Hama. “I fight and kill to avenge my family, to maintain their legacy, to make sure that what happened to them never happens again. I do it because I *love* them. Why do you strive for perfection? So you can love yourself a little more? You’re pathetic.”

*Pathetic* . Azula used the word fairly often herself. She would rather be called pretty much anything else. She leaned forward. “I strive for perfection because it is, and always has been, the word that defines me. I have watched my brother find himself through his honor, my mother through her kindness, and my father through his determination. They all knew what they were. I will not lose what I am to the likes of you. Why I strive for perfection is not something you get to define or take away from me.” Her nails were digging into her palms, maybe even hard enough to cut, but Azula barely noticed.

Hama glared at her. “You think you’re so perfect. I’ll admit, even I was fooled by your façade at first. But you’re just another lost teenage girl who doesn’t know who she is, except she thinks she’s perfect because somebody once told her that a long time ago.”

Hama’s words cut deeper than Azula was willing to admit. “If I’m lost, then so are you.” Azula leaned forward. “Look at you. You’ve taken something as pure as your family’s love and turned it into violence, and a hatred so strong that you allowed others to manipulate you into killing for them. You don’t even kill for yourself anymore.” Her nails dug into the table. “ *Why* do you kill, Hama? Why so violent? Why so *strong* ?” Her voice parroted the old woman’s mocking tone from just moments ago. “Maybe I am lost, but I can admit it, and I can strive for perfection, even if it becomes impossible. What do you have left? You built yourself around this façade of a murderer because it was easier to turn to violence than to fully realize your grief over the loss of your family. You kill because of hatred, even if you tell yourself it stems from a desire to protect. What will you be without that façade?” In a moment of boldness, she leaned forward and grabbed Hama’s wrist. “It really is no use, Hama. You say you’re driven by love. If you are, you can help protect this city from more death. Isn’t that what you claimed you wanted?”

Maybe it was cruel, but there was something so satisfying about reading someone’s entire story in their eyes, and then laying it out on the table for them to see. It was like finding a hidden room in a library, filled with exactly the information you needed at any given moment.

Hama sighed. “I’m not going to reveal my employer to you.”

“Because?”

“Because I’m the last person in my family, and if I reveal who hired me, they’ll kill me. I refuse to be murdered like my family all were. I’m going to die naturally and peacefully, just as they should have died before their lives were ripped away from them.” Hama planted her fist down on the table. “End of discussion.”

“But you can tell me something else,” said Azula, narrowing her eyes. “I can see it on your face. Go on then, spit it out.”

Hama groaned. “You’re very obnoxious, do you know that?”

“I don’t beat around the bush. But yes, you’re not the first person in the world to tell me that. Now, stop stalling and get to the information.” She smirked. “Case in point.”

Hama smirked at her. “You may be a fool, but there are parts of you that truly do remind me of myself.” She straightened her back, as though motivating herself for something. “All right. I wasn’t the only assassin hired. My employer hired an entire network of them for these murders, to cover their tracks.”

“Did they reveal any motives for killing the people they killed?”

Hama shook her head. “Not to me. I don’t know everyone else they hired, only that others were hired.”

“Do you know *some* others?” asked Azula.

Hama laughed. “You always pick up on specific wording, don’t you?”  
“It’s a talent of mine. I wouldn’t be very talented if I couldn’t recognize the same talent in others, now, would I?”

“I suppose not,” said Hama, with a mix between a smile, a smirk, and a glare. “Fine. You’re right. I know one other person who was hired. He was an assassin, on Assassin’s Lane, like me. Maybe you know him.” She looked up at Azula. “His name’s Jet.”

Azula tried her best to stop her eyes from widening in surprise. “Is it, now?”

Hama smirked triumphantly. “You *do* know him. And you’re surprised.”

“It doesn’t matter whether or not I knew before,” snapped Azula, before regaining her composure. “I know now. And I won’t let him get away with any more murders.”

“Good luck finding him,” laughed Hama as Azula left the room. “And good luck beating him, for that matter.”

When Azula walked back out into the lobby, she found Zuko’s cell phone ringing on one of the tables. She didn’t know where he had gone, but if he had left the phone here, whatever undisclosed location he’d run off to must have been incredibly important.

She debated picking up the phone. On the one hand, it could have been something private. On the other, it could have been relevant to the case. Eventually overcome by simple curiosity, she looked over to see who was calling.

*Unknown Number.*

It would normally mean nothing, but in the context of solving a murder, the sight of it made Azula shiver for a split second. Nevertheless, she picked up the phone.

“Hello?”

“Hello,” responded a slippery, ice-cold voice that Azula recognized as Long Feng’s. “We’re looking for your brother. Is he there?”

Immediately, Azula felt her eyes darting around, making sure no one was lurking nearby. “Unfortunately, no. Can I take a message?” Perhaps she would get lucky, and this was only a pleasantry.

“Unfortunately, no,” Long Feng echoed. “We need information from your brother. The sort of information that can’t be written in a letter.”

“About what?” asked Azula. How much did the Dai Li know about the group’s little trip to Lake Laogai the other night.

“None of your business, Little Charmer.” Zhao’s oily voice seemed to ooze through the phone, and Azula nearly dropped it just at the sound of his words. If he was involved, there was no way that this wasn’t going to be pretty. She didn’t know what they wanted with Zuko, but it couldn’t be good.

She could do her best to protect him from whatever threat this was. *The perfect detective* . This was her chance to prove them all wrong. She wasn’t lost, and she wasn’t confused. She was simply perfect at everything she did.

If you ignored the fact that part of her was maybe, slightly, a tiny bit worried about Zuko.

“Well,” she began, “if you’re looking for information, you should be talking to me. I’m the knowledge-seeker here, I always have been. I’ve been investigating the White Lotus ever since I arrived in this city. You wouldn’t believe some of the secrets I have.&#96;&#96; She leaned closer to the phone so she could whisper. “I know everything anyone would *ever* want to know.” She laughed. “Of course, that won’t help *you* , now, will it? It’s not as though I’m willing to share after the way you treated us all.”

The other end of the line went dead, and Azula put the phone down, deleting the call from its history. She had solved this little problem before it became anything noteworthy. Zuko didn’t even need to know about it. The erasure of flaws was the ultimate perfection, after all.

Katara didn’t listen to Sokka as he frantically yelled at her over the phone to calm down.

“I won’t calm down!” she snapped as she ran through the dark city towards the White Lotus mansion.

She had been *happy* . Her *mother* had been happy, and *alive* , and *real* . And she had died for nothing. No one had benefited from her death, there had only ever been pain. For her, for Sokka, for her father.

The world had been robbed of someone *amazing* .

This monster deserved every drop of Katara’s rage. So no, she would *not* calm down. Instead, she shut her phone off and shoved it into her purse. Out of sight, out of mind.

She stormed up the driveway towards the White Lotus house. She still felt like she was walking in a tunnel, all sights and sounds other than the doorway dissolved into blackness and static. She raised the enormous door knocker, and slammed it against the door.

Instead of the door, she saw Yon Rha’s face. That *fucking* murderous face.

Five times. That was how many times her mother had been stabbed, the police had said. That was how she’d bled so much.

Katara slammed the knocker into Yon Rha’s head ten times.

*One* . For the stab wound in the bottom of her mother’s right foot, the same foot she’d used to kick soccer balls around with Katara when she was four and wanted to learn how to play because the boys at school had told her she couldn’t. Her mother couldn’t play to save her life, but that hadn’t stopped her. She and Katara had kicked the ball in the backyard for hours.

*Two* . For the slit in her left wrist, left by Yon Rha’s knife. Her mother had been right-handed, and the left wrist was where she had always worn the friendship bracelets Katara made for her. They had been hideous, tangles of string with hardly any shape to them at all. But Katara’s mother had worn every one, every single day, and hugged Katara every time she made another, telling them how beautiful they were, how much she loved them.

*Three* . For her right wrist. This was the hand she had used to write letters to Katara when she went to camp for the first time, when she was eight. Katara had absolutely loved it, but the first few nights, she had been so homesick that she’d cried herself to sleep. But her mother had written her multiple letters every day, sent postcard after postcard, so that it was as if she was right there with her the entire time, until she didn’t feel so homesick anymore.

*Four* . Right in the middle of her forehead. Her beautiful face. She had Sokka’s chin and sharp wit, but she had Katara’s smile, and the same passionate glare whenever somebody made her angry. Once, a man at the food market had come and started yelling at Katara and Sokka for getting in his way. Their mother had grabbed her own high heels, and held them in her hands like weapons, glaring at the customer.

“ *Those are my children* ,” she had cried. “T *hey are human beings, and they are innocent, and they* *are a part of this family. They will always have a place at this store, and in our world. You, on the* *other hand, had better get the hell out of here. Now.* ”

Kya had been gentle, but when she needed to be, she had always been fierce and protective, like an orca. Everyone in their family had always been compared to an ocean animal: Hakoda, their father, was a seal, playful and powerful, Sokka was a polar bear (by his own declaration), intelligent and brave, and Katara was a dolphin, friendly and warm.

Kya was an orca. Loving, but full of passion and power just the same.

*Five* . For the slash right through her heart. The source of all the endless love she had given to her friends, to her family. Katara had taken it for granted, but her mother had found the time *every* *single day* to tell her how much she loved her.

She should have gotten the chance to keep finding that time, but instead, she’d been sliced open five times by Yon Rha and his knife.

He had turned Katara into a helpless child, and Katara refused to be one any longer.

Katara raised the knocker again, ready to crack Yon Rha’s head open, but the door flew open before she got the chance. Zuko stood on the other side, looking worried.

She ignored his expression and stormed past him. Instead of a tunnel, her vision had now become shockingly sharp. She saw every small detail about the room she was standing in, so clearly that it was making her dizzy.

“Katara, wait,” said Zuko. “Think about this.”

“Please,” cried Sokka as he raced through the front doors, panting. “Just think about it for a *minute* .”

“And why should I do that? I spent *nine years* thinking about Mom’s death while this scum kept walking the Earth. Now I finally have the chance to do something about it, and you’re telling me to *think some more* ?” Katara laughed bitterly. “You don’t understand. Neither of you.”

“That’s not true,” Sokka said quietly, a pained expression on his face.

Katara glared at him. “It is. Nobody else saw Mom right before she died. Nobody else saw how her life was *ripped away* from her. It was *stolen* . But you just want to let him keep his?” In her anger, she slammed her fist down hard on the small table next to her. “It isn’t fair! It isn’t fair that she died and he gets to keep living!”

“You’re right,” said Zuko, stepping forward. “It isn’t fair. And Katara, you know me. I’m all about justice. But you don’t want murder on your conscience. It’ll only make you miserable.”

“I’m *already* miserable!” snapped Katara. “I had my mother taken away from me! And it’s all because of *him* ! I don’t *care* about my *conscience* , I’ll be miserable as long as that *demon* still walks the Earth.” She turned and began sprinting up the stairs. As she ran, she grabbed the dagger that she’d taken from Azula and pointed it ahead of her, slicing through the air. She could practically see Yon Rha right in front of her.

“Katara!” yelled Sokka as he and Zuko sprinted after her. “Don’t do this! You’re not a killer!”

Katara whirled around, glaring at her brother. “You’re right, Sokka. I wasn’t supposed to be a killer. Because Mom wasn’t supposed to be dead! She was supposed to be alive, and here to help us with this mystery! She was supposed to watch me go to college, she was supposed to talk to me about my first kiss, about parties, and give me dating advice. But instead I had to find her fucking corpse on the floor. And it’s all his fault.” She was shaking now. “And that fucking murderous monster isn’t supposed to be alive. He doesn’t get to live. Not after what he did.” She turned towards the wooden door, knife in hand. “I’m going to make sure he feels the pain of everything he did to her. All five fucking stab wounds. *Don’t* try to tell me he doesn’t deserve it.”

“He does deserve it,” replied Zuko. “But you don’t deserve all this pain.”

Katara drove the knife into the door, leaving a slash in the wood. Inside, she heard a scream. Good. “It's true. I don’t deserve the pain he caused. And neither did my mother.” She wasn’t shouting anymore. Her voice had dropped to practically a whisper.

She kicked the door and sent it flying open, charging in with her knife in hand, shaking with anger, tears streaming down her cheeks.

She froze, stopping dead in her tracks. Her eyes darted around frantically, but nothing changed.

Yon Rha lay at her feet. He hadn’t been stabbed five times, only once. There was a deep slash running through his heart. His eyes were open and glassy, staring at the ceiling. He was already dead.

At the sight of his eyes, Katara let out a cry of pure rage and dropped to the floor, sobbing as she began slicing at his corpse with her knife, giving it four more deep slashes, one for each slash given to her mother, and deepening the wound in his heart. Or, where his heart *would* be if he had one.

She didn’t stop slicing the same five places, over and over again until Sokka and Zuko grabbed her and pulled away.

Yon Rha’s face was still hovering in front of her eyes as she screamed and screamed and screamed.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

TW: Death, blood, murder, stabbing, flashbacks, corpses, knives.

I hope I managed to get the emotions right in that chapter. Katara's arc was something I really wanted the chance to write, but it touches on a lot of delicate points that are hard to get just right in writing. I hope I did her justice!  
If you have anything to say (anything at all!) please leave me a comment, or come talk to me on Tumblr at @theatergirl06.

## Chapter 28: Four and Twenty Blackbirds

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

The group tries to handle the chaos in the aftermath of Yon Rha's murder, but some of their past mistakes are slowly catching up to them, and tensions are running high.

#### Chapter Notes

TWs at the end!

Happy reading!

### Text

Katara wasn’t exactly unconscious, because she wasn’t asleep. She had just lost the ability to comprehend what was around her. She was awake, but she didn’t want to open her eyes. She kept feeling as though her mother and Yon Rha’s bodies were going to appear right in front of her, their blood covering her hands once more, staining the skin beneath her fingernails and never coming off.

“Katara?” Through her strange haze, Katara felt a hand on her shoulder. The hand was cool, and held her shoulder steadily. It wasn’t dangerous, and somewhere deep inside, Katara’s mind knew it. Still, her body tensed up. All she could see were Sokka and Zuko, pulling her off of Yon Rha’s body.

“Katara?” the voice spoke again. “I don’t know if you can hear me. Maybe you can’t, and this is all useless. But you can open your eyes. I don’t know what you think you’ll see, but *nothing* here can hurt you. You’re in my room, and I’m here, and I care about you more than anything. I’m not going to let anything happen to you.”

“It’s not about that,” replied Katara, still not opening her eyes. “Yon Rha didn’t even know me, and he turned out to be a monster. I’m me, and look what I did to his body. There are monsters all around us, and they won’t go away. How can we live in a world like that?”

There was a pause, and then Katara felt the hand on her shoulder slide down her arm and clasp her own. “Look,” said the voice, “I don’t think there’s anything we can do to make the monsters in this world go away. But we *can* protect each other.”

Slowly, Katara opened her eyes to find herself in Yue’s bedroom, sitting next to Yue on one of her bean bag chairs. Seeing the expression on Katara’s face, Yue wrapped her arms around her and pulled her in for a hug. “Katara,” she whispered, “you protected me from a future I never wanted. You saved me from getting arrested for a murder I didn’t commit. I can protect you, too, and so can all of your friends.”

“It’s not enough,” said Katara, gasping for air through the tears that were streaming down her cheeks. “I couldn’t protect my mother. Yon Rha still got to her.” Her voice broke. “He still got to me. He made me into someone like him.”

“No,” whispered Yue, pulling Katara even closer. “You could never be like Yon Rha. We’re all driven by emotions, and sometimes they lead us down unexpected paths. And sometimes, even though we try our best, that doesn’t mean we can protect everyone. But that doesn’t make us monsters. It just means that we have to try our best and love each other every day, and Katara, I don’t know anyone who does that better than you.”

Katara blinked. “You don’t think I’m like him? Not even after what I did?”

Yue shook her head, gently running a hand through Katara’s hair. “Not even close.” She leaned even closer. “Yon Rha couldn’t love anymore. He didn’t feel anything for the people around him, not even remorse for what he’d done. But you couldn’t be more different. You’re *brimming* with passion and life and love. Trust me,” she laughed, “I know.”

Katara sighed, and finally let herself fall fully into Yue’s arms. “It was just...so *scary* , seeing that side of myself. My whole life, I’d thought that a murderer was the absolute last thing I ever wanted to be. But now...I’m not so sure.”

Yue nodded. “I know what it’s like to question who you’re supposed to be. It’s hard, and no one else can do it for you. But I promise you that you’ll find your purpose, Katara, even if it isn’t right now. There’s no way someone so strong could turn into something as weak as Yon Rha. You’ll always be our protector. And I’ll be yours.”

Katara felt herself smiling in spite of her tears. “You promise?”  
Yue laughed softly and planted a gentle kiss on Katara’s forehead. “I promise.”

Azula found Ty Lee sitting on the front steps of the White Lotus mansion. She slid in next to her, still thinking over what Hama, Long Feng, and Zhao had said to her. “What are you doing out here?”

Ty Lee sighed. “I just...needed a minute to think. All of this death and chaos...it’s just *so* much. Sometimes it’s easier for me to just go off into my own little world, where none of it ever happened.”

“I wish I could do that,” replied Azula. She paused and looked over at the other girl. “Would you prefer it if I left? Am I stopping you from reaching your goal?”

“No,” laughed Ty Lee. To Azula’s shock, she leaned over and rested her head on her shoulder. Azula felt her face increase in temperature by a factor of ten. She wanted to jerk away from her, run away, but she couldn’t.

“Want to come into my little world with me?” whispered Ty Lee. It was all Azula could do not to run away right then and there, for fear that her entire chest might explode. “It could be fun.” She was practically falling asleep on her shoulder, Azula realized.

“I think you’re just very tired,” she replied, making sure to keep her tone as cold and clipped as she possibly could, even though it pained her. “You don’t want me in your happy little world.” She made the last sentence sound like a joke, even though she didn’t mean it that way.

Ty Lee widened her eyes, and sat up. “What do you mean?”

This question put Azula in a tricky position. Admitting the truth would mean bringing up the feelings she had finally managed to convince herself that Ty Lee didn’t have. It was easy to brush off the pink-clad girl as just an overenthusiastic friend. It was easier for them both. Every day, Azula’s guilt over her secret came closer and closer to consuming her, and every day, she threw herself into the role of the perfect detective a little harder. She could feel the small parts of her that could be considered human slowly being stripped away. She wouldn’t have a whole heart to give Ty Lee soon, and it hurt Azula too much to give half a heart, and even more so, she didn’t want to hurt Ty Lee’s vibrant, open, enormous heart.

She was just a friend with an exuberant personality. After all, nobody had ever had...those sorts of feelings for Azula before. Why would they?

So, instead of telling the truth, she turned away from Ty Lee. “Nothing. It was a joke.” She couldn’t even look the other girl in the eye.

Ty Lee sighed. “Azula, I want to be your friend. Really, I do. And I know you’ve had some hard stuff happen to you, so I can be forgiving. But you can be so closed-off sometimes. I’m not sure how much more of this I can take.”

Not even friends, then. Perhaps it was better this way, in the end. “I understand.” She couldn’t stop herself. “But...it’s really late. Perhaps we could have a more in-depth conversation about this in the morning?”

Ty Lee nodded, smiling. “That seems fair.”

They were about to head back inside when they heard loud, almost stomping footsteps coming up the driveway. Azula stopped in her tracks, her hand instinctively leaping to the dagger handle in her pocket.

She whirled around, still vaguely aware of Ty Lee’s presence next to her, but it was only Jet from Assassin’s Lane. He was holding a sign that said *Fuck the White Lotus* in giant red letters.

Azula rolled her eyes. “Ugh, *you*,” she muttered. “What do you want?” She leaned forward, dagger still in hand. “And we know you were hired by Hama’s employer to commit murders, so don’t bother lying to us.”  
“Or…”

“Or *face the consequences* ,” Azula hissed. “It’s been a long night, Jet. There was a murder at this mansion, which, by the way, has just gained a new, *unusually convenient* suspect, and everyone is panicking, rightfully so because their lives are in danger. All of this to say,” she taunted, dragging her knife over one of her sleeves, “I have very little patience tonight.”

“I have a better idea,” said Jet, smirking, and in a flash, he had grabbed Ty Lee by the braid, and was yanking on her hair. “How about I show this White Lotus scum what she *really* is? The scum that murdered my family!” He pulled harder. “Think you’ll still be pretty and perfect without that hair of yours?” he screamed at Ty Lee.

“Stop it!” cried Ty Lee. “I never did anything to you! I didn’t help the White Lotus kill your family! I wasn’t even six years old when the White Lotus killed your family. I’m sorry for what they did, but I never did anything to hurt you! I would never!”

Jet paused for a moment, then released Ty Lee, who gasped in relief as she fell to the ground. “Easy prey,” he laughed as he disappeared into the shadows. A police siren echoed somewhere off in the distance.

Against her better judgement, Azula raced over towards Ty Lee instead of following Jet. “Are you badly hurt?” She kept her tone as cold as she could, to hide the worry inside of her that was threatening to boil over.

Ty Lee nodded. “I’m just tired, Azula,” she replied, her voice weary. “Just...leave me alone for now. Please.”

Azula set off in the direction of Zuko’s apartment, her eyes lingering on the acrobat for far longer than she’d wanted, as Ty Lee disappeared back into the lights of the mansion.

“Everyone, calm down!” cried Zuko, as the circle of White Lotus members broke into a shouting match yet again. For four old men, the remaining core members of the White Lotus were surprisingly *loud* . “Shouting at each other isn’t going to keep us safe! Finding the person who did this is!”

Sokka, who was standing next to him, nodded. “We need to think logically!” he shouted. Ironically, the fact that he was shouting made him seem *less* logical. “Yelling at each other won’t catch the murder.”

“Oh, we’ll never catch the murderer,” grumbled Jeong Jeong, who was sitting next to Sokka. “They’re too tricky and clever, like a snake, and they want us to be obliterated. We can’t combat someone who uses violence so freely and without remorse, not without stooping to their level.”

“What’s so bad about stooping to their level?” snapped Piandao. It said something about the gravity of their situation that Piandao and Jeong Jeong, who were two of the closest friends in the group, were so suddenly at each other’s throats. “There are only four of us core members left! If we want to protect ourselves, we need to do whatever it takes to make that happen!” He rolled his eyes. “I swear, nobody appreciates the art of combat anymore.”

“It’s not an art!” cried Jeong Jeong. “It’s a bloody disaster! Just look at the recent murder victims if you want proof of that!”

“That’s not what I meant, and you know it!” replied Piandao. “Unless, of course, you’re accusing *me* of the murders!”

“Jeong Jeong,” interjected Iroh. “Surely you're not accusing one of our own brethren of these murders. This organization is built on trust, and if we cannot have that, we have no hope of…”

“What trust?” snapped Jeong Jeong. “Someone is picking us off like flies, and I, for one, would like to know who it is! Why couldn’t it be one of us? A Dai Li spy in our midst, all along.” He spun around, pointing his finger at Bumi. “You’ve been awfully quiet!”

“You’re accusing *me* now?” cackled Bumi. “That’s funny! I’ve been in this organization for longer than you’ve been alive, probably, and people call *me* crazy!”

“That math isn’t actually right,” hissed Sokka, but no one listened to him.

“At least I’m trying to get somewhere!” cried Jeong Jeong. “I’m looking at the people around me for clues! What are the rest of you doing? You’re all content to be sitting ducks, possibly because one of you was responsible in the first place!”

“Jeong Jeong!” cried Zuko. “You’re not helping anything by accusing everyone! You’re only making things around here worse, for the moment.”

“Yeah,” said Sokka. “You can’t accuse people like this with no evidence. It’ll only increase tension and suspicion when we need to work *together* to figure this out.”

There was a moment of silence.

“I am *not* a sitting duck!” yelled Piandao suddenly. “I’ve been proposing efficient solutions to this murder problem for the last half hour! It’s *you* who won’t listen to me!”

“It *is* awfully suspicious that you keep blaming everyone here but yourself,” mused Bumi.

“What?!” screamed Jeong Jeong. “I don’t believe this! This is treason against the White Lotus.”

“If anyone’s a traitor, it’s you,” Iroh said calmly, sipping a cup of tea.

“That’s not true, either,” chimed in Sokka, even though no one other than Zuko was listening to him. “Actually, mathematically, the chances that any one of you is betraying the rest are about…”

“We need to do something!” snapped Piandao. “Something besides indulging in this idiocy of accusing one another! If we want to survive this, we must present a united front!”

“Or we could do nothing!” pointed out Bumi. “Perhaps this is a good moment to wait for the storm to pass, and then we can truly bring about some changes to our city, just like we’ve all always dreamed.”

“See?” snapped Jeong Jeong. “This is what I mean! You all want to do nothing while some killer is out there, trying to wipe us out!”

“Then propose a solution,” said Piandao coolly. “Since you won’t listen to any of mine.”

“Find the killer in this room,” spat Jeong Jeong.

“There is no killer in this room!”

“That’s what they all want us to think!”

“Enough,” said Iroh in a low, gravelly voice. The entire room, including Zuko and Sokka, turned to face him. “There may or may not be a killer in this room. I myself am certain that there is not. But the small possibility of it is not the important thing. The important thing is that someone is trying to kill us, and in dangerous situations like this, the only thing we can do is try our best to protect one another.” He looked around the room at the three men and two teenagers. “We may be unable to discern who is committing these murders, but if we all give a little bit of energy to protect one another, we will be able to present a united front that this murderer will be unable to break.”

The room was silent for a moment. Then, Piandao stood up. “If that’s the case, then this united front needs to go and confront a killer.”

“But, uh…” Sokka interjected “you don’t actually know who the killer is. I thought that was, like, the entire point of this conversation.”

“But we know where they’ll be,” snapped Jeong Jeong. The other three White Lotus members nodded.

“Really?” said Sokka. “Because, last I checked, we didn’t really know that, either.”

“But we always have,” hissed Piandao, with rare venom in his voice. “We knew from the very beginning. And as more and more of us are being picked off, it’s only becoming more clear.” “The Dai Li,” finished Jeong Jeong.

“Wait a sec,” said Sokka. “You guys can’t just go storming after the Dai Li. You have no proof that they did this to you.”

“Besides,” added Zuko, “there are only four of you. We confronted them with *six* people, and we barely made it out alive. You won’t stand a chance.”

“Don’t underestimate us,” chuckled Iroh, who also didn’t seem too keen on the group’s idea. “My nephew and his friend are right, Piandao. We are being too rash. We need to think this through.”

“We’ve thought it through plenty,” said Bumi. “I may be a fan of waiting for the right moment, but they haven’t bothered us once since the murders started. Don’t you think that’s a little suspicious?” He turned to Zuko. “Detective?”

The whole White Lotus was suddenly staring at him.

Zuko sighed. He had a feeling that nothing he said would ever be enough. “I can’t give you any more evidence than you already have. But I can tell you this: the White Lotus is valuable to all of you. If you still want to keep it safe, keep yourselves safe. The Dai Li is playing a dangerous game, and someone will defeat them soon. But it doesn’t have to be you.”

“Yes, it does,” snapped Piandao. “They murdered us. We cannot let that stand.”

“But you have no proof of that!” cried Sokka. “You’re jumping to conclusions based on your past grudges!”

Nobody listened to him.

Zuko turned to Sokka. “If the White Lotus is gearing up to attack, the Dai Li will know about it within an hour. We *need* to stop this before the Dai Li does something awful.”

It was late at night as Toph Beifong crept down the hallway of the Dai Li headquarters. She didn’t normally leave her room so late at night, but the hushed voices down the hall had caught her attention. The voices gave off the impression of two people sharing secrets that nobody else could hear. So, of course, Toph intended to listen to them.

“This is the information,” hissed a slippery, deep voice that Toph recognized as Long Feng’s. She pressed her ear closer to the wall. “The White Lotus suspects us for the murders of their members, and they’re planning some sort of attack. We must be ready.”

“But, Sir,” replied an oily-sounding voice that Toph had never heard before, “we *were* involved with those murders. In a way.”

Toph nearly jumped at the sound of a body smashing another body into the wall. “Don’t you ever say that again,” snapped Long Feng. “Unless you want your head to roll on the floor.”

“Please,” oozed the voice of the other man. “Just *try* to find another Master of Pain as good as me.”

“After tonight, I doubt I’ll have to,” whispered Long Feng. “There’s a reason I’ve brought you here. We cannot fight the White Lotus. Even as a small group, they are too powerful. But if we gained some sort of dark secret, something we could use against them, we would still be able to defeat them.”

“Aaah,” replied the oozing voice. “But where would we find such a secret?”

“By any means necessary,” replied Long Feng in a slow, menacing voice, “including, perhaps, from an unwilling participant.” There was a rustling sound. “My dear Master of Pain, you wouldn’t happen to know anyone who possesses the knowledge we seek, would you? In all of your recent...travels around town, might you have come across someone?”

The oily voice laughed, and Toph felt a shiver shoot down her spine. “You heard her, yourself, Long Feng. Today, even.” He laughed even more loudly, with more confidence. “Our little charmer was *oh so eager* to tell us how much she knew.”

“Then it’s settled,” replied Long Feng. “We get the information we need.”

Toph heard something that sounded like a blade being unsheathed. “Through any means necessary.”

Azula was in the early stages of sleep, where she was unconscious of the world around her, yet still almost capable of thought. Zuko, her mother, Ty Lee, and Hama’s faces all swirled through her dark mind in an anxiety-inducing whirlpool.

Fortunately, the darkness of true sleep was creeping up on her, and Azula could feel the imagery slowly drifting out of her mind.

Something pinched her left arm, hard. Azula tried to open her eyes to see what it was, but found that her eyelids were significantly heavier than usual. She managed to get her eyes half-open, open enough so that she could see the two figures standing over her.

She tried to move, but her limbs felt like lead. She could feel the inky blackness creeping back in, this time an unnatural one, and her eyes drooping shut yet again. She opened her mouth, but no sound came out. She felt unfamiliar hands and arms wrap around her, lifting her out of her bed as the inky blackness surrounded her completely.

“Oh, Little Charmer,” she heard before she dropped completely into darkness. “I suppose you should learn to be more alert while you sleep.”

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

## Chapter 29: The Case of the Missing Lady

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

A frantic search begins, but time is running out.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Mentions of abduction, high anxiety.

Happy reading!

### Text

After nearly an hour of trying to talk the White Lotus out of attacking the Dai Li, Sokka and Zuko returned to Zuko’s apartment, both completely exhausted.

“Phew!” sighed Sokka, flopping down on the sofa. “Think we convinced them not to attack?”

“I don’t know,” replied Zuko. “I don’t have a good feeling about any of this. But I think we might have gotten them to hold off, at least for tonight.”

“Good thing, too,” muttered Sokka, already drifting off to sleep. “I’m exhausted.”

“Me too,” sighed Zuko as he headed towards his bedroom at the other end of the apartment. “You sure you’ll be okay on the sofa? I can call you a cab home or something.”

Sokka said nothing, but gave him a halfhearted thumbs-up instead. Zuko had just hung up his coat and hat when Sokka came walking into the office.

“I thought you were going to sleep.”

“I was,” said Sokka, sinking into Zuko’s chair, “but your apartment’s *so* quiet. Can you put on some music or something?” He was clearly still half-asleep, and Zuko could already see his eyes drooping shut.

“I wish,” said Zuko, rolling his eyes, “but my sister would probably kill me if I did. She almost always sleeps like she’s half awake. If I move half an inch, she’ll leap out of bed with a knife.”

“Can you at least *ask* her?” murmured Sokka. He got a ridiculously dopey grin on his face when he was tired like this, and Zuko found himself smiling softly at it in spite of himself.

Zuko sighed. “Okay, I’ll ask her. But if I don’t come back, you know what happened to me.”

Sokka laughed softly, his laugh turning to a snore as Zuko left the room. Crossing the apartment, he knocked softly on his sister’s door. “Azula, you’re going to hate me for this, but Sokka said he wanted music, and I was wondering if we could put some on.”

There was no answer.

Zuko frowned. Unless she was buried deep in some sort of project, it was unlike his sister not to answer her door, or at least shout some sort of response.

“Azula? You could at least yell at me to go away if you didn’t want music. You don’t have to give me the silent treatment just for this.”

Again, there was no answer.

Zuko sighed. His sister could be so stubborn sometimes, though he supposed he wasn’t one to judge on that particular front. “Azula, if you don’t answer me right now, I’m coming in so that you can answer me then.”

There was nothing but silence.

Zuko sighed as he pushed the door open. He had to push a little harder than usual because the door had stuck, almost as though someone had slammed it shut *really* hard. Strange.

“Azula, the least you could do was say ‘go away’ if…” he stopped short. Azula’s bedroom was completely empty. Not only that, but her bed was a complete mess, the sheets pulled into a bunch at the end. For someone else, this would be normal, but Azula’s bed was absolutely never anything but perfectly made. Right now, the sheets looked as though they had been flung around.

This didn’t feel quite right, and there was something about it that made every bone in Zuko’s body uneasy. Quickly, he darted through the rest of the apartment, looking even in the most unlikely nooks and crannies, hoping that he’d missed something obvious. It *was* after midnight, after all.

Sokka stumbled out of Zuko’s office, yawning and bleary-eyed. “What’s going on?”

Zuko turned to him, frowning. He wasn’t worried yet, but the edges of worry and suspicion were starting to creep into his mind. “Have you seen my sister? I thought I saw her leave the White Lotus mansion, but she’s not here.”

“That’s weird,” said Sokka. “Have you called anyone at the White Lotus to see if she’s still there?”

“No,” said Zuko, already pulling out his phone, “but that’s a really good idea.”

The phone only rang once before it was picked up. “Hello?”

“Hi, Ty Lee,” replied Zuko. “Listen, have you seen my sister? We thought she’d come home, but she isn’t here.”

“That’s weird,” said Ty Lee. “I saw her leaving the mansion. I was literally in the doorway. Unless she snuck back in, she definitely isn’t here.”

“Any idea where she was going?”

“Back to your apartment, I think. I saw her holding a ticket for the Middle Ring.”

Zuko sighed. “Thanks, Ty Lee. Go get some sleep.”

“I hope you find her,” said Ty Lee, and Zuko could hear her worry even through the phone. “She...she means a lot to me. And you, obviously.”

“I know,” replied Zuko, realizing that Ty Lee’s words were true, in a strange sort of way. “I’ll let you know what happens.”

“I hope she’s safe,” said Ty Lee before hanging up the phone.

“Me too,” muttered Zuko, even though Ty Lee wasn’t even there to hear him anymore. The worry from the edge of his brain was starting to fill all of his thoughts. No matter how he looked at this, he couldn’t shake the feeling that something was *profoundly* wrong.

Azula was the powerful one. The prodigy. She wasn’t supposed to disappear without a trace.

Just as he was wondering what to do next, his cell phone rang. Before he even knew he was moving, he had picked it up. “Hello?”

“Zuko!” cried the voice on the other end, and Zuko quickly identified it as belonging to Toph. “Listen, I overheard something important!”

“Look, Toph, how important is this?” groaned Zuko. “I’m sort of in the middle of something big.”

“This is *really big* !” snapped Toph. “I overheard Long Feng talking to someone called the Master of Pain”

Zuko froze. Sokka stared at him, wide-eyed, and mouthed *what?* “Toph,” Zuko said into the phone, “what were they saying?”

“Something about the White Lotus,” replied Toph. “They said that the White Lotus suspected them of the murders, and that they actually *were* involved, but that they couldn’t risk the White Lotus attacking them, so they needed to get some sort of White Lotus secret in order to stop them.”

The bad feeling in Zuko’s mind was slowly taking over everything, and the more information he found out, the worse it got. “Anything else? Where did they say they were getting this secret?”

“From an ‘unwilling participant,’” said Toph. “I don’t know what they meant, but they said it was someone who was ‘eager to share what they knew.’ They called her a...little charmer? I thought it sounded weird.”

The bad feeling had morphed into concrete suspicion (and worry, if Zuko was *really* being honest with himself.)

It couldn’t be a coincidence that his sister, who spent half her time walking around Ba Sing Se as if she knew everything, had disappeared from her bedroom on the same night that Long Feng and the Master of Pain were searching for an unwilling ‘little charmer’ who was eager to share what she knew.

Zuko slammed his phone on the table and turned to Sokka. The emotions rising up inside of him were hard to discern, but he refused to leave Azula alone in the hands of these people, if that was really where she was. *That* he was sure of.

“Zuko?” Sokka stepped forward tentatively. “What’s going on?”

“I hope you’re not too tired,” replied Zuko, already headed for the door. “We’re going back to Lake Laogai.”

“Wait a second,” said Sokka as they rushed through the dark forest. “You’re saying that you think these creeps have Azula? Isn’t that kind of a far-fetched theory?”

“I know it,” replied Zuko. His face was pale, and his eyes were almost dilated with fear and determination. “There are too many things that don’t add up. It’s the only explanation.”

“I’m sure it isn’t,” said Sokka, grabbing Zuko’s shoulder. “Look, Zuko, I think you might be jumping to conclusions. I know you’re worried about Azula, but there’s got to be an easier explanation for this.”

“You don’t know her like I do,” replied Zuko. His eyes almost looked like they were reflecting the image of a blazing forest fire. “Azula is always organized and punctual, and...and perfect. She’s consistent, and if she’s on your side, she’s reliable. If she disappears without a message, something is *wrong* .”

“But it doesn’t have to be this,” said Sokka as Zuko began dragging him down the trail. He recognized the ever-present determined stare on Zuko’s face, but this time, it was accompanied by a layer of pure fear. Zuko was a risk-taker, and Sokka knew that that level of fear only appeared on his face when someone he cared about was in real danger. “You don’t know that.”

“Yes I do,” said Zuko. “I know it sounds silly, but I know my sister. Call it a feeling, or a detective’s intuition, or something. I don’t care. Please, just listen to me.”  
“Zuko, I want to believe you, but I don’t want to jump to conclusions while Azula could be in actual trouble.”  
Zuko sighed, whirling around to look Sokka in the eyes. “Look, Sokka. Logic can’t explain this. It isn’t logical. Just like it isn’t logical that I’m even worried about Azula at all after everything she did to me while we were kids. But she broke that logic when she came here and started helping us. I thought I would never be able to look her in the eye again, and now…” he turned and looked at Sokka. “I couldn’t live with myself if she died while she was trying to help me.”

“And this lead?”

“I just know it. Can you trust me on this one? Just once? I know it sounds dumb.”

Sokka looked away, and Zuko sighed, reaching through the dark and grabbing his hands. “She’s *my* sister.”

Sokka sighed as they reached the entrance to Lake Laogai. “Fine. But...try not to get hurt. Please.”

Zuko gave him a soft smile. “Hopefully, no one has to get hurt tonight.”

He turned and kicked the door open, and the two of them raced down the stairs into the green, glowing underground fortress. It didn’t take Sokka long to notice that something was different about it.

The fortress was even quieter than Zuko’s apartment had been. There were no footsteps of guards, no clanking of prison cells opening and slamming shut, no sounds of explosions from the laboratory section. Just the water dripping from the recent rain and the eerie, green glow.

“If you’re looking for the rest of them, they’re gone,” said a familiar voice from the darkness.

Zuko whirled around to find Joo Dee standing behind them. Rage raced through his body like a lightning bolt, and in a flash, he had her pinned against the wall. She was the reason Mai had been captured and almost tortured. She had pretended to help him and then betrayed him, and there were few things in life that Zuko hated more than that.

“ *Where* is my sister?”

“I don’t know!” cried Joo Dee, tears streaming out of her eyes. “I don’t know what they want with your sister! I don’t know anything!”

“We both know that’s a lie,” snapped Zuko. “You led us down here and trapped us. You know *way* more than you’re letting on.”

“But I *don’t* !” cried Joo Dee. She sighed. “It’s true that I have known about the Dai Li’s sinister practices for longer than I’d like to admit, but I promise you, I was never in agreement with any of it!”

“That’s what you said last time!” Sokka said indignantly. “You’re going to need to do better than *that* if you want us to believe you.”

“I don’t know how to convince you,” said Joo Dee, still sobbing. “At first, I believed in what the Dai Li was doing. I thought that enforcing the law and bringing order to the city would help everyone here, and I was happy to help. I was only the secretary at the police station, and I never thought that I would become important to the organization in any way, but...they started to take notice of me. I never officially changed jobs, but I slowly became the Dai Li secretary. It was perfect; I was able to do my job well and support a cause I believed in. But then, I began filling out more...disturbing documents. Records of illegal prisoners, lab reports written by the Mechanist of his experiments. I began to discover the truth of what they were doing, and I wasn’t going to stand for it. So I quit my job and bought a bus ticket to go and tell some sort of government outside Ba Sing Se’s walls.”

Zuko sensed a *but* coming. “What happened?”

Joo Dee was now crying so hard that she could barely speak. “They...they found my sisters. My little sisters, Jin and Song. I don’t know how they found them, or even knew that they existed, but they found them. The Master of Pain took them, him and the Mechanist. Long Feng threatens them every single day, and all I can do is watch if I want them to live.” Joo Dee let out a sigh. “Watch...and stay in line. Do my job.” She looked up at Zuko. “Trick people like you.”

“What do you want from me?” snapped Zuko. “If you’re trying to cook up some pity story to manipulate me, it won’t work.”

“Zuko,” whispered Sokka from his right, “I think she’s telling the truth.”

“I am!” cried Joo Dee. “Please, just listen to me. If you defeat the Dai Li, I can finally have my sisters back. I want to help the people I care about, just like you!”

Zuko blinked. Was that his relationship to Azula now? Until now, he hadn’t really thought to put it into words. She had become a sort of staple in his mystery-solving life, and he wasn’t used to the fierce protectiveness he felt at the thought of her being in danger because of him. But did that mean he *cared* ? After everything that had happened?

He shoved the question into the back of his mind and turned back to Joo Dee. “What happened here?”

“I...I’m not sure,” said Joo Dee. “Earlier today, I heard Long Feng talking about the White Lotus suspecting us...I mean, them, and coming after us...I mean, them. He said they would come for us here, that they needed to move quickly.”

“Move where?” asked Zuko. Joo Dee trembled as she looked away. He decided to play her cards right back at her, hoping her story was true. “Joo Dee, I’m trying to save my sister. You can understand that, can’t you?”

Joo Dee’s lower lip trembled for a moment, but she nodded, pulling an old-looking, rolled-up piece of parchment from her pocket. “The Dai Li has one more place they might have taken her. You’ll find this place behind a waterfall to the west of the city. Long ago, it used to form part of a prison, but parts of the tunnels have collapsed. The Dai Li rarely uses this place anymore, but if they need a last resort, that’s where they’ll be.”

“And do you know exactly where this is?” asked Zuko, snatching the map out of her hands and studying it. It only showed the inside of the fortress.

Joo Dee sighed. “No,” she said. “This is where they alway kept my sisters. I knew that it existed for filing purposes, but they never told me where it was.”

Zuko reached absentmindedly into his pocket, then froze as his hand brushed against an object that Azula had given him. “I might just be able to fix that,” he said, already racing up the stairs again. “Joo Dee, get in touch with some sort of government from outside the city. Get as many people as you can. We’re going to need to storm this place.”

“Do you think we can trust her?” gasped Sokka, as they sprinted up the stairs and back into the forest.

“We don’t have a choice,” replied Zuko, panting. “There isn’t enough time.”

He was correct. There wasn't enough time. Azula could already be severely injured, or even worse. It was all Zuko could do not to race into the western woods right then and there, but he stopped himself. Going into the woods now wouldn’t do any good if he couldn’t track down his sister.

Luckily, he knew how to find her, and thirty minutes or so later, Zuko slammed the silver coin that Azula had given him a few days ago down on Xu the fork man’s counter in Assassin’s Lane. “I need to find the woman this summons. Now.”

“Ah, I remember you!” chuckled Xu. “A real feisty one! What brings you out this late at night?”

“My sister,” said Zuko, glaring at Xu and enunciating every syllable. “I need to find her.”

“I see,” said Xu, still chuckling, but with an extra flicker of seriousness in his voice. “Let me go into the back,” he replied, grabbing the silver coin off the counter and disappearing.

Sokka turned to face Zuko. The gentleness of his hand on his shoulder nearly made Zuko jump. Every muscle in Zuko’s body had tensed up, and was pulsing with fear and adrenaline. “Are you okay?”

Zuko sighed, shaking his head. “Whatever they do to her is going to be my fault.”

“ *No* .” Sokka’s voice was firm. “Azula knew what she was doing when she came here. She wanted to get to know you better, Zuko. Maybe she never said it, but she was trying to get closer to you. It took you a while, but...you let her in. I think you gave her something she hasn’t had in a really long time. And I think that’s more important to her than her complete safety. She’d rather have this. Whatever they do to her won’t matter. She’ll already have the most important thing you could have given her.”

“Which is?”

Sokka laughed, slightly sadly. “You care about her, silly.”

There was that word again. Maybe it was true after all.

Xu emerged from the back, followed by a tall woman with dark hair, tattoos on both shoulders, and the most enormous dog that Zuko had ever seen in all his nineteen years.

“So,” said the woman, “you’re looking for the golden-eyed girl?”

Zuko nodded. “How did you know?”

The woman laughed. “You look like her. Besides, I don’t give these out every day. It was pretty obvious that this girl would need it.”

“What do you mean?” asked Zuko, as he and Sokka climbed on top of the enormous dog.

“The name’s June,” said the woman as they began to run. “And that girl was like a ticking time bomb. She was using façades to make her way through life. The second somebody sees through those façades and stops believing in your power, you’re toast.”

“Really?” said Sokka. “She always seemed kinda...indestructible to me.”

June laughed. “No one is indestructible, kid, no matter how indestructible they seem. We can put on confident façades and push ourselves to our limits and pretend we’re perfect all we want, but at the end of the day, we’re all just humans, trying to make up for the fact that we hate ourselves so much. Someone is bound to tear us down soon enough.” She paused, and the dog sniffed at a fork in the path before dashing off to the right. They were entering the woods now.

Sokka glanced at his phone. “This is the county government,” he whispered to Zuko. “Joo Dee got them, and they’re on their way.”

Zuko nodded, then turned and glanced at the dark path ahead of them. He was full of churning worry, anger, confusion, and maybe even something like love, but he couldn’t make sense of any of them right then.

*We can put on confident façades and push ourselves to our limits and pretend we’re perfect all we* *want, but at the end of the day, we’re all just humans, trying to make up for the fact that we hate* *ourselves so much. Someone is bound to tear us down soon enough.*

Somehow, they had managed to get everything and everyone they needed to rescue Azula. The only question was, would they get there quickly enough?
