## Chapter 30: Dead Man's Mirror

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

It's dark, and she's in pain. That's all she really knows at first.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Physical violence, restraint, blood, knives, cutting, syringes, drugs, hallucinations.

If you have any serious triggers on the above list, I advise skipping this chapter. This is a bit of an intense one.  
For those of you who are okay with the above trigger warnings, happy reading!

(If I forgot any triggers, please let me know!)

### Text

Even before she opened her eyes, Azula could feel the ache in her left arm. The entire upper half of it felt heavy and sore, as though someone had pumped it full of liquid pain.

The next thing she noticed was the feeling of *restraint* , a feeling she knew from her days as a very young child, before she’d grown up enough to learn how to avoid it. She recognized the feeling of rough ropes on her wrists and ankles, the bent position that meant your body had been draped around a chair. The ropes were tight, too tight to try and break them.

A cold draft ripped through her body, and, still drifting in and out of slumber, Azula shivered. She felt more exposed to the cold than she remembered, though in her hazy, half-asleep state, she couldn’t quite put her finger on why.

Slowly, still groaning from the pain in her arm, she opened her eyes. It took her vision a moment to adjust to the pitch-black darkness, but once she did, she saw the faces of Long Feng and Zhao looming over her.

An enormous spike of fear and adrenaline instantly coursed through her body, but Azula did her best to ignore her twice-as-fast-as-normal heartbeat and put on a confident façade. Right now, that was her best chance at survival.

Slowly and carefully, she allowed her mouth to curl into a confident smirk, despite the fact that her hands were trembling behind her back.

“Well, it seems I am an honored guest. To what do I owe this pleasure?”

Long Feng smirked, and Azula had to admit that, in this moment, his smirk terrified her. “I believe you are already acquainted with the Master of Pain?”

“Please,” said Azula, forcing a laugh. “We go way back.”

“Then you surely know what is in store for you tonight if you refuse to cooperate.”

So they needed something from her, and they needed it badly enough to resort to torture. She could use that. Right now, she was going to use any scrap of an idea that came to her. It was all she could do. She hated feeling so helpless, possibly more than any other feeling on Earth, but what choice did she have?

“I understand perfectly.” She kept her tone even, praying that it wouldn’t reflect her shaking body or rapidly beating heart.

“Wonderful,” replied Long Feng, and Azula noted how *slithery* his voice still sounded. It sent chills running down her spine. “Now, we’re searching for information on the White Lotus. No doubt you already know that they’re planning to attack us tonight.”

“Actually,” Azula said as casually as she could. “I wasn’t aware of that.” If she could make it seem as though she knew nothing at all, maybe she could actually make it out of this alive, somehow. It seemed like her best chance, at least for the moment. *Just try out everything that comes to mind* *until you find something that can save you.*

“You lie,” growled Zhao, stepping forward. Azula barely had time to blink before his fist collided hard with the left side of her face, and barely time to gasp for air before it collided again with the right. It took every ounce of her energy not to wince, but Azula knew that she couldn’t afford to. This was only the beginning of what the Master of Pain was capable of, and they both knew it.

“I don’t, actually,” said Azula, using the same aloof tone she’d been attempting to maintain. “You know, that’s not the first time I’ve been told that. My brother accused me of lying a lot when we were younger, but the funny thing was, he only ever accused me when I told him truths he didn’t want to hear. Never when I was actually lying.” If she could make it seem as though she could read their minds, perhaps they would be threatened by her. So she looked up and stared Zhao right in the eyes. “Perhaps that’s something you should think about.”

“Enough,” said Long Feng before Zhao could do or say anything else. “Listen, Azula. This does not have to be drawn-out or painful. We simply want to know the secret of the White Lotus.”

Azula’s mind flashed briefly to the Box of Lost Confessions, as she and Katara had dubbed it. Could this be what the Dai Li meant? Should she tell them? Since their secrets were already out in the open and protected by the detectives, it seemed like a rather small price to pay in exchange for her life.

“You mean the old box with everyone’s letters about how sorry they are for something that happened over a decade ago?”

Zhao laughed. “We know all about that miserable box. It means nothing to us.”

“Really?” asked Azula, trying to keep her voice monotonous and unassuming. “How might you have come to know about that?”

“Insolent girl!” cried Zhao. He lunged forward in a flash, gripping Azula’s arm and twisting it so that Azula could feel her bones nearly breaking. Tears sprung to the corners of her eyes, but she ignored them, instead staring straight ahead, full of determination. “We ask the questions here.”

But Azula was starting to enjoy this. She couldn’t get out of here, that much was becoming more and more clear with every second, but they *needed* her, or at least thought they needed her. And if they needed her, she couldn’t be killed.

And she could mock her captors to her heart’s content. After all, they *had* kidnapped her. They deserved it.

“Do you? Because I don’t think you really have anything to ask me. If the box means nothing to you, then I have nothing else to be of use.”

“We are not looking for you to be of use, Azula,” said Long Feng. She hated that he kept using her name. “We are looking for the White Lotus’s dark secret. Their equivalent of Lake Laogai...which isn’t where we are, by the way, so you’re out of luck. And you seem to be quite the authority on the topic.”

In that moment, Azula cursed her past self for every single time she’d boasted about her knowledge concerning the White Lotus.

“Well, I apologize that I can’t help you indulge your revenge fantasies, but if the White Lotus has a scheme equivalent to the one at Lake Laogai, I certainly don’t know about it. “

“Are you being honest?” murmured Zhao, stepping forward. Azula swallowed, hoping she could swallow away her fear. “I suppose we’re about to find out.”

In a flash, he yanked a knife out of his jacket and sliced it through the air. Instinctively, she tried to throw up her arms in self-defense, forgetting that her arms were tied to the chair. She squeezed her eyes shut, but the blow never came. She simply felt a slicing motion, and heard something soft fall to the ground.

Carefully, she opened her eyes to find uneven chunks of her hair littering the floor. She wanted to cry; her bangs had been perfect for so long that they had practically become a part of her, but if she wanted to survive, she couldn’t take that chance.

Zhao gave her a wicked smirk. “Tell us what you know, or next time I won’t miss.”

An easy threat, but it still made Azula shiver. Knowing how easy it would be for him to end her life right then and there was terrifying. She had never felt so....breakable.

If telling them she knew nothing wasn’t going to convince them to leave her be, she would need to use other methods to convince them to let her live.

“But if you slice my throat, how are you ever going to get your hands on the White Lotus’s secret?”

Zhao, who was tossing his knife from hand to hand, froze, and the knife clattered to the floor. Azula tried to kick it (to the best of her ability with her ankles bound), but Zhao stomped hard on her foot before she could. Long Feng leaned forward. “What secret?”

The more she talked, the more her fear turned into adrenaline, and the more she thought that there might be some small glimmer of a chance at survival after all. “Well, if I told you now, you would have no reason to keep me alive, would you?” She forced a laugh, though she needed to force it much less than before. “Why would I throw my life away when I could stay alive for as long as I desire?”

In response, Zhao sliced his knife through the skin of her face. Azula felt blood pouring down her cheek, but said nothing, instead looking directly at him. He was smiling cruelly at her, a smile that probably reflected Azula’s own. “Cooperate, or I’ll make your life so incredibly painful that you’ll wish it was over.”

“You underestimate me,” replied Azula. “I have a very high tolerance for pain.”

In response, Zhao pulled out a metal ring with a sharp point, even sharper than his knife, and brandished it in front of her.

Long Feng sighed, stepping forward. “It doesn’t have to be this way, Azula,” he said reproachfully. “We have a lot in common, you know. We’re all pragmatic, we’re all ruthless, and we’re all clever.” He leaned forward, cupping the uncut side of her face in his hand. It was a tactic that she, herself, had used many times. “You can help us, Azula. You should. Because in the end, you’re not so different from us. You can deny it all you like, but we can tell” He gestured to Zhao, who was still brandishing his ring at her. “You could become this. So try to help us. Understand us.” His voice became worse with every word he spoke.

All Azula could do was let out a laugh, in spite of the fear that filled every nook and cranny in her body. It was a laugh of relief more than anything else; relief that, even in her sleep-deprived, tortured state, she could still find weaknesses to exploit in her enemies. But Long Feng didn’t need to know that. “Really? That’s what you have for me? A ‘we’re not so different’ monologue?” Tears were starting to spill from Azula’s eyes, partially from laughter, partially from the profound sense that her life could end at any moment. “I already know I could be like you. My own monstrosity has never surprised me, and it never will. I don’t know who you think you’re interrogating, but if you want an angelic victim, I suggest you look somewhere else.” She rolled her eyes. “I’m unimpressed.”

Long Feng sighed. “Young Lady, you have no option but to cooperate. The Dai Li holds absolutely *immense* power. You are completely power *less* . We could make you disappear without a trace here, and no one would even care that you’re gone. So I would rethink that ‘unimpressed’ remark if I were you.” He leaned forward, snatching the knife out of Zhao’s hands and holding it to her throat. “Or else you might regret it.”

Perhaps it was just more fear, but Azula couldn’t think of anything to do *but* laugh now. Her laughter sounded slightly insane, and perhaps it was, but she didn’t even care. Laughing in the face of pain and potential death was easier than confronting it head on. “You’re absolutely *pathetic*,” she cackled. “You’ve built up this elaborate organization, but once that’s all stripped away, all that’s left for you to do is play the *Big*, *Bad* *Villain*, and boy, are you awful at it! I mean, I’m more terrifying than you are, and I’m not even technically the villain!” She threw her head back and laughed, then, to prove her point, allowed all traces of humor to leave her face, shooting Long Feng a fiery glare. “I may act lighthearted now, but mark my words, the second this is all over, you won’t have anyone else to play the Big, Bad Villain for, because I will end you, and the entire Dai Li, with just a simple flick of the wrist.”

Long Feng glared at her for a moment, eyes seething with hatred, and then stepped aside to clear the path for Zhao, who was still displaying the same wicked grin. “You may do the honors. This little brat has yet to experience true pain. I trust that you can fix that.” The boiling anger in Long Feng’s voice sent small shivers running down Azula’s spine, but she tensed every single muscle in her body so as not to show it.

As Zhao approached her, Azula did her best not to look away from him. If she looked away, the two of them would interpret it as a weakness, and they would pounce on it like panthers. She *could* *not* have that if she wanted to survive this.

As his hand slammed into her face, chest (but not her heart) and shoulders over and over again, it took more energy than Azula had ever used before in her life to keep herself from wincing, from sobbing, from crying out in pain as the blade pierced her skin, as Zhao pounded pain into her body time and time again. By the end of it all, she had at least twelve new gashes all over her body, and she was so exhausted that she now hung limply in her chair, her choppy hair hanging around her soldiers, held up almost solely by the ropes that bound her. She couldn’t see herself, but she would wager that she looked like a ghost.

When her eyes began to droop shut again from the sheer exhaustion of it all, Zhao drew back at last, laughing, and Long Feng once again made his way forward.

“Well, Little Charmer…” his use of Zhao’s nickname for her made Azula shudder, “are you ready to tell us what you know?”

“I told you,” replied Azula, through a blood-filled smirk. “I don’t know anything at all.”

Long Feng frowned and stepped back. His expression was less angry than before, which should have made Azula glad, but instead, she felt worse. His expression was cold and calculating, as though he was slowly losing all regard for humanity.

He turned to Zhao. “Go get the Mechanist, if you please.”

Azula couldn’t stop her eyes widening as Zhao left, and Long Feng smiled cruelly at the sight of it. She knew what was in store, and it was becoming harder and harder to conceal her fear. “You’ve backed yourself into a corner, you know.” The confidence in her voice was beginning to sound forced, even to her own ears. “You have no way of knowing if I truly have the information you seek, so I could be completely useless, but you can’t kill me, because I *could* have the information that would save you all. It’s really quite an unfortunate predicament.” She smirked, ignoring the blood that now coated much of her face.

Long Feng’s sinister smile only grew. “Oh, dear, naïve Azula,” he sighed. There was something about his out-of-character condescending words that made Azula stop breathing for a split second. Long Feng wasn’t the boastful type, and wouldn’t express such confidence if it wasn’t earned. They both knew it.

It felt like hours of sitting in the dark, feeling the sting of each new gash in her flesh, the dull pain of every bruise on her face and collarbone, wondering what fate was about to befall her, before Zhao appeared again, followed by a small man wearing a lab coat, and missing several chunks of his eyebrows. Azula didn’t recognize him, but she did recognize the blue substance in the syringe it was holding.

Azula’s eyes widened, and even she couldn’t stop the shock from showing on her face as she put the final pieces of the puzzle together. Still, she attempted to retain some shred of calm in her voice. “What good am I as a lab rat if I don’t give you the information you seek?”

Long Feng took the syringe out of the Mechanist’s hands and began toying with it. Zhao laughed quietly and maliciously behind him, and Azula hated knowing that he would take great pleasure from watching the syringe plunge into her arm. “But you see, this is no ordinary experiment. This substance is...special.”

“How so?”

Long Feng’s malicious smile extended into a grin. His teeth were so perfectly aligned with one another that it was eerie, and Azula could see every single one of them because he was so close. He was so close that all he needed to do to be heard was whisper. “This is our new pride and joy, Azula. You may be strong, but what will you become...if you are forced to live out your worst nightmare?”

He plunged the syringe into her arm, and everything became a dark blur.

*She was standing in her bedroom, back in Zuko’s apartment. There was sunlight streaming* *through the windows, the books on the bookcase were lined up as neatly as could be, the floor had* *been swept, the bed was made, and every piece of clothing had been placed neatly into its* *respective drawer. The entire room was perfect. The only imperfection was Azula herself.*

*She stared at her reflection in the mirror. She wore the same robe she’d worn earlier that night,* *but it was in shambles, torn into strips that barely managed to stay hanging on her body. Her face* *was a bruised, swollen mess, blood pouring out of the cut on her left jawline, and her hair was* *even worse, a choppy, tangled disaster that looked as though it had been cut by a small child.*

*Was this what the Dai Li had done to her? Had they truly managed to fuck her up so badly?*

*As Azula stared deeper into the mirror, cracks began to form, spiralling out from the center of her* *chest, the only part of her that had remained uncut, though it was still bruised. Soon, the reflective* *glass was nothing but a web of cracks and tiny shards. Azula could barely even make out her own* *image in the broken glass. Sort of like she could barely make out her own image through her* *fucked-up, broken past.*

*“Azula?”*

*Azula whirled around to face the door, and instantly, the room brightened. A quick glance at* *herself informed Azula that all of her imperfections had vanished. No more cuts, bruises or scars,* *just flawless skin, a neat topknot, and a perfect outfit. Everything she’d always tried to be.*

*Zuko stood in the doorway, smiling at her. Even in her strange state, Azula could tell that there was* *something off about the way he smiled; it was a little too big, a little too exaggerated, slanted a* *little ways to the right. He walked towards her, extending his arms. Azula took a small step back,* *but let him wrap his arms around her anyway. This wasn’t real, it wasn’t Zuko, but it had been so* *long since Azula had been so close to her brother that she couldn’t find it in her to break away.*

*Was this what they could have been, in another life?*

*All of a sudden, Azula felt a sharp pain in her lower abdomen. She looked down and saw an* *enormous spot of deep crimson blooming on the white dress she was suddenly wearing. She looked* *up at Zuko, who was now glaring at her with intense hatred in his eyes.*

*“You lied to me.” His voice was cold, full of scorn and betrayal.*

*Azula couldn’t stop the tears from falling, partially from the pain, partially from Zuko’s words.* *How could this have all gone so wrong? “It was never because I wanted to harm you.” Her words* *felt weak and pitiful compared to what she’d done, but it was all she could say.*

*“Never wanted to harm me? You could have gotten me killed!” Zuko’s screams echoed on a higher* *frequency that made Azula’s brain feel like it was exploding. “You’ve been tricking me since the* *moment you showed up on my doorstep, pretending that you needed me!”*

*“I didn’t have anywhere else to go,” Azula replied, her voice faint. Somewhere in the back of her* *mind, she wondered how much blood she’d lost. “I never meant to lie to you. But I didn’t know if* *you’d have given me a chance if I told you the truth.”*

*“So you tricked me into risking my life for you?” snapped Zuko. “Yeah, I don’t think I would have* *given you one.”*

*Azula could feel her knees weakening, her body sinking to the ground. “I’m sorry. I...I wish things* *were different. I only wanted something like what you have. I wasn’t trying to put you in danger!”* *Her vision was blurring again, and the temperature was dropping. Was she dying?*

*Zuko laughed, harsher than he ever laughed in reality. “You’ll never have what I have. Not* *someone like you.”*

For a moment, Azula rested peacefully in blackness before she fell back to reality, feeling the biting air on her skin, the ropes on her wrists and ankles, the freezing metal of the chair on her back. She could barely keep her eyes open, and could feel the blue substance burning in her veins, like acid. It was seeping the energy out of her, almost as if she’d actually been stabbed, and she wasn’t sure how much longer she could keep this up.

She was vaguely aware of the tears streaming down her cheeks, stinging her wounds, as Long Feng and Zhao laughed.

“Well, well, well…” Long Feng leaned forward and wiped a tear off her face, “it seems that the indestructible heiress isn’t so indestructible after all.” He straightened his back and began to face as Azula fought with every fiber in her being to stay conscious. “You do have fear.”

“Every human has fear,” Azula muttered weakly. “You just need to know where to look for it.”

“You speak the truth,” replied Long Feng. “But yours was particularly hard to unearth.” He leaned forward again, cupping her chin in his hand. Azula had so little energy that he essentially needed to support her entire head in order to prevent her from falling forward. “For someone so devious, I didn’t expect such a simple fear, I will admit that.”

“It won’t do you any good,” replied Azula. “I’m already dying.” At least, she thought she was.

Long Feng’s lips curled into a smirk. “But it *will* . You see, we are very close to making that nightmare a reality, if we so desire.”

Azula managed a weak, whispering laugh. “Except for the fact that you have no idea what I was lying about.”

“We don’t need to,” replied Long Feng. “Your fear is not the discovery in itself, but the damage it will lead to. Tell us, will your brother act with any less malice or suspicion if he is unaware of the specifics, but knows you lied? After all, he’s looking for any excuse to prove that you are unworthy of him.” Slowly, he took a knife from his pocket, and traced a delicate line along her chin. Azula was so weak and exhausted that she hardly even noticed the pain.

Long Feng could see her answer in her eyes, though she said nothing. He stepped back, leaving her entire body to slump forward. “We can reveal you for the monster you are, Little Charmer.” Zhao’s nickname was somehow a thousand times worse coming out of Long Feng’s mouth.

Azula’s eyes were still closing, faster and faster, and she felt the life leaving her. Perhaps it was better this way, if the Dai Li was truly going to reveal her secret. Better to die than to live forever as a monster, unloved and alone.

As Azula’s last line of vision was fading away, the door flew open, and an entire crowd poured into the dark room, led by a familiar figure.

“Zuko,” murmured Azula, managing a small smile, “you managed to use that strange silver coin after all.”

With no more energy to spare, and her safety ensured (if she wasn’t already dead), she finally allowed herself to succumb to the quiet darkness.

Seeing Azula’s body hanging limply in a chair, beaten and bruised, made Zuko’s anger spike so strongly that he felt like every cell in his body was going to explode. As the Mayor and the police that Joo Dee (true to her word, for once) had called swarmed the room, Zuko charged over to Long Feng, with Sokka close on his heels. The two men next to Long Feng had already fled into the darkness, but Zuko pinned the Dai Li leader to the ground before he could even really think about it.

Up close, he could see just how pale Azula had become. She looked like a corpse. She *could have* been a corpse, for all he knew.

“What did you do to her?”

Long Feng laughed as the police crowded around him, slapping handcuffs on his wrists and slowly dragging him away. Zuko should have felt triumphant, but all he felt was anxiety.

“A little...experiment.” He nodded towards an empty syringe on the floor, and Zuko could have sworn his heart dropped into his stomach at that very moment. He would have strangled Long Feng if he could. “None of the damage is permanent...hopefully.”

Zuko could still hear his laughter echoing down the corridors long after the police had dragged him away.

Hurriedly, he dropped to the floor next next to his sister and began untying her, wincing as he got a closer look at her gashes and bruises. He was used to seeing her so *perfect* . Seeing her like this, cut up and bloody and damaged, was disturbing.

Sokka placed his hand to her wrist, and examined the empty syringe. He grabbed a paper strip from his coat pocket and pressed it to the inside of the beaker, examining it, then feeling Azula’s wrist again. Zuko stared at him anxiously.

“What?”

Sokka offered him a smile. “It’s okay. I think I recognize some of these ingredients, and they aren’t deadly. Her pulse is steady. She’ll be fine.”

That should have made Zuko feel better, but looking at her nearly unrecognizable state, all he could feel was guilt for letting this happen to her in the first place.

As Zuko looked at his sister, Sokka turned to the Mayor, who had come with the police and was standing behind them. “Thank you, Mr. Mayor,” he said, “for coming when Joo Dee warned you.”

“Don’t mention it,” replied the Mayor. “I want to thank *you* for helping me see the truth. And...I apologize for not believing you before.”

“It’s all right.”

Zuko barely heard anything they said. As gently as he possibly could, he took Azula’s limp body from the chair and lifted her up. She was surprisingly light, and holding her, Zuko was reminded of how *small* she was. Azula had such an intimidating, larger-than-life presence that it was easy to forget how young and small she really was. She was only seventeen.

Azula shivered as they stepped outside into the October air, and Zuko realized for the first time that she was wearing shorts and a tank top, both stained with blood, neither of which belonged to her, neither of which she would ever wear by choice. The fact that the Dai Li had done that to her made Zuko even more furious, but right now, he was more worried about getting his sister home.

The police had lent them a car to take them back to the apartment, and the ride passed by quickly. Sokka left the siblings at the apartment door, giving Zuko a quick hug, and whispering that he’d call him in the morning.

Back in the apartment, Zuko laid Azula softly on the couch and put a blanket over her shivering body, just like he’d done back when they’d first seen the blue substance at the Dai Li’s hidden factory. He’d hated her then. It felt like a lifetime ago.

It had taken him a while to realize it, but he was starting to care about her. Sure, she was messed up and a little strange, but so was Zuko himself. And she was trying her best. He could see it every single day.

He couldn’t sleep. He couldn’t bring himself to leave her alone out here. Not after everything that had happened. So instead, he sat on the arm of the couch with his head in his hands until she stirred, her golden eyes slowly opening, reflecting the dim lights of Zuko’s apartment.

“Zuko?” her voice was still soft and uncharacteristically breathy. Her eyes were wide and slightly wild.

Zuko nodded. “Don’t worry. We’re back home.”

“This isn’t my home,” murmured Azula. “Are we safe?”

Zuko couldn’t find anything to say about the first statement, but he squeezed her wrist, and she didn’t seem to object. “We’re safe. They arrested Long Feng. He won’t be able to do this to you, or anyone else again.”

“Good,” she murmured. A pause, then. “Thank you.”

Zuko blinked. “What for?”

“For coming after me.”

“Azula, you’re an innocent citizen. That’s my job. I’d have come after anyone.”

“But I’m not anyone.” Azula sighed. “It takes more to come after me, and we both know it. So...thank you.”

Zuko wasn’t sure he’d ever heard Azula thank anyone before. “You’re welcome,” he said after a moment, sliding onto the floor. “Why did they want you, anyway?”

“Oh,” murmured Azula. “They thought I knew something they could use against the White Lotus. They were wrong.”

“That’s weird,” muttered Zuko, mostly to himself. “How could they have gotten that idea?”

“Because I told them,” said Azula in a half-whisper. Her eyes were drooping shut again, and Zuko could visibly see her skin becoming paler. It was obvious that she still wasn’t in great shape. “I made it seem like I knew everything.”

Zuko’s eyes widened. “Why would you do that?”

“Once for self-protection in the moment,” she said weakly, “and once to help you.”

“What?” Zuko couldn’t help the small shred of anger from entering his voice. “Why?”

“Because,” said Azula, mostly asleep, “I need to be the perfect helper. After all, that’s the only reason I’m here. You never would have let me stay as myself. But I thought...if I could be useful, maybe I could stay. Obviously, that was a fantasy.”

Zuko said nothing for a moment, before reaching over and squeezing her hand. Even in her half-asleep, drugged state, she looked up, surprised.

“Azula,” said Zuko, not really sure where to start, “look. I know what it was like for you growing up, at least a little. I know what Father always told you, and I know that you think the only way to be accepted is to be something more than human. But you don’t have to be perfect...or anything to be loved here, okay?” He turned and faced her. “I came after you tonight because you’re an innocent citizen, but also because, well...I care about you. In our weird, hard, messed-up way, I care about you. And it’s not because you’re the perfect assistant. It’s because you’re my sister.” He smiled. “And my friend.”

Azula’s eyes were closed, but she was smiling, an indication that she’d heard every word he’d said. “Thank you,” she murmured after a moment. “I care about you, too,” she added after a pause. “I always have, even if I didn’t always know how to say it.” Her voice was thin like a dried leaf in the fall, full of cracks and small tears.

She said nothing more, and Zuko knew that she had drifted off to sleep.

## Chapter 31: The Voice in the Dark

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula and Zuko deal with the aftermath of an objectively traumatic event, and the group makes an important decision.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Mentions of blood and torture.

This chapter was a little tricky (I re-wrote the beginning three times!) so hopefully it's okay.

A big thanks and lots of love to everyone who's actually managed to read this far. Happy reading!

### Text

When Zuko woke up the next morning, his sister was already awake, sitting on the edge of the couch with her body bent over and her chin cupped in her hands. She wasn’t limp anymore, but she still looked smaller than usual, her dangling limbs thinner, her newly cut hair seeming to swallow her shoulders. She looked...like a damaged seventeen-year-old.

He sat up, and even though he was sure that she heard him, she made no movement towards him, nor did she even indicate that she knew he was awake. “Are you okay?”

Azula turned to face him, and Zuko was startled when he saw her eyes. They were still golden, but the gold seemed thin, like a breaking leaf in the fall that had been stretched to its limit. Underneath was a deep, swirling darkness that made her entire face seem hollow, as though someone had taken her confidence, her determination, her spirit, and beaten it out of her.

Zuko found himself hoping with every fiber in his body that they hadn’t beaten *everything* out of her.

“Of course I’m okay. You know as well as anyone that I have an unusually high tolerance for pain.”

“That doesn’t mean you’re okay. I wasn’t there, but they...they did everything they could to you. This isn’t just a random slap here or there, this is *torture* .”

“It doesn’t matter,” sighed Azula. “I *refuse* to let this prevent me from solving these murders. Especially now that I know what those people are capable of.” With each word she said, the gaping hollowness in her eyes seemed to grow and grow.

Zuko recognized the gleam of determination that was starting to appear in her eyes. It was something they had in common. And he had solved enough cases to know how dangerous it could be. “Azula...I know you’re trying to be a good detective, but...”

“What I said last night has nothing to do with this.” She looked away. “And we don’t need to talk about that. I’d rather not discuss my weaknesses again.”

“You don’t understand!” snapped Zuko. “What happened to you isn’t a sign of any sort of failure, and if you’re not okay yet, it isn’t a failure! Every detective has something like this happen to them at some point. It’s part of the job. You told me yourself when you started helping me that you accepted the dangers of doing this. Accepting those also means accepting what’s already happened to you, and accepting that it’s actually possible to get hurt, not just being willing to take risks.”

There was a moment of silence. “Wow,” said Azula with a slight laugh. “That might be the most intelligent thing I’ve ever heard come out of your mouth.”

“I’ve been in this business for a long time,” replied Zuko. “If you’re not okay yet, it only means that you can remember what they did to you, and it’ll make you stronger, and even more determined when the time comes to defeat them.”

Something resembling fire flashed in Azula’s eyes, which looked slightly less hollow than they had a moment ago. “I will obliterate every single soul that had anything to do with that inhuman blight on this Earth.” She hid it well, but Azula could be just as dramatic as Zuko, from time to time.

He glanced at her bangs, which still looked sloppy compared to the rest of her, which was slowly starting to look like herself again. “Do you want to make an appointment to fix your bangs?”

Azula got up and studied her reflection in the glass of Zuko’s window. From here, he could see the red marks the ropes had left around her ankles. “Actually, I think I’m going to keep them the way they are.”

Zuko blinked. “Why? When I said to remember what happened to you, I didn’t mean…”

“I know,” Azula interrupted. “And maybe it’s silly, but...whenever any Dai Li member sees my bangs, they’ll know what I’ve been through, and they’ll know I *survived* . They’ll know exactly how strong I am before I even have to show them.” She turned and looked back at him. “I think this is my way of dealing with this. So...please let me.”

“I would, but…” Zuko sighed, not wanting to ask what he was about to ask “What is Father going to say when you come home with your bangs looking like that? An outfit he can’t see is one thing, but this is risky. *Really* risky.”

Azula turned away. Zuko couldn’t see her face, but she was gripping her hands together very tightly. At long last, she turned back, a somewhat fake-looking confident smile plastered on her face. “He’ll just have to accept them, and if he doesn’t...I could always go somewhere else. That wouldn’t be so bad, right?” She laughed, her laugh sounding slightly broken, like a tape recorder that was half static. “I survived *literal torture* ! How much worse could living away from Father be?” She tossed her hair. “After last night, what’s left to fear?”

“Death,” replied Zuko. “Azula...you *are* planning on going back to Father, right?”

Azula studied him for a moment. “Would it be so bad if I didn’t?”

Zuko didn’t know how to answer. If she went back to Father, he wouldn’t have to deal with all of the complicated feelings that arose whenever she was around. But the longer she stayed, the more he found himself thinking that a place by Father was the absolute last place Azula should be. “No,” he said at last. “It would be okay. But you would need to tell me.”

Azula stood still for a second, shuddering like a figure in an old movie that had been paused between frames. She smiled. “Don’t worry, Zuko. I’m going back to Father as soon as this case is done. I’ll be out of your hair soon.” She disappeared into her bedroom.

Just as Zuko was throwing on a set of clothes that *hadn’t* spent last night carrying his bleeding sister, and his coat (which somehow managed to never get bloodstained, no matter how much blood touched it), the phone rang.

“Hello?” said Zuko. It could have been Sokka, but it was too early for that, and besides, Sokka was usually the type to show up in person (usually without being invited), not call someone on the phone.

“Detective Zuko?” said the voice on the other end. It wasn’t a very familiar one, and it took Zuko a second to identify it.

“Mr. Mayor. Uh...good morning. Is there a problem?”  
“Not at all!” cried the Mayor from the other end of the phone. “I just wanted to thank you, on behalf of myself and all of Ba Sing Se. You are the ones who helped us bring down the Dai Li. And to think that I was being manipulated by them all this time…” he sighed. “I’ve failed as a Mayor.”

“Not at all!” cried Zuko. “Manipulation happens to the best of us, and, when push came to shove, you did the right thing. That’s what really matters.” He paused. “But...if it’s okay to ask...what made you start believing us? Until last night, you hated us.”

“Well, to be honest,” said Kuei, “it was really Joo Dee. I worked closely with her throughout the years, and I’ve always trusted her. When she came to me and told me the truth, it just confirmed my suspicions which had already been spurred by the White Lotus’s party.”

“You went to that?” said Zuko. “I don’t remember seeing you.”

“That’s because I was mostly near the food and drinks,” laughed Kuei. “But seeing that assassin there made me begin to think that there was more at play than I’d originally imagined.”

“Well,” said Zuko, “I think it was brave of you to confront the Dai Li with us. You’re a credit to your city, Mayor Kuei.”

There was a moment where all Zuko could hear were muffled noises. “Are you...crying?” he asked, bewildered.

“I’m just... *proud* ,” sobbed Kuei from the other end of the line.

Zuko groaned as quietly as he could. He was happy to have the Mayor on their side, but dealing with his wackiness was *definitely* going to be a challenge. “Mr. Mayor, can you give me any updates about the Dai Li?”

“Right!” squawked Kuei. Zuko thought he heard papers rustling on the other end of the line. “Uh...Long Feng has been safely placed in custody, as have a lot of the agents who were working last night. But...the other two men there, as well as a lot of Dai Li agents, are gone. We...uh...don’t know where they are.”

Zuko sighed. No matter how much fighting he did, sometimes it seemed as though the fight would never end, like he would never be able to stop struggling, screaming, banging his fists into walls, and feeling like he was reaching for something impossible. “What about the prisoners?”

There was a beat of silence. “What?” said Kuei quietly after a moment.

“The Dai Li has *prisoners* , Mr. Mayor! Have we found them?” Zuko knew the answer even before the Mayor said it, but he needed to hear it anyway, just to make sure it was real.

“Oh,” said Kuei in a squeaky voice, “no. We don’t know where the prisoners are.”

Zuko could feel something igniting inside of him. It was the same feeling that ignited whenever he sought justice, to protect his city, his family and friends, his people, and his home.

He hung up the phone, and only seconds later, there was a knock at the door. Before he could reach it, Azula darted out of her room and over towards the door. Zuko couldn’t help noticing her outfit. She wore a form fitting red sweater with a flame pattern in reds and oranges, black jeans with holes in the knees, and studded black boots. Combined with her new choppy bangs, she looked almost like a rock star.

“You’re okay!” cried Katara, flying through the door and throwing her arms around Azula. Sokka followed closely behind her, giving Zuko an awkward wave. “I’m so sorry I wasn’t there last night, but after the whole thing with Yon Rha and my mother…” she sighed. “I was exhausted. I didn’t even know what happened until this morning, but trust me, if I’d been there last night, not a single Dai Li soldier would have made it out of there unscathed.”

Azula laughed. Up close, Zuko could see that she applied a few layers of makeup to cover her bruises. It was the most makeup Zuko had seen her wear since the party on her first night in Ba Sing Se. The party where Pakku had been murdered. It felt like so long ago. “Katara, I’m perfectly fine. But you’re right. Any Dai Li soldier that tries to come near either of us had better watch out.”

“Oh!” said Katara. “Before I forget…” she pulled Azula’s silver-and-ruby dagger out of her pocket and placed it in her hands. “This helped me so much at Lake Laogai. I only wish you’d had it last night.”

Azula placed the dagger inside her topknot, without it even looking like she’d touched it. “Don’t worry,” she said nonchalantly. “I was asleep when they took me. There was nothing the dagger would have done.”

The room rested in shocked silence for at least a minute, until Azula broke it. “Anyway, I hope you kept this safe for me.”

“Absolutely!” cried Katara with a little too much enthusiasm. “It was safe with me and Yue all night!”

“You and Yue all night?” mused Azula, raising an eyebrow. “Interesting…”

Katara’s face darkened by a factor of ten. “Not like *that* ! She just...lent me one of her bean bag chairs since I was so tired after the whole thing with Yon Rha. That’s *all* !”

“Whatever you say,” said Azula, smirking. As Katara began saying something to Azula about her sweater, Zuko turned to Sokka, who had been unusually quiet ever since he had arrived. “Hey...thanks so much for helping me last night. I know I was a little...intense, but you really helped me. I don’t know if I could have gotten through that if you hadn’t been there.”

“You weren’t intense,” said Sokka. “Well, you were, but not in a bad way. You were just as intense as you needed to be. I’m just glad you and Azula are both okay.” His face flushing, he reached across and placed his hand on Zuko’s shoulder. “You helped me find Katara while she was looking for Yon Rha. We’re solving a murder together. Whatever you need, I’ve got your back, okay?” Zuko smiled. “Only if you’ll let me have yours.” Crap, had he really just said that out loud? What sort of a line was *that* ? Zuko was only starting to understand the way he felt about Sokka, and he was already messing it up. Typical.

As usual, they were interrupted by the sounds of Azula and Katara giggling behind them, and Sokka rolled his eyes, plopping down on the couch next to Azula, who was sitting on the arm, examining the studs on one of her boots.

“What’s our next move?” asked Sokka, ignoring Azula and Katara’s laughter.

“I don’t know,” replied Katara, stroking the sleeves of her velvety deep blue sweater. “There’s still four murders we haven’t solved. And there’s the matter of whoever hired Hama and Jet.”  
“But we don’t know who Jet killed,” interjected Azula.

“Right.”

“Where do we even start?” sighed Sokka. “We have so many suspects, we need to interrogate Long Feng now that he’s in custody, but we don’t know if he’ll tell us anything…”

“He’ll tell us everything he knows,” said Azula, an absolutely malicious gleam in her eye. It was terrifying, and would have been even more concerning if Azula hadn’t just spent more than half the night being tortured by Long Feng. Zuko could understand her wanting to strangle him.

“There’s something else,” said Zuko after a moment, still thinking about what Joo Dee had said to him the day before, about what Zhao and Long Feng had done to Azula just because they thought she *might* have the information they wanted, about what the Mayor had said to him just minutes ago.

Azula must have recognized the look on his face, because she rolled her eyes. “Oh no,” she groaned. “He’s about to say that he wants to go off on some ridiculous, vigilante-inspired, honor-fueled side quest, even though we’re already in the middle of solving a string of murders, four of which are still unsolved, but there’s no stopping him, no matter how hard we try.” She threw her head back dramatically. Was that supposed to be an imitation of *him* ? “Did I guess correctly? Was I right?” She smirked at Katara. “He knows I’m right.”

“Fine,” sighed Zuko, “you’re right. But this isn’t just some ‘vigilante-inspired honor-fueled side quest.’ The Dai Li have real prisoners. I felt bad for leaving them behind before, but we were fleeing for our lives. But now...now that I know what the Dai Li are capable of…” his eyes wandered over to Azula. When he was sitting this close to her, he could see the cuts on her face, hidden under her makeup, “I can’t leave anyone alone with them. Not again. I couldn’t live with myself if I didn’t at least *try* to find them.”

Katara nodded. “I saw how many people they had at Lake Laogai. I was busy trying to rescue Mai, and then...the whole thing with Yon Rha happened, but you’re right. We *can’t* leave them there. Not now that we really have a chance to free them.”

“Hang on,” said Sokka. “Do we really even have a chance? I mean, we don’t know where they are now. They won’t be at Lake Laogai anymore, not now that they know that we know where it is and how to get in.”

“If we had a chance, would you do it?”

Sokka seemed unsure for a moment, but nodded.

Zuko turned to his sister, who sighed, examining her nails. Up close, Zuko could see that the middle fingernail on her right hand was broken right down the middle.

“What happened to your fingernail?”

Azula looked away pointedly. “Zhao’s ring. And don’t look at me that way. You already know that I find your idea incredibly idiotic and reckless.”

“Azula,” said Zuko, sitting next to her on the arm of the sofa, “think about what the Dai Li did to you. They could be doing that right now to who knows how many other people, people who aren’t as strong as you are. You know that no innocent human should have to experience that pain. Don’t you want to help stop it?”

“Of course I do,” snapped Azula. “Every cell in my body wants to leap up, free the prisoners, and slice off Zhao’s head this instant, but Zuko...look at what we’re already doing. Do we really have the time and stamina to go after these prisoners? What the Dai Li did to me was atrocious, but...chances are, those prisoners will still be alive after the case is over. The rest of the city? Maybe not so much.”

Zuko sighed, feeling dejected for a moment before standing up, stucky by a sudden burst of determination. “Look,” he began, “I know this isn’t the best plan in the world. I know it’s a stupid idea.” He glanced at Azula. “But now, we all know the full extent of what the Dai Li can do. Ask yourselves; could you really live with yourselves in the future, knowing that you knew part of what the Dai Li was doing, and you did *nothing* to protect those innocent people?”

There was a beat of silence as the other three glanced around the room, at each other, at Zuko, all of their eyes shifting, never seeming to settle on one spot for too long. Katara was the first to focus her eyes in on one spot. She looked at Zuko. “I’m with you all the way, Zuko. We’re not leaving anyone behind. Not again. We need to protect each other.” She smiled a small smile, though Zuko had no idea why. “That’s what it’s all about.” She turned to her brother. “Please, Sokka. We don’t want to do this without you.”

“You mean you’ll go whether or not I say yes?” said Sokka. “Great,” he added with a sprinkling of sarcasm.

“Well,” said Katara, nervously playing with a strand of her long, thick brown hair, “yes, we will. I know it’s unlikely to work, but Zuko has a reputation for beating the odds!” She grinned at him, and threw her arm around Sokka’s shoulders.

Sokka looked at Zuko. “Of course I’m coming with you,” he said to both Zuko and Katara. “Who else is going to make sure you crazy kids don’t get killed?

Everyone laughed, and then Zuko turned to his sister. “Azula?”  
Azula sighed. “I hate to admit this, and perhaps it’s still effects of last night, but I believe you are correct. None of this is logical, and yet...I couldn’t live with myself if I left all of these people with Zhao and the Dai Li and did nothing. Not after last night.” She glanced around the room. It was only the three of them. “If any of you tell anyone I said that, I will tear each of your fingernails off one by one, and make you eat them.”

“You are strangely good at threats,” said Sokka, and Azula laughed.

Zuko, meanwhile, was looking at the clue board. As Azula and Sokka traded little jabs at one another, Katara crossed the room to stand next to Zuko, following his gaze to a red paper rectangle on his bulletin board, reading ‘prison.’

She turned to Zuko, who seemed lost in thought. “We’ll...get them back, won’t we?”  
Zuko sighed, taking a sip of the tea he’d forgotten about, even though it was stone cold now. “Don’t be silly, Katara. Of *course* we’ll get them back.”

## Chapter 32: The Blood-Spattered Pavement

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

The group goes out on a limb, and soon are forced to face a number of difficult foes.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Physical violence, blood, guns, stabbing, fighting.

Another one of my favorite chapters (and only 10 chapters from the end AAH!) Happy reading!

### Text

It took several hours of sitting in Zuko’s apartment, at least three cups of coffee (or tea) per person, ten notebooks’ worth of theories, and three different maps of Ba Sing Se, for Sokka to finally come up with an idea of where to find the prisoners.

“Guys!” he said excitedly, sitting straight up. “I just had a thought.”

“Do tell,” said Azula, who was the only one still drinking coffee. Sokka would have worried about her if he didn’t...no, he was actually worried about her.

Sokka stared at the map of Ba Sing Se sitting in front of him on the coffee table. “The Dai Li is a complicated organization with several layers. This whole time, we’ve been counting on that, and looking for them in the most obscure, complicated places. But what if the solution was deceptively simple this entire time?”

“What do you mean?” asked Zuko. Of all of them, he seemed the most calm. He still had a spark of determination in his eye, but he seemed to have *purpose* , and it made him calmer and more sure of himself. Sokka was happy to see him like that.

“Well,” said Sokka, “think about it. Where does the Dai Li keep most of their guards in the first place?”

“Long Feng’s mansion,” replied Azula instantly, her eyes widening a second later. “Wait, you’re not thinking what I think you’re thinking...are you?”

“I know it’s a long shot,” said Sokka, “but it makes sense! The Dai Li keep a lot of guards at Lake Laogai, but most of their trained guards are at Long Feng’s mansion. Seems like an awful lot of people just for security, doesn’t it?”

“Are you implying that the Dai Li had three different secret headquarters this whole time?” asked Katara. “That’s kind of a lot to believe.”

“Not in the way that you’re thinking,” said Sokka. It felt like he was putting together a puzzle in his head, and it was exhilarating. Was this why Azula loved solving mysteries so much? He was starting to see why. “Lake Laogai was always the main one. That’s where they kept people for their experiments, trained the guards, and where the Mechanist had his labs.” He gestured to Azula. “The place where we found you was a backup. That was where they went to carry out dangerous tasks if they thought they were at risk of being discovered. The police searched the area there, and didn’t find anyone else. So where were the rest of the prisoners?”

“You’re saying you think they’re in Long Feng’s mansion?” said Zuko.

“Not the mansion itself,” said Sokka. “Hidden under and around it. Just like the White Lotus did. Think about it,” he said, turning towards Zuko. “Where were Joo Dee’s sisters this entire time?”

“The White Lotus and the Dai Li have more in common than they think,” said Azula. “It would make sense for them to utilize some of the same strategies.”

“It *does* make sense!” said Sokka, getting to his feet. “It all makes perfect sense!”

“I don’t know,” muttered Zuko. “It seems like a guess on our part.”

“So does anything else we’d do,” pointed out Azula. “Besides, if there’s nothing there, what have we got to lose? Long Feng has been arrested, and Suki, Toph, and Mai can let us into the mansion. It’s low-risk if he’s wrong.”

“And if he isn’t?” piped up Katara.

Zuko sighed, getting to his feet. “We’ll check it out,” he said after a moment. “But if Sokka’s right...well, let’s just make sure we’re all prepared.”

“I don’t see why you thought there’d be anything here,” said Mai. She, Toph, and Suki were leading the group down the halls of Long Feng’s mansion, and Katara couldn’t help but notice that Mai and Suki were holding hands. “We’ve lived here our whole lives, and we’ve never found anything.”

“Well, maybe that’s just because you never thought to look!” said Sokka, hurrying to catch up with them. As they walked down the hall, Katara turned to Azula, who was standing next to her. She was a little quieter than usual today, still her logical, practical self, but she seemed less willing to engage in an argument than she usually was.

“Do you think Sokka’s right?” asked Katara after a moment.

Azula shrugged. “The evidence makes sense. It’s not impossible.”  
“But it’s unlikely.”

“Well, mathematically…”

“Never mind the math. What’s your intuition telling you?”

Azula smirked, rolling her eyes. “What are you, my therapist?”

Katara scowled. “No, I’m just curious. I was trying to make conversation and distract you from thinking about last night.”

“You don’t need to do that,” said Azula. “But my intuition is telling me that the Dai Li cannot be trusted, and any lead on them is worth checking out.”

“Do you think you’ll be okay if we meet them? Even the ones from last night?”

“First of all, please stop asking me questions, you’re hovering over me like a helicopter, and while I appreciate it, it’s incredibly irritating,” said Azula. “Second of all, the Dai Li is too scared to fight me unless my wrists and ankles are tied to a chair. I doubt they’ll be much of a threat to me if I have to face them head on.”

Katara wanted to answer that, but, true to Azula’s wish, she stayed quiet, and didn’t ask any more questions.

The group stopped at the end of the hallway, and Suki held her phone up to the wall to use as a flashlight. “Lots of guards come here and don’t come back. I’d always assumed they were sneaking out the window for midnight snack breaks or something, but if there are secret passages in this mansion, this is where they’ll be.”

“Well, I don’t see anything,” said Zuko hurriedly. “We’d better leave.” But Azula grabbed his wrist before he could move. She muttered something to him, and he rolled his eyes.

Sokka moved forward, running his hand over the wall. “It’s...odd. It’s almost completely smooth, but there are these little patches that don’t quite match up with the rest of it. Maybe if I press them.” He shoved his hands into the wall, but nothing happened.

“Try having multiple people press it at once,” said Suki. “The Dai Li is all about uniformity and teamwork.” She moved forward and pressed her hand to the left side of the wall, while Sokka kept his in the center, and Mai pressed her hand to the right.

Katara hadn’t been entirely convinced of the theory, so she was completely shocked when the wall split in half, sliding sideways to reveal a stone passageway lined with green torches, identical to the torches at Lake Laogai. She shuddered at the memory of that place, and yet, she was about to willingly walk into another passageway that was almost identical to it.

Justice was worth it, she supposed.

Zuko turned to Suki, Toph, and Mai. “If we don’t come out, go find the Mayor. He’ll get you to the police who aren’t on the Dai Li’s side.”

“Why can’t we come with you?” snapped Toph.

Zuko sighed. “Believe me, we could use your skills,” he said. “But I’m not risking a repeat of what happened at Lake Laogai…” he glanced at Mai “ *or* of last night,” he finished, glancing over at Azula. We need you out here, in case anything happens. *No one* is dying tonight.”

“Take this,” said Suki, grabbing a green torch from the wall. “Your phones won’t be as bright down there. Plus, they double as weapons.” She handed it to Zuko, who smiled at her before descending into the passageway. Azula, Sokka, and Katara all followed him.

Katara was at the back of the group as they walked down the long spiral staircase, longer and narrower than the staircase at Lake Laogai. It seemed to stretch downward for miles, so long and narrow that Katara almost got dizzy counting the steps, trying not to lose her footing. She had no idea how on Earth Azula was managing to do this in high-heeled boots.

At last, they reached the bottom of the stairs, and the sight they found was a grim one. Unlike Lake Laogai, which was a maze of different passageways and twists and turns, this was clearly meant to be one small secret, reserved for only the most important prisoners. They were standing in front of one, long, wide hallway lined with prison cells. Katara could hear faint shrieks and thumps coming from all the way down the corridor.

She couldn’t help herself, and before she even knew she was moving, she was crouching in front of one of the cells with her hands on the bars. Now that she was in the middle of the corridor, she could see one of the Mechanist’s carts sitting next to each cell, stocked full of beakers of the same glowing blue substance she’d seen before.

“The blue liquid is an experimental drug that makes victims hallucinate their greatest fears and reveal them to anyone vicious enough to bear witness to it,” said Azula, who had appeared next to her. Gently, she rubbed a spot on her left arm. “It’s...unpleasant.”

“I can imagine,” said Katara. She turned back to the cell, and nearly jumped back in surprise when a teenage girl appeared on the other side. Quickly, though, her surprise was overcome by worry. She reached through the bars and gently took the girl’s hands. She couldn’t have been older than Katara herself.

“Hi, I’m Katara. What’s your name?”

The girl looked away nervously. “I’m...Song,” she said after a moment.

“Hi, Song,” said Katara. “Don’t worry. My friends and I are here to help you.” Looking more closely, she could see a bandage wrapped around the girl’s left arm, in the exact same spot where Azula had been rubbing her own arm. “Can you tell me why the Dai Li put you here?”

“I don’t know!” cried Song. “They said something about my sister, Joo Dee, but they just dragged me and my twin sister, Jin, here, and started injecting us with that stuff!” She pointed to the blue beakers. “It makes you see *awful* things.”

“Whatever you fear most,” said Azula. Every time she looked at the blue drug, she looked like she was staring into the hollow eyes of a ghost.

Katara turned to her friends, all of whom had come up behind her by that point. “We need to get them out of here,” she said. She turned back to Song. “Is everyone here being treated like you? Are they all innocent?”

“I don’t know,” said Song, “but they’re all being given that drug.”

“What if there are dangerous people here?” said Azula. “We can’t risk letting them go.”

“You’re right, Little Charmer,” said an oily voice from behind them. Slowly, the group turned around to find Zhao, the Mechanist, and every remaining Dai Li soldier standing behind them. “It *would* be a shame to let you go.”

It all happened so fast that it quickly turned into a blur. The guards were running at them, and Zuko had pulled out his pistol, and Zhao had sprinted off down the corridor, and Azula had raced after him, and Sokka was running, trying to keep track of everything around him while also not getting himself killed, and he couldn’t see Katara, and everything was just *insane* .

Something flew past his shoulder and exploded on the wall behind him, and Sokka whirled around just in time to avoid a fiery beaker flying directly towards his head. Quickly, he grabbed the nearest cart and threw it in front of him, using it as a shield. Peering through the bottles, he could see that the Mechanist was the one throwing flaming bottles at him.

The guards kept coming and coming, making it harder for Sokka to see. Through the crowd, he caught a glimpse of the Mechanist leaping onto another cart and careening back towards the entrance, a vial of the blue drug in his arms. In the midst of the fight, vial after vial of it was smashing on the floor.

“Don’t let him get away!” yelled Zuko. “Go after him!”

Sokka looked around. There was an overwhelming number of guards filling the hallway. It would be almost impossible for Zuko and Katara to defeat so many of them on their own. He turned back to Zuko, his expression filled with worry.

Zuko gave him a cocky grin. “Don’t worry about me. These guards don’t know what’s coming for them.”

Sokka had to clench his fists as hard as he possibly could in order to make himself look away from Zuko and leap onto the cart he’d been using as a shield. Tentatively, he leaned forward and gave the front of it a shove. To his surprise, it began to move, and Sokka almost screamed as the cart began hurtling down the passageway at breakneck speed. He plowed through guards like a cow plowing through a stack of its hay, and even though it was hard to steer, he at least managed to keep the cart on the same general path as the Mechanist. *Good* . At least now, he wouldn’t lose him.

“Don’t follow me!” cried the Mechanist, throwing exploding bottles from his cart. Sokka retaliated each time with his boomerang, breaking every bottle in midair before it could even get close to his cart. “I am carrying scientific progress that won’t be replicated for centuries! You don’t want to lose that!”

“That’s not progress!” yelled Sokka, throwing his boomerang again, this time so that it hit the Mechanist in the head, though (unfortunately) not hard enough to knock him out. “Science is about understanding the world and helping it, not torturing people!”

“You study corpses for fun!” chirped the Mechanist, still racing away. “Isn’t that torture!”

“I study corpses so that I can solve murders, dumbass!” yelled Sokka, who was getting fed up with the whole cart-chase-thing. “Not so I can use my knowledge to serve torturers and experiment on humans with dangerous, traumatizing drugs!”

“It isn’t dangerous!” cried the Mechanist. *There was a door up ahead* , Sokka realized. If the Mechanist escaped here, he would never be caught, and his drug would be passed around from city to city until the whole world knew what it was. “It shows humans their worst fear, simply something they should already know!”

Sokka felt rage boiling in his blood. He had lived through a lot of his worst fears. His mother, his father, Katara, Zuko. Shaking with anger and exhaustion, he drew back his arm and threw his boomerang as hard as he could, right into the Mechanist’s head.

The man fell onto his stomach, his vial of the blue substance flying out of his hand and smashing on the floor. Sokka’s cart was going so fast that he needed to leap off it and go flying into the wall in order not to crash.

Quickly, he got to his feet and held his boomerang over the Mechanist’s head. “There’s a difference between studying and living, Mr. Mechanist,” he snapped. “If you ever tried actually interacting with your ‘subjects’, maybe you would know that.”

He smashed the boomerang over the Mechanist’s head, and gave the broken vial of blue liquid on the floor an extra stomp, just for good measure.

For a detective, Zuko had pretty limited experience with his pistol. He always had it on hand, just in case, but he’d rarely actually had to use it. Suddenly, he was in the middle of a horde of guards, all of them armed, shooting this way and that with one hand, and swinging a green torch with the other. It was disorienting.

A guard ran up to him and grabbed him around the waist from behind. Without thinking, he leaned forward and kicked his legs into the guard’s stomach as hard as he possibly could. The guard let out a grunt, and Zuko dropped to the floor. Before the guard could recover, he whirled around, and, seeing the silver key on a thin string around his neck, grabbed the key and pulled. The guard gasped for a moment, but then the string broke, and the key fell right into Zuko’s hand. Quickly, he closed his fist around it before any of the guards could make a grab for it.

“Katara!” he shouted to the only member of his group that he could see. She whirled around, and he threw the key, praying that she’d be able to catch it before the guards. She leaped forward, and her fist closed around the key just as another guard caught hold of the string. They pulled, locked in a tug-of war for a few moments before the already-broken string slipped out of the guard’s hand.

“Get them out of here!” yelled Zuko, gesturing towards the cells as he turned back around to face the guards. She nodded, and began racing down the long line of cell doors, stopping at each one and unlocking it.

“Come with me!” he heard her yell, and soon, there was a line of newly liberated prisoners following her up and down the passageway. A group of ten or so guards raced towards the other cells, vials of blue drug in their hands. Realizing what they were doing, Zuko sprinted towards them as fast as he possibly could. One of the guards already had a teenage prisoner pulled close to the bars. Zuko froze. He didn’t want to shoot and hit the prisoner instead, and he knew his aim wasn’t good enough.

He sprinted forward and smashed the non-lit end of the torch over the guard’s head. The guard crumpled to the floor.

It felt like he fell into a rhythm as he began fighting every guard that came near him, punching and kicking and striking with the torch, holding up the pistol as a threat, but never shooting. He’d never been formally trained in self defense, but he had spent hours as a child practicing it over and over again, trying to come up with new ways to protect himself. It had never worked, but it had proved useful ever since he’d become a detective, and it had never been more apparent than it was right then.

A cart came flying through the guards, causing some of them to fall to the floor, and others to leap backwards into the walls. Zuko caught sight of Sokka on top of it, and leapt on. They drove through the crowd, Zuko striking any guards who came too close, and Sokka steering the cart to try and get the guards to bang their heads on the walls.

“What’s the plan?” yelled Sokka. He was hard to hear over the shouting, banging, and fighting going on all around them.

Zuko looked over at Katara, who was almost done freeing all of the prisoners, and was leading them towards the door. He couldn’t hear what she was saying to them, but he could see her mouth moving, and he could see her moving her arms passionately. With every word she said, the prisoners seemed to gain more confidence, some of them even punching guards who came too close to the group. “We need to wait until she gets everyone out of here. Once they’re out, they’ll call the police, and if they get here fast enough, we can catch them. We just need to keep them busy until that happens.”

“How are we going to keep them all in here?” yelled Sokka. “There are so many of them!”

Zuko glanced at the cart, and then at the open cell doors. “I have an idea, but it’s crazy!”

“I wouldn’t have it any other way!”

Zuko smiled. “All right, here’s what we’re gonna do…”

The second Zhao ran off down the corridor, Azula didn’t hesitate to race after him. After what he’d done to her, after he had taken her mind and body and used them against her, after he had taunted her and taken her while she was sleeping, this was a fight she absolutely *had* to win. There was no other option.

And she was determined to show him *exactly* how strong she was.

The passageway opened up onto a round room, with several empty cells with broken bars lining the walls, stairways on either side of the entrance, and an elevated platform encircling the room at the top of them, about fourteen feet above Azula’s head. Azula didn’t see Zhao, but she drew her dagger and held it up, ready for a fight. Azula had learned how to fight from a young age, despite never being formally trained. She’d carried a dagger since she was eleven years old, when she’d truly learned that no one was safe, not in her house.

It was only because she’d grown up needing to watch her surroundings so carefully that she heard the slight rustling behind her and whirled around, raising her dagger to block Zhao’s fist before his ring could strike her in the heart. The flat side of her knife smashed into his knuckles, and he cried out in pain before raising his fist again.

Azula wasted no time ducking under his arm and slashing at him again. This time, he was ready for her attack, and raised up his arm to defend himself, but the impact of Azula’s movement still sent him sliding backwards. Even angrier than before, he ran at her again, panting. This time, Azula used a tactic that she and Zuko had practiced as children. As he sprinted at her, she dropped low to the ground, then reached up and grabbed his arm, using his momentum to flip him facedown on the floor.

She got to her feet and stood over him, her dagger pointed directly at his neck.

“What’s the matter, Zhao? Surprised that I can put up a fight?” She laughed. “It’s funny what being outside the confines of a torture chamber can do for a girl.” She leaned in closely, pressing her dagger to his throat. “After what you did to me,” she hissed, “you’ll be lucky if I let you live.”

In response, Zhao spun and swept Azula’s legs out from under her. She fell to the ground, but kept a tight grip on her dagger, and quickly drew her knees towards her, her dagger held up as a defense, ready to spring up again. “You won’t defeat me so easily, *Master of Pain* .” Venom oozed from every word she spoke. “Here’s something you should know about me.” She looked him right in the eyes, and glared at him. Any fear that she felt was completely absent from her expression. “I *never* lose.”

Instead of attacking her, Zhao turned and raced up one of the side staircases, laughing as he ran. “You think you can catch me?” He called down to her. “You overestimate yourself!”

In a flash, he threw something (she couldn’t see what it was) down at her, and Azula winced as it hit her in the shoulder. She felt it cut through her skin, and felt blood soaking her sweater. It was a shame, too. She loved that sweater.

But she still wasn’t scared. Instead, all she could do was laugh as she got to her feet.

Zhao couldn’t even fight her one-on-one. Instead, he had resorted to running away and firing at her from a distance.

He was nothing but a coward.

And Azula absolutely *despised* cowards.

She thought about every cut on her body that was still healing, the laughter as he’d bruised her, made her bleed over and over again. She thought about his laughter as Long Feng had plunged the needle into her arm.

There was almost no one on Earth that Azula hated more than she hated Zhao at that moment.

She turned and glared up at him, her eyes gleaming with passion and vengeance. “I loved that sweater,” she hissed.

She sprinted up the stairs to meet him on the platform, her dagger raised, the pain in her shoulder nothing more than a dull throb compared to the adrenaline pumping through her body. He raced around to the other side of the platform, a long sword raised in front of him. “Don’t come any closer,” he yelled. “Or you’ll know the true meaning of the word *pain* .”

But Azula wasn’t afraid of this man. He was a coward, and she was no longer tied to a chair and at his mercy. She was in the position of power, and she *relished* the feeling.

She threw her head back, allowing him to see the bangs that he’d cut, and laughed, smirking at him. “What’s the matter, Zhao? Afraid to fight me when I’m not tied up? I didn’t think the Master of Pain was such a *coward* !” She sprinted further around the platform, and he ran. “Are you really too weak to fight a teenage girl?” she called, making her voice as daunting as possible. “You’re even more pathetic than I thought!” She stopped running and began tossing her dagger from hand to hand. “Hiding behind Long Feng, only attacking victims who can’t fight back, never making *any* decisions for yourself…” She glared at him. “You’re nothing but a spineless puppet, but you’re the worst kind of spineless puppet.” Using all of her strength, hatred, and determination, she sprinted towards him, and before he could react, she had her knife pressed to his throat, and he was bending over backwards, trying not to fall over the edge of the platform. “You’re a spineless puppet who uses others’ power to prey on the weak for no real purpose except tormenting them.”

“And you’re not the same?” hissed Zhao. “I know you, Little Charmer. You’ve spent your life living off the profits of your father’s riches and success, carrying out his awful orders like it was nothing. How are you better than me?”

Azula laughed. “Oh, I’m awful, to be sure, but I worked for everything I have. Father didn’t hand out approval like candy. You had to be *strong* to earn it, and you had to know how to *fight* .” She pressed the dagger harder into Zhao’s throat. “I know how to fight any opponent, not just the ones weaker than I am. I don’t prey only on the innocent, because I can win any battle. I know how to succeed in *any* situation.” She smirked. “And every fight I partake in is for a specific goal. Right now, my goal is watching you *fail* .” She glared at him, her eyes gleaming.

Zhao laughed. “Don’t waste your threats on me. If you hurt me, you *will* witness the full extent of what I can do. And then we’ll all see how empty your boasting is.”

Azula laughed. “I have no fear of you, *Zhao* ,” she hissed. “I know everything about you. You take joy in inflicting pain on others because you’re absolutely petrified of facing it yourself. You think that if you attack the weak and pretend to be strong, you’ll avoid pain.” A bead of blood fell from his neck. “But you’ve already done your worst to me, and I *survived* .” She ran her hand through her hair. “What do you do with an opponent who you have no power over, one who laughs in the face of pain?” She smirked viciously at him. “You are the Master of Pain, after all. What are you going to do when you have to face some of that pain yourself?” She leaned in closely. “I will make you feel *every ounce* of pain that you inflicted upon me, and when I am finished with you, you will be so weak that you won’t be able to lift a finger to fight back.”

Let him feel the weakness that he had forced onto her. “You made me helpless. You made me the victim. *No one* makes me the victim. So now, you are going to pay with your *pride* and your *life* .”

“I won’t!” cried Zhao, leaning forward and swinging his sword at her. Azula didn’t have time to think; instinctively, she ducked under his swinging blade and swung her dagger up towards his shoulder. Still in motion, she didn’t see it pierce his skin, but it was covered in blood the next time it returned to her hand.

Zhao’s sword clattered to the stone twenty feet below them, and he dropped to the floor, clutching his left shoulder, which was bleeding.

Azula rolled her eyes, pointing her blood-covered dagger at him. “Is your pain tolerance really so low? You gave me a nearly identical wound not ten minutes ago, and here I am.” She laughed. “Pathetic.”

In response, Zhao’s eyes rolled back into his head, and he fell down at her feet. Azula didn’t even need to feel his pulse; his skin was already ice-cold.

She dropped her dagger in shock, and it fell right next to his head.

“Azula?” said Zuko’s voice from behind her. “What’s going on?”

Eyes wide, hands shaking in shock, she turned to face him. He and Sokka were standing side by side on the end of the ledge. “I...I don’t know. I didn’t stab him lethally, I just cut his shoulder, but now...he’s dead. I don’t know how it happened.”

She hated Zhao with a passion. She had thought this would feel different.

“Let me see that,” said Sokka, gesturing to her dagger. She handed it to him, and he examined it closely, frowning. “When was the last time you saw this?”

“I gave it to Katara yesterday,” said Azula. “She had it until she gave it back to me today. Said she never lost sight of it. Why?”

“Because,” said Sokka, frowning with worry, “Azula, the blade of your dagger was poisoned.”
