## Chapter 36: The Affair at the Victory Ball

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

The White Lotus throws yet another party, and although everyone agrees that the parties are getting old, they're in for a surprising evening.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Blood, shooting, guns, physical restraint, threats, knives, cutting.

We're getting into the last stretch of chapters, and I'm so excited! Hopefully you'll find them all worth the buildup. Happy reading:)

### Text

Zuko didn’t stumble out of bed until eleven the next morning, and it was only the sound of his ringing phone that woke him up in the first place. Still rubbing the grogginess from his eyes, he groaned and made his way over to the phone. Azula was still asleep in the next room, so he tried not to make too much noise.

“Hello?”  
“I hear you pulled off an impressive rescue mission last night, Detective Zuko.”

Zuko sighed. “Uncle, I’m really exhausted. Is this important?”

“I only wanted to congratulate you. When I asked you to take this case, I had no idea how much progress you would make. But you have been instrumental not only in solving Pakku’s murder, but the entire string of murders that have followed it. You should be incredibly proud of yourself.”

Zuko’s mind flashed to the strange notes. “It’s not over yet, Uncle,” he sighed, sinking down into one of his chairs. “If you count the poison on Azula’s dagger as a murder, three of these murders are still unaccounted for, and we still don’t know who hired all of these people. Whoever did that is the real threat.”

“You are not giving yourself enough credit for what you have accomplished already,” replied Iroh. “The adventure may not be over yet, but all of you have done so much. The White Lotus will forever be grateful for the help you have given us.”

Zuko thought of the White Lotus’s box of secrets and sighed. “I don’t want the White Lotus to be grateful to me, Uncle. I don’t want to be connected to everything you’ve done. Not like that.”

“I see.” Zuko could hear the hurt in Iroh’s voice. After a moment, “Do you still wish to be connected to me?”

Zuko smiled. “Of course, Uncle.” He wouldn’t have admitted it a few weeks ago, but the more he worked on this case, the more he felt like he was becoming the center of a team. More people were likely to get hurt, but there was something about it (Zuko couldn’t quite put his finger on what it was) that made it *so* much better than working alone. Maybe that made him selfish. “Are you...the rest of the White Lotus, that is, doing okay? I know the whole thing with Piandao must have been a shock for all of you.”

As he spoke, Azula wandered out of her room, wearing an oversized red sweater, a short black skirt, tights, and black boots. She threw on a red corduroy coat and a black beret (her hair was in a half-ponytail again) and waved at him before disappearing out the door. Zuko briefly wondered where she was going before turning his attention back to the phone.

“It was a shock, indeed,” Iroh was saying, “but the White Lotus has always been strong. The three of us who remain now have an enormous amount of resources in our possession. We intend to remain united, and distribute them to the city.”

Zuko smiled. “I think that sounds like a perfect idea, Uncle.”

“Of course, that doesn’t mean there won’t be room for *some* fun,” chuckled Iroh. “What’s life without a little amusement, after all?”

Zuko groaned. He’d only *just* started getting some of his energy back. So much for that. “You’re throwing another party again, aren’t you?”

“The whole city will be invited!” chirped Iroh. “Even those who used to reside under the control of the Dai Li! This party will represent a clean slate for us all. And it would truly mean the world to me if you would come.”

“You could have just started with that,” replied Zuko.

“And miss the chance to compliment my nephew on his accomplishments? Never.”

Zuko laughed. “Thanks, Uncle.”

As Zuko hung up the phone, Azula walked back into the apartment, her face flushed from the October cold. She was carrying two coffee cups, and placed one in front of Zuko before hanging up her coat and sliding into the chair across from him.

“Who was brave enough to call you so early?”

“Azula, it’s eleven-thirty in the morning. That’s not that early.”

Azula rolled her eyes. “That depends on your perception of time. Anyway, the coffee shop down your street carries an insane amount of overly complicated flavors.”

“And they’re *really good* ,” replied Zuko defensively, taking a sip of his drink. He blinked. “How did you know that caramel was my favorite?”

“Katara told me,” replied Azula. “I think she knows the coffee preferences of half the people in this city.”

“Yeah,” muttered Zuko, taking another sip. The drink was overly sweet in the best possible way. He glanced over at Azula, who was drinking with her eyes closed, something she didn’t normally do. “What did you order?”

Azula’s face flushed bright red, and she was suddenly having a very hard time looking Zuko in the eye. “Pumpkin spice,” she mumbled, taking another enormous sip and nearly choking on it. Zuko laughed. “No way,” he snickered. “You’re telling me that *Azula-queen-of-no-sugar* likes *pumpkin spice* ? What would the world say?”

“It’s a recently acquired taste,” snapped Azula, now pointedly refusing to look at him. “Anyway, you still haven’t answered my question. Who was calling you?”

“Oh, it was just Uncle,” replied Zuko, as he grabbed two apples from the kitchen. “The White Lotus is having a party tonight. We’re invited.”

“ *Another* one?” said Azula. “They must have an *insanely large* amount of money if they can afford that mansion *and* all of those parties.”

“They really do,” muttered Zuko, biting the apple. “Anyway, will you come?”

“Are you kidding?” replied Azula. “As if I’d miss a chance to wear that suit I bought yesterday to an actual party.”

“For something you bought in two minutes, it fits you weirdly well.”

“What can I say? It’s a gift.”

“This party feels strange,” Katara said to Yue, as they spun around the White Lotus’s ballroom. Even though she usually liked parties and dancing, Katara couldn’t help but feel like she’d done enough dancing in this ballroom to fill an entire lifetime.

“What about it?” asked Yue, as she twirled her around. Tonight, as opposed to one of her long dresses, she was wearing a jumpsuit. It was white, with thin threads of silver woven throughout, making it appear to sparkle like snow. Her hair was also different; instead of her usual complicated braids, she wore it in a simple braided coil at the base of her neck. She looked terrific (in Katara’s opinion, at least.) “Us dancing? Is that weird?”

“No, silly!” laughed Katara, playfully poking her in the arm. “That’s the *best* part! And I don’t know exactly why it feels strange. There are more people here than usual, but it feels...empty, I guess.”

“We’re missing a lot of really important people,” replied Yue, and Katara nodded. She hadn’t even really known any of the murder victims, yet she felt the weight of their deaths on her shoulders constantly. Did that make her weird? She wasn’t sure.

She let out a laugh of surprise as Yue spun her around. Katara felt her deep indigo velvet dress swirling around her legs, before the heavy fabric nearly made her trip. Yue’s arms wrapped around her waist before she could fall, though, and they continued twirling through the ballroom, giggling.

“That was completely your fault,” laughed Katara. “I’ll get my revenge on you soon.”

“First, you need to learn how to dance.”

Katara’s mouth dropped open as she feigned shock. “Yue of the White Lotus, did you just imply that I am incapable of dancing?”

“I don’t know.” Yue was having a hard time keeping herself from giggling. “We’ll have to see, won’t we?”

Katara smiled, and squeezed Yue’s hands tightly before giving her a quick kiss on the cheek. “I’ll dance with you any day.”

Was it a cheesy line? Absolutely. Did Katara give a fuck? Absolutely not.

“This party is stupid,” said Mai as she took a sip of champagne. She wore a simple black tuxedo with dark red accents, and even though it looked sort of like something a magician from a children’s birthday party would wear, no one could say that she was anything less than completely iconic in it.

“Why do you think that?” asked Suki, who was also wearing a suit, but hers was more form fitting, and it was pale green with gold flowers. A gold flower also pinned her short hair into a sort of bun. “I think it’s kind of nice.” She could have taken Mai’s presumed hatred for the party personally, but she knew better than that.

“Talking to *you* isn’t so bad,” said Mai, which made Suki laugh. “But the rest of this is just one big act. As far as I’m concerned, it’s just three old guys inviting a bunch of people who hate each other into their house so that they can celebrate someone else’s work and run from their problems.”

Suki was so surprised at Mai’s blunt comment (though she really shouldn’t have been) that water flew out of her mouth and onto the floor.

The two girls looked at each other for a short moment before bursting into laughter. Suki hadn’t laughed so hard in a really, *really* long time.

“I had no idea you could be so *undisciplined* ,” said Mai in a fake haughty voice that only made Suki laugh more.

“I had no idea you could be so brutal,” replied Suki. “Wait. Yes I did.”

Mai smirked. “There are a lot of things you don’t know about me. You probably still think I’m a bitch who hates everything and is no fun to be around.”

Suki took another sip of water, smiling. “Oh, absolutely. And you probably still think I’m a stick-in-the-mud with no sense of humor who lives for social events and following the rules.”

“Definitely,” replied Mai. The two girls smiled at each other for a moment before bursting into laughter again.

“I guess there were a lot of things we didn’t know about each other when we started working on this case,” said Suki after they finished laughing. Slowly, she let her eyes wander upwards to meet Mai’s. “I’m really glad we did, though.”

“Me too,” replied Mai.

“You? Happy about something?”

“Shut up!” replied Mai. “I can be happy about important things! There just aren’t a lot of them.”

“Aaw,” giggled Suki, reaching over and taking a sip out of Mai’s champagne glass. “I’m an important thing!”

“Of course you are,” said Mai, in a tone so serious that it caught Suki off guard. “You came and rescued me from eternal boredom. Well, prison, at least. That doesn’t exactly mean nothing to me. And neither do you.”

Suki could feel the heat rising through her face as she sipped her water, trying to think of something to say. It didn’t work.

Instead, she threw out her hand, so aggressively that it nearly knocked Mai’s glass onto the floor. “Sorry!” she spluttered, coughing on some of her own water. “I didn’t mean to do that. What I was *trying* to say is...do you want to dance with me?” It was the question she’d wanted to ask Mai the first time she’d been at a White Lotus party, days ago, so it was about time.

Mai smiled. “I hope you brought your dancing shoes, because you’re about to be severely shown up.”

“I wouldn’t be so sure of that,” replied Suki, still laughing as she took Mai’s arm and they walked together out onto the dance floor.

“I swear I’m getting better at this,” muttered Azula, as she tried to imitate one of Ty Lee’s complicated spins for the tenth time, and only ended up tripping over her own feet. “Or...perhaps not so much.”  
“I think you are!” said Ty Lee. Due to the night’s cold weather, she was wearing a dress with long sleeves. Instead of her usual pink, it was bright red, with a high neckline and colorful fall leaves embroidered all over it. Her hair was out of its braid and tumbling down her back in waves, and if Azula was being honest, perhaps part of the reason she was having a hard time with Ty Lee’s complicated spins was because she was having a hard time keeping her eyes off of Ty Lee herself.

She was quite the disaster, it seemed. What had she become?

Whatever it was, she liked the feeling.

“Okay,” laughed Ty Lee, moving forward and wrapping her arms around Azula’s waist. “No more spinning, I promise. We’ll just dance. Follow my lead.”

“I never got the chance to properly thank you,” said Azula as they began to spin. “For last night, that is. What you said, and…” her face turned a violent shade of red “what you did really made me feel better. But if...if you want to re-discuss it, or if you don’t want to be ‘girlfriends,’ or if it was only to make me feel better, I do understand, I just…”

Just like the night before, she was interrupted when Ty Lee leaned in and kissed her. From somewhere to her left, she heard squealing and giggling that sounded suspiciously like Katara and Yue.

“I want to make a rule,” said Ty Lee after they broke apart. Azula still felt like her face was on fire. “No more second-guessing, or self-deprecation, or thinking you don’t deserve this. Not when we’re talking about us.” She leaned in more closely. “You mean a lot to me, Azula. This makes me *really* happy, and if it makes you happy, too, then you deserve it. I want this to work. Us, I mean. I want us to work.”

“Me too,” replied Azula, and then, without thinking, she leaned in and kissed Ty Lee. She still hadn’t gotten over the fact that *this was something they could actually do now* because *they were* *girlfriends* and *Ty Lee actually felt the same way about Azula that Azula felt about her.*

Even with the murder and the torture and the fear surrounding them, it made Azula feel like she was on Cloud Nine.

“Oh!” cried Ty Lee, as a fast song came on, and the crowd began to collectively leap and twist around them. “I almost forgot! I found you something!” She rummaged in the pocket of her gown (yes, her gown had pockets, and that fact in itself was spectacular), until she pulled out a bright red leaf. “I found this outside earlier today, and I know it’s a leaf, which I guess is sort of dumb, but it was such a bright red, and the color reminded me of you, so I brought it home.” Seeing Azula staring at it, she blushed and looked away. “If you don’t like it, I can always keep it.”

“Stop it!” snapped Azula, perhaps a little more angrily than she’d originally intended. “I’m just...not used to receiving gifts, that’s all.” She gently pulled the leaf from Ty Lee’s hand and placed it in her hair. She had worn it completely down tonight, even with the choppy bangs, so there wasn’t really much to keep the leaf in place, but it stayed behind her ear. “It’s absolutely perfect.”

“It matches my dress,” said Ty Lee. “Not that that means anything.”

“Is that so?” said Azula with a slight smirk. It was nice to see that she wasn’t the only one who was a bit nervous. “Well then, that makes me like it even more.”

“Hey,” said Zuko, walking over to Sokka, who was leaning against a pillar. Sokka turned away. He didn’t feel like talking to anyone, but Zuko didn’t go away. “Are you okay?”

“I’m perfectly fine,” said Sokka, but even he could hear how flat and quiet his voice sounded. It didn’t take a detective to figure out that he wasn’t fine.

“No you’re not,” said Zuko, reaching over and squeezing his hand. Sokka’s eyes widened, but instead of letting go, Zuko kept his hand there instead, which only made Sokka feel worse. How was he supposed to fight crime if he got so nervous over *this* ?

“Come on,” said Zuko. “Come to the food table with me. They have caramel apples.”

Damn it. Zuko knew Sokka too well. If there was one thing he couldn’t resist, it was a really good caramel apple. “Fine,” sighed Sokka, as he allowed Zuko to lead him over to the food table. It was sort of funny to see caramel apples and pumpkin pie sitting next to the White Lotus’s usual array of fancy-looking hors d’œuvres that never tasted as good as they looked.

Sokka took a caramel apple and began crunching away. If nothing else, at least sugar still tasted good.

Before he could get too many bites in, though, Zuko reached over and snatched the apple out of his hand.

“Hey!” cried Sokka. “If you wanted a caramel apple, you should have gotten your own!” He tried to grab it, but Zuko was slightly taller, and held it up just out of his reach.

“You don’t get this back until you tell me what’s wrong.”

“Fine,” said Sokka after a moment, dragging Zuko over to a pillar where not as many people could hear them. “But you have to promise not to tell anyone. It’s *really* embarrassing.”

“Sokka,” said Zuko, staring right into his eyes. In this lighting, Zuko’s amber-colored eyes looked like liquid, and the longer Sokka stared into them, the more the amber liquid seemed to ripple, and the harder it was to look away. “Nothing you say to me could ever be too embarrassing.”

“Okay,” grumbled Sokka, taking a deep breath. “The truth is...I’m really scared. After what happened last night, I just...don’t feel safe anymore. Anywhere. I thought I was just in the White Lotus mansion, but Piandao knocked me out *in the coat closet* and almost froze me to death. It just...feels like these murders are gonna follow me wherever I go.”

“That’s not stupid at all,” said Zuko after a moment. “It’s fair. It’s impossible not to feel like that after something like that happens to you.”

“Then what do I do?” sighed Sokka. “You’re my best friend. You’re...more than that,” he finished softly. “I want to help you, more than anything else, but I can’t work on this case with you if I’m just *scared* all the time. It doesn’t feel right.”

“First of all,” said Zuko, “you don’t have to work on the case for me to like you. I will never, *ever* ask you to put yourself in danger, and no amount of playing it safe or being cautious will ever stop me from being your friend. Second of all, it’s normal to be scared like this. The important thing is remembering everyone who’s gonna be there to protect you no matter what.” He gave Sokka a gentle squeeze on the arm. “We came after you for a reason, Sokka. We’re never going to leave you behind.” He paused, looking away, his face flushing. “ *I’m* never going to leave you behind,” he said after a moment.”

Sokka felt his face flushing, too, and decided to take a giant bite of the caramel apple Zuko had given back to him to stop it. “Hey,” he said when he finished chewing, “that almost sounded like a pep talk.”

“I’m getting better at them,” replied Zuko. “And do not claim that it is the magical properties of caramel lattes. We both know it isn’t.”

“There is no scientific evidence to prove that it isn’t.”

Zuko was just pulling Sokka to his feet when there was an enormous crash at the top of the staircase, and the entire window exploded into millions of tiny shards of glass.

“Not again!” cried Sokka, as a shadow leapt from the window, the room dissolved into chaos, and they ducked underneath a table.

From his viewpoint under the table, Zuko could see a figure hurrying down the stairs, but the figure had a gun, and was shooting out all the lights. Zuko couldn’t make out who was attacking them, but he moved closer anyway.

“What are you doing?” hissed Sokka from behind him. “Do you have a death wish?”

“The last time someone tried something like this, she turned into our biggest source of information,” replied Zuko. “This could get us the last few pieces of the puzzle.” He turned to Sokka. “If we catch whoever this is, we could solve this case for good.”

Unfortunately, the more lights the attacker shot out, the darker the room became, and the harder it was to see where the next bullet was coming from. Zuko could hear screaming coming from all sides as he ran from table to table. All he could do was hope that he stayed out of range of the shooter.

He and Sokka came to a stop at a table near the gym doors, and peered out at the party. Most of the crowd had managed to escape, but the room was a disaster. Tables had been knocked over, shattered glass from the window and the lights covered the floor, and Zuko thought he saw blood pooling under one of the tables, though that could have just as easily been wine. In the darkness, it was impossible to tell.

He could make out a few smaller figures darting from table to table, as well as a few larger ones darting out into the open, probably trying to bait the attacker. He had no idea who they were, and, even more concerningly, he had no idea where the attacker was.

“What do we do now?” hissed Sokka. “How are we supposed to find our information if we can’t see anything? Did you think this through?”

“Definitely,” replied Zuko, lying through his teeth. “I’m just waiting for the right moment.”

“Well, I suppose you won’t have to wait much longer,” hissed a slightly familiar voice from above them. Sokka screamed as there was an enormous *thud* on the table. Zuko ducked and rolled away from the table as fast as he could, but Sokka wasn’t so lucky. Before either of them could do anything, the figure on top of the table flipped the table over, pinning Sokka between the table and the wall. Sokka struggled to free himself, but the attacker simply dragged him away from the table. Zuko could make out the outline of a gun to his head, even in the darkness. He froze, not daring to move another step. He was close enough that he could hear Sokka’s breathing, and it was growing quicker and shallower the longer the attacker held him still.

“Hands off my brother!” yelled Katara’s voice, and before Zuko could do anything, the journalist came sprinting out of the darkness, holding something heavy-looking in her hands. The attacker fired the gun, but Katara was quicker, knocking his arm away from Sokka so that the gun fired up to the ceiling. Sokka dropped to the floor, and Zuko grabbed his wrist and yanked him away from the attacker before they could grab him again.

The attacker turned towards Katara and raised their pistol, but Katara was quicker, raising whatever heavy thing she was holding up in the air and smashing it over their head. The attacker crumpled to the floor and lay still.

Slowly, the shadowy figures of the party guests emerged from behind pillars and under tables. Some of them grabbed torches from the walls. Zuko could see Azula, Ty Lee, Mai, Suki, Toph, Aang, Yue, Iroh, Jeong Jeong (who was bleeding; he’d been shot in the shoulder, Zuko realized), and Bumi. Katara stepped back from the attacker, and, in the torchlight, Zuko realized that she was holding an enormous vase. The flowers it had been holding were now strewn all over the floor.

Azula, who was carrying a torch, raced over to them and held the torch up to the attacker’s face. Katara let out a gasp and nearly dropped the heavy vase she was still holding.

“Who is it?” said Toph from behind them, as the crowd began to murmur, some of them even letting out little shrieks of shock.

Zuko turned back to the familiar face of their attacker. He’d thought he’d never have to see this face again, that he’d been locked away for good. But somehow, he was here.

“It’s Long Feng.”

“Tell us everything you know,” Zuko said to Long Feng the second he regained consciousness. They had dragged him upstairs and made sure he was securely tied to a chair before escorting the rest of the party guests out, and sending Bumi and Jeong Jeong off to the hospital. Only Iroh, Zuko, Azula, Katara, and Sokka remained in the interrogation room with Long Feng. Personally, Azula thought that the room was still rather crowded, but it wasn’t as though she could complain about it.

“Or what?” murmured Long Feng. Azula hadn’t seen him since he’d taken her prisoner, and the sound of his voice both terrified her and made her so furious that it felt like lightning was running through her veins instead of blood. “What will you do to me if I do not reveal my deepest secrets?”

“Worse things than you might think,” replied Zuko, digging his nails into the desk so hard that they left scratches in the wood. “I have *not* forgiven you for what you and your people did to my friends and my sister. You don’t want to test me when I’m angry.”

“Yes, yes,” said Long Feng, sounding bored. “I’m sure you’re very intimidating when you’re furious. But the fact is, I’ve already been arrested. I’m already going to spend the rest of my life in prison. There is nothing left for me to fear, and the only things that are horrible enough to fear, you’re too heroic and noble to actually do. So, forgive me for saying this, but it seems to me as though you are stuck.”

“You’re right,” said Azula, ignoring the fear bubbling inside of her chest and stepping forward, holding her dagger out in front of her and pressing the point to Long Feng’s throat. Like when she had fought Zhao, being in the position of power against Long Feng felt euphoric, as though she was reclaiming an important piece of herself that he had stolen. “He *is* too heroic to kill you, or torture you. But I’m not.” She leaned in closer and pressed the blade to his face, leaving a cut identical to her own. “How does that feel?” she hissed.

Long Feng laughed. “You forget that I know you, Azula,” he said in his slithery voice. “You’re impeccable at making threats, but you never follow through on them. You’re just as weak as the rest of them, no matter how hard you try to pretend you aren’t.”

“Is that so?” replied Azula, leaving a matching cut on the other side of his face to match her own. “I still have *blood* on my *face* from what you did to me, Long Feng. I am very, *very* furious with you right now.” She paused, toying with her choppy bangs. “Let me tell you a bit about myself, Long Feng. I was raised in a house where you had to be brutal and manipulative just to *survive* . I have *never* been given anything since the day I was born; I had to work myself to the very bone just to have a chance at life. You tried to *break me* , and you think I’ll be *merciful* with you?” She laughed, slicing his chin, leaving yet another cut that matched her own. “Think again.”

“You wouldn’t kill me,” said Long Feng, though his voice was beginning to quaver now. “You wouldn’t dare.”

“Want to make a bet on that?” snapped Azula. She took a seat across from him and leaned back in the chair, toying with her dagger. “You may think you control everyone, but I understand you. You were born without power, without safety, so you built up an entire organization to protect yourself. You claimed to want order, you claimed to want peace, but really, you just wanted control, so that you’d never have to feel unstable again. You made sure you could control every last person in the city.” She leaned in closer. “But there’s a problem with that little plan of yours. You relied on your organization to maintain your control. What will you be without your guards, your loyal soldiers, your Mechanist, or your Master of Pain?” She laughed. “You’ll be absolutely nothing, that’s what.” She tossed her dagger up into the air, and it landed point-down on the desk, sticking into the wood like a dart. “You never know. It’s possible that there are small traces of poison left on this blade. You could be dead within minutes.” She picked her dagger up, and pressed it to his throat again. “If I were you, reduced to nothing, I would want to take credit for my accomplishments before the rest of my life was stripped away, one way or another.” She drove the blade into his left shoulder, the same place where she had stabbed Zhao. “So, how about you tell my brother everything you know?”

Long Feng glared at her for a moment, then let out a sigh. “You should take up crime,” he spat at her. “You’re a formidable opponent.”

“Oh, please,” laughed Azula. “We’re not even in the same league.”

The room fell silent, and she realized that everyone was staring at her. “What?” She turned to them. “Oh, come on, I was only attempting to help with the job. I wasn’t actually going to kill him...though I still could,” she added quickly, turning to Long Feng.

Zuko shook his head at her, but thankfully said nothing else, instead stepping forward and turning his attention to Long Feng. “How did you escape from jail?”

“I paid off the guards,” Long Feng replied smoothly. “It’s funny how easy it is to manipulate those who used to be under your command and control.”

“Were you responsible for any of the three unsolved murders that took place over the past two weeks?” asked Zuko.

Long Feng paused. “Tell the truth,” Azula reminded him. “It won’t end very well for you if you don’t.”

Long Feng gave them a vicious smirk, and in spite of herself, Azula felt a shiver run down her spine. “I was responsible for *all* of them.”

Zuko’s eyes widened, and even Azula was surprised, though she did her best not to show it. “ *You* wrote those notes.”

“Indeed,” replied Long Feng, his voice slithering into Azula’s ears like a basilisk. “I hired several assassins to pick off members of the White Lotus. I hired even more assassins to kill members of the Dai Li I deemed inadequate, and to cover my own tracks. I even carried out a few murders myself. *I* sent Hama the orders to kill Pakku, and later, Professor Zei, I snuck into this very mansion the next day and pushed poor Fung off a balcony, I manipulated Arnook, Jet, and Piandao into murdering useless members of my own organization, I sent my own Master of Pain, Zhao, to murder that miserable sack of a man, Yon Rha, and when he discovered my plan in full, I poisoned that knife you’re holding while your friend had it at Lake Laogai. She didn’t even notice.” He laughed. “I planned to lead her to him, but then you escaped from me, and she returned it to you. It seemed the universe was on my side after all.”

“It’s a dagger,” replied Azula coldly, not allowing any of her surprise to show itself in her expression. “Not a knife.”

“Why would you do this?” snapped Zuko. “Why would you murder so many people? Why would you wrap so many people up in your scheme?”

“Because,” laughed Long Feng, “every single person I roped into this is a blight on this city. And now, everyone I wanted gone is either dead or locked away. You may be a master detective, but I was always two steps ahead of you.” He threw his head back and laughed, and Azula had to concentrate very hard to stop her hands from shaking. “You may have caught me in the end, but I’ve still won.”

## Chapter 37: The Man in the Mist

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

It seems that all is finally well in Ba Sing Se, but Azula and Zuko aren't convinced, and it seems they're not the only ones.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Poison, confined spaces.

Double-chapter day! Hopefully, you'll be getting a LOT of chapters tomorrow! Let's hope I finish in time, but if not, they should all be here within the next few days. Also I start school tomorrow, and it's a new school, so wish me luck, and happy reading:)

### Text

“Can you believe this?” cried Katara, as the entire group sat in Zuko’s apartment the next morning. Somebody (Zuko still didn’t know who) had brought a basket of breakfast pastries that was at least twice the size of Zuko’s head, and everyone had chosen a different kind, which was kind of weird and also made perfect sense.

“Believe what?” asked Yue, who was eating a lemon-poppy seed muffin and somehow managed not to get any crumbs on anything.

“That everything is over!” sighed Katara happily, taking a bite out of her carrot-cream cheese muffin (it was weird, but it was also strangely good.) “It’s been so long since I’ve felt safe, you know?” she said with her mouth full, something that was so unlike Katara that Zuko almost dropped his cranberry scone on the floor.

“I don’t know what you’ve been up to!” laughed Toph, who, in direct contrast to Yue and Katara, was eating a cherry danish and had cherry jam all over her face and hands, “ *I’ve* felt safe this entire time! *I* can protect *myself* !”

The combination of her purposely snotty tone and the cherry jam all over her body made the entire group burst into laughter. Looking at everyone around the table, chomping on sugary breakfasts, drinking coffee and tea, laughing and chatting, without death hanging over their heads, Zuko felt *right* somehow. Like this was how they were always supposed to be.

And yet, he couldn’t shake the feeling that something was wrong. That this murder spree had been wrapped up a little *too* quickly and neatly.

Zuko tried to shove the thoughts out of his mind. He was just used to constantly being alone, working case after case. He’d never had a group of friends like this before, nor had he ever handled such a big case. He was probably just a little paranoid.

The thoughts refused to leave his mind, no matter how hard he tried.

“Zuko?” came Sokka’s voice from across the table. “What’s wrong?”

All at once, the entire group was staring at him. Zuko felt beads of sweat forming on his forehead. Everyone at the table was truly happy for the first time in weeks, and Zuko couldn’t find it in himself to take that away from them. But if he was right, the consequences of hiding it would be much worse.

“Do you guys...feel like everything was a little *too* perfect?” He tried to keep his tone light and slightly joking, but it didn’t really work.

“Are you serious?” said Suki. “Zuko, more than eight people are dead, there was a web of assassins hired through a system of cryptically written notes, the last of whom just left the city on a train this morning, and we only caught the person behind it all last night. I wouldn’t call that *too* *perfect* .” Her tone was slightly scornful. “We fought tooth and nail to solve this case, Zuko. Some of us almost *died* .” She squeezed Mai’s hand. “Nothing about this was perfect.”

“I’m sorry,” Zuko said quickly. This was exactly why he hadn’t wanted to say anything in the first place. “I didn’t mean that we didn’t struggle. I just...never mind.”

The group stared at him for one more excruciating moment before going back to their breakfast pastries and idle chatter. Only Azula’s eyes remained fixated on him, her gaze piercing, just like it always was. Zuko could feel her looking at him even when he was turned away from her.

Still, he tried to ignore it and focus on counting the cranberries in his scone instead. Snippets of conversation reached his ears from time to time, and he always tried not to eavesdrop, with very mixed results each time.

“Maybe sometime, I can go to a party with you without being attacked,” he heard Katara say to Yue. “I don’t think we’ve ever finished a dance.”

“We’ll have to fix that,” Yue replied. “I still need proof that you’re capable of dancing.”

Zuko wasn’t looking at them, but he could picture the sentimental looks on their faces in his mind.

“I look forward to proving it to you,” replied Katara, and their conversation quickly dissolved into laughter and whispers, the words of which Zuko couldn’t make out.

“I don’t understand how you can eat that!” came Toph’s voice from Zuko’s right. She was talking to Mai, Zuko thought. “There’s no goo or bright red stuff to get all over your hands! That’s the best part of stuff like this!”

“No,” replied Mai in a bored but amused tone. “The best part of stuff like this is eating food that tastes good. Like my chocolate chip scone.”

“Scones taste like wax paper!”

“It’s a matter of opinion.”

“No it isn’t! It’s an objective fact!”

“Suki, can you weigh in on this?” said Mai. “Toph is sharing several things that are completely wrong. I thought you might want to fix it.”

“Sorry, Toph,” said Suki. “I’m with Mai on this one. I think scones are really good.”

“You’re just saying that because she’s your girlfriend!”

Suki scoffed. “I liked scones before Mai and I started dating. What, do you think I had no personality before that?”

“Pretty much,” replied Toph, taking a purposely loud slurp of coffee.

Suki laughed. “Well, then, I guess nobody knows me well enough.”

“I’d like to get to know you better!” chimed in Aang’s voice. Zuko hadn’t even realized that Aang was sitting next to the three of them. Maybe he was more lost in thought than he’d realized.

“You sure you’re okay?” asked Sokka, sliding into the seat next to him, and bringing his attention away from the surrounding conversations. “You never really finished what you were going to say earlier.”

“You’re going to hate me for this,” muttered Zuko. “I’m sorry.”

“Nothing could make me hate you,” replied Sokka, much more earnestly than Zuko had been expecting.

Zuko sighed. “Fine. You asked for it.” He took a deep breath. “I can’t explain it, not really, but something just feels….off to me. LIke this case was all tied up *too* neatly, *too* easily, *too* quickly. I feel like we’re still missing a piece of the puzzle, and the longer we wait, the further away it gets.”

“Zuko,” said Sokka, reaching over and gently taking his wrists, “I get it. It’s got to feel like a letdown to be finished after working on this case for so long. And after all these twists and turns, it’s normal to anticipate another one. But Long Feng confessed to being behind everything. There’s no reason to be scared about this anymore. You can focus on...other things.” His face darkened at the very end, and Zuko could feel his hands on his wrists.

Zuko sighed. Sokka was right. There was so much else to do, to focus on, to experiment with. There was more crime in the city that needed to be stopped. He couldn’t stay fixated on this case forever.

“You’re right,” he said, taking a sip of tea. “It’s not good for me to be hung up on this case forever. I need to start moving on.

“That’s the spirit!” said Sokka enthusiastically, clapping him on the back so hard that Zuko nearly spit out his tea.

“For the record,” Azula said to her brother after the rest of the group had left (and Ty Lee, promising to call later, had left Azula with a blushing face yet again), “I agree with you.”

Zuko seemed tired as he leaned back in the armchair and munched on a leftover scone. “About what?”

“About the case being solved too perfectly.”

Zuko blinked, sitting up. “You do? Everyone else thinks I’m just being paranoid. Even *I* sort of think that.”

“It’s possible,” replied Azula, taking a sip of coffee, “mathematically likely, even. But this is a *feeling* that you have, and I have. This is Long Feng we’re talking about. The torturer, the manipulator, the organizer.”

“And your point is?”

Azula took another sip of coffee. “My point is that we got that confession out of him far too easily.”

“You did threaten his life.”

“Yes,” said Azula. “But it still feels...odd somehow.”

“He didn’t have to confess to being behind all of the other assassinations,” mused Zuko. “He was already going to jail for life for tortute and keeping so many secret prisons and experiments. He didn’t have to confess to anything at all, and *especially* not anything more than the two murders he committed himself. So why would he? Unless…”

“Unless what?”

Zuko looked Azula in the eye. “Unless someone else asked him to.”

“To cover their tracks, you mean?”

Zuko nodded, taking a sip of tea. “Exactly.”

“And if we’re correct, what do we do about that?” asked Azula.

“We do what we’ve always done. Interrogate the suspects, go over the evidence, and come up with theories.”

“I look forward to it.” Azula smiled slightly wryly.

Zuko blinked at her. “You mean you’ll come with me?”

“Why wouldn’t I?”

Zuko sighed. “It won’t be the same from here on out. The whole city thinks that this case is already solved. If we keep going, people are going to think we’re crazy, and we won’t have the support of the White Lotus anymore. We’ll be the only person on this killer’s trail…”

“If there even is another killer.”

“So the killer will be much more aware of us.”

“And more likely to see us as a threat and attack us,” finished Azula, finally putting all of the pieces together. “I understand.”

“But you’re coming?” asked Zuko, holding the door open.

Azula paused. She could walk away from these mysteries, from the danger, from hiding her secrets, from this dangerous, messy thing she was becoming. She could walk away from it at any moment.

She walked through the open front door instead.

“Where are we going again?” asked Azula as they rode the train through the Middle Ring to the Upper Ring. She was so familiar with this particular train line that she probably could have made a map of it with her eyes closed at this point.

Zuko stared at his notepad, where he had notes on every arrested murder suspect. “I checked, and all of the convicted assassins have been moved to the police station closest to the White Lotus mansion. They’re being held there and interrogated, but if we want to see them, this is how we do it.”

“Excellent,” replied Azula, leaning over and glancing at his hand-drawn map. “Wow. You have quite a talent for making maps.”

“I prefer fighting crime,” said Zuko irritably.

Azula blinked. “Why are you angry? That was a compliment.”

Zuko rolled his eyes. “Making maps isn’t a real job, Azula. If you don’t think I can do anything, just tell me.”

Azula’s eyes were wide with concern. “Zuko, I know it’s hard not to assume the worst of me, but please try. I truly didn’t mean to hurt you with that comment.”

Zuko sighed. She was right; he was being unfair. “I’m sorry,” he groaned. “Old habits die hard, I guess.”

“It’s all right,” said Azula, adjusting her half-ponytail so that it was absolutely perfect. “You’re not the only one.”

They eventually stepped off the train, grabbing coffee on the way to the police station. Zuko couldn’t help noticing that Azula was drinking a pumpkin drink again. “Wow, you’ve really jumped on the pumpkin spice train, haven’t you? I always thought you’d be a black coffee girl forever.”

“I am,” Azula replied rapidly, her face reddening slightly. “This is just...an exception to the rule.” She glanced at him. “Besides, who are you to judge? You only like caramel-flavored drinks because Sokka was the one who introduced them to you.”

Zuko felt his face heat up. “What? That’s not true!”

Okay, it might have been true, but Zuko wasn’t about to admit that to his sister. “I don’t even want to know what Father would say if he saw you with that.” It was something he said to Azula fairly frequently, but he kind of couldn’t help it. He still couldn’t quite wrap his head around how... *rebellious* she seemed to be becoming.

“Perhaps that’s part of why I like it so much,” quipped Azula, taking another long sip of her pumpkin spice drink.

Zuko laughed as they kept walking. Even though they were still chasing a murderer, it was nice to just walk down the city streets, enjoying the fall with his sister. For the first time ever, things between them felt almost normal. There were moments where it felt like they could have been any other pair of siblings making their way through the city and drinking coffee.

Not every moment was like that, and it probably never would be. But it was something.

The sugary coffees were long gone by the time the two of them arrived at the police station, and Zuko wished he’d brought a bottle of water, because he could still feel the artificial sweetness of the caramel coating the roof of his mouth.

“Hello?” Azula said to the receptionist. “We’re looking for the assassins involved in the most recent string of murders.” She slid a sheet of paper across the table. “These should be their cell numbers.”  
*Thank goodness for the internet,* thought Zuko.

The receptionist stared pointedly at the siblings over her horn-rimmed glasses. “I’m going to need to see some form of identification.”

Zuko pulled out his detective ID. It wasn’t exactly a real thing, but it was verified by the city, and it served as concrete proof for anyone nosy enough to ask that he was indeed a real private eye.

The receptionist (who looked so bored that Zuko thought she might drift off to sleep the second he and Azula left her alone), nodded and made a note on her clipboard. “And you?” she said to Azula.

Azula’s face turned slightly pink. “Oh, I...don’t actually have any form of ID.”

Zuko looked at her, surprised. “Not even your driver’s license?” he asked. “It’s pretty dumb to go on vacation without it.”

Dumb, and very unlike Azula. Azula never forgot anything that might be useful to her, and never anything as important and irreplaceable as a driver’s license.

“I know,” laughed Azula, looking slightly uncomfortable, though Zuko wasn’t sure why. “Pretty out-of-character for me, right? I suppose it’s my fault for catching a late bus to Ba Sing Se and staying up so late doing schoolwork that I forgot to pack.”

It wasn’t like her, that much was true, but she sounded so genuine despite her discomfort that Zuko was having a hard time *not* believing her.

“Well, Miss, I’m going to need some form of identification, otherwise you won’t be able to enter,” said the receptionist, looking more bored by the second.

Azula rummaged around in her purse for a moment, then pulled out something that looked like an ID. “This is my student ID from my school. Will this suffice?”

The receptionist stared pointedly at the ID card, then at Azula’s face, then back at the ID card again. “The girl in this photo looks very different from you, Miss.”

“That’s because that photo was taken when I was eight,” replied Azula. All traces of her earlier discomfort were gone from her face, and all that remained was her usual eerie calm. “Look at the eyes in the photograph. They’re unmistakably mine.”

The receptionist looked into Azula’s piercing, golden eyes and gulped. Zuko didn’t blame her. Even when she was in a good mood, Azula’s eyes were intimidating at best, and downright terrifying at worst. They were so golden that they looked almost...inhuman, like liquid electric fire that could come pouring out of her skull and burn you at any moment if you looked at them for too long.

Zuko had once had a nightmare as a child that a melting, golden substance had come pouring out of Azula’s eyes. It was thick and sticky and scalding hot, and it had filled the tiny room Zuko’s dream self had been standing in as he screamed.

He wasn’t sure how or why he still remembered that dream now.

“All right,” sighed the receptionist after a moment of eyeballing Azula. She handed Azula back her student ID, then yawned. “You two can go on in.”

Zuko opened the metal door, and the siblings entered into the back hallway. The hallway was dark, only lit by a couple of dim, fluorescent lights on the ceiling, and made entirely of metal. It was lined by several identical doors, each containing a tiny glass window at its center, each marked with a number.

“This entire hallway itself could be a jail cell,” mused Azula, running her fingers over the metal. “It’s quite fascinating, actually.”

“I’m sure,” murmured Zuko, not really listening as he peered through a window into one of the cells. It was empty. Odd. He glanced at the sheet in his hands. According to it, this was where Hama was supposed to be. That was weird. He ran and checked the cell next door, the cell that supposedly held Arnook. Also empty. He ran and checked the next one. Empty.

Empty, empty, empty. Azula was checking the cells on the other side of the hallway, and based on her expression, he would guess that she was reaching the same conclusion.

He was beginning to get a very, *very* bad feeling about this.

“Zuko?” Azula’s voice sounded slightly shaky as she knelt down at the other end of the hallway and picked something up. “I think you should come and see this.”

He walked over and snatched the object out of her hands. Somewhere inside his mind, he knew what it was before he really even touched it.

It was a note, written in the same sloppy handwriting as every single note that had been addressed to the assassins.

*Stay out of this, if you know what’s good for you.*

Zuko felt a chill run down his spine, just as Azula let out a shriek. He whirled around and saw pale yellow gas seeping out from one of the cell windows, which was broken (how had Zuko not noticed that before?) It was oozing slowly down the hallway towards them.

“Fluorine gas,” whispered Azula. “It’ll kill us in an instant if we don’t figure out a way to stop it.”

“You’re the one who aced high school chemistry,” he hissed back, even though he didn’t really know why they were whispering. “You can figure it out.”

“You’re the one who’s used to dealing with near-death situations!”

“We’ll work it out together!” snapped Zuko. “How do we stop this stuff from killing us both?”

“We need to stop ourselves from inhaling it!” replied Azula. “These cells should be airtight. If we can trap the gas inside one of the cells, we’ll be safe.”

Zuko looked at the gas. He looked around, searching for anything that could help them.. “Azula...there’s air circulating through here, isn’t there?”

“Yes.”  
“If that’s the case, then there has to be a vent somewhere, even if it’s covered! We just have to find it!”

Azula’s eyes widened. “If we find that, maybe the air can push the gas away from us! But how are we going to get it into a cell?”

“One of us is going to have to run and open a cell door.” He looked at her. “You’re short, and you’re quick. Do you think you can do it?”

She stared at the gas with a determined expression on her face, her golden liquid eyes gleaming. “I’ll either do it, or die trying.”

The truth of her words was a little terrifying.

Zuko looked around as the gas seeped closer. At last, he spotted it; four metal panels in the hallway ceiling, folded one over the other. “There’s the vent!” he yelled. He quickly backed up against the wall. “Jump and use my shoulders as a base!”

Azula stared at him. “Are you sure? I’m not positive I can do it without hurting you!”

“Better than dying!”

Azula nodded, then took a running leap, bounced off his shoulders (it did hurt, but not too much), and grabbed onto the metal panels. Zuko could see her fingers struggling to grip them, and her nails beginning to break. Quickly, he ran underneath her and grabbed her ankles, placing them on his shoulders for support.

After a moment, the vent flew open, and Azula fell backwards, nearly hitting her head on the wall before Zuko caught her. Both of them held their breath in anticipation.

Miraculously, a gust of wind came barreling out of the vent towards the gas, slowly pushing it down the hall, just to the left of its center.

“Run!” Zuko called to Azula, who took off sprinting towards the last cell on the right, just as the gas was beginning to ooze towards the right half of the hallway. The more the gas travelled, the faster she ran. Both of them got closer and closer, and still Zuko feared that she wouldn't be fast enough.

She reached the cell door and flung it open before sprinting back down the hallway towards Zuko, away from the gas. She nearly tripped over her own feet at the end, out of sheer exhaustion, but Zuko caught her before she could hit the ground.  
As the air from the vent blew the last of the gas into the cell, they sprinted together up the hallway and slammed the door, trapping the poison inside.

Exhausted and gasping for air, they stumbled out of the cell block as quickly as they could, collapsing against the receptionist’s desk. The receptionist, Zuko noted, was long gone.

“Do you realize what this means?” he asked Azula, after they stopped panting, and he could finally breathe again.

Azula shook her head. “In general, yes, but the specifics of what you’re thinking at this exact moment? No.”

Zuko stared at his hands, still shaking with adrenaline. “It means there’s still someone out there. Someone who’s been behind these murders all along. It wasn’t Long Feng.” He turned and looked at his sister. “And whoever it is, they know what we’re doing.”

“And they’re determined to stop us,” Azula finished.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

Thank you for reading! Azula and Zuko's teamwork in that chapter was especially fun to write.

## Chapter 38: The Edge

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula and Zuko reflect on how much things have, or haven't changed.

#### Chapter Notes

TW: Drugging, mentions of suicidal thoughts (one line.)

I am SO SORRY that this chapter is coming so late! I started school this week, and I have had absolutely no energy for writing or posting! I now have a long weekend, so hopefully I'll be able to publish the last few chapters in the next few days! These last ones are some of my very favorites! Writing the climax of all the buildup was so satisfying!

Anyway, this one was absolutely cathartic to write. Happy reading:)

### Text

“Why is it,” asked Azula as the pair of siblings arrived back at Zuko’s apartment, “that every time we come back here, we’re always absolutely exhausted?”

“Part of the job,” replied Zuko, falling onto the couch. “People who have other jobs can go to work for half the day, get a little tired, come home, recharge, and go back out. But us? We spend our days out on the streets, chasing justice, never stopping until we’ve reached our limit. We don’t have time to relax.”

“I would criticize you for being over dramatic if I didn’t understand absolutely every word coming out of your mouth,” moaned Azula as she fell into one of the armchairs.

“Azula?” Zuko wasn’t even really sure he wanted to ask, but the question had been plaguing his mind ever since Azula’s encounter with Long Feng and Zhao.

“Yes?”  
“Why are you still here?”  
Azula let out a slightly bitter laugh of disbelief. “What’s *that* supposed to mean? Do you think I’d abandon you in the middle of a case?”

“No, not like that,” Zuko said quickly. “It’s just...this is so dangerous. Look at everything that’s happened to you. Everyone else was more than happy to leave this case alone, but you’re still here. Why?” He turned to look at her. “You could have gone back home to Father any time, and been treated like a princess, and been safe from all of this death and destruction. But instead, you’re here. And I don’t understand it.”

There was a moment of silence before Azula responded, leaning back in her armchair and taking a sip of water from a glass she’d grabbed the second they’d arrived back at the apartment. “It’s not as perfect as you think. When Father suggested this vacation, I just...wondered if I could use a change. So I took the opportunity, but...I feel different here. More like *myself* than I have in a while, if that makes sense. I suppose that, for me, it’s worth the risk and the danger. For that.”

“It does,” replied Zuko, flipping over and hanging upside-down. “It’s exactly how it felt when I first came here.”

Azula blinked. “Really?”  
Zuko nodded. “Realizing that who I was didn’t depend on what other people said? Yeah, that...sort of changed everything.”

“You’re different,” said Azula after a moment. “Different from when I last saw you, I mean. You’re more confident, more sure of yourself. You have a purpose that’s important to you. I’ve never seen you like that before.”

“I’ve never seen *you* like this, either,” replied Zuko. “I don’t think you’ve even *talked* to me this much since...well, *ever* .”

“I suppose times change,” Azula said softly, giving him a small smile.

“Either that, or this city is good for us,” said Zuko.

Azula laughed. “Right. The city full of murder sprees and poisonous gases and knife-throwing assassins is good for us.”

“First of all, it’s usually not like this, and second of all, that sort of makes sense for us, doesn’t it?”

Azula burst out laughing. “I do suppose it does,” she replied, still giggling. “Only we would be improved by the city with the murder spree.”

Zuko couldn’t help smiling. He still couldn’t get over how weird it was to be this open and honest and... *normal* with his sister, but the more they talked, the more it felt like there was a part of them that was integral to who they were, and only the two of them completely understood every aspect of it. It was...nice.

Their conversation was interrupted by the phone in Zuko’s office ringing. “I’ll get it,” Zuko sighed, dragging himself off the couch. “Try not to burn down the apartment while I’m on the phone.”

“As if you’d be able to stop me if I decided to.”

As Zuko talked on the phone in the other room, Azula found herself drifting away into her thoughts.

Zuko was right. So much had *changed* since she’d gotten to Ba Sing Se. Before she’d come to the city, her entire life had felt like an endless Sisyphean task that would never be finished. Each element was under her control, and had its specific space in the routine of her day. Each day, she would get up, drain every last drop of physical and mental energy from her body, be told by her father that it wasn’t quite enough, sleep as little as possible while still maintaining her strength, and then get up and do it again.

In some ways, that routine had been comforting. She had known exactly what she needed to do every day, and she always knew where any element in her life would be at any given time. There were no surprises, except for her father’s moods, and she had long since learned how to survive those. Life had been brutal, barren, and lonely, but it had been simple.

Now, nothing was the same. Every single day brought unexpected twists and turns, and for the first time, Azula felt as though she was working towards an attainable goal, and not a far-off standard that she could never truly achieve. Those around her were there to protect her, to build her up, perhaps even to love her, if that was even possible. There wasn’t a constant, threatening force hovering over her shoulder, telling her that she wasn’t enough, wasn’t perfect, wasn’t worthy, needed to work harder, rest less, exhaust herself more.

The lack of that threat made Azula feel like a weight was lifting off her chest. It wasn’t entirely gone, but a little bit of it subsided each day, and each day, it became a little easier to speak freely, to take risks, allow for the possibility of error, open her heart, believe that others would want to enter it, believe that others would want her in their hearts.

It wasn’t a lot, and there were times when all Azula wanted was to turn back time and never come to the city. Sometimes she wanted to throw herself out the window and leave it all behind right then and there. But the more time went by, the easier it became. Azula wasn’t positive about what she was searching for, but she liked the new patterns that were starting to appear in her life. They made her feel genuine, happy, and seen.

They made her feel *human* .

She was torn out of her thoughts by the sight of Zuko walking back into the room. Instantly, she noticed that something was wrong. His skin was pale, his black hair matted, as though he’d banged his head against the wall or something like that. His eyes were flashing in anger, and his fists were clenched. He was standing stick-straight, almost as if his muscles had frozen.

Cautiously, Azula slid onto the arm of the chair. “Wow,” she said, trying to keep her tone light, “whoever called you on the phone must have really had something to say, didn’t they?”

Zuko said nothing. He just stood there, staring at her, his eyes burning, his fists clenched.

Azula felt the playful smile slide off her face. The longer Zuko stood there, the more a nagging anxiety kept poking at her brain, telling her that something was wrong, something far worse than anything that had happened to them so far.

“Zuko? Are you okay?”

Zuko let out a harsh laugh. “That’s a funny question, coming from you.” His voice was like an out-of-control flame, containing absolutely nothing but pure, unfiltered fury. “It’s not like you care.”

This Zuko was so different than he’d been not ten minutes ago that it was practically giving Azula whiplash, and she couldn’t stand it. “Stop being cryptic,” she snapped. “If you have a grievance with me, just let it out. I’m not going to pounce on you or anything.” Had she committed another social misdemeanor and been unaware of it? He seemed like he was reacting too strongly for that, but then again, it *was* Zuko.

“You lied to me.” Zuko’s voice was shaking slightly under all the layers of loathing. “You’ve been lying to me since the moment you showed up on my doorstep, two weeks ago.”

*No* .

Azula could swear her heart dropped out of her chest right then, and splattered into a bloody mess all over the floor.

“Zuko, I can explain…”

“Explain what?” snapped Zuko. “Explain why you put my life in danger? Tricked me and almost forced me to face the very thing I ran away from without even *asking* me?” He glared at her. Was he crying? “You could have told me the truth, Azula. That’s the saddest part. I could have helped you.”

“I didn’t know if you would,” admitted Azula. She couldn't bring herself to speak at anything louder than a half-whisper. “I didn’t think you’d accept me if I told you what I really needed.”

“Of course I would have!” yelled Zuko. “Because I’m a good person, Azula, and I’m not selfish, and I don’t put other people in danger just so I can get what I want! Something you’ll never understand!”

“Stop it!” cried Azula. She could feel tears beginning to prick at the corners of her eyes, and she was having trouble breathing. “I promise, I never intended to hurt you. I was trying my absolute best to avoid it.”

“Never meant to *hurt* me?” Zuko’s voice oozed sarcasm, hurt, and rage. “Azula, the entire reason you made up for coming here was a complete lie. You were never on vacation. This was never temporary. You ran away.” He looked up at her. “Didn’t you?”

Azula couldn’t find it in her to respond, so she simply nodded.

“And you didn’t tell Father where you were.”

She nodded again.

Zuko laughed harshly. “Do you even *realize* how much danger you put me in? Never mind the fact that I just don’t want to see Father because I’m worried I’ll have a fucking panic attack, or he’ll burn me again, or I’ll lose an eye, he could have accused me of *kidnapping* , Azula! You’re seventeen! I could have gone to jail forever for that! Hell, Father could have killed me! And all because you didn’t have the honesty to tell me the fucking truth.”

Azula was crying now. “I’m sorry,” she managed through her tears. “I had nowhere else to go. I had no money, no connections outside of Father. I knew of no one who had managed to truly escape from him except you. So you were the one I looked for.”

“So you wanted to follow in my footsteps?” snapped Zuko. “Yeah, that’s ironic, because the second you came here, you put our Father right on my trail.” He gestured angrily towards his office. “Do you know who that was on the phone?”

Azula shook her head.

“It was our fucking father!” yelled Zuko. “The father who I swore I was never going to see again, because I feared for my life! And you brought him down on me! This is your fault!”

“I’ll tell him you didn’t do anything!” cried Azula in desperation. “I’ll make sure he doesn’t do anything to you, I promise!”

“You’ve never tried to stop him before,” hissed Zuko, his voice as cold as ice. “Why should I believe you this time?”

“Zuko,” Azula shakily reached out for her brother, but Zuko slapped her hand away, “I’m not trying to hurt you. Please, just let me explain. This was *never* about you.”

“Funny,” laughed Zuko bitterly. “I seem to be paying the price for it.”

Azula took a deep breath. “I didn’t plan on running away. I had been living alone with Father for a while, but the pressure was slowly becoming more and more crushing. I had no friends, I spent hours each day trying to get perfect grades, perfect hair, the perfect body. Father barely had five seconds for me each day, only to remind me to do even better the next time. It felt like I was falling down a pit of despair and loneliness, as though I was climbing an endless mountain, and Father kept raising the peak, pushing me to every limit until I broke, and then pushing me more. I felt so alone, as though no one would give me any love, because Father never did, and the longer you were gone, the harsher he was with me, the more ready to give out criticism, the less willing to remind me that I was a person. Soon, I stopped feeling like a person at all. I felt like a puppet on strings, performing the dance he’d crafted for me, day after day after day. It was unbearable.” She took a breath. “You have to understand, Zuko, I was never like you. I wasn’t clashing with Father’s ideals and forging my own path, I was being slowly obliterated by the weight of his expectations. It felt as though I had no soul, no mind, *nothing* that was my own.” She sighed. “I don’t know what it was about that day. Maybe the thunderstorm, I’m not sure. But something inside of me just realized that I couldn’t live like that anymore, or I’d slowly destroy myself. I took all the money from my desk, snuck out the back door, and bought a bus ticket to Ba Sing Se.” She sighed. “I hadn’t seen you in two years, but I knew you had a life, a job, friends, and an identity of your own. I wanted that so badly, more than anything, so...I decided to come and find you.” She sighed. “When I got to your front door, I couldn’t tell you the truth. I had nothing, and I didn’t think you’d accept me if I told you I needed a permanent home, or that Father could show up at any minute.”

“I wouldn’t have.” Zuko was still glaring at her, his amber eyes full of hatred.

“I know,” Azula replied sadly. “That’s why I lied.” She took another breath. “I never planned on staying very long, but the more involved I got with your case, the more I started to find what I’d come to Ba Sing Se looking for in the first place. I couldn’t leave it behind, not after I’d been without it for so long, and it was tearing me apart not to tell you, but I couldn’t bear the thought of losing everything, let alone betraying you. So I kept lying, and hoping Father wouldn’t show up.” She looked Zuko right in the eyes. “Zuko, I know I was selfish. I was so desperate to get away from Father that I put you in danger, and I’m sorry. But I will do absolutely everything in my power to stop him from hurting you, and I did not in any way do this to lead him to you. What I said the other night was true,” she finished, looking him in the eyes. “I do care about you. I never lied about that.”

“You’re lucky the Mayor talked Father down,” replied Zuko after a moment. “Because he was just about ready to come here and murder me in cold blood.”

Tears were streaming down Azula’s face now. “I’m sorry…”

“Save it,” snapped Zuko. “I know you’re not sorry. If you were really sorry, you wouldn’t have kept this up for so long.”

“I never meant to…”

“It doesn’t matter what you meant to do!” cried Zuko. “That’s not what matters! What matters is that you prioritized what you wanted over my safety, all while pretending to fucking love me, Azula, that’s what matters.” He let out a laugh that was filled with a mix of heartbreak, rage, and bitterness. “Get out,” he said coldly after a moment.

Azula blinked. “What?” Even though she had never seen Zuko this furious before, she hadn’t expected this.

“You fucking heard me.” Zuko’s voice was low and crackling with angry energy. “Get out of my apartment. Get your things, and leave. I *never* want to see you again.”

“But…”

“You don’t get to protest!” yelled Zuko. “Damn it, Azula! I trusted you! I really trusted you! I thought you were getting better, I thought you were my *friend* ! I was actually starting to think that you understood me better than anyone else.” He laughed. “Isn’t it funny how you didn’t care this whole time if I even lived or died?”

“That’s not true,” Azula said quietly.

“Sure,” snapped Zuko. “Deny it all you want. Pretend you’re good, pretend you’re my friend, pretend you’re actually a fucking normal sister. Pretend all you want, Azula, but you’ll always be a selfish, lying, conniving monster.” He slammed his fist into the wall, so hard that the doorframe shook. “I can’t believe I let you in,” he muttered quietly.

Each one of Zuko’s words felt like a knife in her chest, more painful than anything the Dai Li had done to her. She meant what she said. Sha cared about Zuko. He was her family, possibly her only family. He’d seen her as human, given her a life, an identity. He didn’t *ask* her to repay him; she simply stayed because it was where she belonged. If anything happened to him, she knew she would find the perpetrator and rip their heart out with her bare hands if she had to.

Was that what love was? Was that her strange, twisted version of love?  
She supposed it didn’t matter now. Zuko hated her, he didn’t even think she was human, and Azula didn’t even feel like herself, because she couldn’t stop crying.

“Okay,” she said, more to herself than to Zuko, because she couldn’t find it in herself to be any louder. “I’ll go.”

Still sobbing, trying and failing to control her tears, to maintain some façade of composure, because now that Zuko despised her, she would have to go back to their father, endure the consequences of running away, and go back to being a perfect, soulless puppet.

It was what she deserved.

She walked down the very same stairs she’d told her first lie on when she’d arrived in the city two weeks ago. It felt like an eternity. Zuko slammed the door behind her, and it took every single ounce of her power not to look back as she left the building and walked out onto the streets.

Zuko paced back and forth in his office. He was trying to focus on his clue board, which now featured Hama, Arnook, Jet, and most recently Piandao’s notes, photos from all of the White Lotus parties, and several new murder victims with their faces crossed out in red ink, but he couldn’t concentrate.

He had let himself care about Azula. He had decided that she was worth the risk, and now he was paying the price. She had been manipulating him all along, just like she’d always done. She was as awful as she’d ever been, and he’d just fallen right into her trap.

How could he have been so stupid?

A little voice in his mind told him that Azula had been in a hard position, and that maybe it hadn’t been so black and white, but he ignored it. Those were Azula’s manipulative snakes of phrases, sneaking their way into his mind. He had learned to ignore them as a young teenager. He could learn to ignore them again.

Instead, he turned back to the clue board. Without Azula, he was alone in this case now, all alone to find the mastermind who had made victims and killers out of so many citizens, many of whom had simply been living their innocent lives. The same mastermind who knew who Zuko was, and was out for his blood.

It was better this way, Zuko told himself. This way, he could devote everything he had to catching the killer. No distractions, no one to put in danger, no one to betray him. Just like it had been before.

He paced back and forth a couple of more times, then stared at the clue board. He didn’t know what he was looking at before on the clue board, but the more he thought about Azula’s betrayal, the more he remembered the small signs of it that had been sprinkled here and there throughout the past two weeks. Why she hadn’t wanted to call home. Her missing driver’s license. The pattern had been there. He’d just been too stupid to pick up on it.

Maybe that was what he was searching for. A pattern.

He turned back to the photos and began to study them again, just as a car pulled up outside.

Right. He had a meeting.

Just as he was about to walk away from the board, it was like a lightbulb went off in his brain. There was the same face, appearing over and over in every photo. There was the same motif, plain and simple, in every single note.

*Who else would want this?*

Suddenly, everything made perfect sense. Zuko was so surprised by his own revelation that he let out a laugh, purely out of instinct.

And that was when a figure emerged from the shadows and clapped its hands over Zuko’s mouth.

Zuko began kicking and tried to scream, but the figure was holding a cloth over his face, and the more he struggled, the more his vision blurred, and the harder it became to stay awake.

It was funny that, as his vision blurred and he felt arms begin to wrap around him, his last thought was a cliché line that he had read in a million mystery novels before.

*He knew too much.*
