## Chapter 39: The Veiled Lady

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula makes some surprising discoveries.

#### Chapter Notes

Sorry for the delay (again!) I'm doing my best.  
No TWs for this one (I think.) Only four chapters left…and this is another one of my absolute favorites!  
Happy reading:)

### Text

Azula truly couldn’t believe she had sunk so low. With absolutely nowhere else to turn, she found herself slouched over a table in her uncle’s tea shop, with several empty cups of tea spread out in front of her. She looked like someone from a depressing post break-up sequence in a movie, except she hadn’t broken up with anyone, and instead of empty wine glasses, she had empty mugs of tea.

She had finally been starting to craft a new life for herself, one where she could feel authentic and loved, and it was all being taken away from her, because she hadn’t been able to stop being selfish and *just tell the fucking truth.*

She really had been a monster all along, hadn’t she?

“Azula?” Iroh’s face appeared from behind the counter. He was being irritatingly kind to her, despite what she had done to Zuko. He had closed the tea shop the second she had appeared. “Can I get you anything else?”

Azula was finding it hard to speak, so she simply shook her head. She wanted to despise her uncle for leaving her alone with her father, for never giving her an escape route the way he’d done for Zuko, but he seemed to be trying to make up for it now. It wasn’t everything, but it was something.

She supposed she wasn’t in a position to judge, after what she’d done.

It was a strange feeling, this rock-bottom. She’d spent her whole life ignoring her flaws, burying her emotions, and chasing after higher and higher standards, building up a glass dome of perfection around herself, trying so hard to believe the illusion of flawlessness that she convinced herself it was true. Then, she’d had that illusion stripped away, and built herself a new identity, one of cleverness, confidence, bravery and loyalty. All traits she wished she had.

But now, all of that had been stripped away, too, and all that remained was a monster.

*This was where she was always meant to end up.*

“If I may,” said Iroh gently, sliding into the seat across from her. “What’s on your mind, Detective?”

The use of the title brought a harsh laugh to Azula’s lips. “I’m not a detective. I never was, and I’m *certainly* not one now.”

“I wouldn’t say that,” chuckled Iroh. “Even without Zuko, you have still been instrumental in solving these murders. You do not have any *other* defined occupation. I’d say that makes you a detective.”

“I don’t deserve that title,” Azula said bitterly. “Being *deserving* of what you have is something you’ll *never* understand.”

“Azula, you do not have to achieve impossible standards to be worthy of love.”

“That’s not what I mean!” she snapped. His kindness towards her was so unnatural that it was beginning to be unnerving. “Look at you. You’re a mass murderer who never went to prison for his actions. You abandoned me to my father while you gave Zuko an escape, and as far as I can tell, you had no good reason to do so, because I was a *child* . And yet you play the role of the good, kind, old man who runs a tea shop and is beloved by all. Well let me tell you this,” she hissed, leaning forward. “In my eyes, you will never be worthy of that title. You can pretend all you want, but you haven’t earned the title of ‘good and kind’ any more than I have.”

Iroh was silent for a moment, before reaching out and pouring more tea. Azula had never had so much tea in her life, and thought she might be sick if she drank any more of it. “I’m sorry,” he said after a pause.

Azula sighed. “I know a thing or two about ignoring my own flaws,” she said. “It tends to blow up in your face sooner or later.”

“Perhaps,” said Iroh. “But perhaps there is a middle ground between running from the past, like I sometimes find myself doing, and constantly dwelling on the worst aspects of myself, like you’re doing.”

Azula glanced up. “Elaborate.”

Iroh took another sip of tea. How much tea did the man *drink* ? “Well, I have done horrible things, but I have also done a lot of good for this city. I have made friends, and I may have failed you, but I did manage to help Zuko, at least, I hope I did. My point is, we all have good and bad inside of us. The trick is to acknowledge them both; that is what makes us human.”

“Right,” laughed Azula. “Easy for you to say. Your good things are so clear, so... *pure* . It makes me sick. But I was tainted by my father’s image before I was even born. That doesn’t make me human.”

“Is that so?” mused Iroh. “From what I have observed, you are often torn between believing that you are only capable of what your father set out for you, such as lying and manipulation, and believing that you can do more. You may have lied to Zuko, but you were also an impeccable ally and friend to him.” Iroh placed his hand on her shoulder, and Azula nearly dropped her mug. “It took me a long time to see it, but you, too, are multifaceted, Azula. Like all of us, you have made mistakes, and done good things. Only if you believe you have no choice but to be nothing but the worst parts of yourself do you become anything other than human.”

Was there merit to what he said? Did she only become a monster if she believed it hard enough? Could she really be more than ruthless and brutal? No one had ever called her anything else, not since she was a child.

But perhaps it wasn’t up to everyone else.

The fact that Iroh’s advice was actually useful was incredibly irritating. Azula was torn between wanting to thank him and wanting to slap him.

She settled for simply sipping her tea. A middle ground.

“There...may be some merit to what you say,” Azula admitted. “I only wish I could repair things with Zuko.”

“It is true that some mistakes are unfixable,” said Iroh, “but I do not believe that this is one of them.”

Azula blinked. “After I lied to him and put his life in danger? That’s a nice wish.”

“You’d be surprised,” said Iroh. “Many think our past mistakes will define us forever, but oftentimes it is the good that does so instead. It is not Zuko’s responsibility to forgive you, but if you show him that you care, and remind him of the kind of sister you were, it is possible that eventually, the mistakes will be covered by a new layer of memories. Think of it like bear tracks in the snow that become covered by a new coating of snow after a storm.”

Azula was trying to decide if she agreed with him or not, when a feeling like a switch flipping echoed through her brain.

*Like bear tracks in the snow.*

Quickly, Azula whipped out her phone, and began scrolling through her photos, until she found a photo of Jet’s note from whoever had orchestrated all of the killings.

She zoomed in on the strange shape over the *i* , and let out a gasp.

It was a paw print.

*The paw prints on the rug in the Mayor’s office.*

It was like puzzle pieces were being pulled together by a magnetic force inside of her head.

Each time an assassin had attacked a party, the Mayor had been there, even for the murder that started it all. He’d claimed to just enjoy parties, but what if there was more going on?  
What if he’d been making sure his plans were implemented properly?  
All of those times Long Feng had pretended to manipulate the Mayor, had it really been an act? In all of those meetings behind closed doors, had *he* been the one pulling the strings all along?

Azula’s mind flashed back to one of the first times she’d met the Mayor, after Jet had murdered the Dai Li soldiers, when Long Feng and the Mayor had questioned her, Suki, Mai, and Toph.

And why had he been there in the first place, if not to ensure that they didn’t come too close to discovering his secret?

*“You’re just going to let them go?* ” he had cried. *“I want a word with that one!”* he’d said, pointing at Azula. *“In private.”*

Had he been trying to end her life, even then?

Azula had never actually seen Long Feng put in prison. When the Mayor had come with Zuko and Sokka to rescue her, had it really been to ensure that Long Feng would escape? When he’d arrested her for Zhao’s murder, had he been trying to get her out of the way, perhaps so he could make sure none of the Dai Li agents revealed him?

He had been everywhere, all along. Lurking in the shadows, working with the White Lotus and the Dai Li at the same time. And no one had ever taken him seriously because of his ridiculous façade.

But it had all been an act. That was the only explanation.

Because who else would dot their *i* s with paw prints?

“Azula?” Iroh’s voice cut through her mind, and she glanced up, realizing that she’d been staring at nothing for the past three minutes. “Is everything all right?”

“Everything’s fine.” Azula’s mind was moving so fast that she could barely concentrate on the conversation at hand. Abruptly, she stood up from the table, her mind still racing. “I just...need to do something.”

“Should I call one of your friends?” asked Iroh. She must have seemed completely insane for him to be *that* concerned.

“No,” said Azula hurriedly. If she was right, then she couldn’t waste time telling too many people. She needed to prove this, once and for all, before anyone else got hurt. “I just figured something out.” She paused as she headed for the door. “Thank you for the tea. And the advice. Maybe I’ll use them someday.”

Sha dashed out of the tea shop into the October air. It was unusually cold, even for the season, and she shivered. She was wearing a thick red sweater over her black jeans, but she was still shivering. She started rushing off, not even really knowing where she was going, just knowing that she needed to tell *someone* about this before time ran out.

She was halfway down the block before another realization hit her like a bolt of lightning, and she stopped dead in her tracks.

*Zuko.*

*“You’re lucky the Mayor talked Father down,”* Zuko had said to her. *“Because he was just about* *ready to come here and murder me in cold blood.”*

Why would the Mayor talk their father out of coming directly after Zuko...unless he had the intention of splitting the siblings up and getting Zuko alone?  
Unless he’d never intended to keep Zuko alive, and had simply gained a new ally who was eager to finish the job.

Unless he was working with their father.

The realization should have surprised Azula, but it didn’t surprise her at all. Her father had always bordered on being a criminal. Now, hand in hand with a Mayor who had the whole city fooled, he had taken a leap into the realm of actual murder.

As quickly as she possibly could, Azula jumped on the nearest train and rode it to the other side of the Middle Ring, where she could only hope that Zuko was safe, and would be absolutely furious to see her back on his doorstep.

For the first time since moving to the city, she wasn’t afraid of his rage. She had already faced his fury at her lies being discovered. She could face it again, if it meant that the Mayor would never lay his devious, murdering hands on her brother.

The moment she arrived at Zuko’s apartment, gasping for air and shivering, hurriedly tying her hair up into a ponytail, she knew something was wrong.

The door was unlocked.

After a lifetime of hiding from their father, ducking into secret passages, hiding behind closed doors and curtains, and knowing exactly how to disappear somewhere safe, Zuko *never* left the door unlocked.

Cautiously, Azula pushed the door open and crept into Zuko’s apartment. All of the lights were out, despite the fact that it was only eleven at night, and Zuko usually didn’t go to sleep until two in the morning. Sliding her shoes off, she used her socks to slide over the cold floors. She slipped from room to room, not wanting to wake Zuko if, by some miracle, he was here.

She found no one. The apartment was unquestionably empty.

When she got to Zuko’s office, she froze. The photos from the clue board had been ripped off, and were strewn all over the floor. There were no other signs of a struggle, but Azula knew that Zuko would never have done this himself. Kneeling down, she began to pick up the photos and pin them back up on the board, exactly where they’d been before. She always *had* loved a good bulletin board, after all.

When she put all of the photos back up, there was a gaping hole in the middle of the board where the Mayor’s photo should be.

That could only mean that the Mayor himself had been here and taken his photo, or at the very least hired someone to take it, so that no one searching for Zuko would even consider him as a suspect.

But he hadn’t counted on Azula. He probably assumed that she’d be long gone by now. Exactly as he’d planned.

Azula had always been the one who followed other people’s plans, and took whatever path was laid out for her, usually by her father. For almost her entire life, it was all she’d ever known, until she’d moved to Ba Sing Se. The second she’d moved to the city, she’d begun to break away from other people’s plans before, and tonight, she was going to *ruin* the plan that had been laid out for her.

Because those murderers were not going to lay a finger on her brother. Not if she had anything to say about it.

She could feel the beginnings of a plan starting to form. But first, she needed backup.

“Let me get this straight,” said Katara as she tried to keep up with Azula’s rapid footsteps towards City Hall. “You think the *Mayor* ...our idiotic, puppy-like Mayor, has been behind these murders the entire time?”

“Yes,” said Azula. “The notes, and the evidence missing from Zuko’s apartment prove it.”

Katara remembered how the Mayor had always been at every interrogation, every party, interacting with every murderer.

Somehow, it made perfect sense.

“What do you need me to do?”

Azula sighed as they approached the building where (apparently) the Mayor was keeping Zuko. Katara was ready to storm the building with a squadron of police, but Azula warned her not to.

“We need concrete proof against this man if he’s to be convicted. He’s the Mayor. He holds immense political power. No one is going to convict him without all the evidence, and if he’s acquitted, he’s clever enough to slip away and do this all over again. We can’t take that risk.”

“I can’t just let you go in by yourself!” cried Katara. “He’ll kill you!”

“You can, and perhaps he will,” said Azula. “But if I die, I’ll die trying to make up for what I did to my brother. And I’ll be absolutely sure to take that murderous bastard down with me.” She turned to Katara. “But I need you. You’re the heart and soul of this strange group we’ve built. I need you to find every single one of our allies, plus any law enforcement officials you can find. Give them all the evidence I’ve just given you, and bring them outside City Hall.” She squeezed Katara’s hand. “The second you feel like it’s been too long, get everyone to storm the building, and even if I’m dead, you’ll get the Mayor before he can escape.”

“Azula, think about this,” said Katara. “This whole thing seems really, *really* risky.”

“I know,” said Azula. “I’m used to formulating several plans at once. Right now, I only have one.” It was only then that Katara noticed that she was putting extra effort into shoving her choppy bangs into a perfect topknot. “But it’s all I’ve got, and time is running out, so it has to work.” She shoved her dagger into her topknot, and adjusted it one last time.

“Why does your topknot need to be perfect?”

Azula gave her a wry smile. “It’s complicated. But if this is going to work, I need an impenetrable façade. Luckily, that’s something I’m very good at.”

Even looking into Azula’s eyes, Katara had absolutely no idea what her plan was. Instead, she pulled her friend into a hug. “I’ll do everything you asked me to. You can count on me.”

“I know,” replied Azula. “That’s why I called you.”

“Be careful,” said Katara, breaking apart from her friend, and trying not to think about the fact that this could be the last time she ever saw her alive.

“I can’t afford to be careful,” replied Azula. “But I *can* save my brother and put an end to this.”

Katara watched as Azula raced up the steps of City Hall, her footsteps echoing through the unusually silent city streets. There was no moon, and this part of the city was dark. She wasn’t even halfway up the steps before she disappeared into the darkness.

But Katara couldn’t afford to wait and worry about her. They had a plan in motion, and they couldn’t afford to stop it now.

She checked her watch...eleven-forty-five at night, and began to run.

## Chapter 40: The Baited Trap

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko finds himself in a face-off with several familiar faces, but no one is ever what they seem.

#### Chapter Notes

Hi everyone! I am SO sorry for the three-week hiatus in between the last chapter and this one. I started school and became busy, and I just lost all time, energy, and motivation to work on this. I know you were all used to consistent updates, so I apologize a million times for disappointing all of you. The fic is now finished, so I'll be posting the last 3 chapters consecutively, before I lose the motivation again. If you're still here, thank you so much for reading, and I hope you stick around for the ending.  
TWs at the end for this one.

### Text

The puzzle pieces came rushing back into Zuko’s mind just before he regained consciousness. As he hovered in the black, hazy space between sleep and waking, he felt his discovery from moments before everything had gone black return to him.

*The Mayor.*

He had been coaching Long Feng on murder every time he’d been meeting with him behind closed doors. He had been making sure the killers he’d hired were doing their jobs correctly every time he’d been present at a party that had been attacked, all while claiming to just enjoy a good dance.

It made sense, after all. Hama and Jet had been right; the White Lotus and the Dai Li, for all their good intentions, had been destroying Ba Sing Se for decades, both directly and inadvertently. Zuko could understand wanting to get rid of them, especially as a new mayor.

But murder was too far. And Kuei had dragged too many people into his schemes to be let off the hook.

Zuko wasn’t sure what he could do at this point, but he was going to do absolutely everything in his power to make sure that Kuei didn’t get away with this. It was his job, after all.

Slowly, ignoring the slight ache in his chest from whatever it was that he’d breathed in, he opened his eyes. At first, his vision was blurry, and the lights blinding, but as his eyes adjusted, the room in which he sat came into focus.

Zuko was sitting in a back room at City Hall. He could tell that was where he was because of the view out the window. If he leaned out far enough, he could see the building’s front steps at the other end of the block. He’d never been in this room before, but based on the position of the window, he would guess that they weren’t far from, if not directly next to, the bell tower.

Both Zuko’s wrists and ankles had been locked together with metal cuffs, attaching him not only to the chair he was sitting in, but the desk behind him. Both pieces of furniture were bolted to the floor, making it nearly impossible to move at all.

Closer to the window, in a leather armchair, sat the Mayor, toying with his glasses and wearing an innocent-looking smile as though nothing was out of the ordinary. But if Zuko looked closer, he could see the sinister glint in his eyes, the slight smirk in his smile that hadn’t been there before. It was as though someone had taken the Mayor Zuko knew, made a portrait of him, and gotten everything right except a couple of small details, but those details, once you looked closer, ruined the entire portrait.

But this *wrong* version of the Mayor, this ruined portrait, wasn’t wrong at all. It was what the Mayor had really been all along.

“Detective,” said the Mayor. His voice, too, was different, less happy and bouncy, more cocky and vicious. It reminded Zuko a little bit of his sister when she was interrogating suspects, except somehow, even more sadistic than that. “So nice of you to join me.”

Zuko refused to comply with the Mayor’s pleasantries. He had no time for that. So he glared at him instead, and asked the obvious question. “Why am I still alive?”

“Honestly,” said Kuei, leaning back in his chair, “it’s not my choice. It’s nothing personal,” he added quickly. “I actually quite like you. And if you hadn’t been getting too close to discovering the truth, I wouldn’t have needed to do this.”

“Save it,” snapped Zuko, “and answer my question.”

“I see you haven’t lost any of your characteristic spirit or stubbornness,” laughed the Mayor. “But fine. I have an ally, one who’s been funding my little...city improvement plan.”  
“My father,” realized Zuko. “That’s why you talked to him.”

“Perhaps,” said Kuei. “Perhaps not. Anyway, my investor has been very helpful. He’s provided weapons for my killers, funding to make people disappear, even consultation from time to time.” He glanced over at Zuko. “He claims he has a personal grudge against you, though I can’t imagine why. He wanted to work it out.”

Realization washed over Zuko. It wasn’t exactly surprising, but there was still a part of Zuko, deep inside, that hurt at the thought of it. “You mean he wants to kill me himself.”

“I wish it hadn’t come to this,” said Kuei, turning his back to Zuko and facing out the window. “You’re a good person, Zuko. You’re not like the White Lotus or the Dai Li. You’re not hurting the city at all, in fact,” he laughed, “you even brought some of my biggest adversaries down *for* me.”

“Like Long Feng.”

“Ah, yes,” laughed Kuei. “The man actually thought he was manipulating me. I must admit, I *thoroughly* enjoyed slowly turning the tables on him.” He glanced over his shoulder at Zuko. “Thank you for bringing him down, by the way. It made my job a lot easier.”

“I don’t want your thanks,” spat Zuko. “Long Feng may be a murderer and a terrible person, but you pretended to be his friend and then made him take the fall for *your* murders. You’re despicable.”

“I’m not, though,” sighed the Mayor, facing the window again. “I don’t want to be a murderer. I take no pleasure in death, or killing.”

“Then why do this at all?” snapped Zuko. “What made you this way?”

“It’s a long story,” replied the Mayor. “I don’t think it’s worth telling to a nosy little detective who’s in over his head.”

“Why not?” said Zuko. “I’m a dead man walking. What have you got to lose?”

The Mayor regarded him for a moment, then nodded, facing the window again. Zuko could see his face reflected in the glass, and could tell from his eyes that his mind was beginning to drift somewhere far away. “I never wanted to go into politics as a child, you know. My parents were politicians; city councilmen, the both of them. They were always busy trying to fix the city, so busy, in fact, that they never had time for me. It seemed I wasn’t worthy or important enough to them.” His eyes darted toward Zuko’s reflection in the window, just to the right of his own. “I believe you might know a thing or two about that.”

Zuko didn’t stop glaring at the murderer, but he nodded.

“Anyway,” said Kuei, “I did have one friend as a child. A dog named Bosco. He was...the only living being kind enough to take me seriously, to listen to me, to indulge my goofiness as a child. To this day, he’s the kindest living creature I’ve ever met.”

Zuko could sense a *‘but’* coming. “What happened?”

Kuei sighed. “I never got the chance to live out a whole life with my best friend. When I was seven, my parents were sent on a mission to calm down a group of protesting anarchists. I was desperate for their attention, and begged them to bring me along. Reluctantly, thinking it would be a low-risk mission, they did. They even allowed me to bring Bosco.” He laughed sadly. “I wish I hadn’t begged so hard.”

Zuko recognized the look in his eyes. It was the same look he’d worn when his mother had disappeared. “They died, didn’t they?”

Kuei nodded. “The anarchists were more dangerous than anyone had imagined. They murdered my parents, and my dog got caught in the crossfire.” He sighed. “My parents may have been cold, but even as a child, I knew they were good people. And my dog was *better* than any person I ever met.” He glanced at Zuko. “Those anarchists later fed into the White Lotus and the Dai Li, making them the superpowers they are today. Murderers of innocent beings.”

“But that’s what you’ve become,” said Zuko. “You’ve become the very thing you claim to hate.”

“But I haven’t,” said Kuei. “Because I didn’t make a vow to kill that day. I vowed to better this city, to finish what my parents started, to make up for the loss of my best friend, and I vowed to do it however possible. And that means getting rid of the monsters who poison it.” At last, he turned and faced Zuko fully. “Everyone knows that the White Lotus and the Dai Li need to be gone for this city to flourish, Zuko,” he said. “I’m just the only one brave enough to actually do what no one else will.”

Zuko paused for a moment before looking Kuei in the eye. “Maybe the city would be better off without them,” he said. “But if that’s true, then you can lock them up for the crimes they’ve committed against our people. You can’t take their lives away from them, target their loved ones, threaten the innocent, because some people belong to the groups you’ve decided are bad. We’re all human,” he added. “No one is automatically good or bad because of where they fall.”

“Name one White Lotus member who isn’t a monster. Or a Dai Li member.”

“Chief Song,” spat Zuko. “He was a police chief doing his job. Or Piandao, the fencing instructor who lost his best friend. What about Arnook, the man whose daughter was on trial for the murder of his closest colleague? Or Jet, the teenager who was left behind by society. Hama, the last remaining member of a culture that was exterminated too soon. Even the Dai Li guards were just people doing their jobs!” He stared Kuei right in the face, his eyes flashing. “They’re not perfect, but they’re still people, and they deserve to live their lives. And you...you made killers and victims out of them all. I don’t care how good you think you are, Mayor Kuei. That’s unforgivable. And it makes you worse than any of them.”

Kuei glared at Zuko for a moment. Zuko had never seen the Mayor so angry, and it made his heart beat a little faster. It was easy not to think about it when he was defending something he believed in, but the truth was, Kuei could end Zuko’s life at any moment, and no one would know. Zuko’s death would be marked as a tragic accident, and the Mayor would go on killing and making others murderers.

Zuko would do everything in his power to ensure that the latter didn’t happen, but if worst came to worst, he was fully prepared to go down fighting.

“I think my advisor has arrived,” said Kuei coldly. “And I believe he’d *love* to speak with you.”

Zuko gulped as a shadow loomed in the doorway. He could try as hard as he wanted to force the terrified child out of him, but the truth was, he was still scared of his father. He could hurt Zuko in a way that no one else could. He had spent so long tormenting him that he knew exactly what his weaknesses were, and how to drag them out.

But today, Zuko was fighting for the innocent citizens of Ba Sing Se. He refused to bend to his father’s will, not when there were lives on the line. Just as he had two years ago, when he’d learned to prioritize himself for the first time in his life, tonight he would prioritize others, and do his best to place his fear aside.

That didn’t stop his heartbeat from getting a little faster, though, as the shadow in the doorway grew larger and larger, before a person stepped into the light. He looked exactly as Zuko remembered him, except there was one single, grey hair in his black beard.

“A pleasure to see you, Detective.” His voice oozed sarcasm, disappointment, and sadism. Zuko turned and stared him right in the eyes, the amber eyes that were exactly the same shade as Zuko’s own.

“Hello, Father.”

The room fell silent.

Kuei cleared his throat. “I believe I...have some papers to fill out in the other room. Finalizing the transfer of the murderers. I’ll leave you two alone, but,” he said pointedly to Ozai, “he had better be dead before I get back.”

Ozai nodded, a malicious smirk slowly spreading across his face. “Understood,” he said, as the Mayor walked out of the room, leaving Zuko handcuffed to a desk and a chair, at the mercy of his father.

It was hard not to scream.

Ozai turned to face him, his eyes gleaming in the light. “I see you’ve made quite the career out of ruining others’ lives. How fitting for you.”

“I don’t ruin their lives,” Zuko replied coldly. “They ruin their own lives when they make the decision to kill. All I do is protect the rest of the world.”

“Please,” chuckled Ozai. “You’re chasing some fantasy of justice and perfection, where everyone is as weak as you. In the real world, people do what needs to be done to be efficient and productive. That, *Detective* , is something you have never understood.”

“Maybe you’re right,” said Zuko, not taking his eyes off his father. “Maybe I don’t understand the world. But I do understand this; I’m not weak. I was strong enough to decide for myself what I believed, and I will *never* stop believing in what’s right, no matter what the world says. *That’s* why I do what I do.”

“An admirable goal,” laughed Ozai. “But you never possessed any talent.” He fingered his beard thoughtfully. “By sheer luck, you have come close enough to the truth that we have no choice but to end your life. It will be pleasurable.” A malicious grin was growing on his face. “You were always a blight on my existence, on the family name. But I was willing to let you go, until you kidnapped my daughter.”

Zuko laughed. “That’s what you think I did?” he spat. “Your opinion of me doesn’t matter, but I’m offended that you think I’d stoop so low. I would *never* kidnap anyone.”

“Please,” laughed Ozai. “My daughter would never run away from me. She left me a note saying she’d been planning to go on an educational trip for school. It was only through my colleague the Mayor that I even learned she was with you.” He leaned forward, grabbing Zuko’s face and gripping it so tightly that his nails dug into Zuko’s skin. “Your existence is nothing but an embarrassment and a bother, but I have learned to accept it, so long as you do not attempt to interfere with family business. But Azula,” he hissed, “is different. She is everything I ever wanted. She knows what to do, and how to do it. She is the epitome of perfection, and I refuse to let you bring her down in your miserable quest for some lost justice.”

“I didn’t kidnap her,” repeated Zuko. “Your perfect little daughter’s not as perfect as you think. She came here of her own free will to stay with me. She ran away from you.”

“As if I’d believe your lies. I’m not foolish enough to believe someone like you.”

“You can hate me for being a failure,” said Zuko. “Hate me for not being enough like you, if that’s what you truly want. Hate me for being like you, but choosing the path you secretly wish you’d chosen, all those years ago. Fine. But don’t hate me for stooping down to your level when I never would, not even if my own life was on the line.”

“I’m glad you say that,” said Ozai, yanking Zuko’s head upward so hard that Zuko could feel every ounce of strain on his neck, “because your weak, miserable, short life is on the line, and it’s about to end right now.”

Zuko had never had his neck snapped before, obviously. He wondered what it would feel like.

There was a knock at the door, and Ozai dropped Zuko’s head so suddenly that it banged on Zuko’s chest, and he winced, letting out a sigh of relief despite himself. Ozai noticed, and flashed him a hideous smirk.

It was the Mayor. “Sorry to interrupt this,” he said, “believe me, I want this little inconvenience finished with as much as you do. But...there’s someone here to see you. She claims to be an ally, and she claims to know everything.”

“Do you know her?” replied Ozai, raising an eyebrow in suspicion.

“You both do,” said a familiar voice. Zuko couldn’t keep the shock off his face as his sister stepped into the light.

In some ways, she looked exactly as she had looked when he’d last seen her; same red sweater, same black pants, same black boots. In others, she was completely different. Her choppy bangs were completely hidden in the tightest, most perfect topknot he had seen her wear since her arrival. She bore no mark of the tears that had been spilling down her face when he’d last seen her a few hours ago.

It was *her* fucking fault that he was about to die.

Still, there was a part of him that pitied her, seeing her like this again, next to her father, the pinnacle of *his* expectations, *his* definition of perfection, *his* desires.

Had Azula ever really had any choice in anything?  
He still hated her for lying to him, but she had been desperate. That much, he could understand.

“Daughter,” Ozai said coldly, “you know not of the matters you are meddling in. Go back to wherever you are residing, and leave us be.” He saw Azula’s eyes dart over to Zuko, and he smiled coldly at her. “Don’t worry. Your brother is being taken care of...as I see fit.”

“But I can help you,” replied Azula. Her tone was colder than he’d ever heard it before in his life, and it was such a surprise that...well, he couldn’t think of anything to do at all. She stared directly at her father, and wouldn’t look Zuko in the eye. “You’re planning to kill him, yes?”

Ozai paused for a moment, then nodded, still looking wary. “We do not need your assistance in that.”

“I didn’t say you did.” The way Azula spoke to their father sounded the most like him that she ever had, including sounding slightly more defiant, slightly more commanding against him than Zuko remembered. “I’m here to form an alliance.” She gestured to the Mayor. “This man wants to better the city. *You’ve* been helping him...in exchange for what?”

Ozai looked away for a second, then said “A position of power in this city.”

“Of course.” Azula began to rub the points of her fingernails together. “Well, I’m here to help you.”

Ozai’s lips curled into a cruel smile. “In exchange for what.”

Azula’s lips formed a vicious smirk that mirrored her father’s. “A place by your side when you’re finally the one running this city.” She glanced at Kuei. “And yours, of course.”

Ozai laughed. “You haven’t changed a bit.”

“Now, wait just a minute!” cried Kuei. “I’ve seen this girl! I’ve seen her working tirelessly with *him…* ” he pointed at Zuko “to solve this mystery! She may be your daughter, but how do you know she’s telling the truth?”

“My daughter would never lie to me,” Ozai replied coolly. “She knows the consequences if she tries.”

Zuko looked at Azula, trying to find something, anything, to indicate the Azula he’d seen just a few hours ago, the one he’d been starting to think of as family again, after all these years. But there was nothing there but a stone-cold, picture perfect reflection of the father who was about to end Zuko’s life. The face of a puppet on strings, one who’d never broken free, was too cruel to want to, and too weak to try.

In a strange, twisted way, he still pitied her.

“But what about him?” cried Kuei. “He’s the one she’s been living with!”

“He kidnapped her,” growled Ozai. “He couldn’t bear to see her succeed where he’d always *failed* .”

“Oh, no,” laughed Azula. “He didn’t even know I was coming.”

Zuko blinked. Was she defending him?

“You see,” said Azula, turning and smirking directly at Zuko, her eyes flashing. Where there had once been light and fiery determination, there was only emptiness and horror where a soul should have been. “I’ve been playing my idiot of a brother from the start.”

Even though he was already furious at her, even though she’d already betrayed him, it felt like she’d driven a knife into Zuko’s back.

“Elaborate,” said Ozai in a slithery voice that reminded Zuko of Long Feng.

“It was rather brilliant, actually,” said Azula, making her way over towards Zuko. “You see, I came to Ba Sing Se looking for a little fun, but when the murders started, and I realized how powerful the targets were, I knew you had to be involved, and I knew that I would be a failure as a daughter if I didn’t offer my assistance.” She paused, and Ozai nodded, looking more and more gleeful with every second. He must have loved seeing his own monstrous side appear in his daughter. “Solving the murders was the only way to find you, and Zuzu was playing quite the little detective game.” She laughed, and Zuko couldn’t even look at her. Even as a child, she had never been this malicious. “So I decided to use his information for my benefit.” She looked up at Ozai. “And it worked.”

“That’s preposterous!” cried the Mayor. “I saw how you acted around him!” he pointed at Zuko. “That wasn’t acting!”

“I haven’t even gotten to the best part yet!” cackled Azula. “I got to play the best little game with Zuzu while I was looking for you. It was just like when we were children, but now, I’m so much better.” She smirked, walking over to Zuko and leaning on his shoulder. He looked away. He didn’t know how much of her cruel expressions he could take. He’d tried *so hard* to love her...and she’d been playing him this whole time.

Just like she always had.

“Zuko’s always been... *weak,* ” said Azula. “He wastes all his time believing in love and trust.” She laughed. “Well, if he didn’t already know, he knows it now.” Her tone grew bitter. “Love and trust leads to nothing but betrayal and heartbreak.” Her tone became light and cocky again. “I pretended to be pitiful, damaged, and oh so sorry for everything I’d ever done, and he fell for it hook, line, and sinker.”

“That’s not true!” snapped Zuko, unable to stop himself. Even though the evidence all said otherwise, he couldn’t really believe what he was hearing.

Azula knelt down so that she was facing him. “Poor Zuzu,” she cooed condescendingly. “So naïve, so determined to be good, but it was always *my* game. You’re nothing but a pawn, and I played you like a fiddle.” She ran her hand slowly across his face. “It’s a shame you have to die. I must admit, I did enjoy toying with you.”

She was a monster.

How had he been stupid enough to believe otherwise?  
And why was there a part of him that still thought she was worth saving?

“She’s a sociopath,” remarked the Mayor, in a tone that was a mixture of awe and fear. “I’ve never seen anyone like her.”

“It’s quite useful,” replied Ozai. “She’s always been the perfect protégé.”

Azula smiled, standing up and walking over to the window. “Convinced yet?”

Ozai laughed. “Oh, Daughter, you’re too smart to fall for his weakness. I never doubted you.” His eyes darted over to Zuko. “You, on the other hand…” In a flash, he uncuffed Zuko’s wrists and ankles and pulled him up, gripping his arms with a hand like an iron fist, too hard for Zuko to pull himself free. “It’s a wonder I ever thought that you would amount to anything, even for a moment.”

“Are you finally getting rid of him?” said Kuei. “That’s good. The longer he stays alive, the riskier it gets for us.”

“He’s no risk,” said Azula. “He’s too stupid to escape.”

“Maybe so,” said Ozai. “But I’ll still take immense *pleasure* in seeing this blight on my legacy finally meet his end.”

“Quite dramatic, aren’t you?” said the Mayor. He seemed judgemental for a moment, then laughed. “Aren’t we all?”

Zuko kept his mouth shut as Ozai began dragging him out of the room. He refused to scream. He wouldn’t give Ozai that satisfaction.

“I have some paperwork to do,” was the last thing he heard the Mayor say as Ozai pulled him through a door and began dragging him up a spiral staircase. *The bell tower* , Zuko realized.

“So,” he said, doing his best to remain calm, even though half of his mind was still reeling from Azula’s betrayal, and the other half was racing a mile a minute with fear, “how am I going to die?”

“Rather obvious, isn’t it?” laughed Ozai.

It wasn’t, but Zuko refused to say anything more.

As they reached the top, Zuko looked around. He’d never been up here before, but it was creepy. A dark room with a deep pit in the center where the bell was hanging, and a balcony running around the side. Cobwebs covered the ceiling, and Zuko got the feeling that no one had come up here in a long, long time.

He didn’t know why he was thinking about that, considering that he was about to die.

“Well,” said Ozai coolly, “I think we’ve wasted enough time, don’t you?”

And with that, he shoved Zuko backwards. Zuko felt his feet fly out from under him, and before he even registered what was happening, Ozai was dangling him out the window.

He could see the street far below, too far a fall to survive, and thought he heard someone's voices from the other end of City Hall. His father smiled coldly down at him, and Zuko ignored his racing heartbeat.

“Are you scared yet?” said Ozai. “You were never as terrified of me as you should have been.”

Zuko looked at his father and glared at him. “I’ll never be afraid of you.” It was true. He may have been afraid of dying, but not his father, never his father. Not anymore. “If you kill me here, I’ll die fighting for justice, just like I was always meant to do. At least I won’t die as your puppet.” He stared him right in the eyes. “You will *never* control me.”

Somewhere in the bell tower, he thought he heard the creaking of footsteps. Was he hallucinating now?

It didn’t really matter.  
“Such a shame that you will never listen to me,” said Ozai. “You could have been great, you know, but you were *always* destined to fall.”

His expression grew bizarre, almost manic, his eyes distracted and wide.

With that, he let go of Zuko’s wrist, and let him fall.

## Chapter 41: The World's End

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

The detectives stand on the precipice of death, both tipping over the side. A dangerous struggle will determine the outcome of it all.

#### Chapter Notes

Hello again! (if anyone really is still here.)  
TWs at the end! This one's a little short, but it's sort of the climax, so I didn't want to drag it out. I hope you all enjoy, and happy reading:)

### Text

It felt like Zuko was falling for eternity, even though he was only in the air for a split second before another hand (a smaller one) grabbed him around the wrist and began pulling him back up through the window. Dazed, Zuko barely registered what was going on until he was back inside the bell tower, and standing face to face with his sister, who was doubled over from the exhaustion of pulling him through the window.

Ozai lay on the floor, unconscious, and beside his head was a metal pipe. Zuko spotted traces of the orange rust on the pipe covering Azula’s hands.

He blinked, turning to her. She looked different than she had just a few minutes ago. Her hair had fallen out of its topknot and was now in a ponytail, and the coldness and cruelty had disappeared from her expression. She looked just like she had all week, up until ten minutes ago.

But Zuko couldn’t shake the sound of her vicious laughter, the image of her malicious, empty eyes, from his brain.

Unable to completely process what was happening, he gestured to his father’s body on the floor. “Did you do that?”

Azula nodded. Once Zuko got over the shock of seeing her without her cruel smirk, he realized that she looked anxious, biting her lip slightly, refusing to look him in the eye for a moment before glancing up at him. “He had no idea it was me. He didn’t even see me.”

“And the Mayor?”

Azula shook her head. “He doesn’t know I’m here, either.”

Zuko still felt like they were floating in a fog. It was like he had three different sisters running around inside his head, and didn’t know which was real. “Why would you do that? Don’t you want to see me die after everything Father said to you?” His tone was harsher than he’d meant it to be. Maybe he was angrier with her than he’d thought.

Azula’s expression softened, and she looked guiltily at the floor. “Zuko, I’m sorry for what I said in there. It was the only thing I could think of to get them to let me in, and I had to make them believe my act if I wanted to save you.” Cautiously, she reached over and grabbed his wrists (more gently than she usually did), and looked him in the eyes. “I didn’t mean any of it. I promise.” “Why should I believe you?” snapped Zuko. “It's not like a promise from you means anything. Not really.”

“You’re right,” said Azula, and the starkness of her tone came as a surprise. “There isn’t a logical reason for you to trust me.” Her eyes darted over towards Zuko. “You really believed me?”

Zuko nodded. “Every word.”

Azula sighed. Even though what he’d said was a testament to her skills, she looked distraught (in a controlled, careful, Azula-like sort of way.) “I wish there had been another way, but I had no time.”

Zuko sighed. It wouldn’t make any sense for her to betray him now, and, if he was being honest, even after everything, there was a part of him that still trusted her, maybe even with his life. He didn’t know why. “It’s all right.” He turned and looked her in the eye. “I believe you.”

Azula possibly looked the most relieved he’d ever seen her. “I’m glad you’re still alive, by the way.” Her tone was light, possibly in an attempt to hide how worried she’d been. But for once, Zuko didn’t fall for her act, not even for a second.

Trying not to think about everything she’d have to work out with Zuko later, Azula turned her attention to the stairs. “Look,” she said. “I know you probably still don’t trust me, and maybe you would rather jump off this bell tower than work with me, but can we please work together long enough to get out of here?”

Zuko nodded, starting down the stairs without missing a beat. “I’m not spending any more time this close to him.”

Azula had to force herself not to look at their father as they hurried down the stairs. She had told one last lie to Zuko, and the last thing she’d said to her father was still echoing through her mind.

*Find someone else to be your puppet.*

If Zuko still hated her, what did that mean for her future? Did she still have a home?

But this wasn’t the time to worry about that. They had an escape to make.

Or so she thought, until they came hurtling around a corner and ran smack into the Mayor, who was standing in the middle of the stairs, holding an enormous kitchen knife and smiling malevolently.

Azula, who was in front, shrieked despite herself and stumbled backwards, nearly knocking Zuko over.

“Good evening,” the Mayor said smoothly, even though it was now past midnight. “I had a hunch you might come here. Though I must admit, I don’t understand why you would take such a risk for *his* sake.” He gestured towards Zuko. “Vigilantes like him are a dime a dozen.”  
“If I’m like that, then so are you,” replied Zuko, glaring at the Mayor, eyes full of flaming anger.

It took every ounce of Azula’s energy to maintain her composure. “Really?” she said in a teasing tone, toying with a strand of her hair. “Did you really think I was lying all along? If I were you, and I had thought that, I wouldn’t have let myself climb the bell tower and follow my brother.” She leaned forward, raising her own dagger in defense. “Do you want to know what *I* think?” She let out a laugh. “I think you fell for my little psychopathic act, hook, line, and sinker.” She echoed the words she’d said to him only minutes ago. “Isn’t it funny?” she taunted. “You managed to carefully plan out a flawless string of assassinations, but you can’t even see through the lies of a seventeen-year old. That’s what I’d call *pathetic* .” She glared at him. “Believe me, I have little patience for pathetic people, especially those who pretend to be strong.”

From behind her, she felt Zuko pull her phone out of her back pocket. Reaching back as subtly as she could, she typed in the password, praying she hit the right keys, and let Zuko start recording.

Now all she needed to do was keep him talking, long enough for Zuko to find what he needed.

She could do that.

“You think you’re so much better than me,” hissed the Mayor. “You’re nothing but a lying, conniving little bitch. You’re not a threat to me.” He brandished his knife. “This city *needs* me, and I’m not about to let two teenagers stand in my way.”

“Oh, you’re absolutely right about all of those things,” said Azula playfully. “I am a...what was it...lying, conniving little bitch.” She leaned towards the Mayor, brandishing her own dagger in response. “But I’m a lying, conniving, little bitch who’s currently very angry at you for trying to murder my brother. And I don’t think you want that.”

“You think you can scare me?” laughed the Mayor. “I’ve dealt with the most dangerous assassins in Ba Sing Se, and I was able to control all of them. I’ve seen every type of murder under the sun, and I’m still here. I’m not a weak, incompetent child like I pretended to be. That was an act.” He smiled widely, flashing his teeth. “I believe you know a little something about that.”

“But you *are* a child,” said Zuko, stepping out from behind Azula and passing her the phone. “Everything you’re doing, you’re doing because you’re trying to finish what your parents started. You’ve become obsessed with not being that weak little boy anymore. You’re so fixated on your younger self that you can’t escape it.”

“It doesn’t matter why I am the way I am!” snapped the Mayor. “I’m not weak, and you two would be foolish to believe otherwise! I orchestrated an entire string of murders, met with the most dangerous criminals in Ba Sing Se, and survived attack after attack, all to make a difference in this city!”

“Why, Mr. Mayor!” cried Azula. “Are you saying that you planned all of this, the murders, the assassins, the planted notes, the attacks, because you thought it was *right* ?!” She laughed. “That’s some fucked-up shit if I ever saw it.”

“That’s exactly what I…” the Mayor’s eyes dropped to the phone Azula was holding in her hand, and she realized she’d forgotten to hide it. “No.”

In a flash, faster than Azula would have expected, the Mayor lunged forward and began reaching for the phone in her hands. The two of them crashed to the floor, with him on top of her. She ignored the spike of pain as her back smashed into the stairs, concentrating all of her energy onto keeping a tight grip on the phone.

“You clever little bitch,” hissed the Mayor. “You’re not so much better than me after all, are you?” Azula was about to try and throw the phone to Zuko when the Mayor, keeping her left arm pinned to the floor, reached out, wrapped his hands around her neck, and began to squeeze.

At first, she just felt the pain of his fingers pressing harder and harder into her skin. Pain on a superficial level. The longer and harder he squeezed, the deeper the pain began to go, seeping down into the center of her neck, then following her blood flow towards her chest.

As breathing became harder and harder, the world began to blur. It took every ounce of her strength not to let it all slip away, and somewhere in the corner of her consciousness, she felt her grip loosening on the phone.

With the last of her strength, and a flick of her fingers, she threw the phone as far away as she possibly could.

Black was starting to seep into her vision, and the Mayor didn’t let go.

Would it be better to let it all go? They had the confession. What was left for her in this city, in this world, once this was over?

There was a clang, and all of a sudden, the Mayor’s grip loosened. Air came pouring back into Azula’s lungs, and she gasped, stuttering, her vision clearing rapidly, still dizzy and dazed as she shoved the Mayor’s now-unconscious body off of her and sat up.

Zuko was standing over the Mayor, holding a pipe identical to the one she’d used earlier. The siblings stared at each other, and Azula, for her part, found herself at a loss for words.

*I wasn’t sure you’d save me.*

*I thought you hated me.*

But she couldn’t say any of that. So instead, she said “Did you save the confession?”

Zuko held up the phone. He, too, seemed not to know what to say.

Carefully, Azula pulled herself to her feet, realizing that there was blood on her back from falling so hard into the stairs. Zuko had blood on his wrists, too, probably from the handcuffs he’d worn earlier.

“Is it really over?” she asked after a moment, as they stood over the Mayor’s unconscious body.

Zuko nodded, and Azula found herself letting out a sigh of relief despite herself. “I think it is.”

It felt like a blur as the police, accompanied by Katara, Sokka, Suki, Mai, Toph, Aang, Ty Lee, Yue, the remaining White Lotus members, as well as several people Zuko didn’t even recognize, swarmed the building. After Chief Song’s death, Zuko hadn’t thought about the idea of the new chief, but he bore a great resemblance to Sokka and Katara. The police quickly took Kuei away, and the rest of the group found themselves standing on the steps of City Hall, still hearing the sirens as they drove away, the shouts of pedestrians as they passed by and wondered what had happened.

Only a few members of the police had actually been let into City Hall, and most of Zuko’s friends (he could call them that now, he decided), were waiting on the steps.

When he and Azula walked out the doors, both of them still in a bit of a daze from the adrenaline of it all, there was a collective cry from the crowd on the stairs, and everyone started talking at once.

Ty Lee came flying (literally) out of the crowd, and hugged Azula so hard that they both fell to the ground. Zuko was close enough that he could see Azula wince as she fell into the steps, but she was laughing.

“You’re alive!”

“Barely,” murmured Azula, slowly getting to her feet. Of the two of them, she seemed the most shell-shocked. Zuko could see bruises beginning to form on her throat. Seeing Ty Lee’s worried expression, she managed a smile. “But don’t worry. We’re all safe now.”

Zuko’s attention was brought away from Azula and Ty Lee as he felt a tap on his shoulder. He turned and found Sokka standing directly behind him, fiddling with the sleeves of his sweater (which had obviously been thrown on in a hurry), and staring nervously at his feet.

After everything, it felt like they shouldn’t be nervous anymore. But Zuko could still feel his hands shaking ever so slightly.

“I was worried about you,” said Sokka after a moment. “Really worried.” His tone was flat, not in a cruel way, but the sort of flat tone that people use when they have no idea what to say.

“Well,” said Zuko after a moment (in a similar flat tone, he realized as he spoke), “you didn’t need to be.”

“It doesn’t matter if I need to be,” said Sokka. “I just...you know. Care about you.”

The silence between them was like a balloon being blown up by a child, growing bigger and more delicate by the second. The air felt so tense and awkward that Zuko felt like there was an elephant sitting on his chest.

“Oh, forget it,” said Sokka after a moment, and, seeming to forget the awkwardness in the air, he leaned forward and kissed Zuko.

Zuko’s eyes widened in surprise. He’d sort of known all along...but he’d never let himself believe it. Not really.

Until now.

They broke apart, and Sokka toyed awkwardly with his hair. “So...uh...yeah. That was a thing. That I did.”

Zuko smiled. “Long time coming.”

Sokka’s eyes widened in surprise for a second, before his face broke into a ridiculously huge smile. Zuko would have laughed, if he hadn’t known that he was wearing an identical expression.

“Within a week of this case being finished,” said Azula’s voice from behind them. They turned, and saw her standing with Katara, a couple of steps above them. Both girls were laughing. “Katara, I believe you owe me an iced coffee.”  
“You *bet* on our *relationship*?” squawked Sokka indignantly.

“Obviously,” said Azula. “It was too good of an opportunity to miss.”

“We couldn’t resist,” said Katara, looking slightly sheepish but mostly smug.

“You knew?” said Zuko, turning to the girls.

“Zuko,” said Katara, looking at him slightly condescendingly as Azula giggled in a rather un-Azula-like way, “we have eyes.”

Still a little bit in his own head, Zuko allowed his fingers to intertwine with Sokka’s as they began to walk down the steps, followed by the rest of the group. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw Aang and (for some reason) Appa bounding down the stairs, followed by a grinning Toph and a slightly worried-looking Suki. To his right, Mai was saying something to Yue and Ty Lee, both of whom were laughing. Azula and Katara were behind them, speaking in hushed whispers, and smirking at each other. Occasionally, their eyes would wander over to where their girlfriends were standing.

What a strange group they’d formed, in search of answers. Zuko would never have guessed that he would end up working with all of these people, and yet, he found himself almost indescribably happy that they were all safe, that they’d all survived.

At long last, they could breathe again.

### End Notes

## Chapter 42: The Last Seance

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

The siblings find themselves thinking about the past and the future, endings and beginnings, and strangely enough, they're not alone anymore.

#### Chapter Notes

I can't believe this is the last chapter. I've been daydreaming about this fic since March, and now it's September, and it's finished. I never ever thought I'd be able to write something this long or complete, and it's sad to be done with it, but I'll always love Detectives Zuko and Azula.  
This was written for the Secret Tunnel Big Bang, and I'm so lucky that I had the opportunity to participate. It was such a wonderful experience for me, creating content with a community of other fans, and Iris, the moderator, was absolutely lovely, and patient with my inconsistencies.  
This fic also featured art by @wortvermis on Tumblr. They are one of the most talented artists, and one of the kindest people I've ever met. They made several incredible art pieces for this fic, and were always patient with my inconsistencies in posting. I'm eternally grateful to have been paired with someone so kind and talented. I don't think this fic would be complete without the art they made.  
This chapter is a little bit sentimental. I think it's my love for this fic seeping into the writing. Happy reading:)

### Text

There were a lot of things that went unsaid as Azula and Zuko walked back to Zuko’s apartment. Azula had almost expected Zuko to tell her to go away, but as they made their way home, away from the death and destruction and the chaos, neither of them could think of the right words.

Perhaps it was simply pure exhaustion. Azula barely even remembered getting back to the apartment and falling asleep. The next thing she knew, she was waking up again, sunlight streaming through the curtains she’d forgotten to close.

Someone (probably her uncle) had brought her suitcase in, and she was relieved to find it sitting at the foot of her bed. For the first time in a while, she gave little thought to her outfit. She was still worn-out from the events of the night before, and knew she wouldn’t have the energy to do much for very long.

Still, that didn’t mean she didn’t give a small smile at her reflection as she left her room. It was still chilly, so she’d thrown on black pants, a black top, and her favorite cropped red jacket. It had been her mother’s, she thought. For once, the resemblance in the mirror didn’t bother her.

She threw her hair into a topknot, albeit a loose one, but left her choppy bangs hanging down around her face. She liked them better that way.

She’d found something special here, she realized. It was a shame she couldn’t stay. Somewhere between sleep and waking, it had occurred to her that today would be her last day in the city.

She’d find somewhere else to go. She wasn’t worried about that anymore. But she would miss it, much to her own surprise.

At least she had today.

As usual, Zuko was already sitting on the couch when she made her way into the living room. He was reading a book (the same romance novel Ty Lee had given her weeks ago, Azula realized), and sipping tea out of a mug. Wordlessly, he gestured to the kitchen, and Azula found the coffee machine already on when she entered.

The air wasn’t thick with tension and anger, despite the uncomfortable feeling that still hung in the air between the two siblings. It was simply that neither of them knew what to *say* .

“Please tell me there’s extra coffee.”

Azula turned around. “Mai! How…”

“Zuko let me in.” Mai smiled wryly, and Azula handed her a mug of coffee.

“What brings you here?”

Mai gestured to Azula’s outfit, and it was only then that Azula realized that she’d subconsciously dressed herself for travel. “Are you leaving?”

Azula nodded. “Who told you?”

“Your uncle did,” said Mai. “He seems to think that everyone should make a point of saying goodbye to you.”

Of course he’d known. He was irritating that way. Azula didn’t think she’d ever love him the way Zuko did, not even close, but there were parts of him that she could understand, even occasionally appreciate.

Azula rolled her eyes. “Believe me, I don’t need the fanfare.”

“Oh, there’s nothing worse than the fanfare,” said Mai. “But I thought you might want a warning from your only normal friend before you get bombarded with hugs.”

Azula laughed. “A true friend,” she said, raising her cup of coffee. As she lowered it, her expression softened. “For what it’s worth, I am glad I met you, you know.”

“Me too,” said Mai. “This is the most fun I’ve had in years.”

“I don’t know whether or not I should be concerned that a murder is the most fun you’ve had in years.”

“You’re one to talk.”

Azula laughed. “Fair enough.”

“I think you’re brave, you know,” said Aang, who had come to the apartment just a little bit after Mai.

Zuko blinked. “Bravery is overrated.”

“What do you mean?”

Zuko sighed. He was still tired. “It can get you into trouble. Too much of it.” He glanced at Aang, only four years younger than he, but it seemed like so much more. Even with everything he’d been through, he was still so...happy. Zuko didn’t think he could ever be like that.

Aang blinked. “But...isn’t it worth it? I mean, you’re *Zuko* . There’s nothing you care about more than protecting this city, and doing what’s right. Isn’t that worth a little danger?”

Zuko laughed, albeit a little bitterly. “How do you stay so positive all the time, Aang?”

Aang, who was also sipping tea, smiled at him. “It’s what I care about. I care about feeling at peace. But you care about honor, and justice.” He reached across the table and squeezed Zuko’s shoulder. “I hope you never forget that.”

Zuko sipped his tea, turning Aang’s words over in his mind. “I won’t,” he said after a moment, putting his tea down. “I hope you don’t forget yourself, either. Peace is important.”

“Don’t worry about me,” said Aang, with a smile. “I’ll always have everything I need.”

Sometime later in the morning, Azula was doing a crossword puzzle (Zuko had gone out to get coffee, he claimed, but she knew that he was really off with Sokka. Her brother was a terrible liar), when she heard a knock at the door. Opening it, she found Suki and Toph standing on the other side.

“What were you going to do?” asked Toph, brushing past her into the apartment. “Leave without telling us?”

“Of course not,” said Azula, closing the door behind them. “It’s just...happening a little quickly.”

Mere weeks ago, she never would have admitted that.

“That makes sense,” said Suki, sliding onto the couch. “But we’ll miss you, you know.”

Azula smiled as she leaned on the back of the armchair. “I know.”

“No ‘I’ll miss you, too?’” snapped Toph indignantly. “You really don’t know a lot about goodbyes, do you?”

Suki poked Toph in the arm, but Azula wasn’t angry. She simply nodded. “I don’t.” She paused, then smiled sadly. “I’ll miss you, too.”

“Finally!” said Toph, leaning back on the couch. “I thought you’d never admit it.”

Azula smiled. Toph’s spunk was strangely charming, despite her bluntness. It was true. She *would* miss them.

Suki pulled Azula into a hug. “You helped me, you know.”

Azula blinked. Helping people wasn’t something she normally did. “I did?”

“Sure,” said Suki. “I don’t think I’d have ever broken free from the Dai Li without you, and I feel more like myself than I ever have, now that I don’t have to conform to what they want me to be. Life is better that way.”

Azula nodded, as Suki and Toph each hugged her one last time. “It is.”

The outer streets of Ba Sing Se, near the White Lotus mansion, were coated in multicolored leaves, as Katara and Yue walked through them. Katara had spent the night on Yue’s beanbag chair again, the two of them sleeping peacefully for the first time in weeks, without the threat of death hanging over their heads. Now, they were winding their way through the streets, nowhere to go, nothing to think about except each other.

It reminded Katara of the night they’d walked the streets together, after Yue had been released. Though the danger hadn’t been over then, it had felt like they were flying freely for the first time in days.

The feeling was so exhilarating that it made Katara spin through the streets, kicking up leaves and laughing. Yue blushed for a moment, but then laughed and ran after her. Katara’s foot slipped on a leaf, but Yue wrapped her arms around her waist before she could fall, and the two of them found themselves embracing before they knew it.

Katara leaned in and kissed Yue, feeling the cold air on both their faces as they broke apart. They said nothing for a while, just kept walking through the streets, hand in hand.

“I’m really, *really* glad I met you, Yue,” said Katara, after a moment. “I...well, I don’t know how I would have gotten through this without you.”

Yue smiled, the wind blowing her white braids every which way. She looked like a goddess. “Me too.”

That was how they’d *all* gotten through this, Katara realized. By leaning on one another.

Packing was strange. It wasn’t like Azula had many things to pack, in fact, quite the opposite. Most of her things were already in her suitcases. She only had to pack up the romance novel that Ty Lee had given her.

She held it in her hands, unable to pack it away just yet. She may have ruined her relationship with Zuko, but it felt like with Ty Lee...she’d done something *right* , somehow. She was sad to let it go.

And she loved her. She couldn’t say it out loud, it wasn’t the right moment, but she knew she did.

Still holding the book in her hands, she made her way to the door when she heard another knock. Saying goodbye to everyone was strange. She’d never expected to have anyone to say goodbye to.

Ty Lee was standing on the other side of the door. She was trying to hide it, but Azula could tell she’d been crying.

She felt her chest ache at the sight of her. She hated this.

Wordlessly, she pulled Ty Lee into a hug. Azula still wasn’t used to initiating hugs, or anything of that sort, with other people, but it felt necessary this time.

As they pulled apart, Ty Lee’s eyes wandered to the book in Azula’s hand. “That’s the book I gave you.”

Azula nodded. “I read it five times,” she admitted. “I didn’t expect to, but...I loved it.”

*That’s how I feel about you* , she thought but didn’t say. “Do you want it back?”

Ty Lee shook her head. “You can keep it. You can use it to remember me.”

Azula nodded, trying to keep the tears out of her own eyes. This was so much harder than she would have ever expected. “Look, Ty Lee,” she said after a moment. “I need you to know...after everything that happened with me and Zuko, it’s not right for me to stay here. But I never wanted to leave you. You’re incredible, and so special, and I’ve never known anyone like you.”

Fuck it. She was leaving anyway. If this wasn’t the right time, there would never be one.

“I know it’s crazy, and it doesn’t make logical sense, but...I think I love you.”

Ty Lee’s eyes widened, and her mouth dropped open slightly. For the first time, Azula thought she’d managed to catch the acrobat by surprise.

“I love you too,” said Ty Lee after a moment, still looking shocked. “I just wish you didn’t have to leave.”

“Me too,” said Azula, something she hadn’t admitted to anyone until now. “But we’ll see each other again.” She squeezed Ty Lee’s hand, and Ty Lee leaned forward and kissed her.

“Do you know what you’re going to do now?” asked Ty Lee after they broke apart. “What’s your life going to look like?”

“I don’t know,” admitted Azula. “But I do know that I want you in it. And I won’t let that go, no matter where I am.”

Ty Lee looked at her with shining eyes. “You promise?”

Azula pulled her girlfriend into a hug. “I promise.”

Zuko and Sokka were sipping identical drinks, trying to blink the sleepiness out of their eyes with coffee. It wasn’t working.

“Everyone’s making fun of us for not getting together sooner, you know,” said Sokka, grinning sheepishly.

Zuko groaned, but he was smiling. “Of course they are.”

“We were sort of idiots.”

“Huge ones,” said Zuko, smirking, sipping his coffee. “But we figured it out eventually.”

“I’m glad we did,” said Sokka.

“Me too.”

“So,” said Sokka, leaning back in his chair and sipping his coffee (he drank hot coffee with a straw, something that Zuko *profoundly* did not understand), “what are you going to do now?”

“What I’ve always done,” said Zuko. The future was a blur, but that much, he was sure of. “Protect this city, and everyone in it that I love.”

“That’s noble of you,” said Sokka. He paused, staring at his nearly-empty coffee cup, and blushing. “Think you might have room for a budding forensic scientist on any future escapades?”

Zuko smiled, reaching across the table to take Sokka’s hand. “I wouldn’t dream of doing it any other way.”

Sokka smiled. Zuko didn’t know exactly what he was thinking, but he valued Sokka more than anything. He was the best friend Zuko had ever had (more than that now, Zuko supposed.) Hopefully, Sokka knew that now.

As Zuko wandered home, he found his mind wandering to his sister.

He still felt hurt, but he couldn’t find any anger inside of him anymore. After last night, after everything she’d done to get him back...he couldn’t find it in himself to believe that she’d truly wanted to hurt him all along. Seeing their father again had reminded him just how terrifying he was.

Had Azula acted perfectly? No. But really, did anyone? Zuko knew he hadn’t, especially when he’d first moved to the city. He’d been obsessed with proving that he could handle himself, so that no one, like his father, could ever hurt him again.

All Azula had really wanted was to get away from their father. That was something Zuko could understand.

And despite his hurt, he still cared about her. He had for a while. After everything they’d been through, they were still family. And not just in the sense of being related by blood, because Zuko didn’t really consider that family, not anymore.

Azula was his family because she’d lied to their father in order to come after him, and he would have done the same for her. She was his family because they understood each other, because they’d gone through hell and back, and still stuck together, even after they’d broke apart.

Zuko sighed. He had some thinking to do.

After Ty Lee left, Azula found herself on the couch again. It was only after she’d been left alone that she had managed to pack the romance novel in her suitcase. Ty Lee was special: she’d find a way to stay with her, no matter where she ended up.

She didn’t leave, even though she was all packed. Even if Zuko hated her, she wasn’t going to take off without saying goodbye.

Not like he’d done two years ago. They were better than that now, and Azula intended to keep it that way.

Zuko didn’t get home until the sun was setting. His face was wind-chapped, and his hair was a complete disaster. He looked as though he’d been walking around in the wind for a very long time.

“How was the coffee shop?” asked Azula, unable to think of anything better to say.

Zuko simply nodded. He looked lost in his own head, as though his spirit was somewhere else. Azula raised an eyebrow. “You haven’t been possessed by some sort of evil spirit, have you? So soon after all this trouble?”

Zuko laughed slightly and shook his head. “Not that I know of.”

Azula smirked. “They all say that.”

It was *so close* to normal, and yet miles away.

Azula sighed. If she had learned one thing today, it was that the right moment to say what you really wanted to say never came. You had to make it the right moment.

She got to her feet, grabbing her suitcase in her left hand, trying her hardest not to cry. She would miss this city more than she’d ever imagined, and she had no one but herself to blame.

Still, she was going to leave on the best note possible.

“Look,” she said to Zuko, who was sitting in the armchair. “I’m sorry. For lying to you. You’re right: I can be selfish. I care too much about protecting myself, and sometimes, I can get other people hurt. And I never wanted to hurt you. So I’m sorry.” She sighed. “You don’t have to forgive me. I don’t think you will. But I wanted to tell you before I go that I do care about you. Even if I’ve made mistakes, these past few weeks...working with you, solving this mystery, getting to know your friends, this city...they’ve been the best weeks of my life. I wouldn’t trade them for anything. And I hope that…” she sighed. How could she say this without sounding entitled? “I hope that, even with everything I did, you found something good in them, too.” She turned and headed towards the door. “Goodbye, Zuko.”

It took everything in her power not to look back, to see his face. Had he even heard what she’d said? Did he care?

At least she’d said it. At the end of the day, that was all that mattered.

She was halfway out the door before she felt a hand wrap around her wrist.

“Azula, wait.”

She turned to find Zuko standing there, looking her in the eye for the first time all day. She froze in the doorway, then slowly, almost cautiously, made her way back into the apartment. “Yes?”

Zuko paused, looking away for a moment, then back at her. “You don’t have to leave.”

Possibly for the first time in her life, Azula’s mind was unable to comprehend what she was hearing. “You can’t be serious. After what I did to you?”

Zuko sighed. “I did a lot of thinking when I was out today, especially after we saw Father. And...I don’t forgive you. Not completely, not yet. But I think I understand why you did what you did. You were scared.” He paused, looking down at her. “It doesn’t mean you don’t love me.”

Love was a word the siblings had never used before in their lives. Growing up, it had always been a weakness. If they had somehow managed to cultivate it despite everything...they were even stronger than Azula had thought.

“Understanding doesn’t equal forgiveness,” Azula murmured, still waiting for the other shoe to drop. To mess up this badly and still be welcomed was a foreign concept to her.

“It doesn’t,” agreed Zuko. “But it’s not just that.” He sighed. “I’ve really loved these past few weeks, too. You came to the city and...basically changed everything. You’re the one who got me working on the case with everyone else. You understand me. I’ve never had someone to work with before, and I...I think I need it.” He smiled at her. “We make a good team. We always have. And...you know. I still care about you. And I think that all of that...outweighs the mistakes we’ve made. Because we’re trying. And...I think it’s worth it.”

Azula was speechless. She never could have predicted this.

After a moment, she closed the front door behind her. “Are you saying...you want me to stay?”

Zuko nodded. “I think the city will be better for it.” He paused. “And so will both of us.”

Azula stood still for a moment before pulling her brother into a gentle hug. The sensation was foreign to both of them, but neither of them let go. “I think you’re an idiot to trust me. But in this case, I’m very lucky that you are.”

Zuko laughed. “Does that mean you’re staying?”

Azula finally allowed herself to smile, and admitted what she’d been thinking all day. “I never wanted to leave.”

They stood in silence for a moment, before, on a whim, Azula made her way to Zuko’s window. The two siblings stood there together, staring out at the city. Their city.

Ba Sing Se was strange. It had no rhyme or reason. Sometimes it was dangerous. It was full of puzzles, and excitement, and people Azula had found herself loving. She knew Zuko had, too.

This had been the first mystery of the city, but Azula knew, somewhere deep inside, that it was far from the last.

They had a lot of adventures ahead of them.

And they were home.
